en: The third chapter, titled "Consecration," which is the great summary concerning the characteristics of the accomplishment of the extensive range of all activities, beginning with the Vajra Master.
Homage to the glorious Kālacakra!

Salutation to that Buddha, the sole Teacher, by whose great power of merit and wisdom the tenfold gifts, such as horses and so forth, were bestowed upon those seeking charity; and by whom Māra and the other adversaries were utterly destroyed after he had consecrated the entire universe within the glorious, stainless Maṇḍala of the Lord of Speech, the Dharmadhātu.
Having thus prostrated before Kālacakra, the Great Bliss, the supreme of the three bodies,
the foremost of the three vajras of the three mandalas, the syllable-less Ghoṣavajra, [I shall compose] a commentary on the chapter concerning the initiation.
Based on the realization of the Root Tantra,
I shall here write [this] in the tantra for the sake of attaining the fruit of merit and primordial wisdom.

Here, in the glorious Kalāpa village, in the southern Malaya Garden, at the end of the eastern door of the Kālacakra Maṇḍala house, in the great pavilion of precious jewels, Mañjuśrī—residing upon a great lion throne of precious jewels, having manifested a created body (nirmāṇakāya) by King Yaśas, and being requested by Sūryaratha and prophesied by the Tathāgata—taught the first verse of the Initiation Chapter in the *Laghu-tantra*, which sets forth the purpose of Sucandra’s request from the *Paramādibuddha*.

That very *Mahoddeśa* is now being expanded by me, Lokeśvara, through this commentary (*ṭīkā*)—in the form of an emanated body (*nirmitakāya*), as prophesied by the Tathāgata Puṇḍarīka and urged by Mañjuśrī—beginning with the words "The measurement of the universe within the body," and so forth: "The measurement of the universe within the body, the timing of day and night, the divisions of the lunar months and transits (*saṃkrānti*), the subtle enumeration of the channels (*nāḍī*), the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the Person (*puruṣa*) according to the systems of the heretics, the Veda, the Creator (*kartṛ*), and the distinctions of the *Śruti*—having heard that the Maṇḍala must be taught by me, the Sugata, together with the Moon, proclaims the Kālacakra Maṇḍala."
From the passage beginning with "In this body, the measure of the universe" up to "the mandala is to be shown," there is the request of Sucandra.

Having heard the words of Sucandra, the Sugata speaks the response of the Tathāgata in all the verses of the Initiation Chapter, beginning with "The Kālacakra mandala," and so forth; thereafter, until the end of the chapter, there is no further request.
In this regard, Sucandra says: "O Bhagavān, in this body..."

That which was spoken by the Blessed One in the *Adhyātmapaṭala*—beginning with "The measurement of the universe, the time of day and night, and the divisions of the months and transits," and ending with "In the Veda, the distinction of the agent and so forth"—has been heard by me; the meaning is that all of this has been understood.

Therefore, now, for the sake of sentient beings’ acquisition of merit and gnosis, the mandala must be taught by the Blessed One for the purpose of bestowing empowerments upon disciples and for performing the consecration of images and so forth, as well as for achieving the mundane siddhis associated with the ten principles. According to the *Vimalaprabhā*, by way of mundane truth, the mandala extends up to the Akanistha realm; however, by way of ultimate truth, there is no drawing of a powder mandala (*rajomaṇḍala*), because it has been prohibited by the Blessed One. Thus the Blessed One said in the *Ādibuddha*: "The laying down of the vajra-lines and the scattering of the colored powders..."
One should not act according to the reality of the mantra; for one who acts so, enlightenment is difficult to attain.

Thus, if here, by means of the reality of mantra—where "mantra" refers to gnosis because it protects the mind—if the Vajrācārya performs the laying of the foundation lines and so forth for the sake of attaining the Mahāmudrā-siddhi, then for him who does so, enlightenment (*bodhi*) becomes difficult to attain; such is the rule of the Tathāgata.

For that reason, this request of Sucandra is for the purpose of accomplishing worldly siddhis and for the purpose of accumulating merit (*puṇya-sambhāra*), not for the purpose of accomplishing Mahāmudrā-siddhi and for the purpose of accumulating gnosis (*jñāna-sambhāra*).
In this regard, another triad of mandalas for the sake of attaining gnosis was taught by the Blessed One as follows:
the body-faculty, the bhaga, and the mind constitute the threefold mandala of the vajras of body, speech, and mind; there is no other five-colored [mandala].

Thus, for this reason, there is no *rajo-maṇḍala* (powder mandala) for the sake of accomplishing great bliss (*mahāsukha*), nor for the purpose of bestowing the higher initiations (*uttarābhiṣeka*). This is Sucandra’s request.
Having heard those very words of request—the speech of Sucandra—the Sugata speaks pre-eminently; the meaning is that he teaches the entire *Kālacakra* mandala.
"All [is taught] according to the sequence to be explained" is the summary statement of the teacher and the requester.

Now, for the sake of propitiating the Guru, he describes the examination of the Vajrācārya with the second verse, beginning with "In the beginning": First, the Guru must be served; he should be a holder of the commitments (*samayin*), mounted upon the Vajrayāna, a meditator on reality (*tattva*), free from greed, devoid of impurity, possessed of patience, one who abides on the path, the giver of the way to disciples, the remover of the fear of hell, a true celibate (*brahmacārī*) in essence, and a thunderbolt-staff against the Māras. On the surface of the earth, he is renowned as Vajrasattva.

In this system of Mantra, disciples who desire mundane and supramundane accomplishments must first serve a guru; and having thoroughly examined him according to the procedure prescribed for the examination of a Vajrācārya—for otherwise, by propitiating a guru who lacks the characteristics of one properly examined, a perversion of the Dharma occurs for the disciples—and because such a perversion of the Dharma leads to rebirth in hell, it is said: "At the outset, the guru must also be served with the observance of the pledges (samaya)."

In this context, the *samaya* is twofold—external and internal—and is to be understood according to the provisional (*neyārtha*) and definitive (*nītārtha*) meanings as will be explained [in the following]. One who possesses such *samaya* is a *samayin*; the Guru must first be served in the correct manner. This means he should be propitiated with one’s sons, wife, and so forth.
[This is the meaning in] the second and third verses of the chapter.
[This concludes] the Great Chapter on the Characteristics of the Means for Accomplishing the Extensive Array of All Rituals, beginning with the Vajra-Acarya, for those mounted upon the Vajrayāna.

Here, the Vajrayāna is the vehicle of the perfectly awakened ones (*samyaksambuddha*); it is called the Vajrayāna because liberation (*vajra*) is traveled by means of it, being as indestructible as a diamond (*vajra*) against the vehicles of the non-Buddhists, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas. One who has mounted upon that is "mounted on the Vajrayāna" (*vajrayānādhirūḍha*), meaning one who meditates on reality (*tattva*).

In this context, reality (*tattva*) is twofold: that which accomplishes worldly attainments and that which accomplishes perfect enlightenment; this will be explained in the fifth chapter, the "Chapter on Knowledge," within the *Paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*.
The meaning is that one whose nature it is to meditate upon that very reality is [the subject].
"Free from greed" means one who is indifferent toward one's own body, including sons, wife, and so forth.
"Free from turbidity" (*vyapagatakaluṣa*):

"turbidity" (*kaluṣa*) refers to the collection of passion, hatred, delusion, pride, envy, and avarice; he from whom that very [collection] has departed in various ways is "free from turbidity," meaning one whose conduct is characterized by patience (*kṣāntiśīla*).

His natural inclination toward patience is independent of any fruit; his path is the way of the perfectly enlightened ones (*samyaksambuddha*). Because he abides therein, this Guru, when propitiated, becomes the giver of the path to disciples and the remover of the fear of hell.

In reality, he who has attained the bliss of the supreme unchanging syllable (*paramākṣarasukha*) is a celibate student (*brahmacārī*). He is like a vajra-staff against the four Māras—the Māras of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*), the afflictions (*kleśamāra*), death (*mṛtyumāra*), and the son of a god (*devaputramāra*)—and thus he is a "vajra-staff.
On the surface of the earth, he is renowned as Vajrasattva through his emanation body (*nirmitakāya*); this is the rule for serving the Vajrācārya.

Now, for the purpose of examining the faults of a corrupt teacher, he speaks here with the third verse beginning with *mānī*: "One who is arrogant, overcome by anger, devoid of the commitments (*samaya*), greedy for wealth, unlearned, and seeking to deceive disciples; whose mind is lost regarding the state of supreme bliss, who has not been consecrated, who is attached to enjoyments, negligent, harsh in speech, lustful, and devoted to the objects of the senses—he alone is to be avoided by the wise like hell, even for the sake of enlightenment."

In this system of Mantra, a guru who is possessed of defects such as pride (*māna*) and the like must be avoided by disciples; even if he has been made a guru for the sake of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), he is regarded by the wise—the learned—as being like hell.
One who possesses pride is called "prideful" (*mānī*);

and pride is of many kinds: the conceit of being a scholar (*paṇḍitābhimāna*), the conceit of wealth and power, and the conceit of one's knowledge of the ten principles (*daśatattva*), the path, form, and so forth. He who possesses such [pride] is to be avoided.

One who looks down upon sentient beings as being lower and lower is conceited; one who looks upon the most excellent of sentient beings becomes free from pride, for he is a knower of the right path. Therefore, the conceited person, who is devoid of compassion, is to be avoided. Likewise, one who is overcome by anger is devoid of the *samaya* (vow/discipline); being seized by those things loathed by the world, he becomes devoid of the *samaya* through his manifest conduct. He too is to be avoided. Furthermore, one who is greedy for wealth—specifically one who consumes the property of the Sangha, of a stupa, or other heavy assets—is "greedy for wealth"; likewise, one who accumulates wealth for the sake of worldly enjoyments is also to be avoided.
One who is "unlearned" is a fool, devoid of instruction in the true path;

likewise, one who seeks to deceive good disciples and is a speaker of falsehood should be avoided, for his mind is lost regarding the state of supreme bliss and he is not sprinkled with [the nectar of] truth.
One who teaches the tantra without having received initiation is to be avoided.

"Attached to enjoyments" means being thoroughly (ā) and in every way (samantāt) attached to external worldly pleasures; thus, "negligent" refers to one who is distracted by the drinking of wine, and such a person, being unconcentrated, is to be avoided. This is the meaning.
"One who lusts after the objects of the senses" means one who lusts for the pleasure of the two organs; such a person is to be avoided—this is the rule of the Tathāgata.
Now, was it not stated by the Tathāgata in the Mantra system as follows: "The qualities of the Ācārya are to be accepted, but his faults never at all"?
Success arises from the perception of virtues; there is no success from speech concerning faults.
Thus,
the Vajrācārya who has received the supreme consecration is worshipped by the Tathāgatas residing in the world-systems of the ten directions, coming from the three times.

(Gu0 Pa0 2) Therefore, the qualities of the teacher should be accepted. Regarding what will be said here in the future by ignorant people—that because the teacher has lost the true path, his qualities should be accepted—this will be the statement of certain who have strayed from the path; therefore it is said: "faults [of the teacher] should never be [considered]."
That is not so; why? Because the examination of the faults and virtues of the preceptor for the sake of propitiating him was taught by the Tathāgata as follows:
"A disciple who is wise should not honor a preceptor who is merciless, wrathful, cruel, arrogant, greedy, unrestrained, or one who exalts himself" (Guhyasiddhi 7).
Therefore, according to this statement, even if he has been accepted as a preceptor, one who acts contrary to what should be done must certainly be abandoned by a disciple seeking liberation.
Likewise, in the *Āvibuddha*, it is said: "A householder who enjoys a small hut, a servant, a plowman, a merchant, or a fool who sells the True Dharma—he is not a Vajradhara on this earth.

By such statements, three types of gurus are described in the *Ācāryaparīkṣā*. Furthermore: "Due to the thorough knowledge of the ten principles (*daśatattva*), among the three [types], the monk (*bhikṣu*) is supreme; the one called a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) is middling; and the householder (*gṛhastha*) is the lowest of those two.
Therefore, a householder should not be appointed as a guru by a king without the acquisition of land [as an endowment].

In that regard, one who possesses the marks [of renunciation] must indeed perform the thorough knowledge derived from hearing [the scriptures]. When a householder is honored as an Ācārya without having attained the spiritual stages (*bhūmi*), then the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha fall into disrespect. [As stated in the third chapter: "The consecration and other rites for monasteries and the like must always be performed by one possessing the marks [of renunciation], never by a householder wearing white robes, even when the Three Jewels exist in a single location. Thus it is said.

Thus, regarding the examination of the teacher in various ways, the Blessed One stated that the Guru should be propitiated by disciples; this previously mentioned rule is for the purpose of avoiding one who is possessed of faults. Likewise, his qualities have also been described as follows: "Steadfast, disciplined, intelligent, patient, upright, and free from deceit; skilled in the application of mantra and tantra, compassionate, and proficient in the scriptures; a knower of the ten principles (*daśatattva*), an expert in the rites of drawing the mandala, an expounder of mantras, a teacher (*ācārya*) of serene mind and conquered senses. (Guhyasamāja Tantra 8–9) And so forth.
Furthermore, why not consider the statement expressed in the subsequent verse:

"For he who has obtained the supreme consecration" (Guhyasamāja Paṭala 2), and so forth? This statement is to be understood by the wise according to ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), conventional truth (*laukikasatya*), definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), and interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).

In this regard, the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is first stated: here, beyond the vase, secret, and wisdom-knowledge empowerments (*kalaśa-guhya-prajñājñānābhiṣeka*), there is the final [empowerment] characterized by perfect awakening (*abhisaṃbodhi*), which is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), and the moment of great immutable bliss (*mahākṣarasukha*). It is indestructible (5). That which was obtained by the Blessed One at the foot of the Bodhi tree is "obtained through the supreme empowerment. Indeed, because it is indivisible from body, speech, and mind, the Vajra Master Śākyamuni Tathāgata is so called.

In this regard, he whose body, speech, and mind act indestructibly like a vajra for the sake of sentient beings within these three realms is the Vajrācārya; he is all-pervading and omniscient, and is thus [praised] by the Tathāgatas residing in the world-systems of the ten directions (*Guhyasamāja Tantra* 2). Here, those who are Bodhisattvas in the ten directions have crowns made of the seven precious gems; according to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), these are called "world-systems."

Among those crowns, those Tathāgatas who abide in the form of the family-mudrās (kula-mudrā) reside in the world-systems of the ten directions; and those Bodhisattvas, arriving during the three times, perform prostrations to the Buddha Bhagavān. By means of those prostrating Tathāgatas situated upon the crowns, even the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are worshipped as the Tathāgata—this is the definitive meaning (nītārtha) of the Bhagavān. Furthermore, the interpretable meaning (neyārtha) is stated by way of metaphorical convention: here, according to the statement "as it is externally, so it is within the body," the word "world-system" (lokadhātu) refers to the bodies of the disciples residing in the ten directions.
Those situated in underground chambers and those situated above, such as in the Tripura palaces and so forth—
among them, the five aggregates are called Tathāgatas; likewise, those residing in the world-systems, acting as disciples, come at the three junctions of the day to pay homage to the Guru.

The statement that "the guru is also venerated by those five aggregates who perform the salutation" is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*); [this is because] the suffix *cha* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), and there is no elision [of the final vowel].
The portion stating "the qualities have also been described" does not exist at the foot of the Bodhi tree.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the consecration: here, the Vajrācārya is to be saluted three times a day by monks wearing the saffron robes, but not by householders, nor by those who are junior, except through the exposition of the True Dharma (*saddharma*).

For example: "A householder or even a junior person, having placed the True Dharma and so forth before them, should be saluted with the thought that he is a Buddha by those who uphold the vows, in order to avoid the censure of the world. Likewise: "The one who upholds the vows should perform all these acts—providing a seat, rising to greet, performing services, and showing respect—with the exception of saluting those engaged in improper actions."

In this case, if even a householder or a novice monk becomes equal to a Vajrācārya, then what need is there for the washing of his feet and so forth? Having abandoned the five-limbed prostration (*pañcāṅga-vandanā*), one should show honor with wealth and other offerings when the Guru arrives at his own place. At the time of exposition, one should perform prostrations while placing the True Dharma and so forth in front, in order to avoid public censure. Here, "public censure" refers to that which arises regarding householders and novices due to their laziness, because they do not adopt the higher marks [of ordination] and lack thorough knowledge of the *Prātimokṣa* and its study.

If there is no pride regarding indolence, then for what purpose do they not follow the words of the Blessed One concerning medicine and so forth, which state that one should first understand the monastic vows (*bhikṣusaṃvara*) and only afterwards understand the Mahāyāna? Therefore, householders acting as teachers are not to be propitiated by monks; furthermore, when a monk is a Vajradhara, he is to be propitiated by a king in every possible way.

Likewise, in the *Ācāryaparīkṣā*, there is the following connection: "That evil-souled one who feels shame because of begging and red garments is to be saluted and honored by widows, Buddhists, and those who have lost their way. Similarly: "When sinners, who delight in the religion of the Mlecchas and are fond of the white-robed [Jainas], see the red garment, they feel aversion.
Thus, in this context, the Buddhist system never [prescribes] a white cloth.

For instance, Mañjuśrī, in other regions and monasteries, when a monk or a temple attendant commits a *pārājika* offense, he is expelled from the monastery after being given white robes and made to take back his saffron robe;
even a Vajrācārya is likewise removed from the royal mantra-monastery by the king’s decree.

But here, in this noble land, how can a layman wearing white robes become the preceptor for those wearing saffron robes, performing the consecration of monasteries and so forth? This is a great insult to the Saṅgha, and indeed a profound lack of discernment on the part of the followers of the Sugata, that they do not exclude those who have fallen into a state of transgression. It is not right.
The heavens [are filled] with those who possess the wealth of vows and the true Dharma.
One should perform worship and salutation while remaining in a comfortable posture.
From salutation,
it "becomes"; thus, it "does not exist."
At that time (tadā),
the Teaching (śāsanaṃ) likewise.
It is summarized in the chapter [of the *Āryaviṣaya*], verse [number].
The Great Chapter on the Characteristics of the Means for the Extensive Application of All Rituals, beginning with the Vajrācārya, even though there exists a Vajradhara who is a monk.

Therefore, having examined him in every way, a teacher who is free from faults should be served, while one possessed of faults should be avoided; this is the rule for the examination of the teacher, known as the "Instruction on Examination. Now, the characteristics of a good disciple are described for the purpose of the empowerment of wisdom (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*) by means of the verse beginning with "profound" (*gambhīra*), etc.: "One whose mind is profound and noble, who delights in the teacher’s rules, who is disposed toward renunciation, who recognizes virtues, who seeks liberation, who is devoted to the *tantra*, whose heart is not fickle, who is well-guarded once the reality has been attained, and who has abandoned the company of the wicked—he alone is the disciple to be accepted by a highly skilled teacher for the sake of the empowerment of wisdom and so forth. Another, moreover, is the middling type, for the sake of merit. In this system of Mantra, the disciple is of two kinds: one is a seeker of the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, and the second is a seeker of worldly accomplishments (*laukikasiddhi*).
He who seeks the accomplishment of the great mudrās should be initiated by means of the *seka*—such as the vase, the secret, and so forth—for the sake of cultivating the path of emptiness.

He who seeks the accomplishment of worldly siddhis should be initiated by means of the sevenfold consecration for the sake of cultivating the mantra, mudrā, and maṇḍalacakra; this is for the sake of middling merit.
The inferior candidate is [initiated] by means of the *abhiṣeka*.
He is not to be gathered [as a disciple]; rather, the rule is that such a lay follower (*upāsaka*) is to be gathered through the training.
Here, one whose mind is directed toward this profound and vast Dharma, which consists of emptiness and compassion, is said to have a "profound and vast mind. Such a person is the best of disciples:
one who delights in the precepts of the guru, is free from the fourteen root downfalls, and delights in the ten virtuous dharmas.
"One whose nature is renunciation" means one who is free from all attachments; "one who is indifferent to wealth and the like";
"one who knows virtues" means one who has faith in the Three Jewels;
and "one who seeks liberation" means one who is indifferent to worldly accomplishments.
"Devoted to the tantras" means one who observes the vows (*saṃvara*) taught in the tantras;
"one whose heart is not fickle" means one whose heart does not stray toward worldly paths— that is, one whose heart is not fickle.

"Secretive regarding that which has been attained" (*labdhatatve'tigupta*) means that as long as one does not possess personal realization (*svato'nubhava*) of the reality (*tattva*) that has been attained, one remains secretive or extremely secretive.
"Destroyed by association with the wicked" (*duṣṭānāṃ saṅganaṣṭa*):

here, those householders who act as teachers for the sake of wealth, as well as ascetics who enjoy the use of monasteries and temples for the sake of a single individual, are the wicked. Association with them is the path of the ten unwholesome actions; he in whom this [association] has perished is "destroyed by association with the wicked."

A great disciple of such a nature should be accepted by a highly skilled teacher who knows reality for the sake of the initiation of the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñānaseka*); and by the word "etcetera," he alone,

being another [type], possessing middling qualities, should further be accepted for the sake of the merit [of the ritual] and for the sake of the fourth initiation, as well as for the seven initiations.
Furthermore, even an inferior person may be accepted for the sake of the five precepts if he honors his guru and does not cause him harm; such is the Blessed One’s rule.
This concludes the rule for examining disciples.
O sir, there is no movement toward the object of knowledge and so forth.
Mu. The reality-seeker,
the servant,
[is] all-secret.
That [person] does not exist, nor is there one of middling merit in the consecration.
O, that does not exist in the Upāsaka-śikṣā;
[it is] 12. ca. 13. apekṣa 13. ka. therein.
14. ca. sya so'ca 15. ka. kha. cha. anubhāvo 16. bho. 'na' is not present.
17. ga. For the purpose of the consecration of the knowledge of reality (*tattvavijñānābhiṣeka*) and so forth; ka. kha. ca. cha. *prajñāseka*; 17. ca.
"again" (*punaḥ*) is not present;
19. ca. Therefore, the examination of the disciple (*śiṣyaparīkṣā*).

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the consecration: now, for the purpose of drawing the mandala, bestowing the consecrations, teaching the tantra, and performing worship of the yoginīs, the rule concerning the white lunar festival (śuklaparvan) as declared by the Blessed One is set forth beginning with the words "from Caitra," etc.: "At the end of Caitra, on the white festival day, the Guru who benefits others, having drawn the mandala, should bestow the seven consecrations which remove the stains of defilement, for the sake of the merit of his sons."
Worship is for the sake of the teaching of the Yoginīs, who are a treasury of all virtues; in the absence of worship, the Guru’s teaching does not occur for one year in the *Tantrarāja*. || 5 ||
In this noble land, the Blessed One Śākyamuni attained perfect enlightenment at the rising of the sun on the full moon day of Vaiśākha;

then, during the fifteen lunar digits from the first day of the bright fortnight until the entry into the first day of the dark fortnight, he set the Wheel of Dharma in motion and taught the three vehicles. Thereafter, in the twelfth month, on the full moon day of Caitra at the glorious Dhānyakaṭaka, he manifested the Maṇḍala of the Lord of Speech of the Dharmadhātu, characterized by the division of sixteen digits, and above that, the glorious Nakṣatra-maṇḍala consisting of six divisions—the Maṇḍala of the Ādibuddha expanded from that very Maṇḍala.
How is it known that this is the *nakṣatramaṇḍala*?

It is said: Here, outside the shrine (*caitya*), twenty-eight pillars have been erected in the four directions according to the purification of the twenty-eight lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) by means of a seven-pronged division—brought from the east by Viṣṇu, from the south by Kārttikeya, from the west by Brahmā, and from the north by Śaṅkara.
Because of these [pillars] arranged outside the shrine according to the lunar mansions, the inner mandala of the shrine is called the "Glorious Lunar Mansion Mandala" (*śrī-nakṣatramaṇḍala*).

Thus, by means of the division of the twenty-four lunar digits (*kalā*) of the waxing and waning phases, there is another *pātāla*-maṇḍala consisting of sixteen divisions, which is the nature of the maṇḍalas of body, speech, and mind, through the purification of the sixteen emptinesses and compassion;

such is the rule for the location of the maṇḍala. In that very place, on that same day, having bestowed the Buddha-consecration, the Tathāgata gave the prophecy of Buddhahood to the gods, asuras, and others in the future time.
Therefore, on this full moon day, the Tathāgata’s ordinance for the Vajrācāryas in the Kālacakra was as follows:

"At the end of Caitra, on the white fortnight, having drawn the mandala, the Guru who benefits others should bestow the seven empowerments that remove the stains of defilement upon his sons for the sake of merit."

Here, first, for the purpose of engaging in the bestowal of the seven empowerments (*saptābhiṣeka*), for the sake of mantra recitation (*mantrajāpa*) and mandala meditation (*maṇḍalabhāvanā*), there is the accumulation of merit (*puṇyasaṃbhāra*). Therefore, for the sake of that accumulation of merit, the seven empowerments should be given. Then, the twenty-five vows (*vrata*) beginning with non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) should be given. After that, for the sake of the accumulation of gnosis (*jñānasaṃbhāra*), the three higher empowerments (*uttarābhiṣeka*) should be given. [These are for] the purpose of giving even one's own flesh and what is most dear, and for the purpose of meditating on emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects (*sarvākāravaropetaśūnyatā*), while abiding in the *bodhicitta*—the seminal essence (*śukra*).
ga. In the twelfth [chapter], O Bhagavān, [the section on] the Sixteen Parts (*ṣoḍaśakalāvi0*) titled "The Detailed Analysis" (*vibhāga*).
In manuscripts ka, kha, ga, and ca, the word "maṇḍalaṃ" does not appear.
ga. ca. this maṇḍala;
ka. ca. twenty-eight;
ga. ca. not superimposed.
ka. cha. [refers to] the past Sugatas;
ka. kha ca. cha. [refers to] the maṇḍala-cakra.
