[Chapter on the Meaning of the Syllables, Verse: This is the great chapter concerning the characteristics of the means for accomplishing all activities, beginning with those of the Vajrācārya. Because the accumulation of gnosis (*jñānasambhāra*) has that [accumulation of merit] as its meaning, the higher initiations (*uttarābhiṣeka*) must be bestowed for the sake of that cause, the accumulation of gnosis; and these, together with the fourth initiation, are to be explained by means of the oral instruction (*upadeśa*).
Such is the Blessed One’s rule regarding the initiations.

Thus, O Caitra, having begun with the full moon of Caitra, the Vajrācārya should bestow empowerments during twelve full moons; he should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of images and so forth, as well as on other days endowed with auspicious lunar mansions (nakṣatra). This is the rule for empowerment and the like. Now, the rule for the worship of the Yoginīs for the purpose of teaching the Kālacakra is stated:

having drawn the mandala on the full moon of Caitra, worship of the Yoginīs should be performed with food, drink, and so forth; or even in the absence of drawing a mandala, [worship is performed] for the sake of teaching this King of Tantras, which is a treasury of all virtues.

O Caitra, when due to the lack of the assembly of conditions there is an absence of worship on the full moon day, then for one year there is an absence of teaching from the Guru, the Vajrācārya, according to the *Tantrarāja*.

Now, if an absence of worship occurs and some worthy disciple seeks the meaning of what has been heard, then he listens after performing the worship of the Yoginīs during twelve full moon days; by his accumulation of merit, others also listen.

In this context, the worship of the Yoginīs for the purpose of pacifying external obstacles should always be performed on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days according to one's means; an offering (*bali*) should be given daily to the spirits (*bhūtas*) and others; and the worship of the Buddhas, the maṇḍala, and so forth should be performed—this is the rule for wealthy householders.

However, for disciples who are *avadhūtas*, there is no fixed rule regarding worship, nor is there any rule for the Guru concerning the teaching of them, because the Buddhas and Vajrayoginīs accept the [disciples'] intention (*āśaya*), not the material objects such as worship. This concludes the rule for worship in the teaching of the Tantra. || 5 ||

Now, the characteristics of the ground and so forth for the purpose of initiation are stated: Having understood the examination of the site, the division of directions in forests, cities, towns, and villages, the preceptor should perform all rites for the results of inauspicious and auspicious [actions], such as pacification (*śāntika*) and so on;

likewise, the characteristics of the fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*), the colored powders (*rajas*), the oblations, the ritual stakes (*kīla*), and so forth, as well as the gathering of disciples and the drawing of the mandala of the Supreme Victor. (6)

Whatever has been taken up here in this chapter concerning the ground and so forth, which is to be explained in what follows, all of that the Vajrācārya should perform for the sake of the fruits of auspicious and inauspicious karma, such as rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and the like; this is the rule that he should act after knowing how to gather disciples and how to draw the mandala. For a corrupt teacher who acts out of a lack of thorough knowledge, or one who deceives others out of greed for wealth, there will be rebirth in hell; such is the instruction of the Teacher. The [verse] beginning with "the examination of the ground for the sake of initiation" is easy to understand. || 6 ||
Six. For the purpose of destruction, 4.
Six. *Māyām* (in manuscripts kha, ca, and cha, the word *ca* does not exist).
In the *Kālacakra Tantra*, [the word] "abhiṣeka" does not appear in the Ka and Cha recensions;
Bhoṭa hears it.
And [the words] "of the wretched," etc., and "of the self-grasping," etc.
(yaduktaṃ). What was said:

Ga. Gha. Ca. Gha. Now the characteristics of the earth are described: In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is said that the birth of the earth is fourfold according to its qualities—Śūdra, Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, and Brāhmaṇa—and it should be known by its color as black, yellow, red, and white like the moon.

By its taste, the Earth (Vasumatī) becomes salty and has the fragrance of a lotus; [the others] have divine fragrances in sequence. The Śūdra earth is sour and salty; the Vaiśya and Kṣatriya are sweet and pungent; the other, the twice-born (Brāhmaṇa), is otherwise. (7)

By the words "of the earth" and so forth, it is meant that here in worldly convention the birth of things is fourfold; that [birth] is to be understood as being according to the four castes (*caturvarṇataḥ*), such as the Śūdra and others, by way of the black color and so forth.
Here, according to worldly consensus (*lokasaṃvṛtyā*), the black-colored earth is the Śūdra, the yellow is the Vaiśya, the red is the Kṣatriya, and the white is the Brāhmaṇa caste.

Likewise, according to odor: a Śūdra woman has a putrid odor, a Vaiśya woman has the odor of alkaline salt, a Kṣatriya woman has the odor of a lotus, and a Brāhmaṇa woman has a divine fragrance; such is the sequence for caste. Similarly, according to taste: one of Śūdra birth has the taste of sourness and alkalinity; one of Vaiśya birth has the taste of sweetness and pungency (through the experience of sweet); and a Kṣatriya woman has the taste of pungency; while another taste, bitter or astringent, belongs to the twice-born (Brāhmaṇa). Thus is the rule of caste determined by taste. || 7 ||

Now he describes the ground for the purpose of pacification and so forth: "White for pacification, and [the ground] resembling a cloud leads to nourishment; black for killing and driving away; red for attraction and subjugation; resembling excellent gold for paralyzing and deluding.
Indeed, in all ritual applications, the fifth [type], which is green and of the lowest caste, is the 'all-tasting' scent; it should be known by yogins as a treasury of all qualities. (8)
Regarding the passage beginning with "white" (śveta) and so forth:

here, in rites of pacification (śāntika), the ground is white; in rites of enrichment (puṣṭi), it is black in color for both killing (māraṇa) and expulsion (uccāṭana); it is red for attraction (ākṛṣṭi) and subjugation (vaśya); and it should be yellow for paralyzing (stambhana) and bewildering (mohana).
By the use of the word "and" (ca), the rule applies respectively even to [rites such as] poisoning (nirviṣa) and so forth.
In this entire section on ritual action (*karmabhāga*), green earth is effective for all rites;

furthermore, the fifth [element], the lowest caste, which is the source of all flavors, possesses all fragrances, is a treasury of all qualities, and is characterized by the element of space—this is to be known by the yogi. This is the rule regarding the characteristics of the elements (*bhūmilakṣaṇaniyama*).

In this regard, if such a fixed rule for the characteristics of the ground were intended for purposes such as rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth, then it would not be the case that in every instance—whether in forests, cities, or other directional divisions—the ground is endowed with these characteristics.

Therefore, the Blessed One stated in the *Mūlatantra*: "In this world, wherever a rite such as a mandala is to be performed, if the ground there is not suitable according to the requirements of the rite, then one should dig a pit down to the water level or to the level of rock; thereafter, one should fill the pit with other earth in accordance with the requirements of the rite."

In this regard, for the sake of the "earth-scent" (*bhūgandha*), one should saturate white clay with sandalwood water; red clay with lotus water or red sandalwood water; yellow clay with the urine of a donkey, a horse, or a human;
and black clay with putrid flesh and [the urine of] the twice-born caste.

This is the great chapter on the characteristics of the means for accomplishing the entire expansion of activities, beginning with the Vajrācārya. One should meditate upon [the vessel] with water; for the purpose of tasting the flavors, one should throw salt-water into it when it is black, molasses when it is yellow, the three pungents (trikaṭuka) when it is red, and bitter and astringent substances when it is white. Since nothing need be added when it is green because it performs all activities, likewise, [these substances] should be placed within the womb of the earth.

Human bone is used for killing during the *kṛṣṇā* [tithi]; crow feathers for expulsion; donkey bones for inciting hatred; during the *pītā*, horn of a ram for pinning; yellow orpiment for paralyzing; a snake for bewildering; during the *raktā*, *gorocana* for subjugation; vermilion for attraction; realgar for immobilizing; during the *śvetā*, crystal for pacification; a conch for nourishment; and pearl for removing fever and burning sensations. During the *haritā*, nothing at all should be cast in.
Now, if that *haritā* is for a general purpose intended to fulfill all desires, then one should cause five jewels to be placed within the earth.
Even when the [deity] is white or red, one should avoid cruel substances in all rites;

by the term "all rites," the six rites beginning with pacification (śāntika) and subjugation (vaśya) are meant, and not the six beginning with killing (māraṇa) and piercing (kīlana). This is the rule for the procedure of examining the ground. || 8 ||

Now, the division of directions for the purpose of pacifying rites and so forth is stated: In the northeast and the north, there is indeed the attainment of worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*), as well as pacification (*śāntika*) and enrichment (*pauṣṭika*). In the southeast and the eastern part, killing (*māraṇa*) and expulsion (*uccāṭana*) are clearly and invariably established.

In the southwest and the south, subjugation (*vaśya*) and summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*) are always manifest. O supreme lord of men, in the northwest and the west, there is paralyzing (*stambhana*) and bewildering (*mohana*). || 9 ||

With the words "In the northeast," and so forth, it is taught that here in an ordinary village, one should perform rites for pacification (*śāntika*), enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), or the removal of fever outside the village in the northeast, or even in the north; however, in a great royal capital, there are the eight cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*)— such as the burning of corpses— in the eight directions, and therefore [rites for] pacification and enrichment do not succeed there.
Therefore, one should perform rites for pacification (*śāntika*) and enrichment (*pauṣṭika*) to the northeast or the north of Rājagṛha;

the remaining rites are to be performed outside the capital city as in the case of a village. This is the rule for the rites of pacification and enrichment. Likewise, killing (*māraṇa*) is in the southeast; causing hatred (*vidveṣa*) and expulsion (*uccāṭana*) are in the east; subjugation (*vaśya*) is in the southwest; summoning (*ākṛṣṭi*) or paralyzing (*stobhana*) is in the south; deluding (*mohana*) is in the northwest; and immobilizing (*stambhana*) and pinning down (*kolana*) are in the west.

The mantra-practitioner should perform the all-purpose maṇḍala, the sacrificial pit, and the fire-oblation in the center of the village; this is the rule for performing rites according to the directions. || 9 ||

Now the fire-pits for rites such as pacification (śānti) and others are described: In the eight directions of the village, the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) invariably arises as circular, square, semi-circular, pentagonal, heptagonal, and triangular, according to the influence of the qualities of nature (guṇas).

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is said that there are also hexagonal and octagonal pits according to the family (kula). And their central emblems are: the lotus, the wheel, the knife, the sword, the arrow, the vajra-hook, the chain, and the serpent. [10]

In the eight directions of the village, starting from the northeast (aiśānī) and proceeding in order, the fire-pits (kuṇḍas) for the various rites are as follows: for pacification (śānti), a circular pit; for nourishment (puṣṭi), a square pit; for killing (māraṇa), a bow-shaped pit; for creating enmity (vidveṣa), a five-cornered pit; for subjugation (vaśya), a seven-cornered pit; for attraction (ākṛṣṭi), a triangle; for delusion (mohana), a six-cornered pit; and for immobilization (stambhana), an eight-cornered pit.
The characteristics of these should be explained in detail in the forthcoming ritual procedure for the fire sacrifice (homavidhi).

Now the marks for the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) are described: here, in a circular pit, the mark on the lotus pericarp is a lotus; in a square pit, a wheel; in a bow-shaped pit, a knife (*kartī*); in a five-cornered pit, a sword; in a seven-cornered pit, an arrow; in a triangular pit, a vajra-hook (*vajrāṅkuśa*); in a six-cornered pit used for subjugation (*mohana*), a snake; and in an eight-cornered pit, a chain (*śṛṅkhalā*).
In these two [types of] pits, there is a reversal of the marks due to the power of the meter; such is the rule for the marks. || 10 ||

He states their measurements: one, two, and a half cubits; zero, four, zero, and two finger-breadths (aṅgulas); zero, three, and zero aṅgulas; half an aṅgula; and six parts. By the division of Varuṇa (four) and Ravi (twelve), there are zeros and nights (seven).

O King, for the rites of pacification (śānti) and nourishment (puṣṭi), you should fashion the altar (vedī) and the lips (oṣṭhas), as well as a series of marks above the altar according to the family tradition on all sides. Outside the altar, you should also make lotus petals, and not others. || 11 ||

Regarding "one" and so forth: a circle is one cubit; a square is two cubits; a bow-shaped [semi-circle] is half a cubit; a pentagon has the same measurement as the circle; a heptagon is forty finger-breadths (aṅgulas); a triangle is twenty finger-breadths; a hexagon is thirty finger-breadths; and an octagon is sixty finger-breadths. The excavation (khāni) is half the measurement of the pit (kuṇḍa); the altar (vedi) within the pit consists of six parts; the rim (oṣṭha) consists of twelve parts of the pit. The series of marks (cihnāvalī) is equal to the altar. Outside that, for rites of pacification (śānti) and nourishment (puṣṭi), there are lotus petals. Regarding the remaining [mandalas], another different [measurement] will be stated outside the Veda.
Or else, the vajra symbol should be known as [the mark] in the center of the fire-pit for all rites. || 11 ||

Or the vajra may be used for all rites; it is also the great [implement] in the eightfold division of the kīlaka. [The materials are: wood from the nyagrodha, aśvattha, iron, khadira, mango, or bilva, as well as the lotus.
In the triangular [diagram] for attraction, there is a seven-pointed [vajra];
in the triangle, an arrow; and in the seven-pointed [diagram], a vajrāṅkuśa.

In this chapter, [the section] on the great summary (*mahoddeśa*) concerning the characteristics of the practice for the expansion of all activities, beginning with the Vajrācārya: Thus, there are crystal vases, those made of excellent silver, glorious skull-bowls, those made of iron, those called copper, golden vases, as well as those clearly prescribed as being made of wood or clay. (12)

In this regard, for pacification (śāntika), stakes are made of *nyagrodha* wood; for the purpose of pinning down the quarters and so forth in rites of enrichment (puṣṭi), they are made of *aśvattha*; for killing (māraṇa), they are made of bone; for expulsion (uccāṭana), they are made of iron; for subjugation (vaśya), they are made of *akhadira*; for attraction (ākṛṣṭi), they are made of *cūta*; for delusion (mohana), they are made of *arka*; and for immobilization (stambhana), they are made of *vilva*. This is the rule for the stakes; for rites applicable to all purposes (sārvakarmika), they are made of *udumbara*.

Now the vases are described: for pacification (śāntika), crystal vases; for enrichment (puṣṭi), silver; for killing (māraṇa), human skulls; for expulsion (uccāṭana) and creating enmity (vidveṣa), iron; for subjugation (vaśya), gold; for attraction (ākṛṣṭi), copper; for immobilization (stambhana), clay; and for delusion (mohana), wood—thus there are ten vases. || 12 ||

Now, the characteristics of the ritual jar (*kumbha*) for the purpose of pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*) are described: circular, said to be eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in width, ten finger-breadths high, with lips two finger-breadths thick, a neck six finger-breadths long, and an opening eight finger-breadths wide; white as the moon, and no others [are used] for pacification and nourishment.

During the eight watches (*yāma*) starting from the forenoon, at every daily time, there should be [these jars] for pacification, nourishment, and so forth; thus one should perform the eight rites there during the half-watch of day and night.

In this regard, regarding the *kalaśagarbha* verse: "Eight finger-breadths [in width] are prescribed; sixteen finger-breadths are prescribed; they are raised by twice ten [finger-breadths]. Thus, from the base of the *kalaśagarbha* to the end of the lip, the height is twenty finger-breadths. "With lips of two finger-breadths" means those whose two lips hang down for two finger-breadths each. From the mouth as the reference point, the neck is six finger-breadths, and the face is eight finger-breadths.

From one lip-end to the other lip-end, the mouth is eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas) wide; having divided these eight finger-breadths into three parts, the throat-opening is made with two parts, and the length of the two lips is one part. These [lips] should be as white as the moon for the rites of pacification (śānti) and enrichment (puṣṭi), and no other [colored] jars should be used.
In the absence of crystal or silver pitchers, earthen jars—specifically those made from the *akālamūla* plant—should be made white by coating them with rice-flour paste or sandalwood paste.

Likewise, it was said by the Blessed One in the *Mūlatantra*: "For the rite of killing (*māraṇa*), one should fashion the hell-guardians (*naraka-pāla*) black with the charcoal powder of a cremation ground, smeared with human fat.

For the rites of expulsion (*uccāṭana*) and inciting hatred (*vidveṣa*), they have long necks and faces eight finger-breadths wide; their bodies are black, twelve finger-breadths in circumference, twenty-four finger-breadths in height, with lips one finger-breadth thick and mouths six finger-breadths deep. For the rites of subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), they should be fashioned by an artisan according to worldly custom. For the rite of paralyzing (*stambhana*), they are short, with equal circumference and height of sixteen finger-breadths, and necks four finger-breadths long. [The same applies] for causing division (*vibheda*).
In this chapter, [verse]:

The great summary concerning the characteristics of the practice for the expansion of all activities, beginning with the Vajrācārya: Dūrvā grass, grain, meat, as well as poison, likewise rājikā, red flowers, bilva, discarded garlands, and golden flowers—these indeed [are used] in the five and so forth. (15)

For the rite of delusion (*mohana*), fuel-sticks born from the *unmatta* plant are used; for the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*), those born from the *vilva* plant. All are half a cubit long, measuring twelve finger-breadths from the little finger up to the thumb;
beyond that, they should not be accepted if they are shorter or longer—this is the rule regarding sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*).
Now the substances for the fire offering (homa) are described—beginning with "milk" and so forth.
Here, in rites of pacification (śāntika), the homa is performed with cow's milk and dūrvā grass;

in rites of nourishment (puṣṭi), with ghee and the five grains; in rites of killing (māraṇa), with blood together with meat and poison; and in rites of expulsion (uccāṭana) and inciting enmity (vidveṣa), with human fat. [The rule for the jar is: it should have six finger-widths for its mouth, thick lips, and [be held] by two thumbs.

The rule is that for all rites—such as those of pacification (*śānti*) and subjugation (*vaśya*)—those [times] previously mentioned should be adopted. Now, the times for pacification and so forth are stated, beginning with "forenoon" (*pūrvāhṇa*): here, every day there are eight watches (*prahara*), each consisting of three hours; among these, one should perform *uccāṭana* (expulsion) during the fourth watch of the forenoon, and *vaśya* during the fifth. Thus, the watches for pacification and the other rites are established.

Thus, there it is said "by half-watch periods": during the first half-prahara of the forenoon, one should perform rites of pacification (śāntika), and during the latter half, rites of enrichment (pauṣṭika). In this same way, it applies everywhere;

likewise at night, during the first half-prahara, one should perform rites of pacification, and during the latter half, rites of enrichment as well—the mantra practitioner should thus carry out these activities.

If one is unable to perform the *homa* for one *prahara* after assuming the seat that will be described, then one should accomplish the goal by performing the *homa* for half a *prahara*; thus both cases are stated.
Furthermore, the specific rule regarding the time for the worship and accomplishment of the Goddess will be explained in the fifth chapter. || 13 ||

In the first [period] there is pacification (*śāntika*); in the second, nourishment (*pauṣṭika*); in the third, killing (*māraṇa*); in the sixth, attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*); in the seventh, delusion (*mohana*); and in the eighth, immobilization (*stambhana*), which is to be avoided. Now, the prohibition regarding cruel times and ascendants for pacification and nourishment is stated: at midday and midnight, during the periods of day and night, an ascendant occupied by a malefic planet causes fear of death; it is well known to be just like that. For pacification and nourishment, [fuel sticks] with sap are used; for killing, human bone; for inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*), crow feathers; and for attraction, [sticks] made of *khadira* wood or *kiṃśuka* flowers. || 14 ||

In this context, at midday and midnight every day, one should avoid [performing] rites for pacification (*śāntika*) as well as those for prosperity (*puṣṭika*). Likewise, an ascendant that has risen while occupied by a malefic planet, or one associated with Mars, Saturn, or the planet Kālāgni, is forbidden, because it causes fear of death; however, that very same [ascendant] should be employed for rites of killing (*māraṇa*) and expulsion (*uccāṭana*)—this is the rule.
Now, the sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*) for the *śāntika* and other rites are described, beginning with the words "with milk" (*sakṣīra*).

Here, for *śānti* and *puṣṭi*, the fuel sticks are made from milky trees (*kṣīravṛkṣa*)—namely, the *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *nyagrodha*, *parkaṭī*, and *madhuvṛkṣa*—numbering five hundred. For *māraṇa*, there are five hundred human bones fashioned into the shape of the little finger. Likewise, for *vidveṣa* and *uccāṭana*, there are five hundred peacock feathers. Similarly, for *vaśya*, they are made from *khadira* wood; for *ākṛṣṭi*, they are made from *palāśa* wood. || 14 ||

The measurements for the *vilva*, *unmatta*, and *ardhahasta* [are as follows]: they are used for paralyzing (*stambhana*) and bewildering (*mohana*) when counted by hundreds of arrows. In the fire-oblation (*homa*) of milk, clarified butter, blood, fat, sweat, water from a thunderbolt, water, phlegm, wine, and so forth, [the substances are used] together with black mustard and salt for subjugation (*vaśya*); with sweat and flowers of the red oleander (*raktakaravīra*) and others for attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*); with urine, bilva leaves, or its fruit and grain for paralyzing; with phlegm and a garland of discarded offerings (*nirmālya*) for bewildering; and with wine and datura flowers for bewilderment. Such is the rule regarding the materials for the oblation in rites such as pacification (*śāntika*). || 15 ||

O King, the teacher’s seat is in the south, the southwest corner, and [the seats] of Varuṇa and Vāyu; the colored ground for the two types of rites should also be divided within the lotus. For rites such as pacification (śāntika) and so forth, [the colors] are white, black, and yellow;

white, black, and yellow; and white, black, and yellow on the outside according to the divisions of the Buddhas. In the directions of the gods, Yama, and Varuṇa, and in the north, is the colored ground. || 16 ||

In this context, for the rite of pacification (*śānti*), the seat should be made in the south as will be described; for nourishment (*puṣṭi*) in the southwest corner; for killing (*māraṇa*) in the west; for expulsion (*uccāṭana*) or causing enmity (*vidveṣa*) in the northwest; for subjugation (*vaśya*) in the northeast; for attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*) in the north; and for delusion (*mohana*) in the east, and for immobilization (*stambhana*) in the southeast. This is the rule for the seats of the sacrificial fire-pits (*homakuṇḍa*) in rites such as pacification and the rest. Now, the procedure for the colored powders (*rajas*) is stated: here, in the two types of rites beginning with pacification, the falling of the powder occurs either in the center of the fire-pit or in the mandala.

White powder is for pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*); black powder is for killing (*māraṇa*) and expulsion (*uccāṭana*); red for subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*); yellow for delusion (*mohana*) and immobilization (*stambhana*); and green for all rites (*sarvakarman*). Alternatively, white, black, red, yellow, or green may be used together.

Thus, whether in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or the mandala, on the ground in the east, south, west, or north according to the specific Buddha, the scattering of powder follows the procedure taught in the Tantra; or it may be according to the color of the faces of the Blessed One. This is the rule for the application of colors. || 16 ||

The sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or the colored ground (*raṅgabhūmi*) is prepared according to the family lineage (*kula*), and the application of colors is likewise performed on the ground. The placement (*nyāsa*) and sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of the deities, as well as their dismissal (*utsarjana*) by means of the vajra of one’s own heart, must be performed by the Master (*ācārya*) according to the sequence that will be explained; this is the rule. Now, the characteristics of the argha-vessel are stated: In an argha-vessel made of crystal or other materials, there should be an eight-petaled lotus measuring twelve thumb-breadths (*aṅguṣṭha*). At the tip of its handle, there is a vessel for anointing (*añjati-pātra*) and a cup (*culuka*) for the performance of oblations (*āhuti*) in the fire sacrifice (*homa*). || 17 ||
In this context of pacification (*śānti*), the crystal vessel for the offering of the *argha* water is shaped like a shallow bowl (*śarāva*), meaning it has the form of a *kacola*;
everything measures twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and consists of a pericarp with eight petals.
Thus, in the crystal and other *argha* vessels, there is an eight-petaled lotus measuring twelve thumbs-breadths (*aṅguṣṭha*).
In this [mandala], the pericarp is four finger-breadths (catur-aṅgula) and the eight petals are likewise four finger-breadths each; thus it is twelve finger-breadths in total.
Furthermore, for rites such as those for prosperity (puṣṭi), the procedure is performed in vessels made of silver, skull-cups, iron, gold, copper, wood, or clay.
Likewise, the vessel for the purpose of the oblation (āhuti) is called the *dhruvaka*.

Here, at the tip of the staff—one cubit in length—is a vessel shaped like a hollowed palm, square and one finger-breadth high. On its level surface is a lotus made of lotus-petal tips; on the inner side of the rim is a five-pronged vajra, and in the central prong there is an aperture for the flow of clarified butter, like the exit of the stream of urine or semen. Regarding the offerings, the rule in the Root Tantra is that "the vessel" (pātrī) refers to the offerings, and it extends from the one-cubit staff up to the vajra from the heart-lotus.

Likewise, for the purpose of the fire-oblation (*homakārya*), there is a hollow at the tip of the handle reaching from the *ūrṇā* location to the heart, or else a horizontal division from the mouth; right there, a lotus of six finger-breadths according to the measure of the palm [is formed]. This is the rule for the oblation vessel: the substance-oblation is in the hollow, and the vajra symbol is on the back of the handle. || 17 ||

Now, the form of the deity for pacification and other rites is described: the deity becomes peaceful, fierce, or passionate according to the family (kula), and likewise possesses a rigid form in the two types of activity; thus the presiding deity in the mandala is fixed and manifest.

The Lord of Jinas has five aspects as he exists within the threefold existence through the divisions of the aggregates, elements, and so forth; therefore, the deities in the powder mandala also possess five aspects. ||18||

In this pit (*kuṇḍa*), within the maṇḍala of the fire deity (*agnidevatā*), the leader (*nāyaka*) is peaceful and white in color for rites of pacification (*śānti*) and enrichment (*puṣṭi*); he is fierce and black in color for killing (*māraṇa*), expulsion (*uccāṭana*), and so forth; he is passionate and red in color for subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*); and he is rigid and yellow in color for delusion (*mohana*), paralysis (*stambhana*), and so forth—such is the color of the deity. For all rites beginning with pacification, he is green; thus, his form possesses a slight smile and passion. This is the rule regarding the deity. Now, the purification of the colored powders (*rajas*) is described, beginning with the words "fivefold" (*pañcākāra*).

In this context, the Lord of Jinas is Vajrasattva, who indeed possesses five aspects because, through the radiation of rays of fivefold gnosis, he pervades the three realms by way of the divisions of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases being free from obscuration; for that reason as well, there are deities with five aspects in the powder maṇḍala—this is the rule regarding the powders. || 18 ||

The Great Chapter on the Characteristics of the Accomplishment of the Entire Range of Rituals, beginning with the Vajrācārya. Now, the characteristics of the thread (*sūtra*) are stated: The thread should be eight cubits long; it is circular, being one finger-breadth thick. It is triple-stranded, made from the thumb-thread of the master (*ācārya*), and follows three paths; there is only this one [type of] thread and no other. Regarding the postures: the *paryaṅka* (cross-legged) posture is prescribed for rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth; the *vajra* (diamond) posture is for wrathful rites (*abhicāruka*). The *utkaṭa* (squatting) posture is another variety. The *ardhaparyaṅka* (half-cross-legged) posture has two types: that in which the feet are placed upon the anus, and that which serves as a seat according to the distinctions of ritual action.
Regarding the statement "the thread is eight cubits," and so forth:

here, having wound the thread made by a maiden into many strands consisting of three threads each, one should then have it tripled. According to the measure of the thumb-joint of the Vajrācārya, that very [thread] is eight cubits; it may be double or quadruple the size of the maṇḍala, up to sixteen cubits. One single thread must be prepared according to the hand of the Ācārya.

And there is no other characteristic regarding the mandala; the mandala always exists through its own internal division, starting from one cubit up to a thousand cubits. Therefore, the rule for the cord and the rule for the mandala are according to the hand of the Ācārya. In this regard, since it is a fixed rule that "the mind-mandala (*cittamaṇḍala*) in the *Ādibuddha* should be made twelve cubits," the cord must be twenty-four cubits. Wherever the cord is double the length of the mandala, that is the rule. Thus, in the *Ādibuddha*, one should construct the mind-mandala as twelve cubits, and by that rule, the cord is twenty-four cubits.

Thus, the rule is that the speech-maṇḍala is sixteen cubits and the body-maṇḍala is twenty cubits, based on the doubling of the [mandala’s] circumference. However, it should not be said that in a maṇḍala of one thousand cubits, the laying of the lines is performed with a thread of two thousand cubits, because that would be extraordinary.
But surely, in another tantra it says: "The thread is divided into twenty-two parts; how can it be double the length of the maṇḍala in both its circumference and its length?"
Will there not be the statement of someone that [the circumference] is one *yava* in width and eight cubits (*hasta*) in length?

Therefore, it is said: here, if in every mandala the circular line is twenty-two parts, then in a mandala of one thousand cubits, the door, which occupies one part of the wheel, will be one hundred and twenty-five cubits;
twenty parts of that constitute the circular line, which is six cubits and six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length.
By that sūtra measuring two thousand cubits, who is this teacher who will perform the laying of the lines on the mandala ground?

Therefore, this statement regarding the measurement of one cubit and so forth applies to an ordinary mandala, and not to the circular layout of the sūtras beyond that; such is the rule of the Blessed One.
In general, the body of humans is four cubits;

therefore, twice that body is eight cubits. That which has entered the three paths—the channels of body, speech, and mind—becomes unified as one. By means of that, one should mark out the maṇḍala up to a thousand cubits, repeatedly casting the thread at the places for the threads from the center of the wheels outward; this is the rule for the procedure of the thread.
Now, the seats for the purpose of accomplishing rites such as pacification are described, beginning with the words "the cross-legged posture" (*paryaṅka*).
In this context, the postures for rites such as pacification (śāntika) occur in sequence;
therein, for pacification, the "lotus posture" (paryaṅka) consists of the right foot placed upon the left knee with the sole turned upward. This is the lotus posture.

For nourishment (*puṣṭi*), the vajra-posture (*vajrāsana*) is formed by placing the right foot upon the top of the left thigh; this is the *bhūta-sūtra*. [In the manuscripts] ka, kha, and cha, it is doubled (*dviguṇa*).
ka. kha. cha. should perform; ka. kha. ga. [the word] "of the door" (dvāravi) is present; bho. the word "uncommon" (asāmānya) is absent; ca. commentary (vṛtti).
ga, ca, bho, ka, kha, cha: *ryanta*.
ga: *śāntikādi*.
ka: *āsanam ucyate*.
"Ṅka" (refers to) *ka*, *kha*, and *ga*. Regarding the left foot:
"The left foot also, extended crosswise upon the right thigh with the sole upward, is the vajrāsana. (*Vimalaprabhā*, Abhiṣeka section).

Regarding "the posture of the Daityas" (*daityāsana*): for the purpose of slaying *daityas*, it is like the *karmapāda* posture; however, for the purposes of eradication (*uccāṭana*) and inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*), the *utkaṭa* [posture] is used.

In the *utkaṭa* posture, both feet are placed evenly on the ground with the ankles joined at the base of the buttocks (*phiccaka*), while the two knees and the two thighs are raised upward. This is the *utkaṭa*.
"The half-paryaṅka has two varieties" means:
here, in the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*), the left foot is in the *paryaṅka* position while the right is in the *utkaṭaka* position, bent slightly toward the right; this is the first variety.

In the rite of attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*), the second variety is the right foot in the *paryaṅka* position and the left in the *utkaṭaka* position, bent slightly toward the left. Thus, the half-paryaṅka has two varieties.
Regarding "the foot placed upon the anus":
here, in the rite of subduing (*mohana*), the left foot is placed upon the anus and the anus rests upon the foot; the right [foot] is like that of one sitting in the *utkaṭaka* posture.
In the rite of paralyzing (*stambhana*), the right foot is placed upon the anus and the anus rests upon the foot; the left [foot] is like that of one sitting in the *utkaṭaka* posture.
Thus concludes the rule concerning the eightfold classification of postures.

Now, for the purpose of mantra recitation (*jāpa*), the rosaries (*akṣasūtra*) for pacification and other rites are described: for mantra recitation according to the families of the Sugatas, the rosary should be made of crystal, pearls, or the teeth of humans or donkeys, or of *putrajīva* seeds, or lotus seeds;

it should be fragrant. For worship, one uses white flowers along with pungent and astringent substances; for fierce incense, one uses red and yellow [substances], as well as urine, feces, and meat mixed with honey and blood; and for astringent incense, one uses astringent decoctions.

With the words "made of crystal," and so forth, [it is taught that] here, for pacification (*śānti*), there is a rosary made of crystal; for nourishment (*puṣṭi*), a pearl; for killing (*māraṇa*), one made of human teeth; for expulsion (*uccāṭana*), one made of donkey teeth or bones; for subjugation (*vaśya*), a rosary of *putrajīva* seeds;
for attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*), a lotus-seed rosary; and furthermore, one made from red sandalwood seeds.

For the rite of delusion (*mohana*), a rosary of *riṣṭa* seeds; for the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*), *īśākṣa* [seeds]; by "*īśākṣa*" is meant a rosary of *rudrākṣa* seeds—this is the rule regarding the rosary according to the lineage of the Sugata family—as will be stated later.
Now, the flowers for the purpose of worship during rites such as pacification (*śānti*) and so forth are described, beginning with the words "fragrant" (*saugandhaiḥ*).

In this context, for pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*), there is worship of the deities and others with fragrant white flowers; for killing (*māraṇa*), expulsion (*uccāṭana*), and creating enmity (*vidveṣa*), [one uses] black flowers with pungent substances and thorns;
for subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*), red flowers; and for delusion (*mohana*) and immobilization (*stambhana*), yellow flowers—such is the rule for flower worship.
Now, the incenses are described, beginning with the word "cold" (*śīta*).

For pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*), the incense is cool; an incense made of *aguru*, *sika*, and camphor, combined with honey and sugar, is called "cool incense" because it consists of cool substances. Likewise, for killing (*māraṇa*) and expulsion (*uccāṭana*), there is "flesh incense" mixed with sweet-smelling blood;
for subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*), there is "excellent incense."
*guggulu*—ka. ga.; "vāmo mūrdhni" is not present in ka.; *kramapāta*—cha.; *kūrmapāta*—bho.; *utkuṭakaṃ*—Tsog Pu.
ca. sphicakamūlā;
ka. kha. cha. utkaṭā, bho. utkuṭa;
ca śāntikādyakṣa; ga. śāntikādīnya.
ka. kha. crystal;
kha. [the portion] "for eradication, [an image] made from donkey's teeth" does not exist;
and sandalwood.
And those indeed;
with pungent substances;
in cold substances.
ga. Incense is sweet; ka. ga. Meat is for pacification and so forth.

In the chapter [on the] Great Chapter on the Characteristics of the Accomplishment of the Extensive Application of All Rites, such as those of the Vajrācārya and others: "Lac, resin of *sarja*, *kunduru*, *śrīvāsa*, and molasses—this is the fierce incense (*ugradhūpa*).
Likewise, for the rites of deluding (*mohana*) and paralyzing (*stambhana*), there is the decoction incense (*kaṣāyadhūpa*);
powdered *harītakī* mixed with molasses is the decoction incense.

Such is the rule for incense. Likewise, regarding the food offering (*naivedya*): for pacification (*śānti*), it is rice with milk; for nourishment (*puṣṭi*), rice with curd; for killing (*māraṇa*), black gram (*kāla-ja*); for expulsion (*uccāṭana*), meat; for subjugation (*vaśya*), rice with ghee; for attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*), rice with sesame oil; for delusion (*mohana*), mixed mung-bean rice;
and for immobilization (*stambhana*), chickpeas and fish-rice.

Thus, for pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*), sandalwood is the unguent; for killing (*māraṇa*) and expulsion (*uccāṭana*), with red charcoal; for subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), with saffron and *gorocana*; or with red sandalwood for delusion (*mohana*); and for stupefaction (*stambhana*), with turmeric and yellow arsenic (*haritāla*). This is the rule regarding perfumes, as well as for the lamp.

The rule for the lamp is as follows: for *śānti* (pacification) and *puṣṭi* (nourishment), a lamp with ghee; for *māraṇa* (killing) and *uccāṭana* (expulsion), human fat; for *vaśya* (subjugation) and *ākarṣaṇa* (attraction), sesame oil; for *mohana* (delusion) and *stambhana* (paralysis), *jyotiṣmatī* oil, *bhallātaka* oil, and so forth.

Likewise, for *śānti* and *puṣṭi*, [the offering] is *akṣata* (unbroken rice) or *śāli* rice; for *māraṇa* and *uccāṭana*, black mustard (*rājikā*); for *vaśya* and *ākarṣaṇa*, white mustard (*sarṣapa*); for *stambhana* and *mohana*, lentils (*masūrikā*), or other grains.

Likewise, for the rites of pacification (śānti) and nourishment (puṣṭi), all articles of worship such as clothing and so forth should be white; for killing (māraṇa) and expulsion (uccāṭana), they should be black; for subjugation (vaśya) and attraction (ākarṣaṇa), they should be red; for paralyzing (stambhana) and deluding (mohana), they should be yellow; and for all rites, they should be green. This is the rule for the procedure of worship. || 20 ||

The drawing of the yantra may be done on a banyan leaf, a cloth from a funeral pyre, a leaf with many veins, an arka leaf, or śrīkhaṇḍa; using rice flour, charcoal from a funeral pyre, red minerals, poison, saffron, white flowers, the juice of triphalā, kuśa grass, or tālaka for the ink; and a pen made of dūrvā grass, śītā, bone, gold, khadira wood, bilva, or arka. (21)

For nourishment (*puṣṭi*), one uses water mixed with rice flour and *dūrvā* sprouts with a cool pen; likewise, for killing (*māraṇa*) and driving away (*uccāṭana*), one uses charcoal from a cremation ground and poison on a cloth from a cemetery with a pen made of human bone; for driving away, with a pen made of a crow's feather; for subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*), on birch bark with saffron and *gorocanā* using a golden pen; for attraction, with a *khadira* pen and powdered red sandalwood; and for paralyzing (*stambhana*) and bewildering (*mohana*), on a ripe leaf of the *arka* plant with yellow-colored *triphalā* juice, *tālaka*, and turmeric, using a *vilva* pen—for bewildering, this is the rule.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, the procedure for the installation of the yantra is now stated: here, for the rites of pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*), one should wrap the yantra drawn on a leaf or similar material with a white thread until the leaf is no longer visible; likewise, according to the division of activities, one should wrap it with a black thread, a red thread, or a yellow thread. || 21 ||

The placement of the yantra on clay, a slow fire, a skull of Śrī, the three sweets, blood, a vessel wrapped in beeswax, a moist spot, a pure place, the surface of a funeral pyre, heat from fire, or the earth, should be understood by the mantra-practitioner according to whether the result is inauspicious or auspicious; [the results] follow in sequence for the Moon, a ghost, a camel, a deer, a horse, a beast, a jar, and a corpse. (22)

Then, for pacification (śānti) and nourishment (puṣṭi), one should place it in a hollowed pair of shallow bowls (śarāva-sampuṭa) containing the three sweets (trimadhu)—mixed with honey, ghee, and milk; for killing (māraṇa) and expulsion (uccāṭana), one should place it in a skull filled with blood; for heating by fire, one should wrap it in beeswax and place it in a hollowed pair of shards (kharpara-sampuṭa); and for subjugation (vaśya), attraction (ākṛṣṭi), immobilization (stambhana), and delusion (mohana), one should place it within a brick filled with yellow arsenic (haritāla) water.

In a moist and pure place, one should place [the vessel] upon a mandala for rites of pacification (śānti) and nourishment (puṣṭi); for killing (māraṇa) and expulsion (uccāṭana), one should deposit it in the ground of a cemetery or a burnt pit; for subjugation (vaśya) and attraction (ākarṣaṇa), on the surface of a hearth; and for paralyzing (stambhana) and bewildering (mohana), one should deposit it in dry ground—this is the rule by which the practitioner should understand the results of auspicious and inauspicious rites.

Now, the rule for the exterior of the written yantra-cakra is stated: here, for pacification (śānti), one should encircle the cakra on the outside with a lunar disc; for nourishment (puṣṭi), having drawn it out, one should encircle it with an elephant; so that the cakra remains within the body of the elephant; for killing (māraṇa), within the body of a *preta*; for expulsion (uccāṭana), within the body of a camel; for subjugation (vaśya), within the body of a deer; for attraction (ākṛṣṭi), within the body of a horse; for delusion (mohana), within the body of a goat or a ram; for immobilization (stambhana), within the body of a corpse—just as the yantra-cakra is situated, so should the form be made on the outside; then, one should encircle it with the previously mentioned thread.

Likewise, there is a rule regarding the *vidyā* for the rites of pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*): for *vidyā*, a silver tube should be placed in the center; for killing (*māraṇa*), a tube of human bone; for expulsion (*uccāṭana*), a tube of crow bone; for subjugation (*vaśya*), a gold tube; for attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*), a copper tube; for delusion (*mohana*), an iron tube; and for immobilization (*stambhana*), a tin tube—such is the rule.

In this context, the rite of inciting hatred (vidveṣa) should be performed by the very same procedure as that for eradication (uccāṭana); and the rite of pinning (kīlana) should be performed by the very same procedure as that for immobilization (stambhana). However, in the case of pinning, one should fashion an image using the excrement of an enemy mixed with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and then pin it at the six centers (ṣaṭcakra) and at the joints of the hands and feet using *madanakaṇṭaka* thorns. The remainder is like that of immobilization and the other rites.
By that very [means] comes the drawing [of the lines], and by that very [means] the production of fever; however, one should smear an effigy with mustard seeds and salt and heat it over a fire.
By that very [means] comes the rite of pacification (śāntika) in this chapter, verse—

Having understood the twelvefold ritual procedure—namely, the Great Chapter on the Collection of the Grounds and so forth preceded by the Wheel of Protection, and the removal of the poison of evil views—the Master, if he performs it according to the sequence to be described, will certainly obtain its fruit through the command of the Blessed One.
However, for one who performs it not for the benefit of others but for his own sake, nothing at all is accomplished here; for wicked teachers, there is only the exhaustion of mere affliction.

Therefore, according to the rule stated in the Tantra, it shall be performed by an independent preceptor who has attained supernormal knowledge for the sake of benefiting others; this will be the rule as it is to be explained later, and for that reason it has not been described here in detail. || 22 ||

Thus ends the first great chapter, concerning the characteristics of the accomplishment of all ritual activities such as the Vajrācārya and others, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghukālacakratantrarāja* following the *Mūlatantra*.

(2) The Great Chapter on the Collection of the Grounds and Other Elements Preceded by the Protection Wheel: Having bowed to the terrifying Vajrabhairava, the hero Kālacakra who holds a skull-cup, the conqueror of the three worlds, the subduer of those difficult to tame.
I shall explain the ritual for protecting the site and for drawing the mandala,
as well as the expulsion of malevolent beings and the consecration of the ground and other elements.
As it has been stated by Mañjuvajra and others in the *Tantrarāja*,
I shall expound all the ritual procedures through this commentary for the sake of attaining the fruit of Buddhahood.

Here, the Blessed Lord Mañjuśrī, having been requested by Sūryaratha according to the previously stated procedure, appeared in an emanated body as King Yaśas. For the purpose of drawing the mandala, he uttered the response from the *Paramādibuddha*, the Blessed Buddha, beginning with the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*) and so forth, as taught in the Tantra starting with the twenty-third verse: "O Śrīvajra, in all directions... and so on. All that which was spoken in the Tantra, I shall now expand upon through this great summary (*mahoddeśa*), beginning with the words "O Śrīvajra": "O Śrīvajra, [the yogin] should burn the entire host of Māras situated in all directions; thereafter, within the ten-spoked wheel, he should visualize the host of wrathful deities located in the cardinal and intermediate directions. In the center of the wheel is the Lord of Wrath (Krodhendrarāja), who has two hands more than the Conquerors (Buddhas), possesses the speed of a thunderbolt, and has four faces. Therefore, whatever is desired should be accomplished by practitioners, provided it is conjoined with the Guru’s instructions. (23)
"'Vajrācārya, etc. does not exist, O Bhagavan.
The *māyājāla-tantra* [begins with] "O Bhagavān, Primordial Buddha," followed by "Śrīvajra," and so forth; [the rest] does not exist.
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, [Chapter] 13:
[Consecration] 14.
"In this context, first of all, the Vajrācārya must contemplate the protection of the places within his own body; afterwards, the disciples... 15.
One must perform the gathering of the poor and the acquisition of land and so forth.

Therefore, first the mantra-practitioner, having gone to the ground prepared for the mandala, sits in the center facing east upon a soft seat and performs the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) with the venerable vajras.
The placement (*nyāsa*) upon the forehead with the syllable *oṃ* on a white moon-maṇḍala; the placement upon the throat with the syllable *āḥ* on a red sun-maṇḍala. 18.
The placement upon the heart with the syllable *hūṃ* on a black Rāhu-maṇḍala; [the placement] upon the navel with the syllable *hoḥ* on a yellow-colored Kālāgni-maṇḍala. 19.

The placement (*nyāsa*): by means of the syllables *haṃ* and *kṣaḥ*, one performs the placement upon the crown of the head and the secret place respectively, within the green, blue, space-like, and gnosis mandalas.
Having thus meditated upon the six mandalas, within those mandalas there are vajras produced from these seed-syllables in their proper order. 21.

One should meditate upon [the following]: a needle with seventeen points, one with thirty-three points, one with nine points, one with sixty-five points, one with five points, and [again] one with thirty-three points.
Thus, externally, at the joint of the left shoulder and upper arm, there is a needle consisting of the *ka*-group with thirty-one points. 23.

Thus, at the right [shoulder], there is that which consists of the long *ka*-group; likewise, at the joint of the left upper arm, there is that which consists of the short *ca*-group, and at the right [upper arm], that which consists of the long [ca-group]; likewise, at the joint of the left hand, there is that which consists of the short *ṭa*-group, and at the right [hand], that which consists of the long [ṭa-group]; 25.

at the joint of the left thigh, there is that which consists of the short *pa*-group, and at the right [thigh], that which consists of the long [pa-group]; at the joint of the left knee, there is that which consists of the short *ta*-group, 26.

On the right [side] is that consisting of the long vowels; at the joint of the left foot is that consisting of the short *śa*-group, and on the right is that consisting of the long vowels. Thus [ends section] 27.
At the joint is the placement of the *vajra* (*vajranyāsa*).
Thus [ends section] 28.
Likewise, one should visualize sixty seven-pronged vajras upon each of the sixty finger-joints using the seed-syllables taught in the *Adhyātmapaṭala*.
Similarly, one should visualize a three-pronged vajra with the syllables *a* and *ā* on the two ears, and with *e* and *ai* on the two nostrils. 30.

With these two [syllables], *ā* and *ā*, [one places them] on the two eyes; with *o* and *o*, on the tongue and the uvula; with *al* and *āl*, on the vajra and the secret organ; and with *aṃ* and *aḥ*, on the channel of the mind and the semen.
Thus, on the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) and the head, one places a five-pronged [vajra] with *ha* and *hā*. Then, 32.

The tongue [is marked] with *ya* on the palate; by those two (*ya*s), the five [fingers] [are marked] on the palms of the hands; likewise, the two feet with *ra* and *va*; likewise, the anus, left and right, with *la* and *ba*.
In this way, one should meditate upon oneself as having a vajra-body.
Then, by the vajra-flames issuing forth from that [vajra], the entire host of Māras—who harass sentient beings—would be utterly consumed, even though they remain within the bamboo-like stalks. 35.
[He] would burn them away.
With green flames above, blue flames below, black flames in the east and southeast, red flames in the south and southwest, white flames in the north and northeast,
and yellow flames in the west and northwest— having thus burned the host of Māras, thereafter, within the ten-spoked wheel, [he visualizes them] gone in every direction and intermediate direction.
"One should meditate on the circle of wrathful deities" means that here,

according to the sequence to be explained, the mantra-practitioner should meditate on the protection wheel for the purpose of trampling upon Māras, obstacles, and Vināyakas, and for the purpose of protecting the site.

By Śaśin: "In the *Vimalaprabhā*, all [deities] are situated on the sun; or likewise, on the lunar day (*tithi*), all are situated on the moon according to the distinction between wealth and debt. Thus, by way of the division of the body, they are situated on the moon in the cardinal directions and on the sun in the intermediate directions; likewise, by way of the division of the internal state (*bhāva*), they are situated on the moon in the intermediate directions and on the sun in the cardinal directions. Likewise, in the west and south, they are situated on the solar seat; in the north and east, they are situated on the lunar seat—this is the rule according to the division of the solar and lunar [mandalas]. By that [rule], the mantra-practitioner should establish the host of wrathful deities; this is the rule. Thus, having emanated through the door of the right ear, one should place Sumbharāja, blue in color and produced from the long syllable *HĀ*, upon the sun on the surface of the vajra-ground. Likewise, having emanated Vighnāntaka, black in color and produced from the modified syllable (*vikāra*), through the door of the left nostril, one should place him on the lunar mandala on the eastern spoke, or on the sun. Likewise, having emanated Nīladaṇḍa, black in color and produced from the syllable *YĪ*, through the door of the right nostril, one should place him on the sun or the moon on the southeastern spoke. Having emanated Prajñāntaka, red in color and produced from the syllable *RA*, through the door of the left eye, one should place him on the lunar mandala on the southern spoke, or on the sun. Likewise, having emanated Ṭakkirāja, red in color and produced from the syllable *RŪ*, through the door of the right eye, one should place him on the sun or the moon on the southwestern spoke. Likewise, having emanated Padmāntaka, white in color and produced from the syllable *VŪ*, through the mouth of the tongue, one should place him on the moon or the sun in the north. Likewise, having emanated Acala, white in color and produced from the syllable *VŪK*, through the door of the urethra, one should place him on the sun or the moon on the northeastern spoke."
Likewise, having emanated yellow Yamāntaka, produced from the syllable *lḷ*, through the anus-door, one should place him upon the moon or the sun on the western spoke.

Similarly, having emanated yellow Mahābala, produced from the syllable *llū*, through the door of the Vajroṣṇīṣa, one should place him upon the sun or the moon on the northwest spoke. Now, according to the intention of the *Laghutantra*, all [deities] should be placed by the practitioner upon the solar mandalas;
such is the arrangement of the inner wheel (*garbhacakra*).
Then, outside the *kūṭa*, one should emanate the deities of the Brahma-realm (*brahmakāyika*) and so forth, as well as the earth-totality (*pṛthvī-kṛtsna*) and so forth.

Then, having visualized the peak-syllables *gha*, *jha*, *ḍha*, *bha*, *dha*, and *dhaḥ*, one should again emanate the ten guardians of the directions (*daśadikpāla*) within them.

Śukra and Bṛhaspati, produced from the bubble [of water], are situated in the north and northeast within the water-maṇḍala; Ketu and Śanaiścara, produced from the petals of the lotus, are to be visualized in the west and northwest within the earth-maṇḍala;
thus are the planetary guardians of the protection outside the enclosure.

Then, for the purpose of guarding the five walls, one should visualize the Naga kings; therein, upon the solar mandala, the syllables *kha*, *cha*, *ṭha*, *pha*, *tha*, and *tha* are to be visualized. From these, *Jaya* and *Vijaya*, produced from *kha* and *kha* respectively, are to be visualized as standing within the void mandala, with a width equal to the interior span of the five walls.

Thus, Karkoṭaka and Padma, produced from *chi* and *chī*, are situated on the wind-maṇḍala in the east and southeast; likewise, Vāsuki and Śaṅkhapāla, produced from *ṭha* and *ṭhū*, are situated on the fire-maṇḍala in the south and southwest; likewise, Ananta and Kulika, produced from *phu* and *phū*, are situated on the water-maṇḍala in the north and northeast; and Mahāpadma and Takṣaka, produced from *thlṛ* and *thlu*, are to be visualized on the earth-maṇḍala in the west and northwest. Then, outside the five enclosures, one should visualize the spirits (*bhūta*) and asuras for the sake of protection.

There, having visualized the *kacaṭapa* syllables upon the solar mandala, one should contemplate palatial mansions (*kūṭāgāra*) within them; in these, according to the measurement of the outer wall's width, one should visualize a Vetāḍa above and a Kumbhāṇḍa below—these two being produced from the syllable *ka* and situated in the mandala of emptiness. To the east, a Kiṃnara with the face of a dog, produced from the syllable *ca*, stands in the wind [quarter]. In the southeast, a Kiṃpuruṣa with the face of a crow, produced from the syllable *ṭa*, likewise [stands]; and a Gandharva with the face of a pig, produced from *ṭūṭū*, and a Bhūta with the face of a vulture, stand in the fire [quarter] to the south-southwest.

In the north-northeast, the Rākṣasa with a tiger’s face stands in water; the Preta with an owl’s face is produced from *pū-pū*; in the west-northwest, the Apasmāra with a jackal’s face stands on the ground and is produced from *skṛ-la*; and Garuḍa is indeed Garuḍa himself—this is the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*).
