Chapter on the Wheel or Lotus, titled "The Great Section on the Construction of the Mandala. Om. Also

The seats of the deities and so forth shall be three times that of the Lord; furthermore, in the Brahma-position, there shall be a row of pillars and vajras with twelve squares (arkakoṣṭha) and one square (śaśin).

The lotus of the Buddhas and others arises from four [squares], and the outer row of vajras arises from one square; between the goddesses and the Buddhas, there shall be a seat of a jar or a skull, consisting of three squares.
Regarding its essential nature, more has been stated by the two verses beginning with "forty-five" (*dvayabdhyekāndhyekasūryaiḥ*) and so forth; this is the fixed rule (*niyama*).
Therefore, whatever measurement is expressed by these half-finger-breadths and grid-squares is for the purpose of the teacher’s detailed exposition (*prapañca*).
Furthermore, that which was stated by means of divisions such as "two oceans" and so forth is for the sake of awakening the young disciples;
therefore, regarding those sūtras which are to be omitted, they are not to be applied— this is the rule in the alternative method.

Therefore, following the Root Tantra, the layout of the lines (*sūtrapāta*) is described as "the purification of the digit of the moon free from conceptual proliferation" (*niṣprapañcacandrakalāśuddhi*);
likewise, the Blessed One said: "Having made the ground square and even, [one should divide it] into sixteen parts."
Having abandoned the body-maṇḍalaka, it is again divided into sixteen parts.
One should first construct the mandala of speech and so forth, and then abandon the mandala of speech;
one should then construct the mandala of mind, divided again into sixteen parts.
Thus, having purified the mandala consisting of three qualities over three fortnights,
one should then lay out the lines for that threefold mandala using divisions of two, four, and so forth.
This rule regarding the laying of the lines (*sūtrapāta*) in the mandalas of body, speech, and mind was taught by the Blessed One in such sūtras;

therefore, the Vajrācārya must perform the laying of the lines according to the procedure stated in the Root Tantra, excluding those lines that are to be erased—this is the rule. Here too, in the case of a three-mandala structure measuring four cubits, the divisions are said to consist of twelve threads and half-finger-widths.
In that regard, among the sixteen divisions, each individual division is twelve and a half finger-breadths (*ardhāṅgula*).
Thus, in sixteen such divisions, there are one hundred and eighty finger-breadths;
therefore, first, the ground surface for the purpose of the mandala should be divided into sixteen parts.
Then, on the outside, having set aside four divisions in the four directions and having set aside eight divisions on both sides for the sake of the *vāṅmaṇḍala*,

one should divide that same eight-part section of the *vāṅmaṇḍala* into sixteen parts by placing a thread through the middle of each individual part; therein, the sixteen divisions shall be six and a half finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) each.

Furthermore, among those [parts], for the sake of the mandala of the mind, one should set aside four parts in the east, likewise in the west, and likewise in the north and south; then, in the remaining center, one should divide the eight parts into sixteen sections.

Having placed a thread within each individual section, sixteen [lines] are to be cast there—[as specified in various versions]: *ka*, *ga* read "in front" (*purataḥ*); *ka*, *kha* read "clod" (*loṣṭha*); *ga*, *ca*, *cha* read "three and five" (*tripañca*); *ga*, *ca*, *bho* omit "should be cast" (*pātitavyāni*); *cha* does not mention it; *ca* reads "section" (*bhāgaka*); *ca* reads "two" (*dvaya*); *ca*, *bho* lack the syllable "vi"; *ga* reads "ten fingers" (*daśāṅgu*); *ga* reads "division" (*vibhā*); *cha* reads "part" (*bhāgaṃ*); *ca* reads "then" (*tataḥ*); [the measurement is] sixteen half-fingers (*ṣoḍaśārghāṅgulāni*). In the west (*nub*) according to *bho*; in the left (*vāme*) according to *ga*, *ca*; in the north (*byan*) according to *bho*. In the Vimalaprabhā, in the section on the initiation, in the Mind Mandala (*cittamaṇḍala*), they are three and a half fingers.

Thus it is: by forty-eight *vasuyuga* units—that is, sixteen divisions consisting of three and a half finger-breadths (*tryardhāṅgula*) each—the Blessed One has stated that two parts to the left and right, and two parts to the front and back from the Brahma-thread, are for the purpose of measuring the four gates in the *cittamaṇḍala*. Likewise, four parts of three and a half finger-breadths each have been stated for the purpose of the gates of the *vāṅmaṇḍala*.
Likewise, it has been stated that eight parts of three and a half finger-breadths are for the purpose of the doors of the body-maṇḍala;
thus, in the mind, speech, and body maṇḍalas, the door consists of one-eighth of the wheel, according to the measurement of its respective wheel,
and the wheel, along with the enclosure wall and so forth, should be understood as being defined by its boundary.
It is likewise in the three spheres.

From that position, the stage-ground (raṅgabhūmi) extends for twelve squares; indeed, up to three lines in the cardinal and corner directions, there are sixteen lotuses for the scents and other offerings.

With one and a half [squares], it becomes three-lined; with six seasons (six squares), there are doors and gate-towers (niryūha); likewise on the side, there is a skull (kapāla) with three [squares], and the great altar (mahāvedikā) is half [of that].

In half of that [space], there is a jeweled band made of *naṣṭakāla* units; the door-area should have pillars and an archway (*toraṇa*). From the base of the door, one should exclude half a line multiplied by thirty (thirty units) at the top;
at the end of the half-necklace (*ardhahāra*), there is a *bakulī*. Below the archway, in six squares, there is a band for the Yoginīs, joined with eight lotuses.
From the Brahma-thread, one should drop two auspicious half-threads to the left and right, and to the east and west;
this is for the pericarp of the central lotus to serve as the seat for the Principal Deity, and for the deities at the four gates to have lotus seats.
Then, in the directions of north, south, east, and west, there are four half-finger-breadths each for the lotus petals, which constitute the "ocean."
The lotus of the central leader (nāyaka) is three times the size of the seats of the remaining deities and goddesses;

thus, in the place of Brahmā, by twelve half-finger-breadths (arkakoṣṭha), there is the lotus of the Blessed One. The rule is that the pericarp (kaṇikā), which is one part of the lotus, shall be four half-finger-breadths. Having laid a thread through the middle of the petals in the cardinal directions, the remainder—three and a half finger-breadths—is divided into two parts; by a division of two and a quarter finger-breadths, there are three lines in the inner mandala, and by the other [division], the side-petals (pakṣaka) are formed.
Then, outside the lotus petals, there is the location for the vajra-garland by means of one half-finger-width portion.

Then, with four half-finger-widths, there are the lotuses of the deities. Having laid down a thread through the center of the lotus, there are three and a half finger-widths together with the portion of the previous vajra-garland.

Having laid a thread through the midst of those [points], at the location of the cheeks: north, south, east, and west (*uttara-dakṣiṇaṃ pūrva-paścimam*). For the sake of the four gates (*caturdvārārtham*): here the *mātṛkā* is fragmentary; the shadow-copy is not beautiful. Everywhere, in place of "left" (*vāma*), [read] "north"; in place of "other" (*apara*), [read] "west"—[and thus] south. Half a finger (*ardhāṅgula*). *Bho. sor phyed*. (*Ardhāṅgulam*).
The height of the *sārghārgha* is three finger-breadths; thus,
O venerable one, it becomes three finger-breadths, being unprecedented (*apūrva*).

[In the *Kapālapaṭala*, verses 38–39: The great chapter entitled "The Drawing of the Maṇḍala" states that the enclosure walls, the ground, and the archway pillars exist with a division of one and a half [units] each. Then, outside the seat of the Buddha by half a finger-breadth, there is the outer vajra-garland; in the middle, within the courtyards of the Buddha and the goddesses, there are eight seats for either jars or skull-cups.
By a division of two and a half finger-breadths on the left and right, within the space between the sixteen pillars, the remainder is according to the measurement of the Buddha’s seat; then,

having set aside two parts of two and a half finger-breadths for the vajra-garland, one should drop a thread at half a finger-breadth, and from there, with four [parts], one should drop a thread for the purpose of the seats of the goddesses of fragrance and so forth, and the deities of the sense of smell and so forth.
Then, leaving half an *aṅgula* [of space], there are three walls (*prākāra*) measuring one and a half *aṅgulas* each; thus, the ground for the altar (*vedikā*) is double the ground for the walls,
the jeweled band (*ratnapaṭṭikā*) is half the height of the altar, and the ground for the necklaces (*hāra*) and half-necklaces (*ardhabhūmi*) is double that.

Half of the *hāra* ground is the *vakulī*, and likewise the *kavaśīrṣaka*; thus, the *niryūha* is equal to the *hāra*, the *pakṣaka* and the *kapola* are equal to the *niryūha*, and above the pillar, the *toraṇa* is three times the measure of the door.

Thus is the rule for laying the lines in the womb-maṇḍala (*garbhamaṇḍala*). Starting from "The *sūtra* indeed [is drawn] from the Brahma-line" up to "the *vakulī* arises at the end of the half-necklace" (3.39), the first laying of the lines is described. Furthermore, for the sake of the maṇḍala, another laying of both lines in the mind-maṇḍala (*cittamaṇḍala*) is taught, starting from "two, one, four, one" (3.54) up to "the archway (*toraṇa*) by the stated parts" (3.55). This is the rule regarding the mind-maṇḍala. Now, the characteristics of the archway as taught in the Root Tantra (*mūlatantra*) are stated.
In this context, the archway (toraṇa) is everywhere three times the measure of the door;
thus, in the mind-mandala (cittamaṇḍala), the door is six half-fingers (ardhāṅgula) wide, and the archway there is three times that, consisting of eighteen half-fingers.
One should construct that very [archway] as a triple city (tripura).
First, the *pura* is six half-fingers; the second is four and a half; the third is three and a half;
then the *harmya* is two, and the *kalaśa* is two.
Thus, with eighteen parts, there is the triple city and the archway (*toraṇa*).
Therein, in the first city, upon the pillar, a fillet (*paṭṭikā*) measuring half a finger-breadth in width and twenty-four finger-breadths in length;
above that, a *mattavāraṇa* measuring half a finger-breadth in width and eight finger-breadths in length.
Above that, according to the measurement of the *garbhakaṇikā*, there is a square in the center which is the place for the worship-deities (*pūjādevī*);

to its right and left, at a distance of half a finger-breadth, are two pillars; and to the right and left of those two pillars are the places for the deities, followed again by pillars to the right and left.
On the left and right sides of those two, above the gateway pillars, one should display a pair of lions treading upon elephants;
above their heads, by means of a half-portion of the lower fillet, there is a fillet extending over the four pillars with a length of eighteen half-fingers.
Above that is a *mattavāraṇa* (drunken-elephant motif) as in the base, with a length of twelve half-fingers.

Above that, by a division of three and a quarter *aṅgulas* for each pillar, one should fashion three positions for deities or marks at intervals of three and a half *aṅgulas* between each pillar; on the left and right of the two outer pillars, one should place *śālabhañjikā* figures.
Above their heads—and again above the four pillars—one should fashion a frieze (*paṭṭikā*) with a width of half an *aṅgula* and a length of fifteen and a half *aṅgulas*.

Above that, one should construct a *mattavāraṇa* (elephant-head ornament) as before, measuring half a finger-breadth in height and eight finger-breadths in length; above that, one should fashion individual pillars according to a division of half of a quarter-finger-breadth each,
with no gaps between the pillars.

In the side-lobes (*kakṣe*), [the syllables] *svasvā* [are placed], O Venerable One. In the compartments (*koṣṭheṣu*), the half-[units] of the *alyās* are not present as the "jewel-strip" (*ratnapaṭṭikā*).
[Then follow] the necklaces (*hāra*) and half-necklaces (*ardhahāra*).
At the first city-gate, the location for the goddess is one and a half finger-breadths (tyarghāṅgulā). The *sāla* [structure] is half a cubit (*kādyardha-hasta*).

Within that, there are three locations divided according to half the space occupied by the deities of the main city. There, to the right and left of the outer pillars, one should again fashion a *śālabhañjikā* (carved female figure).
Above that, the frieze (*paṭṭikā*) is six finger-breadths (dvādaśārdhāṅgulā) in height.
Above that, a harmikā measuring four and a half finger-breadths in length;
above that, by means of two [units], the kalaśa on the left and right, which is the location for the flagpole (*dhvajadaṇḍa*).

Thus, at the tip of each beam (*paṭṭikā*), there are hanging chowries, a mirror, and a banner; such is the characteristic measurement of the archway (*toraṇa*) as taught in the Root Tantra. Now, the mandala of speech (*vāṅmaṇḍala*) is described: "Below the archway, in six compartments, there is a beam joined with eight lotuses, belonging to the yoginīs."

In this speech-mandala (*vāṅmaṇḍala*), there are four divisions in the four directions, each measuring six and a half finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Of these, by means of two parts, the enclosure wall, the altar (*vedikā*), the jewel-band (*ratnapaṭṭikā*), the *hāra*, the *ardhahāra*, the *vakulī*, and the *kramaśīrṣas* of the inner mandala are formed. Two parts remain;

setting aside one of those parts, in the remaining six compartments, excluding one compartment each at the bottom and top, there is a lotus-band for the eight Yoginīs in the center consisting of four parts, and lotuses in all directions and corners.

Beneath the archway, in the cardinal directions of the second enclosure, one should break the *mattavāraṇa* pillars by a measure of four half-finger-breadths (*ardhāṅgula*) and fashion lotuses for the Yoginīs;
having removed the pair of pillars by a measure of half a half-finger-breadth (*ardhāṅgulārdha*),
if there are no deities (*devatī*), one should again follow the previously mentioned characteristics.

By that same characteristic, everything in the external *vāṅmaṇḍala* becomes double [in size], starting from the gates up to the arches (*toraṇa*); this is the rule. (38–39) Now the *kāyamaṇḍala* is described: From that [center], on the ground of Śrīraṅga, using [the measurement] multiplied by six and doubled [by two], one should indeed draw five lines; in the cardinal and intermediate directions, one should fashion a twelve-petaled lotus with twice as many petals, using twelve solar squares. The inner gate should be doubled, and the outer gate here also [should be doubled] according to the power of the threefold qualities; likewise, one should fashion the arrangement of the three enclosures and the twenty-four spokes.
From the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) onwards:

here, within the body-mandala (*kāyamaṇḍala*), regarding those four sections in the four directions that consist of twelve half-finger-breadths (*ardhāṅgula*) each, two of those sections—namely the wall, the altar-platform (*vedikā*), the jeweled band (*ratnapaṭṭikā*), the necklace (*hāra*), the half-necklace (*ardhahāra*), the *vakulī*, and the arches (*kramaśīrṣa*) of the speech-mandala (*vāṅmaṇḍala*)—have fallen [into place]. Two remaining sections stay [empty];
therefore, from the end of that speech-mandala, the ground of the glorious courtyard (*śrīraṅgabhūmi*) is measured by "twos multiplied by six" (*rasaguṇitayugaiḥ*).
The rule is that there are five lines consisting of twenty-four half-finger-breadths (ardhāṅgula) each.
In the cardinal and intermediate directions of that mandala, there is the "sun-lotus," meaning twelve lotuses; "twice the number of petals" means twenty-eight petals.
"By twelve solar squares," meaning by parts of six finger-breadths each;
having divided those twelve half-finger-breadths into seven sections, one makes the pericarp with the middle section, the second [petal] with the right and left sections,
the third with the right and left sections, and the fourth with the right section.
ca. cha. kava ga. multiplied by ca. 'hāra' ca. cha. kava.
ga ca. 0 śatyardhāṅgu0 cha. There is no [word] in maṇḍaleṣu in ka. kha. cha. 0 dalām.

In the chapter [on the mandala], the great section titled "The Drawing of the Mandala," verses [concerning] the eight petals. (Note: Variants *vahulī*, *viśad*, and *'vi'* appear in manuscripts ka, kha, cha, and ga respectively.)
One should fashion sixteen petals by moving four times to the right and left;
thus one should make twenty-eight petals.
In this way, the door of the womb [is formed] through the influence of the quality of darkness (tamas).

Therefore, the door of the middle mandala is double [the size] due to the influence of the quality of *rajas*; from that, the door of the body mandala is fourfold due to the influence of the quality of *sattva*.

In this way, one should construct the enclosure walls and so forth, the archways and so forth, the arrangement of the three circles, and the arrangement of the circles of water, fire, and air, using twenty-four [units] consisting of three times eight.

At the beginning and end of those, one should construct the circles of the sun and moon and the outer vajra-fence; within the squares below that, in the circle of air and at the edge of the mandala, one should place the wheel.

Below the pillar, the mandala of the serpents arises, as well as that of the goddesses; with the suns, there is a door in the middle of the sky, on the surface of the earth, in the eastern part and the western part.
[41] At the beginning of those three circles, one should draw the circle of the rising of the sun and moon using twelve solar squares;
at their end, one should draw a row of petals using twelve [squares].
Regarding the statement "by twenty-four [spokes] it is filled," therein, the wheel at the end of the door is an eight-spoked one each within the enclosures of wind and fire; by twelve [spokes],
there is the seat for the hooded serpents upon the altar of the outer mandala pillars, which is the wind and other mandalas consisting of twelve.
In the middle of the door, one should fashion a *syandana* (arched pediment) with twelve [units];

right there, in the speech-maṇḍala (*vāṅmaṇḍala*), having excluded twelve finger-breadths, one should make a *syandana* on the second half of the door, equal to the bands for the deities such as Indra, excluding the *toraṇa-kalaśa* (arch-pitcher) at the front and back; in the body-maṇḍala (*kāyamaṇḍala*), one should display the chariot of the sky and the underworld (*ākāśapātālaratha*).
Thus ends the rule for drawing the lines of the mandala.

Now he describes the procedure for casting the colored powders (rajas): "O King, the casting of powders occurs on the colored ground in the various directions using the five jewels beginning with diamond (vajra), or gold, coral, emerald, and pearl; or likewise with grains, or with many kinds of gems ground into colors. According to the divisions of the Buddhas, [the colors] are yellow, white, red, and so forth, in sequence upon the circles of earth and water, and fire and wind."
42. By the words "with the vajra and so forth" and so on,

it is meant that once the laying of the lines (*sūtrapāta*) has been performed here and the site for all the deities has been purified, one should then offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and afterwards begin the application of the colors (*raṅgapāta*).
In that regard, five colors should be prepared according to one's wealth.
If one possesses the wealth of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), one should have powder made from the five jewels, such as the vajra and so forth:
therein, emerald provides the green powder; sapphire provides the black; ruby provides the red; moonstone provides the white; karketana provides the yellow; and mahānīla provides the blue.
In these [verses],
there are twenty-eight [syllables] in the *ga* and *ca* [pādas].
Ga. "The walls" thus, O Bhagavan; and by the division of three times eight (tryaṣṭaka).
O. Half (ardha). Ga. Ca. Maṇḍala.
Ga. Ca. O. Twelve arghāṅgulas.
ga. omits "maṇḍala"; ka. reads "māharet" instead of "āharet".
ka. kha. cha. read "vibhāve";
ga. reads "varṇam"; ga. ca. read "śuklam".

[From the Vimalaprabhā, Abhiṣeka-paṭala]: Likewise, for an ordinary universal monarch (cakravartin), gold powder is yellow, pearl powder is white, coral powder is red, lapis lazuli powder is black, and green is a mixture of four ingredients.
Or with five kinds of grain, such as mung beans and the like, or with unbroken rice; or with various kinds of jewels, powders, and dyes, or with flour and ghee—this is common to all sentient beings.
Just as it is with words, so it is with unbroken grains.
Just as with powders of emerald and so forth, or likewise with ground pigments,

O King, the scattering of colored dust occurs upon the ground of the various directions according to one's wealth; in that very same way, it is done in the maṇḍala by means of the various Buddhas who will be described.
Furthermore, on the outer circle of earth it is yellow, on water white, on fire red, and on the circle of wind black, in that order. // 42 //

Now the description of the colors of the dust-particles (*rajobhūmi*) is stated: in the east there is the glorious black ground; in the south it resembles the sun; in the west it has the luster of gold; and in the north, another is white like the moon.

According to the divisions of the faces of the Wielder of the Thunderbolt (Indra), the ground for the bands and necklaces is arranged in sequence as white, black, and red. The lotuses have the colors of the moon and the sun; and the three lines are stainless like the moon, red, and black.

By the words "east" and so forth, the division of directions in the mandala occurs on the ground according to the presiding deity, the insignia, and the face; by means of the black face and so forth, the glorious black earth appears in the east through the purification of the mind (*citta-viśuddhi*); in the south, it is like the sun through the purification of speech (*vāk-viśuddhi*); in the west, it is golden-hued and yellow through the purification of the wisdom face (*jñāna-vaktra-viśuddhi*); and in the north, the other [earth] is white through the purification of the body face (*kāya-vaktra-viśuddhi*).
In this way, the casting of the powder (*rajaḥpātana*) for the various faces of the Vajrin should be performed;

and having cast it in the directions starting from the northeast (*aiśānī*) with white color and so forth according to the ritual action (*karma*), it is then to be cast according to the division of the faces—this is the rule.
Now, he states the colors of the powder for the altar (*vedikā*) and other parts, beginning with the word "white" (*śveta*).

Here, the altar (*vedikā*) is white, and its supporting band (*paṭṭikā*) is red; above that is a jeweled band (*ratnapaṭṭikā*), and upon it the ground is variegated with jewel-inlays. At the joints of the projecting supports and pillars, there is an inlay of jewels.
Likewise, the ground for the necklaces (*hārabhūmi*) is black, whereon are full necklaces, half-necklaces, mirrors, and chowries.
The *vakulī* is white, and the pillars are yellow.

The white stepped-pyramids (kramaśīrṣa) are the lotuses of the deities, having the color of the moon and the color of the sun; just as in the entire central mandala, through the purity of body, speech, and mind, there are white, red, and black lines for the enclosures (prākāra). Thus [ends verse] 43.

He describes the description of the womb-lotus and so forth: In the center is an eight-petaled lotus, and there should be a green vajra-fence surrounding the pillar. In the directions of Īśāna, Nairṛtya, Agni, and Vāyu, there are [deities] with the forms of the moon and sun, black and yellow respectively.
(The syllables *kha*, *ca*, *raṅga*, and *cha* do not exist.)
ga. ca. by parts; cha. in the part; ca. does not exist; cha. does not exist.
ka. kha. cha, it does not exist; ka kha. ca. kava ca. maṇḍala.

And so, the great chapter titled "The Turning of the Viśu Mandala": Śaṅkha, Gaṇḍī, and Maṇi are the sequence; likewise, at the junction of the eight white pitchers, the Moon arises upon the red lotus, and the Sun above the white lotus. //44//
With the words "In the center," and so forth,

here in the center of the mind-maṇḍala, the lotus of the presiding deity is green and eight-petaled; in rites such as pacification (śāntika) and others, it becomes white in color and so on, but generally it is green, and there should be a row of vajras resembling bees for the purpose of immobilization (stambhana).
Outside the lotus are sixteen pillars, starting from the east, each set of four being adorned with a row of swords, jewels, wheels, and lotuses.

Here, in the four corners of the inner lotus, there are respectively: in the northeast, a conch of moon-like color; in the southwest, the Dharma-gong of sun-like color; in the southeast, a wish-fulfilling gem of black color; and in the northwest, a kalpa-tree of non-yellow (green) color.
Thus, in the sixteen intervals between the pillars in the four directions, there are white jars for the Buddha-deities;
situated upon lotuses in the eight directions, they have lotus-faces. //44//
On the red lotuses of the goddesses, there is a moon as a seat in the pericarp; on the white lotus in the pericarp, there is a sun for the deities.

In the outer directions, there should be a garland of vajras. According to the division of the pervasive lotuses, the altar is white in color, with yellow pillars and a railing (bakulī) with the luster of snow. The archway (toraṇa) is of universal colors.
In this context, for the goddesses there is a moon-seat upon a red lotus; for the deities, there is a sun-seat upon the head of a white lotus;
and even the moon-seats are located within the pericarp, excluding the eight petals, which constitute one-third of the lotus.
In the corners of the goddesses' [mandala] and in the directions of the deities, there should be a row of forests on the outermost perimeter;

it should be made according to the colors of the various lotuses, and the archway (toraṇa) should be made of universal color (viśvavarṇa). This is the rule for the application of colors in the primary mandala. // 45 //

Now he describes the colors of the speech and body maṇḍala deities, the friezes, and so forth: The frieze of the eight lotuses for the Yoginīs is white in all directions; by the power of the Jina, there is a red lotus in the cardinal directions and a white lotus in the corners.

It is devoid of the moon and sun, and likewise, the chowries have twice as many petals. Furthermore, those five lines which are to be eaten (the food offerings) are situated at intervals of one-third, according to the qualities of nature. //46//
Regarding "white-light" (*śvetābhā*):

here, in the speech-maṇḍala, it refers to the yoginīs such as Icchā and the others; in the body-maṇḍala, it is the white-light band (*paṭṭikā*). Furthermore, the eight-petal lotus support-band exists in all cardinal and intermediate directions.
In that direction, there are red-colored lotuses by the power of the Jina— that is, by the power of the Buddha— and a white lotus in the corner;
these are eight-petaled lotuses devoid of moon and sun seats.
Likewise, for the immortals, the strength of the breath is doubled; [there is] a lotus of twenty-eight petals, devoid of the moon and sun.
In the circle of speech (vāṅmaṇḍala), the five lines beginning with *kha* arise by the power of the qualities of nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*); *kha*, *pīta*, *ka*, *kha*, *cha*, and *vṛkṣa*.
ga. There is none;
ka. kha. cha. ca. Eight; ga.
Twenty petals.
ka. kha. 0tāṅga; ga.
shevetā bhavati
O, there are no such [elements] situated within those three parts;
here, in this mandala of speech, the nature is the flow of the mandalas beginning with space.

Therefore, in rites such as pacification (*śānti*) or subjugation (*vaśya*), by means of the leftward movement (*vāmasaṃcāra*) and the yoga of emanation (*sṛṣṭiyoga*), space, air, fire, water, and earth—possessing green, black, red, white, and yellow colors respectively—should be arranged in sequence starting from the womb up to the altar (*vedikā*).
Thus, in rites such as killing (*māraṇa*) or immobilization (*stambhana*), earth and the other elements are to be employed;
they arise according to the power of their inherent qualities (*prakṛtiguṇa*).
Having set aside one part, each individual line is formed by two parts;
therefore, the ground for the enclosure wall should be known as consisting of fifteen parts.
Thus, the ground for the enclosure wall of the inner maṇḍala consists of nine divisions.
Likewise, the nature (*prakṛti*) of the body-maṇḍala is stated: here, in this body, the nature of the five fingers beginning with the little finger is space and so forth.
Therefore, in the peaceful and increasing rites, the lines of the maṇḍala are green and so on according to the division of emanation;
whereas in rites such as killing, they are according to the division of earth by way of the sequence of withdrawal. This is the rule for the lines of the enclosure wall. //46//

Now the seats of the Naga kings are described: at the base of the pillars and at the junctions of the doors, there arises the seat of the hooded serpents, beginning with Māruta (the Wind). In the northeast and in the corner of the Daityas (the southwest), O King, the Moon and Sun are situated upon the circle of the earth;

likewise, there should be the Dharma-wheel, dark as a cloud, together with a deer. Above the outer portion of the door on the right side, there should be a red pot; and in the direction of Kubera (the north) and Varuṇa (the west), there should be a drum and the Bodhi tree. //47//

By the words "below the pillar" and so forth, here in the outer body-maṇḍala, at the location of the pedestal beneath the archway-pillars, at the junction of the door, there arises the seat of the serpents; for the eastern gate, on the right and left, there is the circular wind-maṇḍala, and in the interior, according to the measurement of the lotus, there is the triangular fire-maṇḍala on the south.

From the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it follows that in the west is the square earth-maṇḍala; in the north is the water-maṇḍala, shaped like a half-moon. These are black, red, yellow, and white respectively, marked with the signs of a drop (*bindu*), a svastika, a vajra, and a lotus.
Thus, the gates and so forth are black, red, yellow, white, green, and blue;
the chariots and the cremation-ground wheels have the colors of the moon and the sun, as he will state: "The wheel is white and red" (3.48).
Thus, by way of distinguishing the colors of the Tathāgatas, the ground is everywhere made of dust;
now, the place where the moon and sun rise is described.

Here, at the end of the archway of the body-maṇḍala, there is a yellow-colored earth-circle constructed with twelve half-fingers' breadth; therein, in the northeast, one should show the rising of the moon according to the night.
On the full moon day, likewise,
one should show the setting of the sun in the corner of the Daityas, that is, in the southwest (nairṛtya).
In this manner, the moon and the sun come to be situated upon the circle of the earth.
O King!
Then, on the outer perimeter of the body-mandala, in the upper portion above the gate, at the first city, [there is] the *ka* and *kha* of the archway (*toraṇa*).
6. Ga.
beginning with Rākā; Ga.
in sequence.
ga. ca. bho vibhāgikā; ka. kha. ga. ca. mitāmikā, cha. vitāmikā; ga. ardhavṛtta.
ga. Of lotuses;
nāsti (is not present); ca. Earth.
ga. and ca. do not have it;
ca., ka., and kha. read *spandanā*; cha. reads *0ṅgulī*.
[In the] *pūrṇā* [vase].
The Great Chapter entitled "The Drawing of the Mandala": In the central location, measuring sixteen half-fingers, there should also be a Dharma-wheel with the luster of a cloud;
due to the purification of the Citta-cakra, on the right and left of the wheel are the deer and the doe.
Then, in the other location, the deities of worship are according to their respective colors.
Thus, at the southern archway (*toraṇa*), there is a yellow-colored *bhadraghaṭa* (auspicious jar) through the purification of speech; to its left and right are a conch and a lotus.
[In the directions] of Kubera and Varuṇa, there is a drum and a wheel in the presence of Kubera; [the two] are white, with a staff and a mallet to the left and right.
In the west is the Bodhi tree, yellow; on the right and left are the Kinnaras and Kinnarīs—this is the rule. || 47 ||
Bells, mirrors, and banners white as the moon, as well as hanging arches and necklaces, are white in color according to the family; the chariot in the middle of the gate is likewise.
The wheel is white and red according to the family of its own Jina; O King, at the outer gate of the wind [quarter], there is an external vajra-fence shimmering with vajra-flames. (48)

Likewise, there are bells, mirrors, and banners as white as the moon; hanging arches (*toraṇa*) and necklaces (*hāra*) and half-necklaces (*ardhahāra*) are white in color according to the [specific] family (*kula*). In the middle of the gate, the chariot is white or red according to the family of its respective Victor (*jinakula*). O King, at the exterior of the gate in the northwest direction, there is the outer vajra-fence (*vajrāvalī*), which consists of flickering flames. Here, having placed a *ghuṇaka* (corner-stone) at the beginning and end of the vajra-fence, one should display outside of that a flame consisting of five rays of light.
Then follows the completion of the mandala.

One should arrange the articles of worship between the perimeter of the earth and the summit according to their aesthetic beauty; such is the rule for the colors of the powder in the mandala. || 48 ||

Now he describes the specific defects of the lines of the enclosure wall: "A thick line causes disease; a thin line reveals the loss of wealth; a crooked line indicates death; and likewise, a broken line brings about the expulsion of the king and the people. When the marks of the sun and moon are broken, there is no success for ministers, as it destroys the fear of worldly existence. A mixture of dust colors in the maṇḍala of the Jina family should be understood as the destruction of one's lineage. (49)
Regarding the passage beginning with "sthūla" (thick), etc.:
here, in the rites of pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*), when the line becomes irregular, then there is a reversal of the ritual result.
In that case, a thick line causes disease; a thin line reveals the loss of wealth for either the donor or the preceptor (*ācārya*); and a crooked line [indicates misfortune].
When severed, it reveals death;
likewise, when crooked, it effects the eradication of the entire region.
When the mark is severed, or when the seat of the moon and sun is severed, that accomplishment which destroys the fear of worldly existence no longer exists for the practitioners of mantra.

When the lines are mutually mixed with dust, there is a severance of the lineage within the family of the donor; this is stated in such passages as "it is gross," and so forth, as well as in the inversion of the sentence. Furthermore, that which is curved causes the expulsion of the king, while a bad line [causes] misfortune.
"In that very same way": when the sign (*cihna*) is severed, it reveals death.
This is stated in the *Vimalaprabhā* regarding the lineage of the Moon and Sun (*candrārka*), as well as the lineage of the *Abhiṣeka-ācārya*.
"By that, the entire procedure for the dust [mandala] in the Jina-family mandala should be understood with diligence"—this is the rule.
Now, the characteristics of the symbols are described: here, the wheel (*cakra*) is of two kinds; one is the assembly of deities, and the other is the eight-spoked form of the support.
Among these, the eight-spoked [wheel] is white at the corners and red in the cardinal directions.
It has the form of an aggregate.
Furthermore, by virtue of their respective Buddha-family, the color of the goddesses is according to the color of their respective Buddhas; this is the meaning. || 49 ||

That symbol which was not explicitly taught in the middle of the Tantra, even if it appears clearly in the Jina Maṇḍala for the sake of beauty, must not be given in the family of the Father of the Jinas; that very thing is the symbol of Māra.

Therefore, the symbol as taught in the Tantra should be placed in the maṇḍala according to the respective families, from the boundary of the gates to the end of the half-necklace (ardhahāra); one should create the beauty of the lotus, vase, and so forth, situated upon the circle of the earth.
Regarding the phrase "that which is not":

here, in the Mantra system, whatever symbol (*cihna*) is not explicitly mentioned in a tantra by the Victors, the Tathāgatas, even if it is clearly [known], that symbol must not be placed in the mandala for the sake of ornamentation. Why? Because it becomes a symbol of Māra, due to its excessive nature resulting from perversion (*viparyāsa*).
"In the family of the progenitor of the Jinas, in the family of Vajrasattva, [this belongs] to the Vajrācārya.
Therefore, there is a sign according to the procedure taught in the Tantra.
By virtue of the family, it is at the southern gate of the mandala.
"One should perform [the decoration] at the end of the *hāra* and the *argha*"—this is the rule.

By way of indicating the *ardha-hāra*, one should create the beauty of the lotus and the jar upon the ground-circle (*kṣitivalaya*) at the end of the *vakulī*, the end of the *kramaśīrṣa*, and the end of the body-maṇḍala (*kāyamaṇḍala*). || 50 ||

Now the elevation of the dust is described: From the black [layer] onwards, the elevation of the dust increases by one-quarter (pāda) at each step; from one barley-corn (yava), the lines of the ramparts are tripled, and those of the sun and moon are doubled.

Outside the womb [of the city], O Lord of Men, in this mandala of elevations, the elevation becomes double; at the end of the necklaces, there is one barley-corn in the layers of earth, water, fire, air, and diamond.

By the phrase "of black, etc. and so forth: here, in the central mandala, due to the differentiation of qualities such as air (vāyu) and the rest, there is a downward fall of the *rajas* through an increase of one quarter (*pāda*) and so on.

The height of the black *rajas* is one quarter of a barleycorn (*yava*). Due to the purification of the single quality of touch (*sparśa*), the red [rajas] has two quarters; due to the purification of the two qualities of touch and form (*rūpa*), the white [rajas] in the south has three quarters; due to the purification of the three qualities of touch, form, and taste (*rasa*), the yellow [rajas] in the north [has four quarters]; and due to the purification of the four qualities of touch, form, taste, and smell (*gandha*), the height in the west is four quarters.
Thus, the rule for elevation is that it is double in the speech-mandala and fourfold in the body-mandala.
A barley-corn (*yava*) should also be understood as being one part out of seven hundred and sixty-eight of its respective mandala.
Thus ends the great section titled "The Drawing of the Mandala" from the [Prakaraṇa-]paṭala, verse [number]. The elevation of the walls is tripled, which is the elevation of the yellow powder.
Any other common line for the yellow dust becomes double [the previous].
Outside the petals of the lotuses, for the bands of the lotus-throne, the rule is that the lines of the sun and moon are doubled; or else, from the center, they are doubled in the central mandala.

That is doubled again in this body-mandala, ending with the pearl necklace (hāra) at the edge of the sages' area; there is one barley-corn (yava) at the end of the gradual peak, on the outside in the ground of worship.

Thus, the rule for the elevation of the dust-particles in the circles of earth, water, fire, and air, as well as in the vajra-enclosures and the two Ghuṇaka-sections, according to the measurement of the walls of the body-maṇḍala, is determined by the differentiation of the qualities of the elements; furthermore, the falling of the other dust-particles is uniform everywhere across all levels through the threefold differentiation, such that the threefold measure of the three walls applies to all grounds—this is the purification of the dust-particles. || 51 ||

Now, the purification of the dust mandala through the purification of the world-system (*lokadhātu*) is described: In the mandala of the world-system, from the center to the boundary of the gates and so forth, there is the earth; from the gates to the edge of the *cañcā*, there should be the ocean of salt and the abode of jewels in the triple city of the serpents (*phaṇipura*).

Beyond that, by means of the squares of the Jaina lords (*jainendra*), there should likewise be the circle of fire and wind; outside of that, for the sake of its purification, the earth, water, fire, and wind are to be visualized. (52)
By the words "the womb-sun" and so forth:
as it is here externally, so it is in the body;
as it is in the body, so it is in the other, the *rajo-maṇḍala*.
Therefore, whatever the measurement of the world-system is—four hundred thousand *yojanas*—that corresponds to four cubits (*hasta*) in the body.
Likewise, in the mandala as well, it ranges from one cubit up to a thousand cubits;
for every [mandala] is four cubits according to one's own cubit, because it is divided into units consisting of ninety-six times two and a half finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).

Therefore, the entire maṇḍala consists of four cubits (hasta). By that [measure], from the center to the edge of the doors and so forth, there is the Earth (Vasumatī) extending in all directions up to the gates by twenty-four half-aṅgulas from the Brahma-thread.

Therein, the central lotus is twelve half-aṅgulas; the Tathāgata-layer, according to the measure of fifty thousand yojanas, extends in all directions to the six continents, six oceans, and six mountains, and from top to bottom it is fifty thousand yojanas according to the measure of Mount Meru.
Then, the circle of the earth is twenty-five thousand *yojanas* everywhere;
within the mandala, this extends from the ground of dust up to the gateway.
Thus, the entire central mandala is one hundred thousand *yojanas*.
The rule is that it consists of forty-eight and a half finger-widths (*aṅgula*) divisions.
Thus, from the center to the boundary of the gates and so forth, there is the earth-maṇṇḍala of the world-system (*lokadhātu*).

Likewise, from the four gates in the four directions, extending as far as Cakrikā, there is the ocean of salt-water and the circle of salt-water, with twenty-four half-finger-widths in each of the four directions within the city of the triple-folded serpent. In this way, the maṇḍala of speech (*vāṅmaṇḍala*) becomes two hundred thousand [yojanas] in all directions.
The rule is that it extends from the east up to the *parārdha*.

Therefore, from the gateway of the *vāṅmaṇḍala*, the circle of fire (*śikhivalaya*)—which ends at the summit of the *vāṅmaṇḍala*—is formed in all directions by twenty-four half-finger-breadths (*ardhāṅgula*) using the squares of the Lord of Jinas (*jinendra*) multiplied by three times the cities of the serpents (*phaṇipurai*).
From that location, [it extends] east and west.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, the rule is that the world-system (*lokadhātu*) consists of three hundred thousand *yojanas*.
Thus, from that [central point], there would be wind;

therefore, by means of twenty-four half-fingers (using the *Jainendra* lexicon's measurement), starting from the "head" [of the central square] and extending in all directions to the edge of the gates of the body-maṇḍala, is the wind-circle of the world-system.

Thus, the mandala of the world-system, measuring four hundred thousand [yojanas] from east to west, is divided externally into ninety-six double portions; this is the rule for the body-mandala (*kāyamaṇḍala*).

Furthermore, outside that, at the conclusion of the archways of the body-mandala, according to their respective purifications—specifically the purification of the earth-circle and so forth—one should visualize the earth-circle as twelve half-fingers (half-aṅgulas) excluding Meru, while the remaining circles are each twenty-four half-fingers.

Then, outside of that, having divided the area into three parts on the right and left by means of twelve *vajra*-fences, a *vajra*-fence should be made in the middle with six parts; outside of that, a *vajra*-flame with twenty-four [parts]. This is the rule for the purification of the world-system (*lokadhātu*).
Now, the purification of the upper and lower [realms] is described:

The *uṣṇīṣa*, the face, and the throat are to be purified in the mandala of the threefold city of the serpent (*phaṇipura*). From there, Mount Meru, along with all [the realms], up to the earth consisting of the six times six squares in sequence—the manifest world of the serpents and the seven netherworlds (*pātāla*)—likewise, everything beginning with the earth must again be purified within one's own body.

Successively, by means of two oceans, one ocean, one sun, six seasons, six tastes, and the peaks [seven], and by half-fires [three] and half-time [one and a half], and by time divided by time, by seasons, and also by tastes as portions of the humors;

from the center [the navel] comes the pericarp, then the lotus petals, then the stalk, the vajra-garland, and the lotus, and then the vajra-garland, and then the earth, and then the gates, turrets, and so forth.

O King, the pillars, the enclosure wall, the altar, and again the frieze, the ground for the hanging garlands, the earth, and the fillet are formed by the aforementioned proportions. The archway is declared by these same parts.

Everything outside, such as the doors and so forth, should be double; and that should be doubled again at each successive outer layer. There are lotuses and wheels, and the chariot of the Sun-god, as well as the mandalas.

With the words "the *uṣṇīṣa*" and so forth, here on the external Meru, the *uṣṇīṣa* is twenty-five thousand [yojanas], divided into twelve half-finger-breadths (*ardhāṅgula*); in the center is the womb-lotus (*garbhapadma*), which is of that same division;
from there, the face (*vaktra*) is fifty thousand [yojanas] and the throat (*kaṇṭha*) is twenty-five thousand.
Within those [sections], in the first part is the wheel of the Buddha; in the second, for the sake of the face, is the other wheel consisting of twenty-five thousand [yojanas];
and in the remaining two parts is the ground of dust up to the doors.
Thus, from top to bottom, the mandala of the world-system extends for one hundred thousand yojanas up to the throat.

ga. The first major section (mahoddeśa) titled "The Drawing of the Mandala," [verse]: "On all sides" is the rule for the inner mandala;
likewise, the crown, face, and throat, along with the three-fold serpent, are to be purified in the right and left [channels] within the city-mandala—this is the rule.
Therefore, the entire Meru from the throat to the waist measures one hundred thousand yojanas;
it should be purified on the right and left sides by means of twenty-four and a half finger-breadths [each], multiplied three times by the cities of the serpents above and below.
Regarding the characteristic of the mandala, according to the *Medinī* lexicon, it extends downward as far as the earth; therefore,
by means of six sets of six compartments, each consisting of twenty-five thousand *yojanas* and divided into six parts, [the total] is two hundred thousand [yojanas].

Having clearly divided the world of the serpents (ahibhuvana) into eight parts, including the seven netherworlds (pātāla) and the realm of hells, each should be purified within the body by dividing it into eight parts starting from the waist down to the soles of the feet; this should likewise be purified within the colored powder mandala (raja-maṇḍala).
The rule is that [the purification] extends from the Brahma-sthāna to the end of the body-maṇḍala, reaching as far as the four gates in all directions.

In this way, everything beginning with the ground must be purified once again; furthermore, this applies to all beings, such as humans and others, within one's own body. This is the rule for the procedure of the maṇḍala.
Likewise, another purification taught in the Root Tantra is described here:
the gnosis residing within the hearts of all sentient beings is the unstruck sound (*anāhata-dhvani*), which is eternally characterized by resonance (*nāda*).
Having placed that maṇḍala in the center, it is the heart-wheel (*hṛdaya-cakra*).
Then, taking half the measure from the middle of the throat and the navel, one should form the mind-mandala (*cittamaṇḍala*) of the Blessed One consisting of twelve and a half measures;
one should form the speech-mandala (*vāṅmaṇḍala*) from the throat to the end of the navel consisting of twenty-five measures;
and one should form the body-mandala (*kāyamaṇḍala*) from the location of the *ūrṇā* (the hair-treasure) to the marrow consisting of fifty measures.

Then, there are the four doors of the body: the apertures of feces, urine, semen, and the *uṣṇīṣa*. The doors of the speech-maṇḍala are *lalanā*, *rasanā*, *avadhūtī*, and *śaṅkhinī*, extending from the throat to the limit of the navel.
The doors of the mind-maṇḍala are characterized by the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (*turyā*).
Thus, the maṇḍala of body, speech, and mind consists of twelve doors; it is the *Paramādibuddha*, divided into sixteen lunar digits (*kalās*).
Just as it is externally, so it is within the body; just as it is within the body, so it is elsewhere.
Having understood the threefold mandala, the master should draw the mandala.
Thus, this is the rule everywhere;
the meter has been described by means of [the sequence] two, four, one, and so forth, together with the application of the preceding sūtra.

Now the mantras, symbols, and deities of the mandala are described: Oṃ. Within the lotus of the supreme Victor, born from the gnosis of the syllable Oṃ, above the seats of the moon and sun, the Mother Mātṛkā—the progenitor of the three worlds—is to be established together with the vowels beginning with A and the consonants beginning with Ka, along with the Void (Śūnya).

In the void, within the vowel A and the Visarga, the supreme Vajra of Gnosis—the fourth [body], the source of mantras which produces supreme bliss, the Vajra of Body, Speech, and Mind—is fully manifested.
Oho! Re Mig (Koṣṭha) ga. Samastaṃ ga. Ca. Vibhāgikaṃ.

It is added by means of *oṃkāra* and so forth.

In all these *tantrarājas*, within the *raja-maṇḍala*, the syllable *oṃ* is the *kāyavajra*; by means of it, the maṇḍala is produced, and thus the syllable *oṃ* is said to be "born from gnosis" (*jñānajāta*).

Therefore, in the maṇḍala born from *oṃ*, within the lotuses of the supreme Victors—that is, within the twenty-four lotuses—there are moon and sun seats according to the division of the [twelve] months; twelve moon seats according to the division of the twelve full moons, and twelve sun seats according to the division of the twelve new moons, through the purification of wisdom and method (*prajñopāya-viśuddhyā*).

Upon those seats of the moon and sun situated above the pericarp, together with the vowels beginning with *ā* (the "first ones"), the consonants beginning with *ka*, and the "voids" (*saśūnya*)—meaning accompanied by the *bindu* and *visarga*—there stands the Mother of the Three Worlds, Śūnyatā, who is omniform and whose nature is sound (*nāda*). She is Mātṛkā, the mother of the three realms, the unstruck resonance (*anāhatadhvani*), Prajñāpāramitā, who is to be established upon the basis of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) at the head of all mantras, beginning with the vowels such as *ā* and the consonants such as *ka*, together with those "voids.
Therefore, she is said to be together with them.
In this way, the Blessed One, whose form is great bliss, is also contained therein.

Now, the arising of the body-mantras and so forth for those who practice withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) within the five voids is described, beginning with the word "void": "in the void," meaning in the location of the mantras mentioned in the first chapter; "on the left limb" means the *anusvāra*.
"In the two *a*s, one preceding and one following, in the *visarga* on the right limb, and in the two *bindu*s that follow [the *a*s] and are devoid of vowels"— thus,
in the vowelless *ha* of the *anāhata*.
The vajras of body, speech, mind, and gnosis have arisen;
among them, first of all, the arising of the body is described here: first the *anusvāra*, then the letter *a*, between the two the *visarga*, and at the end of the *anusvāra* the long *ākāra*.

Thus, when a long vowel follows, the preceding *anusvāra* becomes *m*, and when *m* follows, the *visarga* after the letter *a* becomes the letter *a*. Subsequently, through *guṇa* with the letter *a*, there arises the letter *o*.
Then, since there is the elision of a phoneme according to the rules of etymological derivation (*nirukti*), one should separate the *m* and drop the final *ā*.
Thus, the syllable Oṃ, consisting of the three qualities, is called the Body-Vajra as *a*, *u*,
and *m* in both our own and other systems;
now the Speech-Vajra is described.
In this context, the two preceding and following *a*-sounds are lengthened and a *visarga* is placed at the end;
thus, the letter *ā* becomes composed of the three qualities (*guṇas*) and is designated as *a ā*.
Now the *cittavatra* is described:

here first is the vowel-less *a*, then the short *a*, then the *visarga*, then the *bindu*, then the long *ā*. Thus, as before, there is the *ukāra*, with the elision of the initial and final *ā*s of the *visarga*.
Then, the syllable *huṃ*, which consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*),
is said to be *uṃ*; thus, it is born from the mantras of body, speech, and mind, meaning it is the source (*yoni*) and birthplace of mantras.

In this chapter, the great section titled "The Drawing of the Mandala" [is concluded]. Now, the *jñānavajra* is described.
Here, first is the vowel-less letter *ha*, then the letter *a*, then the *visarga*, then the *anusvāra*, then the long letter *ā*.
Thus, as before, from the *visarga* comes the letter *u*.
The vowel *u* from the preceding [syllable] forms a *guṇa* with the letter *ha*; the subsequent *ā* and *a* are elided. Thus, the syllable *ho* consists of the three *guṇas*.
"Ha ā u" is thus said.
In this way, there are three qualities in the Knowledge-Vajra: ignorance (*avidyā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
In the Body-Vajra: name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), and contact (*sparśa*).
The vajra of speech consists of sensation (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*);
the vajra of mind consists of becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
This is by virtue of the form of the *bindu*.

Thus, the fourth [empowerment] is the knowledge-vajra, which generates ignorance and the other [afflictions] and brings about supreme bliss; it is the source (*yoni*) of all mantras. The Blessed One’s rule is that this is everywhere the twelvefold body, speech, mind, and knowledge-vajra.

Now the placement of the mantra-symbols is described: The syllable *huṃ* is in the center of the lotus of the Lord of Jinas, which has all colors and is above the moon, sun, and fire; the initial void (*ādiśūnya*) is on the petals of the cardinal directions, and the *hādi*-void is fourfold on the intermediate petals.

In the northeast, southwest, southeast, and northwest corners, there is the passion of body, speech, mind, and attachment (*rāga*), beginning with the syllable *hī*; thus there is a group of ten for the jars, ending with *haṃ ha*.

In every maṇḍala here, there is a threefold deposition (*nyāsa*), categorized as gross, subtle, and supreme, upon the seats of the moon and sun. Among these, the supreme division is the deposition of the seed-syllables of the mantras; the subtle division is the deposition of symbols such as the vajra, which are the transformation of those mantra-seed syllables; and the gross division is the deposition of the forms of the deities, which are the transformation of those symbols such as the cloth.
Thus, when the deposition of the mantra-seed syllables has been performed according to this sequence, the subsequent depositions of the symbols and so forth are to be understood—this is the rule.
Therefore, in this context, the deposition of the mantra-seed syllables is stated as being primary.
"The syllable *Huṃ* is of universal color, yet green in color, upon the lotus of the Lord of Jinas, above the moon, sun, and fire.
Here, the conjunction of the moon, sun, and Rāhu occurs at the end of the new moon during the time of an eclipse; that very [conjunction] is the mandala-seat "joined with the moon, sun, and fire.
Internally, it is the heart-lotus joined with the lalanā, rasanā, and avadhūtī channels. Upon its pericarp, above the moon, sun, and Rāhu, one should draw the seed-syllable *Huṃ* with blue powder.
Alternatively, one should draw a three-pronged blue vajra transformed from that [syllable].
According to the *Guhyatantra*, the form of the deity should not be drawn in a powder mandala (*rajomaṇḍala*) in order to avoid public censure.
This is the placement of the seed-syllable of the presiding deity.
Then, the placement of the perfections, beginning with generosity (*dāna*), should be performed upon the lotus petals.
Regarding "the first void" (*ādiśūnya*) on the directional petals:
*a* is on the eastern petal, *aḥ* on the southern, *aṃ* on the northern, and *ā* on the western.

Now, the symbols: on the eastern petal is the incense ladle (*dhūpadarvī*), on the south is the lamp (*pradīpa*), on the north is the food offering (*naivedya*), and on the west is the conch (*śaṅkha*).

Regarding the symbol to be placed here according to the rule to be stated later, it says: "Whatever symbol belongs to [a deity], that is the *mudrā* on its right palm, [but] here it is devoid of the lotus," because the placement of the symbols follows the rule that will be stated.
Thus, in the intermediate directions and on the petals, there are four [symbols] beginning with *ha*, which are empty.

in Bo, "Thuni Nu (short)" is additionally inserted.

In the southeast (*śikhin*), the Mind-Vajra; here in the southeast (*āgneyī*) is *Ha*, in the southwest (*nairṛtya*) is *Ihaḥ*, in the northeast (*īśa*) is *Haṃ*, and in the northwest (*vāyavya*) is *Hā*. One should draw [these].

Then, on the outer petals of the intermediate directions, in the four corners: either the Dharma-conch, or in the southwest corner Vāgvajra with *āḥ* and *hūṃ*, or the Cintāmaṇi; in the northwest, Rāga-Jñānavajra with *hoṃ*, or the Kalpavṛkṣa—this is the placement within the inner lotus.
Now, the placement in the second enclosure is described.

Here, in the second enclosure, in the eight sectors starting from the east, in the place of the lotus of the eastern deity: *hi* on the left and *hī* on the right, or two vases; to the east of the southern deity *hu* and to the west *haṝ*, or two vases.
To the south of the western deity is *halu*, to the north is *halu*, or two jars (*ghaṭau*).
To the west of the northern deity is *hu*, to the east is *hū*, or two jars.

*Haṃ* and *haḥ* are at the exit of the eastern and western doors, above and below the Wrathful One (*krodha*), purified by the upward and downward [movements]; thus there is the group of ten beginning with *ho*. This is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seed-syllables of the jars (*kalaśa*).

Then follows the placement of the seed-syllables of the deities: the letter *vi* (vikāra) is on the eastern lotus; the long *ī* is situated on the fire-lotus (southeast); in the south, on the demon-lotus, are the two *ṛ*s, both short and long; in the southwest, on the wealth-giver-lotus (Yama), are the two *a*s, both short and long; in the west, on the wind-lotus, are the two *lṛ*s, both short and long. These are to be assigned according to the distinction of the faces: black, red, white, and resembling excellent gold.
Here, on the eastern lotus at the seat of the sun, there is the letter *i*, a sword, or [the symbol] of formative predisposition (*saṃskāra*).
Located on the fire-lotus and within the lunar disc, there is the long vowel *ī*, a sword, or a blue lotus, representing the wind element.
Likewise, in the south, there is the letter *ṛ*, a jewel, or [the symbol] of sensation (*vedanā*).
In the southwest, for the fire element, there is a red lotus or a moon;
likewise, for the god of wealth (Kubera), there is the vowel *u* or a white lotus for Saṃjñā;
and situated in the north, there is the vowel *ū* or a white water-lily for the water element.
Likewise, in the northwest (Vāruṇya) as well, there is the letter *la* or the wheel (*cakra*) for the form (*rūpa*).
In the wind-corner (Vāyavya), there is *la* for the earth element (*pṛthvīdhātu*), or the wheel; this is the placement of the aggregates and elements (*skandhadhātunyāsa*).
For the space element (*ākāśadhātu*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), there is only a single symbol-vajra (*cihnavastra*) in the pericarp (*kaṇikā*).
The two [faces] in the east and southeast are black; those in the south and southwest are red;
those in the north and northeast are white; and those in the west and northwest are yellow—this is the rule for assigning the colors of the Jina according to the distinction of his faces.

Now, the seed-syllables of the deities and goddesses are stated through the purification of the six sense-faculties and the six objects: on the right of the eastern gate, situated upon a fire-lotus, are the short and long [vowels]; likewise, there is a pair of *ar* syllables; situated on the left of Yama is a pair of *al* syllables; in the west, there is a pair of *aḷ* syllables. *O* and *au* are in Yakṣa and Rudra; in the left of the gates of the gods, Varuṇa, and Yama, together with Yakṣa, are *aṃ* and *aḥ* in sequence; and in the lotuses of the gates, *ya*, *ra*, *va*, and *la* follow the vowels.

In the third enclosure, here on the right of the eastern gate, upon a lotus situated on a solar mandala, is the letter *E*, which belongs to the nose; in the southeast corner, on a fire-lotus situated on a lunar mandala, is the letter *Ai*, which belongs to Sparśavajrā. Likewise, on the west of the southern gate, is the letter *O* for the eye; similarly, in the southwest, is the letter *Au* for Rasavajrā.
Thus is the pair:
likewise, in the west, *alkāra* belongs to the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), and *ālkāra* in the northwest belongs to the nose-faculty (*gandhavajrā*).
Similarly, *o* in the yakṣa [direction] belongs to the tongue, and *au* in the rudra [direction] belongs to the form-faculty (*rūpavajrā*).
"Suravaruṇayamadvāravāme sayakṣa" means:

here, at the north of the eastern gate, on the sun, is *a*, the sense-faculty of mind (*manaindriya*); at the south of the western gate, is the syllable *aḥ*, the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); "candro'yama" means at the east of the southern gate, on the sun, is the syllable *a*, the sense-faculty of hearing (*śrotrendriya*).
In all cases, these are according to the divisions of the four faces of the Blessed One, situated to the left.

To the west of the northern gate of the Yakṣas is the syllable *ĀḤ*, which belongs to Śabdavajrā. This is the placement of the seed-syllables (*bījanyāsa*) of the twelve sense-bases (*āyatana*). Now, the placement of the seed-syllables of the gatekeepers is described: sequentially, *ya*, *ra*, *va*, and *la* are the guardians of the gates in the lotuses of the doors.

Here, in the eastern gate, upon the solar or lunar disc, is the syllable *ya* for the organ of speech; in the south, upon the sun, is the syllable *ra* for the organ of the hands; in the north is the syllable *va* for the organ of the feet; and in the west is the syllable *la* for the organ of the anus. This is the placement. (59)

Now, the rule for the seats of the Moon and Sun is stated: At the eastern gate, on the left side, there is the seat of the Moon for the two wrathful deities, and on the right side, the Sun prevails; and in the other [gates], the lotus-seats of the pairs arise from the divisions of Wisdom and Means. Indeed, the entire arrangement of Moon and Sun seats occurs thus: on the right and at the back, there should be the Sun; for Indra and Kubera, the seat should be the Moon alone. (60)
Here, at the eastern gate—that is, the left-hand gate—there is the moon as the seat for the two wrathful deities; and by the word "and" (ca), there is also the sun.
At the right-hand gate and the western gate, there is the sun, according to the distinction between wisdom and method.
Then, Sūrya is on the seat of means (upāya) and Candra is on the seat of wisdom (prajñā),
each upon their own lotus.
Then, for those whose presiding deity is the eastern fire and so forth, there is a sword;
for those of the south and the southwest, a jewel; and for those of the north and the northeast, a lotus.
The wheel for those of the west and the northwest,

and for the deities above and below, is the vajra; alternatively, according to the distinction of sense objects, it is the lute for sound, the garment for touch, the mirror for form, the vessel for taste, the fragrance-conch for smell, and the source of phenomena (dharmodaya) for the sphere of phenomena (dharmadhātu).

Likewise, the sword is for the organ of speech, and the staff is for the organ of the hand. Now, the seeds of the lotuses are described: The syllables of the *ka*-group and so forth, located within the lotus and divided by the forms of the *bindu*, are arranged in sequence upon the bulb, the stalk, the petals, the filaments, and the pericarp.

Starting from Earth (*bhūmi*) and ending with the vowel *a*—namely *ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa*—these consist of short and long vowels on their respective grounds. The *bindu* is the Moon, and the *visarga* is the Sun; the pericarp above serves as the seat. (61)
By the words "in the form of drops" (*bindvākāraiḥ*) and so forth,
it is meant that here, within the twenty-four lotuses starting from the *kanda*,

the letters of the *ka*-group and other classes are to be assigned as differentiated by the drops (*bindu*) and so on— namely *aṃ*, *aḥ*, *a*, *ā*— according to the family (*kula*) of the respective deity.

For the ear: *kaṃ* in the lotus bulb, *khaṃ* in the stalk, *gaṃ* in the petals, *ghaṃ* in the filaments, and *ṅaṃ* in the pericarp; for the sense of the mind-element (*dharmadhātu*), *kā*, *khā*, *gā*, *ghā*, and *ṅā*; and for the mental faculty (*manaindriya*), *saṃ*, *paṃ*, *ṣaṃ*, *śaṃ*, and *kaṃ*.
The *pa*, *ṣa*, *śa*, and *ka* of the word *śabda* are transformed by these five syllables; for the formation of *kamala*, there are *ca*, *cha*, *ja*, *jha*, and *ña*.
Likewise, for the nose (*ghrāṇa*), there are *caṃ*, *chaṃ*, *jaṃ*, *jhaṃ*, and *ñaṃ*.
*cā cha jā jhā trā* for touch (*sparśa*); *caḥ chaḥ jaḥ jhaḥ trāḥ*;
*ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa* for the eye (*cakṣus*); *ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ*.
For the fire element: ṭā ṭhā ḍā ḍhā ṇā; likewise for the air element;
and for sensation.
For Rasavajrā, the designations are ṭāḥ ṭhāḥ ḍāḥ ḍhāḥ ṇāḥ;
for the tongue, they are pa pha ba bha ma; and [for the palate], they are paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ.

For the water element, there are *pā*, *phā*, *bā*, *bhā*, and *mā* for Rūpavajrā; and for form (*rūpa*), there are *pāḥ*, *phāḥ*, *bāḥ*, *bhāḥ*, and *māḥ*; and for [the earth element], there are *ta*, *tha*, *da*, *dha*, and *na*.

For the body-faculty (kāyendriya), [the seed-syllables] are *taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ*, which belong to the earth element (*pṛthvīdhātu*); for odor (*gandha*), they are *tā thā dā dhā nā*; and for [the tactile object], they are *tāḥ thāḥ dāḥ dhāḥ nāḥ*.
And thus, cha, ja, jha, ña belong to the organ of speech; ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa belong to the organ of the hands; pa, pha, ba, bha, ma belong to the organ of the feet.

The syllables *ta, tha, da, dha, na* are to be known as belonging to the lotus of the *pātrindriya*; thus is the rule for the placement of lotus-seeds (*kamalabījanyāsa*), both short and long, in their own respective locations. Likewise, the seats of the Moon are formed by the nasal dot (*bindu*), the letter *a*, or the letter *ha*; the seats of the Sun are formed by the visarga, the letter *ra*, or the letter *kṣa*. Above the pericarp (*kaṇikā*) is the lotus of the presiding deity (*adhipatikamala*), where [the syllables] *sāṃ, pāṃ, ṣāṃ, śāṃ, kāṃ* are located; and in the pericarp itself are *aṃ* and *aḥ*. *A*.
The placement [of mantras] consists of the seats of the Moon, the Sun, and Rāhu. || 61 ||

Now the seed-syllables (bīja) of the offering goddesses are stated: the six groups [of consonants], by virtue of their short and long natures and qualities, are located on the sides of the pillars of the altar; they reside in their own family-grounds in sequence starting from the eastern part, in their respective directions, beginning with *ga* for touch (*sparśa*).

The Great Chapter entitled "The Drawing of the Mandala": On the exterior, on the altar, there are [circles] divided by points and so forth, multiplied by three suns; likewise, for all the desires, the colors of the Jinas according to their own families and days are distributed everywhere. (62)
With the words "the sixfold group" and so forth,
here in the eastern part of the mandala of the mind, on the base of the archway pillar of the platform, there is *cch-jhjña* on the left for Gandhā, and *cachajajhañā* on the right for Mālā.
Thus, in the south, *ṭ ṭh ū ṇa* belong to Dhūpā;
*ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa* belong to Dīpā; and in the west, *ta tha dha na* belong to Lāsyā.
Likewise, *dadhinā* for *hāsyāyāḥ*,
*pphbbhma* for *amṛtāyāḥ*,
*paphababhamā* for *phalākṣatāyāḥ*.

*Kkhgghṅa* is for Nṛtyā above the eastern gate-arch; *kakhagaghaṅā* is for Vādyā above the western gate-arch; *s ya śa ka* is for Gītā above the northern gate-arch; and *sayay ṣ ś paśa kā* is for Kāmā above the southern gate-arch. Now, regarding the symbols: the conch, rosary, ladle, lamp, crown, necklace, fruit, vessel, cloth, drum, vajra, and lotus—these are to be assigned starting from the eastern side; this is the rule. Now, the seed-syllables for the thirty-six [deities] of Icchā are stated, beginning with "On the exterior" (*bāhye*), etc.
Here, in the outer speech-maṇḍala, on the altar to the south of the eastern gate and on the altar [itself], are *cha*, *ja*, *jha*, *ña*;
on the south are *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ḍa*, *ḍha*, *ṇa*; and on the west are *ta*, *tha*, *da*, *dha*, *na*.
In the north are *pa*, *pha*, *ba*, *bha*, and *ma*;
at the left of the eastern gate are *sa*, *pa*, *ṣa*, *śa*, and *ṣka*;
at the western side of the northern gate are *la*, *va*, *ra*, *ya*, and *ha*.
On the southern gate altar, [one should write] *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṅa*;

on the south of the western gate, *kṣa*. In the speech mandala (*vāṅmaṇḍala*) and the body mandala (*kāyamaṇḍala*), the seed-syllables (*bīja*), signs, or forms of the Protectors should be written using these letters joined with the anusvāra, beginning with the letter *ca* and so forth.

On the inner altar (*garbhavedikā*), all the various deities of worship who are the sustainers (*dhāriṇyaḥ*) are to be drawn; this is the placement of the seed-syllables (*bījanyāsa*) of the *dhāraṇīs*.

Thus, for all [the goddesses of] desire, the colors of the Jinas belonging to their respective families should be understood according to the distinction of colors on all sides, using five-colored powder (*pañcavarṇa-rajas*); this is the rule everywhere. Now, the seed-syllables of Carcikā and the others in the mandala of speech (*vāṅmaṇḍala*) are stated: the short and long *ha* syllables are in the south, behind the gods of wealth (Vaiśravaṇa); the syllable *kṣa* belongs to Vaiṣṇavī and the others; and it is differentiated by the fire, moon, and wind in the west.

The eight letters beginning with *kṣa* located on the petals of the lotus are in the eight directions on the front side; the six letters beginning with *ya*, both short and long, are in the petals of the divine lotus in the southeast, in due order.

By the words "short" (*hrasvau*) and so forth, it is meant that in this chapter on the means of accomplishment (*sādhanapaṭala*) which will be explained hereafter, one should draw Cāmuṇḍā upon a corpse as her lotus seat, and above that, an eight-petalled lotus.

O, Self-Awareness (*svavidyā*)! Regarding the letter *ha*:

in the case of the goddesses, there is *ha* in the pericarp of the lotus for Caṇḍākṣī; for Dhanada, there is *haṃ* in the pericarp of the lotus atop the bull for Raudrī. [From the *Vimalaprabhā*, Chapter on Consecration] 15 20 20. *Ran Rig* (Self-Awareness). *Ha*-sounds: thus, in the case of the goddesses, there is *ha* in the pericarp for Caṇḍākṣī; for Dhanada, there is *haṃ* in the pericarp of the lotus atop the bull for Raudrī.

In the south, the syllable *haḥ* is for Vārāhī upon a buffalo; in the west, *hā* is for Aindrī upon an elephant. Thus, in the cardinal directions, *yaḥ* belongs to Cāmuṇḍā and the others, while *kṣa* and *phā* belong to Vaiṣṇavī and the others.
Thus, in the southeast corner, upon Garuḍa, on the pericarp of the lotus, is *kṣa*. Likewise, for Hari’s Mahālakṣmī, on a lion, is *kṣaṃ*.
In the northwest, for Brahmāṇī, upon a swan, is *kṣā*.
In the southwest (nairṛtya), there is *kṣaḥ* for Kaumāryā upon the pericarp of a peacock-lotus;
in these cases, there is no moon-seat (*candrāsana*).
Such is the rule regarding Daitya according to the distinctions of Carcikā and the others.

1.12 Now, the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the sixty-four yoginīs, beginning with Bhīmā, are described on the lotus petals, starting with the words "hyādyā" and so forth. Here, the syllables begin with *hya*.
There are eight in number; among them, *hi* is for Bhīmā on the lotus petal in front of Carcikā, and *hī* is for Vāyuvegā behind her.
In those directions starting from one's own, in the eastern direction,
there are the six short vowels beginning with *a*;
[the planets] beginning with Mars are arranged by turning clockwise.
Likewise, on the second petal belongs Bhīmā; on the second [of the next set] is Ugrā;
on the third is Kāladaṃṣṭrā;
and on the fourth is Jvaladanalamukhā.
Then, on the fifth petal, Vāyuvegā is stated;
on the sixth, Yu belongs to Pracaṇḍā, whose face is like blazing fire;
and on the seventh, Yla belongs to Raudrākṣī.
In the eighth [petal], there is that of Sthūlanāsā;

or else, in all places such as the pericarp (*kaṇikā*), there is the mark of the pericarp for Cāmuṇḍā and the others. Thus is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in the eastern lotus of the divine lotus. Here, in the directions starting from the southeast (*vahni-pāda*), there are eight syllables beginning with *kṣa*; among them, *kṣi* is in front of Vaiṣṇavī, and [the syllable] of Śrī is [in front of] Śrī.
On the back [of the leaf] is the syllable *kṣī* for Paramavijayā.
Likewise, *yā* is for Māyā, *yī* for Kīrti, and *yū* for Lakṣmī. On the sixth petal is *yū* for Jayā.
On the eighth petal of the Jayantī [lotus], there is the *ṭala* [syllable];
furthermore, the wheel-mark (*cakracihna*) is present everywhere.
This is the rule according to the sequence of the fire-lotus (*vahnipadma*).

Thus, on the southern lotus petal, *ra* and so forth are short and long; on the northern, *ya* and so forth; and on the eastern door, to its right, *la* and so forth are on the petals of the lotus situated in the wind and water directions. The group of consonants beginning with *ca*, differentiated by the Mothers, is short when located on a lotus petal of the Daitya (west), and it becomes long for the Wind situated in the fire corner (southeast).
"Thus, in the southern [direction], there are *rā* and so forth.

Alternatively, in all cases, including those for Vārāhī and the others, the staff is the emblem (*daṇḍa-cihna*).
In the case of Kaumāryā and others, the attribute is a spear;
for Padmā and Khaḍgā, it is a lotus or a sword; for Lakṣmī and others, as well as Raudrī and others, it is a trident.

In the case of the *aindrī* and other [mantras], there is the thunderbolt (*vajra*). In the case of the *brahmāṇī* and other [mantras], there is the sacrificial ladle (*śruci*) or the vessel (*pātra*).
The Lord’s rule is that the seed-syllables and symbols of Saśvacikā and the others are to be written within the speech-maṇḍala.
Now, the seed-syllables of Nairṛti and the others in the body-maṇḍala are stated, beginning with "of the eastern gate" and so forth.
Here, in this body-maṇḍala, there are twenty-eight-petaled lotuses for the twelve deities beginning with Nairṛti.
The sixty-three lunar days beginning with Caitra are the presiding deities.
Among them, the full moon and new moon days are the seeds located in the pericarp,
while the remaining days are on the lotus petals.
Here, Caitra and Vaiśākha constitute the spring season due to the purification of the wind;
by that [purification], the short syllable belongs to the Daitya,
while the long measure belongs to the Wind situated in the southeast corner.
Here, on the first petal to the south of the eastern gate is Ña-ña for Vajrā; thus it is everywhere, just as with the first lunar day of the bright fortnight:
Ña for Vajrā.
Likewise, on the second petal is Tritrivajrā;
in this manner, all lunar days (*tithi*) ending with the name Vajra are to be understood.
The full moon is Prajñā, and the new moon is Upāya.
Thus on the third petal;
again, in due order: ña, ñlṛ, jha, jhi, jhū, jhū, jhalu, jhaṃ.
*Ja* and *ji* are on the fourteenth petal; then, on the pericarp of the full moon, *jū* and *jū* belong to Vajrā.
Then, [the letters] *pa*, *ñca*, *cha*, and *grataḥ* belong to Kumārī. [The letter] *nā* does not exist.

In the letter *ga* is Ahalyā; in *ka*, *kha*, and *cha* is Śuci.
15 20 66. In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the ten petals of the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*):
thus, in sequence, *jṛ jaṃ; cha chi chṛ chu chlū chaṃ*.
On the twenty-eighth petal, [the syllables] *ca*, *ci*, *cṛ*, and *cu* are placed;
then, on the new moon day, the seed-syllable *caṃ* is in the pericarp (*kaṇikā*);
and on the first lunar day (*pratipad*) of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, [it is] on the first [petal].
Cā for Vajrā;
likewise, the names of all the lunar days (tithis) end in "Vajrā.
