Jū jlū jaḥ | Jhā jhī jhu jhū jhūlū jhaḥ | Ñā ñī ñū ñū ñ | [These are] on the twenty-eighth petal.
Then, on the new moon day, the seed-syllable *ña* of the wind [element] is placed in the pericarp; the long vowels and the *ca*-group belong to the wind—this is the rule.
64. Thus, in the south (Yāmya) is the *ṭa*-group; in the southeast (Śikhira), the southwest (Rasa), and the east (Mukha), there are the short and long [vowels] according to their divisions.
On the left (Vāma) and in the northeast (Īśa), the *pa*-group occurs; in the west (Jalanidhi), it belongs to the division of the long [vowels].

For the host of Śakra, Brahmā, and Varuṇa-Pavana, the *ta*-group consists of short and long [vowels]. To the left of the eastern gate is the *ka*-group, belonging to the enemy of Danu (Indra), situated upon the lotus petals.
Likewise, in the southern direction, to the west of the southern gate,
there is the short *ṭa*-group with *ṇa* and so forth on the full-moon dates; [the syllable] "dṛḍham" is in the pericarp of the Fire [deity], belonging to the one whose face is the six flavors.
For Ṣaṇmukha, there is the long vowel;

for the lunar days of Āṣāḍha, it is like the long *ca*-group; and in the pericarp, there is *dṛṇaḥ*—thus, by means of the distinctions between short and long vowels, [the sequence proceeds] on the left, in the north, within the ocean.
The short *pavarga* is for the sake of protection during the full moon and new moon of the month of Śrāvaṇa; in the northeast, it is used with long variations.
In the center of the Vināyaka-gaṇa,
we worship [the deities] on the full moon and new moon days of Bhādrapada;
likewise, for Śakra, there is the short *stabarga* in the Varuṇa [direction].
With the [sound] ṇādi, one should place a drop in the pericarp on the full moon and new moon days of the month of Āśvina;
likewise in the wind.
By this [method], one should place *dṛ* and *naḥ* in the pericarp of the lotus of Brahmā on the full moon and new moon days of the month of Kārttika;
likewise, on the left side of the eastern door, there is the short vowel *a* of Danuripu Viṣṇu, and the *ka*-group on the lotus petals.
With the syllable *ṅā* and so forth, one should place *gṛ* and *kam* in the pericarp on the full moon and new moon days of the month of Māgha.

O King, the short and long vowels occur on the left of Yama; on the north and west, the short and long vowels together with their groups (savarga) belong to Paśupati and Jambhala, O King, [and] likewise on the lunar day (tithi). Or [it is] "cha. Vā.
On the ten petals:
Ka, Kha, Ga, Cha, Māyāṃ,
Bhoḥ— thus [the sequence] is augmented.
ga. Therefore, o Kha. Padma, Bho. ḍṭaṃ.

the right and O, the left.

ga. [The letter] *pa* is short; after this, ka. kha. [have] *pūrṇāvāmā*, while ga. has *pūrṇimā*; ga.
does not have the word "pada."

In the chapter [beginning with] "ga. ca. gṛka," verse 67, titled "The Great Exposition on the Drawing of the Maṇḍala": For the Daityas and others, their own seed-syllable occurs; and on the petals, in the midst of the end of each respective group, there are the letters of their own respective groups according to the day, even upon the twenty-eight petals.
The long [vowels] are on the left; on the east of the left door, the letters beginning with *ka* are in the pericarp (*kaṇikā*) for the full moon and new moon of Phālguna—namely, *ga* and *ṅa*.
Then, on the north, to the west of the north door, the short vowels and the *sa*-group (the labials) are located; by the letters beginning with *ka*, the letter *ṣ* is in the pericarp of Paśupati.
On the full moon and new moon days of Mārgaśīrṣa—
thus at the southern side of the western gate— the long vowel Ā and so forth are on the petals, and in the pericarp (kaṇikā) is "ṢŪ KA" for the Yakṣa, on the full moon and new moon days of Pauṣa.

Thus, according to the divisions of the seasons—spring, summer, the rainy season, autumn, early winter, and late winter—the elements of wind, fire, water, earth, consciousness, and space correspond to the five maṇḍalas through the division of lunar days; and by means of the sixfold division [of each], there is the placement of seed-syllables upon the body-maṇḍala.
Alternatively, there are symbols upon all the petals according to the specific symbols of the central deities.
Here, the symbols for those starting from Nairṛti in sequence within the pericarp are: a sword, a tree, and a spear.
Spears, nooses, and axes.
The vajra, the trident, and the wheel.
The rule for the placement of symbols is: the staff, the trident, and the mace.

For example—the seed-syllables of the Daityas and others arise; and within the strength [of the system], in the midst of their respective groups, on the twenty-eight petals according to the days, there are the syllables of their respective groups. This is the rule for the placement of the thirty-sixty lunar days (*tithi*) as vajras upon the body-maṇḍala.

Now, the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the gatekeepers and the goddesses stationed on the chariots, as well as those of the Wrathful Kings (*krodharāja*), are stated: The syllables *yā*, *rā*, *vā*, *lā*, *haṃ*, and *hāḥ*—these six indeed [reside] at the top and base of the chariots, beginning with the vowels (*svarādi*), on the left and right of the door. The letter *ha* is mounted upon the syllable *ya* and so forth;

the six groups (*ṣaḍvarga*) are also in the form of peaks (*kūṭarūpa*). Furthermore, in the wheel of the directions (*dikcakra*), the groups beginning with *ka* are joined with *ya*, *ha*, *ra*, *va*, *la*, and *kṣa*; and others beginning with *ca* are situated in the moving circle (*calavalaya*) in direct order (*anuloma*).
By means of the mantra *yārā yā rā* and so forth, here at the eastern gate, there is *lāḥ* for Mārīcī and *yaṃ* for Nīladaṇḍa.
At the southern gate is the syllable VĀḤ of Cundā; at the northern gate is the syllable RĀḤ of Bhṛkuṭī.
To the west of Acala is Vaṃ; to that of Vajraśṛṅkhalā is Lāṃ;
and to that of Mahābala is Laṃ.
Through the purification of space, before the eastern gate, is Nīlā with *hāḥ* and *haḥ*;
through the purification of the underworld (*pātāla*), before the western gate, is Raudrekṣaṇā and Sumbharāja with *haṃ*.
Alternatively, the symbols are the staff, the arrow, and the club.
The mace, the thunderbolt, and the trident.
The rule is that the boar, horse, lion, elephant, wind, and eight-legged [creature] are on the chariot;
according to Yama and others, there is a long vowel in *kha* and *cha*.
On lotus petals: *pūrṇimā* and *vā*; in the *ga.* [group]: *pūrṇāmā* and *maṇḍala*; in the *ca.* [group]: *maṇḍala* and *vāyumaṇḍala*.
Indeed, on the right of the lotus,
or else the banner-sign;
likewise at the southern gate, in the eastern and western fire-mandalas.
"Hra hrāḥ" is for the Svastika; "Hva hvā" is for Vāsuki and Śaṅkhapāla in the north, east, and west.
On the water-mandala,
there is either a lotus for Kulikā and Ananta.
To the south and north of the western gate,
on the earth mandala, are the vajras of Takṣaka and Mahāpadma, or [the syllables] *ha* and *hrāḥ*.
Thus is the placement of the signs in the great cremation grounds according to their respective order;
in the circle of directions, there are the classes of consonants beginning with 'ka'.
K, KH, G, GH, and ṄA—
thus [is] the previous wheel; at its head is the knife (kartī), or [it is] SA at the rear.
In the north are *lū*, *v*, *r*, *y*, *ha*;
in the south are those joined with *kṣā* and so forth, namely *la*, *va*, *ra*, *ya*, *hā*.

Having thus formed an eight-spoked wheel in the middle of the circle of immovable fire, one should place the other vowels beginning with *ā* in clockwise order upon it; and in the intermediate directions: *c*, *ch*, *j*, *jh*, *ña* in the southeast (*agni*); *ṭ*, *ṭh*, *ḍ*, *ḍh*, *ṇa* in the southwest (*nairṛtya*); *t*, *th*, *d*, *dh*, *na* in the northwest (*vāyavya*); and *pa*, *pha*, *ba*, *bha*, *ma* in the northeast (*īśāna*).
Now, there is a rule regarding the mark of the agent in all cases.

In the east, south, left (north), [and right (west)], the syllables *Aṃ* and *Aḥ* belong respectively to the Moon and Sun; *Va* and *Ra* to Varuṇa and Agni; and *I* and *Śa* to Īśvara and Vāyu—these are the mantras of the multitude of spirits residing in the world of the funeral pyre.
The syllable *Hūṃ* belongs to the Wheel of Dharma; likewise, the seed-syllable *Kā* belongs to the Jar; *Oṃ* belongs to the Drum; and *Ho* arises for the Bodhi tree, belonging to Varuṇa.
In the east, south, left (northwest), west, southeast, northeast, and northwest respectively— here,
in this circle of the earth, *aṃ* is the seed-syllable of the Moon and *aḥ* is the seed-syllable of the Sun.

The number of the host of spirits (bhūta-vṛnda) residing in the city of Citibhuvana is three and a half crores; the mantras of that host of spirits are infinite, meaning they are equal in number to those [spirits].
Alternatively, there is a rule that various symbols should be fashioned upon the circle of wind (vāyu-valaya).
Now, [follow] the seed-syllables (bīja) of the Dharma-wheel and so forth.

At the eastern archway is the *dharmacakra* with *huṃ*; at the southern, the auspicious vase (*bhadraghaṭa*) with *āḥ*; at the northern, the drum (*dundubhi*) with *oṃ*; and at the western, the Bodhi tree with *ho*.
Hrā, Ga. Hrasvā, Hlahnā, Vala-dvāra.

The great chapter titled "The Drawing of the Mandala" is thus found in the *Mātṛkā*. According to the [respective] families, there is a division of mantras in the mandala, as well as mudrās, signs, and colors; indeed, everything belongs to the Vajrin through the divisions of his faces.

Likewise, there is the fire-oblation (*homa*) in the sacrificial pit, and furthermore, the invocation of the heretics on the glorious ground, the sprinkling, the rite of the offering (*argha*), and likewise the expulsion of Māra.
[The text provided consists solely of vertical bars (||) and does not contain any content to translate.]
Thus, according to the family (*kula*), there occurs a division of mantras within the mandala of the *mātṛkā*. Indeed, the mudrās, signs, and colors arise from all the various faces of the Vajrin.

Likewise, the fire-oblation (*homa*) in the hearth (*kuṇḍa*), as well as the invitation (*āvāhana*) of the heretics (*tīrthika*), the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) on the glorious ground, the ritual of the water-offering (*argha*), and the expulsion of Māra—all this is to be understood according to the sequence to be explained; it is summarized in this verse. This is the rule everywhere.

Now, the disciples are designated for the protection of the doors of the mandala: "For the purpose of guarding the doors, pure disciples endowed with vows and observances should be assigned as yoginīs to the [four] glorious vases, and in the southeast and northeast corners respectively.
O King, the preceptor becomes the glorious Gaṇeśa; in the absence of disciples, Gaṇeśa himself performs the ritual of Karmavajrī, including the fire-offering (homa) and other rites."
With the words beginning with "dvāra" (gate), [it is meant that] for the purpose of guarding the gates here, starting from the east, they are "endowed with vows and observances" (*vrataniyamayuta*);
the "vows" (*vrata*) are the twenty-five that will be described, and "observance" (*niyama*) is the authorization of the Buddha; those joined with that are "endowed with vows and observances."
Pure disciples, free from the fourteen root downfalls,
are to be given [initiation] preeminently; thus,
with vajras and vajra-bells in hand at the gateways, they are consecrated and authorized.
The yoginīs of the Śrīghaṭas are to be given in sequence in the northeastern corner of the grove of Śikhivana,
once they have been purified by the previous vows and so forth;
at that time, O King, the Vajrācārya becomes Śrī Gaṇeśa, for Karmavajrī is his nature.
In this context, the fifth type of excellent disciple is one who is skilled in all ritual actions and has a thorough knowledge of the ten principles (*daśatattva*).
Having appointed such a person as the "Karma-Vajrī" in the section on rituals such as the fire sacrifice (*homa*), the Guru performs the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) in the mandala.
In the absence of such a disciple, Gaṇeśa himself also performs the ritual actions, such as the fire sacrifice and so forth.

The third major section, titled "The Procedure for Drawing the Mandala," in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja* following the *Mūlatantra*, concludes with the words: "and by the word 'also' (ca), other [procedures] yet to be described."

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, the great chapter on the mandala initiation states: "He who consumes the entire oblation— the fuel-sticks and so forth consisting of the aggregates and so on— [is the true consumer]."
Having prostrated before that fire of knowledge, I shall describe the characteristics of its sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is said to be of eight kinds, according to the division of the directions and the distinctions of rites such as pacification (śāntika),
while the ninth is for all rites (sārvakarmika).
It was taught by Mañjuvajrin; it is now being set forth.

Having extracted this from the *Abhiṣeka-mūlatantra* and other sources, it is here set forth in brief according to the *Mūlatantrānusāriṇī* in seventy-one verses. The characteristics of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) for all rites and so forth are now described: The pit is either circular or has four corners, depending on the *kula*; for the rites of pacification (*śānti*) and enrichment (*puṣṭi*), the pit is on the left or at the corner of Rudra (the northeast). Oh, the root-lotus is white and double [the size of the others].

The opening is the size of a lotus; within its interior is the root-lotus with its insignia, marked by lotus-eyes; outside the lotus there may also be a jar, as well as insignias such as a sword and jewels. ||71||

By the words "whether circular" and so forth, it is established that here, in every case within the four-cubit mandala, the circular *kuṇḍa* fulfills all desires for rites of pacification (*śānti*), while the square one, equal to half the mandala, is for rites of enrichment (*puṣṭi*). Furthermore, therein,

according to the [specific] family (*kula*), the knowledge-wheel (*jñānacakra*)— extending from the center to the end of the vajra-railings and pillars— is everywhere half the size of the mandala, by the rule that it measures half of the outer wheel.
The root lotus is half the size of that; for prosperity, it is double the size of that central lotus. It may be two cubits square or circular, and the measurement of the central lotus is one cubit.
In all cases, this is for the sake of merit in the center of villages and other such places.

Then, according to the specific rite, either on the left or in the northeast corner, one should prepare a white dust-mandala outside the vajra-flame border at a distance of two cubits; therein, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is square, measuring two cubits in width, with a depth equal to half the measure of the outer wheel,
and its excavation is the size of a lotus.
In this nourishing pit (puṣṭikuṇḍa), the excavation is the size of a lotus and two spans (vitasti) deep; in its circular form, it is one span deep,
and within its interior is the embryonic lotus (garbhapadma).

Just as there is a four-cubit mandala with its symbols, so it is in the square fire-pit (kuṇḍa); just as there is a two-cubit mandala, so it occurs within the circular pit. Thus, just as there is a lotus in the mandala and outside the lotus, in the cardinal and intermediate directions, there are symbols such as the water-jar and the sword; likewise, within the pit of all fire-pits, the primary lotus and so forth should be made with white powder or clay. Afterwards, according to the specific rite, the color should be applied with flour, rice, and so on, in the case of a nourishing mandala. These are the symbols, just like the symbols of the mandala.
Thus, on the surface of the *kuṇḍa*, one part measured transversely from the Brahma-position [is occupied by] the *vajra*; there is no circle (*vṛtta*) or other [markings].
For the *kuṇḍas*, there is no square or semi-circular mandala.
O Lotus-born One,
or rather, there is none.
There is no [defilement] by means of dust and so forth, O King.
The rule for the marks is in the chapter on the great sacrificial pit (mahākuṇḍa), verse [number].
The Great Chapter on the Maṇḍala Initiation (Maṇḍalābhiṣeka-mahoddeśa), 71: The hand [measure] is square;
likewise, half a part [is used] for the wall of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
In this way, there are two parts each for the east and the west as well.
In the same manner, it should be on the left and right as well;
thus, the rule is that the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be four cubits [in extent], extending from the boundary of the enclosure wall to the locations of the eyes and other [senses].
It may be four cubits square, or half of that (two cubits) circular, or a mandala of two cubits. || 71 ||

The lip is half of that [the width], and the pedestal (vedikā) is twice that; the portion for the pillars (yāma-bhāga) is raised by half the height of the lip. At the top, there is a fixed vajra-garland on the outside, and below it, one should arrange lotus petals and kusa-grass in all directions. At its end, to the west, there is invariably a single door with three lines.
"And with half of that, the lip"— this is the rule:
with half of that lotus, which is the location of the Tathāgata, by way of its horizontal height— that is,
by the measurement of the enclosure wall— there is the horizontal division.
By that same measure, the altar-platform (vedikā) of the mandala should extend [to that extent];

above that, with half of that [measure], the lip (oṣṭha)—which is the outer perimeter line of the mandala—should have its projection and height; thus, up to the edge of the altar-platform, it is perfectly pure and double [the previous size], and from there, the portion for the pillars (yāma-bhāga) of the altar.

Then, extending outward by a horizontal division twice the measure of the inner sanctum (*garbha*), there is a veranda (*vedikā*); in this manner, the ground for the jeweled bands (*ratnapaṭṭikā*), necklaces (*hāra*), and half-necklaces (*ardhahāra*)—extending as far as the *vakulī*—should be made as a veranda everywhere.
Then, the *vakulī* extends outward by a horizontal division equal to the height of the stepped pediment (*kramaśīrṣa*).

There, at the top of the altar (vedikā), having divided the middle portion into five parts, a row of vajras (vajrāvalī) is placed upon the altar using three of those middle parts; it is raised to half the measurement of the rim (oṣṭha) of the all-purpose fire-pit (sarvakarmika-kuṇḍa). When it is made of clay, the height of the central spike (śūka) is half that of the rim; when it is made of colored powder (rajas), there is no fixed rule for the height.
On the outside, lotus petals with their tips pointing downward should be made, reaching down to the ground level and measuring half the height of the altar.
Then, on the ground outside in all directions, one should arrange *kuśa* grass.
Outside of that *kuśa* spread, in the western sector, there is certainly one door, consisting of three lines.

Here, having left two cubits outside the perimeter of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should construct three walls outside using white, red, and black powders. Then, to the west, the door—measuring one-eighth of the length of the wall—is three-lined like the door of a mandala and is provided with an archway (*toraṇa*).
Thus, in all sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), whether large or small, the rule for the three enclosures (prākāra) is that two cubits must be left [from the edge]. || 72 ||

The seat of the Ācārya is indeed equal to the inner lotus (garbhapadma), or else it should be double that size; O Lord of Men, the Argha seat should be on the left, and the vessel for the fire-oblation (homapātra) should be on the right.

For all [deities], there is the vajra symbol; or for the Lord of Jinas, there is the empty lotus. The mouth and the secret part of the Mother are the pit (kuṇḍa); O King, this twofold [pit] exists both externally and within the body. (73)
On the outer [part] of the night mandala.
There is no double-stranded necklace for the Mivakulī.
There is no need for it to be done;
take one-fifth part.
Furthermore, in the downward direction,
there is no "three-lined" [region].
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is stated that there is no seat for the Ācārya; indeed, in a square pit (*kuṇḍa*), the [seat] is equal to twice the central lotus,
which is two cubits square.
Thus, in all the fire-pits (kuṇḍas), the diameter should be one cubit;
likewise, on the left there should be a seat for the arghya-water one cubit in size,
and similarly on the right, a seat for the oblation-vessel (homapātra) one cubit in size.
For nourishment, it is two cubits;
lotus petals should be placed in the middle of all the seats,
and the symbol of the double-vajra (viśvavajra) should be given in the center of the seat.

Indeed, for the Lord of Jinas or for Vajrasattva, the "sky-lotus" (*khapadma*)—which is the mother’s *dharmodaya*—is to be given; thus it is stated in the *Sārvakāmika*: "The mouth is the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) for the purpose of offering grains and so forth, while the secret pit is for the giving of oblations of clarified butter and other nectars.
In this way, there are two types [of pits]; and "the lotus is on the outer body," O King, is the address.
Thus is the rule for the characteristics of the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) used for all rites.
Now, the characteristics of the [pits] previously mentioned for pacification and so forth are described:

here, in a circular pit measuring one cubit, there is a central lotus (garbhapadma) measuring one cubit, white in color; on the pericarp (kaṇikā) and the petals of the lotus are the symbols such as the wheel and others.
The cavity is half a lotus; the lip is one-twelfth of a lotus; its outward projection is nine parts horizontally and half of that vertically.
Its horizontal projection is [nine parts].
The height of the vedikā is one-sixth of a padma;
having set aside two parts from the five parts of the vedikā for the front and back, the lotus garland (padmāvalī) is formed by the remaining three parts.
Then, below the altar ledge on the outside, one should arrange lotus petals and a carpet of *dūrvā* grass;
there shall be three enclosures and a gateway arch, and the seat for the preceptor is situated to the north.
The seat for the *argha* offering and the seat for the *homa* should be placed to the left and right, respectively, of the preceptor’s seat.

In the *pauṣṭika* rite, there are two cubits [in size]; the lotus, the lips, and so forth are divided into twelve parts and so on; the wheel is in the pericarp (*kaṇikā*); on the petals are the symbols such as garments and the like;
in the corners are the symbols such as Locanā and the others;
and on the pedestal (*vedikā*) is a row of wheels.
The remainder is exactly as in the previous ritual;
thus, the pacifying fire-pit (kuṇḍa) is bow-shaped, cut in the middle,
with a lotus twelve finger-breadths wide in the center and a depression half that size.

The lips and all other parts are as before, divided into twelve and so forth; in the place of the lotus petals are the marks, the palms and fingers, and below the garland on the exterior is the arrangement of dead hair; in the pericarp of the lotus is a knife, and above the pedestal is a series of knives.
The teacher’s seat is shaped like a bow and marked with the *kartṛkā* (scissors) and the time;
as for the five-cornered *śānti* sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), its proportions are such that it is marked with a lotus for pacification (*śānti*) and marked with a wheel for nourishment (*puṣṭi*).
Upon the five-cornered altar-platform (vedikā), there should be a row of swords and the central emblem of a sword;
outside, at the bottom, one should fashion a garland of crow feathers made of clay.
The exterior is black in color, decorated with the leaves of the *bhūta* tree;
it is a triangle where each side from corner to corner measures one cubit (*hasta*), and the inner lotus, extending twenty fingers from the corner to the center, measures one cubit.
By that same measurement, the cavity is ten finger-breadths and half a lotus-unit;
the remainder, such as the lip and so forth, is as before, according to the twelve-part division and other proportions.
On the pedestal (vedikā) is a row of arrows;

below are red lotuses, and on the exterior is an arrangement of red flowers. On the pedestal surrounding the double-sided seven-cornered figure is a row of vajras and goads; the remainder is the color of the triangle.
The womb-symbol (*garbhacihna*) is an arrow within a triangle;
for attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*), it is a thunderbolt-hook (*vajrāṅkuśa*).

A hexagon measuring thirty finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) is placed upon the altar (*vedikā*) above the hexagon; the womb-symbol there is a series of serpent-nooses (*nāgapāśa*), specifically a serpent-noose.
With yellow stalks on the outside and a design of yellow flowers,
the eight-cornered [mandala] is doubled as before;
the central symbol is a vajra-chain.
On the pedestal (vedikā) is a row of vajra-chains;

below it, there are three walls shaped like hexagons, leaving two cubits on all sides. The seat for the preceptor (ācāryāsana), as well as the seats for the water-offering (arghāsana) and the fire-oblation (homāsana), are everywhere in the shape of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa).
The rule for the horizontal division is according to the measurement from corner to corner of the pits.
Now the nature of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) is described: here, the pit for pacification (śānti) has the nature of the moon and is marked with the sign of the sun;
the pit for nourishment (puṣṭi) is double that of the moon and, because it is twice the dimension of the sun-subject (dharmi), is marked with the sign of the moon;
the pit for killing (māraṇa) has the characteristic of Rāhu and is marked with the sign of the fire of time (kālāgni).
The *uccāṭana* (expulsion) pit has the characteristics of air mixed with the nature of fire and is marked with its own symbol;

the triangular pit has the characteristics of the fire of time (*kālāgni*) and is marked with its own symbol; the *ākṛṣṭi* (attraction) pit consists of the qualities of earth and fire and is inscribed with the symbol of a hook.
The hexagon, representing Rāhu and the element Earth, marked with the sign of a serpent,
is the fire-pit for deluding and paralyzing; it is the enclosure of Earth from both Merus, marked with both signs—
such is the rule for the characteristics of the fire-pits.

The practitioner of mantras must understand the previously mentioned rules regarding the postures, sacrificial substances, and so forth; this is the rule of the Blessed One in all the *Yogatantra*, *Yoginītantra*, and other scriptures.

Now, the procedure for the fire sacrifice (*homavidhi*) is described: Having performed the protection of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) within the circle of the ten directions by means of the Wrathful Kings together with their goddesses, and having performed the sprinkling and other rites with the glorious vajras, one who is joined in yoga should offer the water-offering (*argha*) to the Fire-god with water and flowers. Then, having meditated upon [the deity] within the lotus of his own heart—[visualizing him] as having one face, white in color, with two lotus-like hands holding a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*) in the left and a lotus in the right, and situated upon the moon at the crown of the head.

One should meditate upon [the deity] holding a staff and a rosary in his left hand, with beautiful tawny matted hair, tawny eyes, and clad in garments; he has the heart of fire and the moon upon his head, and his stainless hands flash like rays.
Whoever indeed draws that Jñānasattva—omnipresent and of equal flavor—with the hook into his own body, O King, in this way the invocation of the Fire in the sacrificial pit becomes perfect.

Outside, having caused the stakes (kīlakas) to be placed with the previously mentioned mantra-words together with the wrathful deities (krodhas) and goddesses, one should then perform the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and other rites with the syllables *oṃ āḥ hūṃ haḥ phaṭ*. With this, using a blade of *kuśa* grass, one should take scented water from the offering vessel (*arghapātra*) and sprinkle it in the ten directions of the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*). This is the first step. Then, relying on that yoga, having established Vaiśvānara (the Fire-god) in one’s own heart and in the fire-pit, one should offer the *argha* to the Fire with flowers and water. Being joined with that yoga, one should visualize the moon within the lotus of one’s own heart for all ritual actions.
In this rite for all purposes, [the deity] has one face, a dark complexion, four hands, and two feet.
The venerable one has a vajra in his first right hand and a rosary in the second; in his left hands he holds a bell and a lotus;
he has matted hair of a beautiful tawny color.
One with tawny eyes and tawny garments [is used] for all rites.

Having thus produced the *samayasattva* as one who bears the head of Akṣobhya, one should then visualize a moon disc in his heart, and above that, a vajra hook with stainless rays flashing forth, transformed from the seed-syllable *jaḥ*. Having drawn in the *jñānasattva* with that [hook], make it of one flavor (*samarasa*) with the *samayasattva* throughout all its limbs.

Thus, having properly emanated [the deity] from one's own heart into the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) by means of the breath, and having performed the invocation with the vajrāṅkuśa-mudrā to be described, one should establish him upon the pericarp of the lotus with the vajra-fist with the thumb raised.
In the rite of pacification (śānti), he is white in color, clothed, crowned with Amitābha,
holding a lotus and a crystal rosary in his right hands, and holding a water-pot and a conch in his left hands.
In rites for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), he holds a wheel and a rosary of pearls in his right hands,
and a lotus and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in his left hands;
in rites for killing (*māraṇa*), he is black in color, clothed in garments, and bears Amoghasiddhi as his crown.
In the rites of eradication and inciting hatred, he holds a chopper and a trident in his right hand,
and a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff in his left; alternatively, in these same rites, he holds a sword and a trident in his right hand.
In the case of subjugation (vaśya), he holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff in his left hand, is saffron-colored and clothed,
and holds an arrow and a jewel in his right hand.
In the left [hand] he holds a bow and a mirror,
wears a crown of Ratneśa,
and in the right [hand], for the purpose of summoning, he holds a vajra-hook and a jewel.
In the deluding [mudrā], the left hands hold a vajra-noose and a mirror, while the right hands hold a staff with a serpent; in the wheel-mudgara [mudrā], the left hands hold a wheel and a mallet.

For the rites of immobilization (stambhana) and pinning (kīlana), one should visualize [the deity] as yellow in color, wearing garments, with Vairocana upon his crown, holding a chain and a mallet in his right hands, and a wheel and a vajra-pin in his left hands.

In this practice, first one should kindle the fire with sandalwood for all rites; however, having brought it from a temple for all rites, one should bring it from the house of a Brāhmaṇa for pacification (śānti) and nourishment (puṣṭi), from the house of a Śūdra for killing (māraṇa) and so forth, from the house of a Kṣatriya for subjugation (vaśya) and so forth, from the house of a Vaiśya for paralyzing (stambhana) and so forth, and furthermore, for killing, one should kindle it by bringing it from the house of a Caṇḍāla. For paralyzing, one should use thorny wood; for subjugation, astringent wood;
and for [subjugation], red wood such as Khadira and others.
For pacification (*śānti*), one should use wood from milk-exuding trees (*kṣīravṛkṣa*);

for all rites, one should use fragrant woods such as sandalwood, agallochum, and deodar, or the aforementioned milk-exuding trees and so forth. Then, one should invoke Vaiśvānara with these mantra-words: "Oṃ! Come, come, O best of gods, ṛṣis, and twice-born beings, great element! Taking up your weapon, O you of great radiance, be present here! Vajradhara commands this—svāhā! Having uttered this, one should summon him with the hook-gesture (*aṅkuśamudrā*).
One should cause [the disciple] to enter with the vajra-mudrā,
bind him with the pāśa-mudrā,
and satisfy him with the bell-mudrā to be described below.
For each of these, one should utter the seed-syllables *jaḥ*, *hūṃ*, *vaṃ*, and *hoḥ*.
Then, having sounded the vajra-bell, one should bring [the deity] under control.
Here, half [of the offering] should be given with: *oṃ pravarasatkāraṃ mahāraśmīn pratīccha svāhā*.
Thus is the mantra for the offering of water (argha).

Then follows the worship itself: "Vajragandhaṃ pratīccha svāhā" (Accept the vajra-fragrance, svāhā), "Vajrapuṣpaṃ pratīccha svāhā" (Accept the vajra-flower, svāhā), "Vajradhūpaṃ pratīccha svāhā" (Accept the vajra-incense, svāhā), "Vajradīpaṃ pratīccha svāhā" (Accept the vajra-lamp, svāhā), "Vajranaivedyaṃ ga. huṃ hūṃ haḥ, bho. huṃ hiḥ, cha. huṃ hraḥ."

ka. tathā tadyo; ca. piṅgaṃ; kha. ga. dhāraṇa; ca. ‘ca’ is absent; ka. kha. cha. sara; bho. gharam; cha. ‘ehi’ is absent; ga. bhaveti; ca bho. hoḥ; bho. the reading “vajra akṣataṃ pratīccha svāhā” is additional. [In this] chapter, verse [section]: the Great Chapter on the Mandala Consecration: *pratīccha svāhā*, *vajralāsyaṃ pratīccha svāhā*, *vajrahāsyaṃ pratīccha svāhā*, *vajravādyaṃ pratīccha svāhā*, *vañcanṛtyaṃ pratīccha svāhā*, *vajragītaṃ pratīccha svāhā*, *vajrakāmaṃ pratīccha svāhā*.

Thus, with the aforementioned substances, one should perform worship in the context of the fire-offering (*agnipūjā*) using these mantra-words ending in *svāhā* according to the ritual procedure; however, the rule is that in the case of the mandala, they end in *namaḥ*. Having thus presented all the water for washing the feet (*pādya*), the Vajrācārya, remaining in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) according to the ritual procedure with the previously mentioned sacrificial wood (*samidh*) and other materials, and the previously mentioned oblation-substances, following the previously described method for the seat.

After burning the sacrificial wood with his hand, he should then cause all the oblation-substances to be offered as oblations (*āhuti*) from the offering vessel (*āhutipātrī*) using the *śruva* ladle.
In the absence of that [fire], one should perform the oblation (*homa*) into the mouth of the fire with one's own hand, using the thumb as the "boon-granting" gesture; this is the rule.
Here, the purification of Vaiśvānara is described:
in this context, Vaiśvānara is threefold—namely, the *dakṣiṇāgni*, the *gārhapatya*, and the *āhavanīya*.
In this context, the Dakṣiṇāgni is lightning,
the Gārhapatya is the sun,
and the Āhavanīya is the consumer of raw flesh.
The fourth fire is Truth, whose nature is knowledge and bliss;
therefore, all oblations are offered below it.
Thus, the Vedānta also says: "I cast away the flesh-eating fire far off; let it go to the realm of Yama, carrying away the enemy."

"Right here let this other Jātavedas, knowing [the way], carry the oblation to the gods" (Ṛgveda)—such is the meaning of the Vedic passage; here too, the meaning is the same. [b] As for the flesh-eating Agni:

By this mantra-phrase—*oṃ sarvapāpadahanavajrāgni vajrasattva sarvapāpaṃ daha daha svāhā*—according to the rule, there is the invocation of the fire of desire (*kāmāgni*). Likewise, here the mantra for the fire that carries the oblation (*havyavāhana*) for the sun is:
*oṃ vajrānala sarvabhūtān jvālaya sarvān bhasmīkuru sarvajanaduṣṭān hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*; by this rule, [there is the invocation] of the sun.
He alone is the Lord of the Seven Days, possessing seven horses and a chariot; "seven-tongued" according to the distinction of the days:

in pacification (*śānti*), he has the tongue of the Moon; in nourishment (*puṣṭi*), the tongue of the Sun; in killing (*māraṇa*), expulsion (*uccāṭana*), and creating enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), the tongue of Saturn (*Śani*); in subjugation (*vaśya*), the tongue of Venus (*Śukra*); in attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*), the tongue of Jupiter (*Bṛhaspati*); in delusion (*mohana*), the tongue of Mercury (*Budha*); and in paralyzing (*stambhana*), the tongue of Mars (*Maṅgala*). Thus, through the purification of each individual day, he has a single face for each respective rite.
The rule is that he has two feet through the purification of day and night,
and four arms through the purification of the four twilights; however, in rites such as pacification, while in the rite of killing, he has two arms through the purification of Ketu.
Kartika holds a skull in his hand;
furthermore, for the purpose of causing enmity (vidveṣa), there is an alternative rule that he holds a sword and a skull in his hands through the purification of Saturday.
On Saturday, by means of the division into the first and second halves,
in all rites, through the purification of Rāhu and the purification of Kālāgni, because of the nature of arising and dissolution,
the deity is both the fire of desire and the Āhavanīya fire, owing to its pervasiveness on all days.
"The fire of gnosis" is to be worshipped by the Vajrācārya according to the previously mentioned ritual; such is the rule for the invocation of Vaiśvānara.
ga. cha. Having sounded all musical instruments (*sarva-vādyaṃ vādayitvā*), bho.
One should offer the oblation with the vessel for the pouring of offerings (*āhuti-pātryā arpayet*).
ka. kha. ga. cha. Its meaning is as follows:
O! *pragrāhaḥ* (Rab hZin):
ka. kha. read *prajādityaḥ*; ga. cha. read *pravahati prajādibhyaḥ*;
ga. reads *sarvam*.
Ka. Kārttika, Ga. Pūrvāparārdha.

Now the fire-offering (homa), mudrās, and so forth are described—in the *Vimalaprabhā*, in the section on Consecration: One should perform the fire-offering into the mouth of the fire with the thumb of the hand displaying the boon-granting gesture (*varada-mudrā*), and with the vajras and limbs of the Lord; [using] hundreds of arrows as sacrificial fuel (*samidh*), along with grain, dūrvā grass, ghee, and milk.
Seated in the cross-legged posture, tranquil, with a steady heart, the preceptor—versed in mantra, embodying the mantra, and holding the vajra of action—offers oblations once again to the fire.
Regarding the passage beginning with "with the thumb" (*aṅguṣṭhena*),

when there is an absence of a ladle (*śruvaka*) here, the Vajrācārya, seated upon the previously mentioned seat, should turn his left hand palm-upward and, with the thumb of his right hand, move the oblation substance and offer it into the mouth of Vaiśvānara, whose mouth has been expanded; and he [the deity] should be visualized as consuming it.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations with five hundred fuel-sticks using these [mantras]: *vajrai rīti oṃ āḥ hūṃ ho haṃ kṣaḥ svāhā*.
Then, for the limbs,
[recite] "aṅgāya hla hra ṛ hrīṃ hrāṃ hrāḥ svāhā" one hundred and eight times.
By virtue of the word "and" (ca), [the mantra] consists of one hundred and eight repetitions with these: "pañcaskandhair dhātubhir a ā i ī ṛ ṝ u ū la la aṃ aḥ svāhā."
Likewise, with the twelve sense-bases (*āyatana*), [one recites] "a ā e ai ar ār o au al ālū aṃ aḥ svāhā" one hundred and eight times.
Then, with the organs of action (*karmendriya*) together with their objects, [one recites] "ha hā yayā rarā vavāla lā haṃ haḥ svāhā."
By these one hundred and eight [mantras],
five hundred and forty are thus comprised under the designation of "five hundred";
for each, the mantra should be recited one hundred and eight times.
The thirty-two major marks (*lakṣaṇa*), the eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*), and—

excluding from those one hundred and twelve the bases of knowledge of body, speech, and mind— the remaining one hundred and eight [are represented] in the rosary: the central bead (*meru*) and the four faces.
Therefore, for all rites, one hundred and eight measures should be used in every homa for the sake of accumulating merit.

Then, even the sacrificial materials such as grain and so forth should be offered according to this very same procedure; the homa should be performed with grain, *dūrvā*, clarified butter, and milk, divided into these one hundred and eight portions, by means of the faces and other [limbs].

The fuel-sticks (*samidhaḥ*) and the offerings (*śasyāni*), smeared with clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and milked *durvā* grass, are to be offered. Then, having filled the vessel with clarified butter while reciting the *hṛdayamantra*, the preceptor (*ācārya*), seated upon a couch, tranquil, with a steady heart, knowing the mantras, and being the embodiment of the mantra, who is like a vajra in his ritual action, again offers it to the one with the crest-lock (*śikhin*). Having given the offering of clarified butter with this mantra—*oṃ h kṣ m l v r ya~*—he then takes consecrated water and performs the rite for well-being (*svastyayana*).

Reciting: *Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svāhā | Namaḥ devebhyaḥ | Svasti prajābhyaḥ | Svāhā rājabhyaḥ | Svadhā pitṛbhyaḥ | Alaṃ bhūtebhyaḥ | Vaṣaṭ indrāya*, he should step outside the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), cast that water and rice-offering outside, perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) there, and then re-enter the maṇḍala-hall. He should also perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth for the fire with water infused with *kuśa* grass, using this mantra:
*Oṃ āḥ hūṃ kāyavākcittasvabhāvaśuddha svāhā*.
At the time of kindling the sacrificial pit, one must not blow on it with the mouth;
rather, for the purpose of inflaming the fire, one should do so by means of the wind from a fan or similar instruments.
|| Herein: Hṛ. Kaṃ Hrīṃ Hrāṃ Hrā; Ga. Hṛhuṃ Hra. Hrīṃ Hrāṃ Haḥ; Ca. Hṛ. Hṛ. Kṛṃ Hrīṃ Hrāṃ Hraḥ; Bho. Hlīṃ Hrīṃ Hrāṃ Hrīṃ Hrāṃ Hraḥ (the six aggregates).
Sarva, Ca. ‘Sa’ is not present.
And: there is no "svāhā," nor are there [other] knowledges; it is milk mixed with sour gruel.
Huṃ ga.
Here, there is no breath from the mouth.

In the [relevant] chapter, verse [number]: The Great Chapter on the Initiation into the Maṇḍala. Having performed the fire-oblation (homa) in sequence, and likewise having offered the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) to both the fire and himself, and having offered perfumes and incense, he should then dismiss the fire of gnosis (jñānāgni) from the lotus of his own heart.

Afterwards, the glorious Guru, a treasury of all virtues, bestows the initiation upon the disciple; first, for the sake of purification, he gives the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) empowered by the vajra of the supreme Jina.

Having thus performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) in sequence, and having likewise offered water for sipping (*ācamana*) to both the fire and himself, he should offer perfumes and other articles according to the previously mentioned order. Then, once again, he should dismiss the Fire of Knowledge (*jñānavahni*) from the lotus of his own heart by means of exhalation, with the mantra:

*oṃ jaḥ gaccha gaccha mahāraśmi svasthānaṃ saṃtṛpto 'ho punarāgamiṣyasi devāsya yadāhvayāmi svāhā*. Having thus dismissed the Fire of Knowledge, the Guru—who is a treasury of all virtues—then bestows the consecration (*seka*) upon the disciple according to the sequence to be described.

For the purpose of the consecration (sekā), first [prepare] the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) empowered by the vajra of the supreme Victor with the mantra *oṃ āḥ hūṃ ho haṃ kṣaḥ*. Having thus consecrated the five nectars seven times, one should place them in a pearl-oyster shell or a conch-shell.
Thus, for the sake of purification, the pill of the five lamps should be prepared in that very conch shell;
this must first be accomplished for the purpose of the seven empowerments— such is the Lord’s rule regarding the procedure for the fire sacrifice in all tantras.

Now, the meditative absorption for the consecration of the maṇḍala is described: When the fire sacrifice with one’s own mantra has been accomplished, when the colored powder has fallen, and when the mantra-symbols have been placed in the corners, the master—facing east and surrounded by five white crystal jars—should draw forth the wisdom-circle (jñānacakra) with the wrathful kings arising from the vajra-lotus and make it of one flavor with the colored powder for the sake of the consecration.
By the words "Siddhe" and so forth, [it is meant that] when the fire-oblation (*homa*) has been accomplished here, by means of "one's own mantras"— that is,

the mantras taught in one's own *tantra* as well as those mentioned in the numerous *Yoginītantras* permeated by the practice of *kriyāyoga*— when the fire-oblation has been accomplished according to the procedure taught in the *tantra* of one's own mantras.

At the first homa, when the powder has been cast within one's own mandala and the circle of the womb (*garbhacakra*) for the host of deities has been provided, crystal-white jars should be placed in the corners according to the procedure taught in one's own Tantra; they are wrapped with five threads for the sake of pacification (*śānti*). The remainder [of the ritual] is performed according to the previously mentioned procedure: [the jars] are wrapped with five threads and their necks are bound with cloth. Among the rites of the five jars, the *jayakalaśa* is placed on the eastern ground outside the mandala.
Above that is the sixth, the Victorious Conch (*vijayaśaṅkha*).
Furthermore, for the purpose of the ten vases, there are eight jars in the eight directions. Jaya and Vijaya are two finger-widths outside the eastern and western vases.
*Bhoḥ! Hoḥ!*
ga. the mark, cha. bho huṃ ga. the pill, ca, the pill.
ga. ca. The ritual for the *rajo-maṇḍala* (powder mandala).
cha. Thus [ends].
ga. *svatantraḥ* svaśca svatantraiśca ga. ca. bho, cihna, the reading found in the root text is *mantracihne*; ga. ca śānto.
In the *ga*, *ca*, and *śeṣa* [recensions], as well as according to the previous rule,
the word "eight" (*aṣṭa*) is not present.

Sixth: Regarding the external *Vimalaprabhā* [commentary], concerning the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), there is the Great Victorious Vase (*mahāvijayakalaśa*) upon the previously mentioned Victorious Vase (*jayakalaśa*), and the conch is the eleventh; such is the rule for the vases.
Likewise, in a vessel of a hundred thousand [measures], there is the great victorious conch for pacification, nourishment, and all rites;
and for fierce rites, the skull-cup.
For subjugation (*vaśya*) and other rites, [the vessel] should be made of copper; for paralyzing (*stambhana*), a golden shell; and for enchanting (*mohana*) and so forth, a bronze bowl (*sarāva*).

Having placed them there, wrapped them with threads according to their respective functions, and fashioned cloth neck-threads, they should be installed by the preceptor with their openings adorned with sprouts.

Therein, the preceptor, seated facing the east, having performed the confession of sins and so forth according to the method of practice to be described, and having performed the *maṇḍalarājāgrī*, the *karmarājāgrī*, the *binduyoga*, and the *sūkṣmayoga*, he then—by means of the wrathful kings arisen from the union of wisdom and skillful means (prajñopāya) and born from the vajra and lotus—should, according to the ritual for the practitioner of the sādhana, draw [the deities] in with the syllable *jaḥ*, cause them to enter with the syllable *hūṃ*, and bind them with the syllable *vaṃ* by means of these mantra-words: *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*.

Having gratified the Knowledge Wheel (*jñānacakra*) with the syllable *HOḤ*, and having meditated upon the Pledge Wheel (*samayamaṇḍala*) within the powder mandala (*rajomaṇḍala*), one brings them into a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) for the sake of initiation.

Then, having performed the consecration (*pratiṣṭhāpana*) and offered the water of honor (*argha*) according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should supplicate thus: "Oṃ ĀḤ HŪṂ HOḤ! O Lord of the Three Realms, Kālacakra, accept this *argha*; O Blessed One, together with your retinue, be the granter of boons to me and to the disciples. Having thus supplicated, one should offer the *argha* after drawing a mandala outside the powder mandala.

Then, having made another mandala one cubit in size in front of the Vijaya-kalaśa, one should cause the previously mentioned perfumes and other offerings, as well as the water for the feet (pādya), to be presented there.
In this manner, the food offering (naivedya) and other items should be given to each deity in all the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Flowers and other such items must not be placed on the ground of colored powder outside the colored powder mandala in any direction.
If there is a loss of powder once the mandala has been established, it results in the destruction of the stupa due to that loss of powder;
therefore, outside the mandala at the eastern gate, the casting of flowers should be performed upon the victory-vase (vijayakalaśa) for the purpose of examining the family (kula).
Otherwise, how could the flower thrown by the disciple fall within the thousand-cubit mandala?
As before, having emitted rays of light, the vajra-flame also extends there for one hundred and twenty-five cubits;
how else could the flower leap over that [flame] and fall in the directions of the family-clans without the empowerment of the deity?
Therefore, having made the five symbols upon the victory flask (*vijayakalaśa*), the throwing of flowers therein as will be described later must be performed;
by that [act], the fragrances and so forth are outside the mandala, not on the ground of colored powders (*rajobhūmi*).

Thus, when the King of Wrath has entered the disciple, he—whose hands are adorned with weapons—reduces to a hundred fragments whatever is stationary or moving that he strikes; and whomsoever from the host of Māras who obstructs the Dharma he threatens with his index finger, he causes to fall to the ground and brings to a state of motionlessness.
Furthermore, with his feet in the *pratyālīḍha* stance and various hand-gestures (*karaṇa*), he performs the "Vajra Dance."

In this context, a disciple who previously knew nothing of the characteristics of dance (*nāṭyalakṣaṇa*), being possessed by anger, performs the *vajranṛtya* in the intermediate space through various gestures (*karaṇa*); thus he dances,
and then he laughs.
Then, even for the enemy— the host of Māras— it becomes mixed with the syllable *huṃ*; likewise,
that disciple who was previously ignorant, once possessed by wrath, performs a song through the accessible sounds of humans and others,
as it has been stated in many other tantras.

Therefore, one possessed by the King of Wrath becomes shameless and fearless due to the power of his qualities and the nature of wrath; and because the other deities are gentle, such as Locanā and the rest—[the question arises: where then are those deities? ka kha.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the rule for the possession (*āveśa*) by the wrathful kings beginning with *Saumya*:
here too, the ten fundamental natures (*prakṛti*) of the other ten wrathful deities are to be understood through the binding of mudrās;
whichever sign arises for which deity, that becomes its "seizing mudrā" (*haratamudrā*).
The rule is that he must be known by her. || 88 ||

Now, the empowerment of the body and so forth of the Wrathful King or the Bodhisattva is described: through the entry into the body, the yogi performs bodily actions by the power of his innate qualities; through the entry into speech, he becomes a victorious speaker among gods, nāgas, and asuras; through the entry into the mind, everything residing in the hearts of others—past and future—is known; and through the entry into gnosis, he becomes a Buddha, a teacher of teachers, possessing great majesty and the sole instructor. (89)

By the words beginning with "kāya," it is meant here that the yogi, having entered the body and being empowered by the vajra of the deity’s body, performs bodily actions according to the influence of the qualities of *prakṛti*—that is, from a nature that is either fierce or peaceful.

Just as the wrathful Bodhisattvas perform the act of traveling through space, so too does the disciple perform the act of traveling to the subterranean realm (*pātāla*), manifests invisible mandalas and the like, and causes mountains to rise; thus he performs such bodily actions, being empowered by the divine vajra of the deity’s body.

Likewise, through the possession of speech (*vāg-āveśa*), the proponent becomes victorious over the three worlds—over gods, *nāgas*, and *asuras*—just as Mañjuśrī; and it is a fixed rule that even a fool disciple becomes empowered by the vajra-speech of the deity.

Similarly, through the possession of the mind of a divine deity (*divya-devatā-cittāveśa*), the disciple knows everything residing in the hearts of others—the past, future, present, and all that is unseen; such is the rule regarding the possession of the mind.

Now, if by the power of latencies from previous births there occurs at some point an immersion into knowledge (*jñānāveśa*), then one attains accomplishment in the mandala and becomes a Buddha; he becomes even the Guru of Gurus, an attainer of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), and a lord of the ten stages (*daśabhūmīśvara*).
"Buddha" is here a figurative expression (*upacāra-vacana*).
Even for a single teacher who possesses supernatural powers (ṛddhimat), there is likewise this fixed rule regarding the characteristics of the empowerment of body, speech, mind, and gnosis. || 89 ||

[213b] Now, the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) by Locanā and the others is described: Through the penetration (*āveśa*) of Earth, the yogi becomes like a mountain; through the penetration of Water, he attains coolness; through the penetration of Fire, he undergoes burning; and through the penetration of Wind, he likewise undergoes drying.

Through the penetrations of Emptiness (*śūnya*), he becomes invisible upon the surface of the earth and attains the state of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*). In this way, all things such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth are to be understood sequentially according to the power of the qualities of the primary elements (*prakṛti-guṇa*). || 90 ||
By the words "the earth" and so forth,
it is meant that here, when a disciple is empowered by the entry into the earth-element as a yogin, he becomes like a mountain; he cannot be moved by hundreds of men,
and the cold of water passes away [from him].
In this case, the yogin empowered by Māmakī embraces even one seized by a burning fever and makes him free from that fever; thus,
there is no "king" (rājā).
O Vajra-speech, this is the body.
Ga yaḥ ga
and "non-existent" (asan) ga.
And may fever depart.

And this does not exist; it does not exist in the chapter [on] verses 89–92.

Regarding the Great Chapter on the Maṇḍala Initiation: when one undergoes combustion here through the possession (*āveśa*) of Vāyu and becomes presided over by Pāṇḍaravāsinī, then whatever one touches, that is burned;
thus, being presided over by the possession of Māruta, one likewise undergoes desiccation.
Whomever he embraces, he causes to be transported many yojanas away;
thus, through the descents of emptiness, he becomes invisible,
and whomever he touches, that person alone becomes invisible.
The rule is that one attains the state of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*) upon the surface of the earth;
thus, everything here is to be understood according to the influence of the qualities of *prakṛti*.
When the descent of the divine eye occurs, then one sees a divine form and even unseen substances.
When there is an immersion into the divine faculty of hearing, one hears the sounds of sentient beings that have not been heard before;
when there is an immersion into the divine mind, one knows the knowledge of others' minds;
when there is an immersion into the divine body-faculty, one perceives divine touch and knows former abodes.
When there is the descent of the divine tongue, then there is the tasting of divine flavors,
and by that, the supernatural power of moving through space occurs;
when there is the descent of the divine nose, then one perceives divine fragrances.
By that, there is the empowerment of all Buddhas; this is the rule. ||90||

Now, the characteristic signs of the arising of divine possession (*divyāveśa*) are described: O Lord of Men, possession indeed occurs for practitioners of mantra through the power of meditation, sometimes by various types of service, and sometimes through the recitation of mantras and other practices according to the manifold rules, as well as by the tasting of the intellect.

For a worthy son within the maṇḍala, it occurs through the power of nectar; however, for practitioners of mantra who lack self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), there is no accomplishment (*siddhi*) despite many and various worldly existences. (91)
By the words "possession" (*āveśa*) and so forth,
[it is meant that] he who possesses divine possession here belongs exclusively to the practitioners (*mantrin*) and teachers (*ācārya*),

through the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) by means of various types of prior service (*pūrva-sevā*), by means of many kinds of methods, by means of the various pledges (*samaya*) being guarded— such as the drops of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta-bindu*) and so forth— and likewise by means of mantra-recitation (*jāpa*) and other practices; thus does possession occur.
Otherwise, it does not occur;

thus, O Lord of Men— this is the address— it sometimes happens for a worthy son in the mandala due to the power of nectar, when tasted by a purified disciple through the succession of the lineage of gurus.
Without self-consecration, there is no accomplishment for mantra-practitioners through the many various paths of existence,
up to the Akaniṣṭha realm; that which has been taught by the Tathāgatas as mundane is, in this context, the descent of the divine ones.
There are other infinite entries (āveśa) belonging to spirits (bhūta), rākṣasas, servants (ceṭaka), and so forth;

their characteristics are to be explained in the fifth chapter on the attainment of knowledge (jñānasiddhi). Furthermore, the characteristic of the Guru’s command was not mentioned here during the entry into the mandala; such is the rule of the Blessed One. || 91 ||

Now, the pacification of the possession (*āveśa*) and so forth is described: After the possession has been released, one who possesses the three vajras (*trivajra*) should perform protection (*rakṣā*) by the Jinas at the head, heart, crown, navel, throat, and secret place, according to their respective family origins.

Then, for the sake of concealment, the initiation of the disciple—who has been given yellow garments and whose eyes are covered—should take place here. Furthermore, those vows that have reached the supreme state should be bestowed upon him. || 92 ||
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the passage beginning with "having abandoned," etc.:
here, when the disciple is empowered by the wrathful deities and so forth, he should then be asked by the master whatever task is desired;
thereafter, having consecrated a flower with the three syllables *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*, it should be placed upon his head.
Then he abandons the possession and goes to his own place;
thus he becomes one whose possession has been relinquished.

Then, after the abandonment of the attire, protection is performed on the head according to the words of the Jinas: with the syllable *Oṃ* on the head, with *Hūṃ* at the heart, and with *Haṃ* on the crown (*uṣṇīṣa*). This is by means of the three vajras of one's own body, speech, and mind for the Upāya.
Likewise, with *Ho* at the navel, *Āḥ* at the throat, and *Kṣaḥ* at the secret place; this is by means of the three vajras of one's own body, speech, and mind for the Prajñā.
In this regard, concerning the vajras of the body, speech, and mind of both, the long *Hūṃ* is the Vāgvajra, and the short [Hūṃ] is the Cittavajra.
Elsewhere, having performed protection over that which exists there, the entry of the disciple into this mandala—while wearing yellow garments and with eyes covered—is to be described.
First, for the sake of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), the vows (*vrata*) up until enlightenment;
"conventional truth" refers to the accumulation of merit and so forth. For the sake of that, for that purpose, those [vows] are said to have proceeded to the most excellent state.

The preeminent Tathāgatas of the Fortunate Aeon (Bhadrakalpa), beginning with the seven starting from Vipaśyin and ending with Śākyamuni, have as their destination the accumulation of merit, ethical discipline, and gnosis. Whatever has gone to that destination is indeed "gone to the preeminent destination" (*pravaragatigata*); these are what must be given by the teacher to the disciple—this is the rule of the Tathāgatas. || 92 ||

In that regard, the Blessed One has declared the vows to be maintained until the end of enlightenment: "Abandon violence, untruth, and another’s wife; likewise, abandon the wealth of self and others, and the drinking of intoxicants. These five are sins, a noose of Vajra in cyclic existence, and the destruction of one's own merit. This command of the Lord of the Universe—which destroys the fear of existence—should be given under the names of those who have appeared at various times as teachers of gods and men, and it must be observed by you as well. (93)

Violence, untruth, another’s wife, one’s own or another’s wealth, and likewise the drinking of intoxicants—these five are the *vratas* (vows); the meaning is that they constitute a *niyama* (rule). Why? Because in this world, these five sinful actions are like a diamond snare that destroys one’s own merit; therefore, the rule is that they must not be committed.

"To whom does [this] belong? To the Universal Lord (Viśvabhartṛ). It should be given under the name of whichever Tathāgata, the teacher of gods and men, appeared at that time. This command of the Universal Lord, which crushes the fear of existence, must be observed by you as well, just as it has been observed by sons of noble family and daughters of noble family for the sake of the accumulation of merit; such is the Tathāgata’s rule regarding the five precepts. || 93 ||

Gambling, eating forbidden food, reciting wicked words, killing a living being, and the five types of slaughter—of a bull, a deity, a lord, a cow, a child, a woman, or a man—as well as treachery toward friends, masters, the Teacher of the gods and men (the Buddha), the Saṅgha, and those who trust him, and the attachment of the sense faculties: these are the fifty transgressions of the Lord of the World.
The Great Chapter on the Maṇḍala Initiation [2152]: Then, if he so desires, other things should be given up.

In that regard, one should not engage in gambling, the consumption of blameworthy food, the recitation of evil speech mentioned previously, the dharma of spirits, ancestral rites, sacrificial rites as prescribed in the Vedas, the dharma of the Daityas, or the dharma of the Mlecchas; these are the five secondary sins (*upapāpaka*).

Likewise, among the ten [sins] of the past and future, one should never commit the first five killings: the killing of a cow, the killing of a child, the killing of a woman, the killing of a man, and the killing of the teacher of the thirty gods and of men—that is, of a statue or a stūpa; such is the agreement regarding the latter [set of] killings.

Similarly, one should not commit the five [sins] of treachery: treachery against a friend, treachery against a lord, treachery against the Buddha, treachery against the Saṅgha, and treachery against those who trust one. Thus it is said.
Likewise, "attachment of the sense faculties" refers to attachment to forms, attachment to sounds, attachment to smells, attachment to tastes, and attachment to tactile objects.

These twenty-five vows of Vajrasattva, the Lord of the World, must be observed by the disciples; thus, they are to be bestowed by the Vajrācārya upon the disciples at the time of initiation. This is the rule for the bestowal of the vows. || 94 ||

Now the entry into the mandala is described: Having consecrated [the flower] with the glorious mantra, one should place a single flower in the hollow of the hands; first, having rotated it three times, the release of the flower from the hollow of the hands occurs upon the mandala.

O Lord of Men, in whichever place the beautiful flower falls, that is certainly his family-line. Afterwards, the sevenfold initiation, here of three types—namely the Unsurpassed (anuttara)—should be bestowed. || 95 ||

With the words "By the glorious mantra," and so forth, it is taught here that first, immediately after the bestowal of the vow, one should bind the face with either a yellow cloth or a red cloth for all rites. For rites such as pacification (*śānti*), one should use a fine cloth of the color corresponding to the deity's color, while reciting this mantra: *oṃ dvādaśāṅganirodhakāriṇe hūṃ phaṭ*.
Then, having closed the eyes and other senses, and having circumambulated the circle three times starting from the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra),
the preceptor stands at the eastern gate in the form of the Leader.
If the deity has arisen within the mandala with the left leg extended in the pratyālīḍha posture and so forth, then the preceptor, having also risen, bestows the consecration upon the disciple.
Then, when they have sat down, the preceptor seated there bestows [the initiation].

Having performed the sprinkling with conch-water upon the head of the disciple entrusted by the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), he should place a single flower consecrated seven times with the three syllables *oṃ āḥ hūṃ* into the hollow of the disciple’s cupped palms. Then, for the sake of the purity of the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), he should release the flower from the hollow of the cupped palms onto the victory-vase (*jayakalaśa*) above the mandala according to the previously mentioned rule. Simultaneously, he should remove the blindfold according to the aforementioned regulation.
Then, having first performed the "release of the flower" (*puṣpā-mokṣa*), one should subsequently remove [the blindfold] with this mantra: *oṃ divyendriyāṇyudghāṭaya svāhā*.

Having thus performed the opening of the eyes, the deity in whichever location the well-placed flower—consecrated with the three-syllable mantra—falls upon becomes that person's family deity (*kuladevatā*).
It is the rule that through her, the accomplishment of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) is attained.

Then, having shown him the family deity (*kuladevatā*), afterwards follows the sevenfold consecration beginning with water; here, as there are three types [of consecration] such as that from the vase (*kalaśa*) and so forth, so too, after worshipping the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), the unsurpassed [consecration] to be described should be entered—this is the rule for the master (*ācārya*) established by the Tathāgata. || 95 ||

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, the procedure for the seven empowerments is now stated: "O King, with four [substances] from a serpent, or with water-pots made of clay or clay mixed with gems, herbs, and perfumes, one should bathe the goddesses in the *jaya* and *vijaya* pots. The excellent Guru bestows the crown according to the divisions of the Buddhas, and the turban according to the Śaktis. The vajra and bell, the sun and moon, and the vow are to be joined with the sense objects and the sense faculties. (96)

Regarding the passage beginning with "by the *nāgas*," here it means by eight or four *nāgas*, that is, by victory (*jaya*) and triumph (*vijaya*) jars; or by five victory jars and five triumph jars in the case of eight jars; or by three victory jars and three triumph jars in the case of four jars; [these being] jars of jewels or gold, or in their absence, jars made of clay or *sarala* wood.

Regarding the phrase "with herbs and fragrant substances," therein the herbs are to be collected according to the previously mentioned *Gandhakakṣapuṭa* with their respective parts, such as two and so forth; from among the twenty-five [herbs], five should be taken by the Master as available, according to the procedure taught in the Root Tantra (*Mūlatantra*).

In that regard, the Blessed One said: "O King, one should place the medicinal herbs in the incense box in sequence, with five groups of five beginning with Brāhmī and the others, according to the parts [determined] by the eyes, the moon, fire, and so forth."
Brāhmī, Nārāyaṇī, Raudrī, Īśvarī, Parameśvarī,
Aindrī, Lakṣmī, Vārāhī, Kaumārī, and likewise Carcikā.
The Earth, Vāruṇī, Jyotis, Vāyavī, and likewise Khecarī;
the Mother, the Sister, the Daughter, the Niece, and likewise the one born of oneself.
The Brāhmaṇī, Kṣatriṇī, Veśyā, Śūdrī, and likewise the Ḍombī are thus remembered;
these medicinal herbs always bestow great siddhis, enjoyment, and supernatural powers.

Thus, the manifest names of these [plants] are now stated: here, Brāhmī is *brahmadaṇḍī* (part 2), Nārāyaṇī is *viṣṇukrāntā* (part 1), Raudrī is *rudrajaṭā* (part 3), Īśvarī is well-known (*prasiddhā*) (part 4), and Parameśvarī is *devadālī* (part 5); this is the first group.

Then the second [set] is described: *aindrī* (Indra’s) is *indravāruṇī*, four parts; *vārāhī* (Boar’s) is *varāhakarṇā*, five parts; *kaumārī* (Kumāra’s) is *adhopuṣpikā*, one part. This is the deposition of the second pentad. The pericarp is two parts. Then the third is described: *pārthivī* (Earth’s) is *muṣalī*, five parts; *vāruṇī* (Varuṇa’s) is *rudantī*, two parts; *jyotiḥ* (Light) is *jyotiṣmatī*, one part; *vāyavī* (Wind’s) is *lajjālu*, three parts; *khecarī* (Sky-walker) is *arkā*, four parts. This is the third pentad.

The Great Chapter on the Maṇḍala Initiation (*maṇḍalābhiṣeka-mahoddeśa*). Thereafter, the fourth arrangement (*nyāsa*) is taught: "Mother" (*mātā*) is *puṭaṃjāra*, one part; "Daughter" (*putrī*) is *kṛtāñjali*, four parts; "Sister's daughter" (*bhāgineyā*) is *ajakarṇā*, five parts; [and] "part" (*bhāga*), two parts—this is the fourth pentad. "Sister" (*bhaginī*) is *sahadevā*, three parts; "one born of oneself" (*svajā*) is *mohanī* (the deluder), *vaṭapatrikā*. Then the fifth arrangement is taught: "Brahmin woman" (*brāhmaṇī*) is *bṛhatī*, four parts; "Kṣatriya woman" (*kṣatriṇī*) is *bhṛṅgarāja*, five parts; "Courtesan" (*veśyā*) is *yaṣṭimadhu*, two parts; "Śūdra woman" (*śūdrī*) is *kaṇṭakārī*, one part; "Ḍombī" is *mayūraśikhā*, three parts—this is the fifth arrangement.

Thus, according to their respective order, the first group of five consists of the collection of grain crops and so forth: *dhānya*, *mahādhānya*, *māṣa*, white *caṇaka* beans, and black sesame seeds;
the second group is: *kodrava*, *mudga* beans, *kalāya* peas, white sesame seeds, and wheat.
The third [group] consists of *mauṭha*, *tripuṭa*, black mustard seeds (*kṛṣṇasarṣapa*), barley (*yava*), and beans (*māṣa*).
The fourth consists of lentils (*masūrikā*), white mustard seeds (*śuklasarṣapa*), *kaṅgu* grain, *tuvarikā*, and *avarvaṭikā*.
The fifth consists of linseed (*atasī*), *varaṭī*, *varṇā*, horse gram (*kulattha*), and black chickpeas (*kṛṣṇacaṇaka*).
Thus, the five grains are to be taken as they are obtained according to the portion of the *kakṣapuṭa*;
here, the number of finger-breadths for the portions follows;
thereafter, the gems are those belonging to the Brahma, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, namely the diamonds (*vajra*).
Likewise, the primary gems are sapphire, ruby, moonstone, karketana, and emerald;
likewise, the metals are gold, silver, copper, steel, iron, and magnetite;
and likewise, the secondary gems are pearl, coral, royal silk, the śūlamaṇi, and the ṣaḍbinduka.
Likewise, the inferior ones— crystal, *jīvajāti*, *ḍoharī*, glass, and green gems—
these are to be taken according to one's means;
furthermore, the gems of the gods and nāgas become five-colored during the great jewel-consecration (*mahāratnābhiṣeka*) of a universal monarch (*ājñācakravartin*).

In the absence of those [precious gems], there is a rule that for the poor, there should be fragrant flowers of five colors; likewise, they may be made of clay or with precious stones. Herein, the green gem is for the *vijaya* conch; the blue gem is for the eastern and western *jaya-vijaya* jars; the black [gem] is for the eastern and southeastern jars; the red [gem] is for the southern and southwestern jars; the white [gem] is for the northern and northeastern jars; the yellow [gem] is for the western and northwestern jars. Likewise, there are iron, magnetite (*ayaḥkānta*), steel (*tīkṣṇa*), copper, silver, and gold.
Likewise, the medicinal herbs (oṣadhyaḥ) are one part in the jar of Jaya and Vijaya,
and two parts in the eastern fire.
It is three parts for Yama and the Daityas, four parts for Uttara and Hari,
and five parts for the West and Vāyu.
Likewise, having placed the varieties of medicinal pills, the grains, the five aforementioned medicinal herbs from the *kakṣapuṭa*,

as well as metals, gems, forest herbs, grains, and fragrant substances into jars, one should again bind them into twenty-five small packets and place them into a victory-conch (*vijayaśaṅkha*) filled with water.

With that [water], one should sprinkle [the disciple] at five places of birth: on the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*), on the right and left shoulder-joints, and likewise on the hip and waist joints. Then, for the purification of the family deity (*kuladevatā*), there is the mantra for casting the flower: *oṃ sarvatathāgatakulaviśodhani svāhā*.
With this mantra, the preceptor causes the disciple to release the flower.
