Then, with this mantra, the unveiling is performed:
*oṃ divyanayanaṃ udghāṭayāmi svāhā*.
Having begun with the central deity, one should show the entire maṇḍala within the maṇḍala of the family deity (*kuladevatā*).

Then, having performed the purification of the lineage at the eastern gate, the preceptor, having led the disciple with his left hand and circumambulated together with the Action-Vajra-holder, leads him to the northern gate. Then, for the sake of purifying the [five] objects of experience (*kāryaviśuddhi*), he takes water from all the ritual jars using the mantras of the goddesses beginning with Tārā, pours it into the victory conch (*vijayaśaṅkha*), and performs the water-consecration (*udakābhiṣeka*) again upon the five places of birth with this mantra: *oṃ ā ī ṝ ū lu pañcadhātuvishodhani svāhā*.

Then, during the crown consecration (*mukuṭābhiṣeka*), one should consecrate [the disciple] at the five places of birth with this mantra: *oṃ a i ṝ u lṛ pañca tathāgatapariśuddha svāhā*. Then, one should fasten a crown of precious gold or a cloth crown.
Through these two consecrations, the purification of the elements (*dhātu*) and aggregates (*skandha*), as well as the purification of the sense-bases (*āyatana*), is accomplished.

Having performed the purification of the body on the ground of the body and speech, one should then lead the disciple by way of the right-hand circuit to the southern door for the sake of purifying speech. There, one should consecrate the disciple at the five places of birth with this mantra during the crown-consecration (*paṭṭābhiṣeka*): *oṃ a ā aṃ aḥ ha hā haṃ haḥ hoḥ pha daśapāramitāparipūraṇi svāhā*.
Then, one should bind a golden band upon a jeweled cloth, or in its absence, a garland of flowers, upon the forehead.
Then, having consecrated [the disciple] at the five places of birth during the Vajra and Vajra-bell initiation with this mantra— *oṃ hūṃ hoḥ sūryacandra viśodhaka svāhā*—
one should place the vajra and vajra-bell upon the head and consecrate [him] with water from a conch shell.

Then, having purified the Speech-Vajra (*vāgvajra*) by means of the two consecrations and having placed the thumb upon the vajra, one should again circumambulate clockwise; then, for the sake of purifying the Mind-Raiment (*cittavastra*), one should consecrate [the disciple] at the five places of birth at the eastern face during the Vajra-Vow Consecration (*vajravratābhiṣeka*) with this mantra: *oṃ a ā e ai ar ār o au al āl viṣayendriyaviśodhani svāhā*. Having bestowed the vajra and bell—which are the command of the Lord of Victors (*jinapati*) made manifest through the wrathful ones, the loving-kindnesses, and so forth—the teacher, possessing the correct measure, should teach the pure Dharma out of supreme compassion.

One should indeed commit the taking of life in the Vajra family; false speech in the Sword [family]; the theft of another’s property in the Jewel [family]; and likewise, the taking of another’s wife in the excellent Lotus family. Then, having offered flowers to the ears and other sense organs, and having consecrated [the disciple] in the five places of birth during the Name-consecration, one should do so with this mantra: *oṃ ha hā ya yā rarā va vā la lā caturbrahmavihāraviśuddha svāhā*.

Then, having tied flower garlands upon the hands and feet— since bracelets, anklets, and so forth are absent— one should perform the consecration by declaring, "You are [the deity] such-and-such. Then, for the purpose of purifying gnosis (*jñāna*), one should dry the cloth of the mind (*cittavastra*) within that *kalaśa* [at the] eye-gate.
ga. purity;
ga. ca. or should bind; ga. cha. garment; ca. vajra.
ga. purification;
ga. ca. having sprinkled;
bho. "vajra" is absent; ga. face.
Six. Huṃ bho. 'Vi' means there is no.
Viśodha.
ga. One should consecrate [the disciple] during the consecration of authorization (anujñābhiṣeka).
bho. [The mantra] "aṃ aḥ" is added.
ga. ca. Having consecrated [him].
ga. hāṭaka;
ka. kha. ga. ca. cha. vajrasattvam iti; in ga. and ca., "vi" is absent.

In the chapter [on the] Great Section on the Mandala Consecration: having performed [the rite], and having again led the disciple by way of the two consecrations in a clockwise direction, one should consecrate him at the western face in the five places of birth during the consecration of authorization with this mantra: *oṃ haṃ kṣaḥ dharmacakrapravartaka svāhā*.

Having bestowed the consecration and purified the vajras of body, speech, mind, and gnosis through the seven consecrations, the preceptor then places the vajra and vajra-bell into the hands of the disciple. Addressing him as "Amukavajra," and having given the vajra and vajra-bell to the two of them, he should teach the pure Dharma with supreme compassion by means of these two and a half verses,
beginning with "One should indeed commit the taking of life in the Vajra family" and ending with "they should be bestowed within the mandala."

Having thus performed the ritual of the seven empowerments in the mandala, the Vajrācārya should then contemplate the Buddha’s blessing upon the disciple. For the sake of determining seniority and juniority, he proclaims the year and so forth: "In this year, such-and-such, during the teaching of the Dharma of King Kalkin; in such-and-such month, on such-and-such full moon day, on such-and-such day of the week, on such-and-such lunar date, under such-and-such constellation, in such-and-such yoga, and in such-and-such karaṇa, I, the Vajrācārya named so-and-so, have empowered the disciple named so-and-so."

In the *Paramādibuddha* or in other mandalas, one who has been prophesied and authorized by me through the seven empowerments [is empowered] for the sake of accomplishing worldly siddhis up to the limit of the Akaniṣṭha realm, as a leader for all sentient beings to attain the fruit of merit and gnosis; such is the rule for the seven empowerments.
Here, in another tantra, it is said that for the introduction of ordinary people, there are five empowerments through the purity of the five Tathāgatas:
the water empowerment by Vairocana and the crown empowerment by Ratnasambhava.
In this regard, there is no contradiction between earlier and later statements;

for in all tantras, it is the Lord’s rule that through the casting of flowers upon the mandala, the disciple’s family deity (kuladevatā) is revealed, and by means of that crowned deity and its corresponding family mudrā, his accomplishment (siddhi) is attained.

Therefore, because of the statement in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*, "He whose crown consists of the nature of the five Buddhas," whichever Tathāgata the flower falls upon becomes the one in the center of the crown,
and not necessarily Ratnasambhava in every case;
likewise, there is no purification by water and so forth in the *Laghutantra*, because another procedure is more powerful.
Now he speaks of the teaching of the pure Dharma, beginning with "one should commit the taking of life," and so forth.
Here, the commitments (*samaya*) such as the taking of life are twofold: according to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) and the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), namely external and internal.

Regarding that, the rule is that when the Blessed One says one should commit the taking of life externally, it refers to those who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*), those who harm the Buddha's teaching, and those who violate the commitments.

Having understood that very same [case of] the five immediate transgressions (*pañcānantarya*) in their prior and subsequent sequence— wherein someone here first commits the five immediate transgressions and later becomes a performer of merit, like Caṇḍāśoka becoming Dharmāśoka— a hell results for the minister from that harmful act due to his lack of discernment regarding auspicious and inauspicious karma. Therefore, as long as the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) have not been attained, the minister must not perform cruel rites, except through the rites of pacification (*śānti*), enrichment (*puṣṭi*), subjugation (*vaśya*), and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*).

In this way, false speech, harming others, taking what is not given, even the taking of another's wife, sexual intercourse with those forbidden by convention or outside one's caste, and even the giving away of one's own body— none of these are for one's own true benefit; such is the reading of all [authoritative sources].
There is no doubt about this,
sir;
(this is the certainty).

In the *Vimalaprabhā*: "Now, when one commits the five immediate transgressions until the end of life, then one should perform the killing of the Blessed One by means of this previously accomplished mantra within the family of Wrath (*krodhakula*) through the meditative absorption of Akṣobhya"—this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
Thus, for the sake of rescuing those who have fallen onto the wrong path, a false statement must be uttered, but not for one's own sake;
likewise, taking what is not given is for the purpose of preventing rebirth in the realm of hungry ghosts (*pretagati*), but not for one's own sake.
Likewise, the taking of another's wife is for the purpose of warding off rebirth in the animal realm and not for one's own sake;
one should partake of the five nectars and so forth for the destruction of the family-grahas.
Thus, for the sake of accomplishing the *karmamudrā*, one should not despise women such as the *ḍombī* and others;
for the accumulation of merit, one gives great gifts.
Having thus accomplished the mantras of the Sword family, the Jewel family, the Lotus family, the Wheel family, and the Knife family, the yogi, endowed with power, may perform everything.
The statement "so that there is no laughter in the world" is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*);

now the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is stated: here, in one's own body, because of the non-transgression of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), there is the "non-killing" (*prāṇātipāta*); one should effect the cessation of the vital breath in the *uṣṇīṣa* within the Vajra family; by that non-killing of the vital breath, the yogi becomes one whose semen flows upward—this is the rule.
And regarding false speech, "false" here refers to speech that is non-abiding;

it is the speech consisting of the cries of all sentient beings according to both the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) and the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), which simultaneously teaches the Dharma to sentient beings. That very [speech] is the rule known as the "unstruck sound" (*anāhatadhvani*) within the heart. Regarding the jewel, this is the property of others.

Regarding the phrase "another's property" (*parasvam*): here, "another" (*para*) is Vajrasattva; his "property" (*svam*) is the jewel, the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*). Its "seizure" (*apaharaṇam*) occurs in the Jewel Family at the throat, the location of the eighth stage; this is the rule. Likewise, in the Lotus Family, "another's wife" (*parastrī*) is to be seized:
"another's wife" is Mahāmudrā, and her "seizure" is the taking of another's wife.

That [power] is to be taken away by one belonging to the Lotus family (kamalakula) at the forehead, which is the location of the tenth stage; this is the rule regarding the "one whose semen flows upwards" (ūrdhvaretas).

Alcohol, lamps, the Buddhas, and all sense objects are to be utilized in the wheel; the *ḍombī* and other women are to be honored in the knife; all women are not to be despised in the boat, and for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, this body along with its wealth must not be preserved by you. O son of noble family, the Conquerors have declared that Buddhahood does not occur otherwise, even after infinite eons. (98)
"Intoxicant, lamps, Buddhas, and all sense objects are to be enjoyed as the wheel"—
here, "intoxicant" refers to innate bliss (*sahajānanda*),
and "lamps" refers to the five sense organs, such as the eyes and so forth.
The Buddhas and the five nectars within one's own body are to be served and consumed in the wheel of the navel-lotus;
externally, this means that the discharge of feces, urine, semen, and tears should be performed—this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Women such as the *ḍombī* and others are not to be despised in the "knife" of the secret lotus; rather, they are to be honored in the lotus of one's own [body], the womb, through churning with celibacy (*brahmacarya*), which externally means by the non-emission of semen—this is the rule.

For the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, one should give away wealth along with sons, wife, and so forth; for the sake of the accumulation of merit, one’s own body should be given away as well.
Likewise, for the sake of the accumulation of ethical discipline (*śīla*), women are not to be despised.
Therefore, in the "Family of the Wheel" (*cakrakula*), there is no [such thing].

The Great Chapter on the Mandala Initiation: Through the accumulation of merit and ethical discipline, as well as the accumulation of gnosis—thus, by means of these three accumulations, you shall attain the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha, O son of noble family, and not otherwise;
this is what has been taught by the Victors over infinite eons. This is the rule for the teaching of the pure Dharma.
In all tantras here. || 98 ||

Now the purification of the initiations is described: Water is the goddesses beginning with Tārā; here, the Victors are the crown; the powers are the hero’s band; the vajra and bell are the sun and moon; the vow is the engagement with the sense objects; the name is the yoga of loving-kindness and so forth; the command is the glory of perfect awakening that crushes the fear of cyclic existence, as integrated within Kālacakra. These seven initiations, which remove the stains of defilement, are to be bestowed in the mandala. (99)

[219] By the passage beginning with "Water is the goddesses Tārā and so forth," it is shown that the water consecration here is the purification and removal of obscurations of the five elements, wind and the rest;
likewise, the crown consecration is the purification of the five aggregates, consciousness and the rest.
The hero’s consecration of the turban consists of the ten powers, such as generosity and so forth, for the sake of fulfilling the perfections (*pāramitā*);
the consecration of the vajra and vajra-bell is the purification of *lalanā* and *rasanā*, which is the removal of the obscurations of the moon and the sun;
the consecration of the vow (*vrata*) is the purification of the sense objects such as form and the sense faculties such as the eyes, which is the manifestation of the divine eye and so forth.

The name-consecration (*nāmābhiṣeka*) consists of the yoga of loving-kindness and so forth through the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), which at all times purifies attachment, aversion, and the like; it is the state of being free from obscurations.

The command-consecration (*ājñābhiṣeka*) is the manifestation of the glory of perfect awakening and the turning of the wheel of Dharma; that teaching of the Dharma crushes the fear of cyclic existence by means of benefiting others.
The rule is that the teaching of emptiness is permeated by Kālacakra and permeated by immutable bliss (*acyutasukha*).

Furthermore, these seven initiations, which remove the stains of defilement, are to be bestowed upon disciples in the mandala by the preceptor; such is the rule of the Tathāgatas regarding the bestowing of the seven initiations for Vajrācāryas. ||99||

Now the fruit of consecration is stated: One who has been consecrated by the seven consecrations, through the power of virtue, attains sovereignty over the seven stages; furthermore, one consecrated by the vase and secret [consecrations] certainly enters the stage of non-retrogression and so forth.

One consecrated by the knowledge of wisdom (prajñājñāna) attains the state of Mañjughoṣa, which crushes the fear of existence. However, if due to the influence of deceit one ever commits a root downfall, this leads to the suffering of hell. || 100 ||
By the words "sprinkled" and so forth,
it means that having been consecrated here by the seven empowerments (*saptābhiṣeka*), one attains mastery over the seven stages (*bhūmi*) through the power of merit upon entering the great mandala,
provided that one directly realizes the mandala-circle; then, by that very body, the seven...
Neither existent nor non-existent, ga.
There is no going.
And in the practice of dwelling in the monasteries.
Kha cha vaite.
And who now [is] the one consecrated seven times?
Then, by this very means,
he attains mastery over the stages of initiation in the *Vimalaprabhā*.

Now, if one dies free from the ten non-virtuous actions, then by the power of that merit, it is a certainty that they attain sovereignty over the seven stages. Through the accumulation of merit, they further enter the stage of the Non-Returner (*avaivartika*) and so forth; being consecrated by the Vase (*kumbha*) and the Secret (*guhya*), and having been consecrated here by these two, they proceed to the Immovable (*acalā*) stage through the power of their ethical discipline.
By the word "etcetera," one goes to the stage of Sādhumatī;
the non-falling of the bodhicitta is Acalā; in the churning of the womb is Sādhumatī, which is the mind of great bliss.

In this regard, one who has been consecrated with the wisdom-knowledge (prajñājñāna-abhiṣeka) attains the state of Mañjughoṣa—which crushes the fear of existence—by the power of the accumulation of ethical discipline (śīla-saṃbhāra);

he proceeds to the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā), and from that Cloud of Dharma comes the rain of great bliss (mahāsukha) which accomplishes both one's own welfare and the welfare of others: such is the rule.
Thus, preceded by the accumulation of merit and ethical discipline, there is the accumulation of gnosis;
from that, Buddhahood for yogins occurs on the twelfth stage—this is the rule of the Tathāgata.

Now, regarding the root [tantra], due to the influence of the deceitful as will be explained, and due to the engagement in the ten unwholesome actions, then all this suffering of the hells arises from the initiation (*sekādi*) and so forth; this is the rule concerning the power of perversion.
[Blank]

Now, the purification of a root downfall is described: The purification of a root downfall indeed occurs for one possessed of qualities who remains for seven days in the *kumbha* [vessel]. There is never purification through the secret [initiation] by force of vows and observances in the higher [initiations].

One who has committed a root downfall enters this mandala again for the sake of purification; having obtained [the status of] kings, he goes once more into the family of the *gaṇas*, [regaining] the name of the eldest and losing his insignificance.
By the words "of the root downfall" and so forth,

it is meant that when a root downfall as will be described here occurs, then for one who possesses qualities and stands within the seven initiations, purification occurs through thirty-six thousand recitations of mantra, provided they subsequently abide in the restraint of non-repetition.

When a root downfall occurs for one who has been consecrated and resides in the "pot" (kumbha) or the "secret" (guhya) [initiation], then, perhaps through the power of vows and observances or the power of the accumulation of merit and virtue, purification may occur; in that case, the preceptor should administer punishment according to the rules of the vow and observance.
Beyond this, there is no purification.
What is the meaning of the statement that when a root downfall occurs for one who has been consecrated with the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*), there is no purification?

In this context, the Master should not inflict punishment upon him; rather, by the power of his virtuous conduct, he himself should perform the confession of sins and so forth, and having gone before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who possess great blessings, he himself [achieves] purification.
"It is the opinion of the Buddhas that one who has committed a root downfall enters this mandala again for the sake of purification.

This means that when one who was established in the seven empowerments— whether situated in the vase empowerment or the secret empowerment— commits a root downfall, then, for the sake of his purification, one constructs this mandala and performs the entry into the mandala and so forth once more.

Furthermore, regarding the vow of non-repetition: having received permission therein, he returns once more to the family of the Gaṇas within the lineage; he who previously held the name of the eldest attains the state of being younger and becomes the youngest. Thus, for the sake of the vow of non-repetition, this rule of the Tathāgata must necessarily be observed by the disciples.
ca. guhyābhiṣeka;
ga. does not exist;
ca, pattava.
And. There is no.
Purity.
O Ga. And, O Bho, purity.
O! There, *ga* [is read as] *bho*. O! Regarding *adhiṣṭhānasthānaṃ*, the reading "it does not fall" (*na patati*) and "it leads" (*nayati*) is excellent; *bho* [is read as] *thob bo* (*prāpnoti*).

Ka. Kha. Ga. Cha. Then follows the great chapter on the initiation into the mandala with permission. Now, the root downfalls are described: The moon-like root downfall for sons occurs from causing mental distress to the glorious Guru; another indeed arises from transgressing his command; likewise, the third from anger toward one's brothers;

the fourth arises again from abandoning loving-kindness (*maitrī*); the fifth from the destruction of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*); the sixth from reviling the established tenets (*siddhānta*); and the seventh from giving the secret [teachings] to an immature person.
Regarding the phrase "root downfall" and so forth:
here, in all tantras, there are fourteen root downfalls.

Among them, each occurs as follows; thus he says: "The first root downfall for sons—that is, for initiated disciples—occurs, O Moon-like One, through causing distress to the mind of the glorious Guru."

In this context, the guru is of two kinds: the true guru and the false guru. These are further divided into two types each based on mental distress—namely, for the sake of others and for one's own sake.
Among these, he whose mental distress is for the sake of others is the venerable guru (*śrī-guru*).
"One whose mind suffers from self-interest is an unvirtuous guru.

Regarding this, it is said that the mental suffering of the venerable guru arises for the disciple through the engagement in the ten non-virtues; therefore, from that mental suffering, a root downfall occurs. However, there is no rule that a downfall occurs for a guru who acts for his own sake through the engagement in the ten non-virtues.
A second root downfall occurs when one violates his command, even if it is done behind the back of the Guru while he is performing the ten unwholesome actions;
likewise, the third occurs from anger toward one's brother.
When one becomes angry while an elder or younger Vajra-brother is being instructed,

it is the fourth [type] due to the abandonment of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Here, the abandonment of loving-kindness is fourfold, distinguished by the categories of weak, medium, strong, and extremely strong.
In that regard, the weak [type of] abandonment of loving-kindness is like a line drawn with a staff on water; it ceases after a mere moment.
The middling [type] is like a line in the sand; it returns to a state of evenness again by the wind.
That which consists of the superior [degree] is like a crack in the earth; it returns to a state of evenness again by the rainwater.

Then, when the mind of non-friendliness (*amaitrī-citta*), having become exceedingly intense and fully matured, is such that it can never again become complete or equanimous—just as a split stone never becomes whole again, or as a ripe fruit does not remain upon the tree—in that same way, there is an abandonment of friendliness toward sentient beings;
by this, the fourth root downfall (*mūlāpatti*) occurs: this is the rule.
The word "arrow" (iṣu) is used here in the ablative case;
"due to the destruction of the bodhicitta" means that in this context, *bodhicitta* is the semen (*śukra*), and from its destruction, the bliss of non-emission (*acyutasukha*) does not arise.
Since for those who lack the realization of reality and yet desire Buddhahood through the pleasure of the two organs, there occurs the fifth root downfall;
the sixth is the disparagement of the Siddhānta—
the chapter on reality within the Mantra system, which is the method of the Prajñāpāramitā— and that which is such disparagement is the sixth.
"Giri" refers to the locative case (*saptamī*).

When a person is unripened—that is, when one is situated on the path of the Śrāvaka—there is an infraction for the masters (*ācāryas*) due to the giving of secrets, that is, the giving of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). Furthermore, the ninth [infraction] is to be outside the aggregates and afflictions; it is a lack of interest in the pure Dharma, as well as the employment of deceptive mantras, conceptualization regarding names and so forth, and the like, which are Rudras.
And from that. And of the wholesome.
Of that, the non-transgression.

ga. ca. yānaṃ; ga. nindāyā;
ka. kha. ga. ca. ayācite; cha, apacite; bho. nindayā sā; ka. kha. ga. 0pattiriti.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is said: "If one commits an offense against a pure being worthy of initiation, or abandons the sun [the Guru] at the appointed time, or indeed feels contempt for all other women, then for those established in the Vajrayāna, Manu [the lawgiver] prescribes punishment. (103)
The eighth [stage] is called "having cast off the aggregates and afflictions" (*skandha-kleśa-avahī*);

because the dwelling in form (*rūpa-vāsa*), such as the aggregates and afflictions, and the cutting of the body (*śarīra-cchedana*) and so forth are said to have been relinquished, it is therefore the eighth.
Furthermore, the ninth [fault] is a lack of interest in the pure Dharma and the Dharma of emptiness, and practicing a deceptive friendliness— wherein there is one intended word on the surface,
but another thought in the heart.
That which is illusory friendliness (māyāmaitrī) is the tenth, named *Dik*;
that conceptualization regarding the reality of the Tathāgata, which bestows bliss free from name and so forth, is the eleventh, *Rudra*;
and in the pure state, due to the fault of the Yoginīs, it becomes the twelfth, *Ravi*.

When the occasion has arrived, through renunciation in the *gaṇacakra*, there is another thirteenth [state] for all women; that which is contempt for [all] women is indeed determined to be the fourteenth, known as Manu— this is the rule.
Of whom? Of those established in the Vajrayāna who have received initiation; this is the rule.
Regarding the many gross transgressions of the Vajra-holder, there is the rule that their punishment is slight. || 103 ||

Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Great Exposition on the Initiation of the Mandala, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja* following the *Mūlatantra*. 4.

The Great Chapter on the Ritual of the Yoga Practice of the Assembly Circle of Consecration: Having prostrated with my head to that Kālacakra who is worshipped by the hosts of gods, asuras, and lords of nāgas and men after performing the consecration, I shall explain the consecration of images and so forth.

Here, from the glorious *Paramādibuddha*, the ritual for consecration is extracted by Mañjuśrī in one hundred and four verses and is now expanded upon with a commentary. O King, one should bathe [the deity] in the center of the pedestal with four jars made of gems, gold, or clay, filled with water containing jewels, medicinal herbs, and perfumes—these being the jars of Victory (*jaya*) and Unconquerable (*vijaya*).

On the eight-petaled lotus bound with the glorious crest by the Nāgas, and on the fourfold seal bound with a cloth, there is the glorious jar; here, omitting the lotus, one should leave out the five lines. || 104 ||

With the words "By the Nāgas," etc., [it is meant that] having first been consecrated here by the consecrations such as the vase (kalaśa) which are about to be described, the disciple—who has understood all the tantras and who has ascended to his vow—is to be consecrated by the Guru as the sovereign Vajrācārya.

Now follows the great chapter on the ritual of consecration, the gaṇacakra, and yogic conduct: "O Śrī Guru, by your grace I have understood the entire path of the Sugatas"—having thus addressed the Guru, he makes this vow.

Having seen the disciple established in his vow, saying, "From this time forward, I shall not worship any other guru, setting aside you, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas," and seeing him endowed with all virtues, then the previously mentioned *jayavijaya* jars—whether by those eight or four *nāgas*, or by a single jar—the lordship should be conferred in three ways:
for a monk (*bhikṣu*), a Vajradhara, or a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) by means of the four [jars]; for a householder (*gṛhastha*) by means of one.
Thus, according to the previously stated procedure, one should perform the sprinkling with jars prepared with medicinal herbs and other substances.

Here, on a level area outside the maṇḍala-hall, having drawn five enclosure lines (prākāra-rekhā) over a space of four cubits, one should draw in the center a two-cubit lotus with eight petals, devoid of the five insignia and in all colors;
this very pedestal-lotus (*pīṭhapadma*) should be drawn upon a cloth with five colors in the middle of that lotus.

Having placed [the vessel] above, one should have a monk place it with eight jars accompanied by Jaya and Vijaya. One should bathe [the image] with ten beautiful maidens, all adorned with ornaments, who have not yet borne children,
and with two young girls whose virginity remains intact.

Having bound a crown upon his head together with the silk ribbon and seal, one should thus make the monk Vajradhara intent on threatening the wicked; at the mere sight of him, the Daityas go to the netherworld (rasātala). Thus it is said.
Likewise, when the *nāgas* have bound the crown upon his head, and the eight-petaled lotus has been bound with a fillet,
then, having again bound the fillet of a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), he is presented with a seal by four maidens.
The central preceptor should cause two young girls to bathe [the image], excluding the dust-marks and lotus, having drawn five lines and provided a central strip; thus [is the procedure].
Then, having applied the "mudrā" (seal) as described, one should bathe [the deity] with a single victorious jar using one girl and one young maiden,
having set aside the five lines.
Having drawn three lines with ordinary ointment and having provided an ordinary seat, the inferior preceptor should perform the bath.

In this manner, according to the sequence, having prepared a seat of four cubits, two cubits, or one cubit, the Vajrācārya should bestow the consecration upon the monks, novices, and householders; this is the rule for the purpose of teaching the Tantra, whether by word or by authorization. || 104 ||

Therefore, the procedure for initiation (sekavidhi) is described: first, one indeed becomes a lay practitioner (upāsaka) in the water; in the [water] jar, one becomes a novice monk (śrāmaṇera); in the secret initiation (guhyābhiṣeka), one becomes a fully ordained monk (bhikṣu); and in the higher cause, one becomes an elder (sthavira). For their sake, as the preceptor (ācārya), the excellent Guru bestows the mudrā, the turban, and the crown according to the power of their own Buddha-family: the vajra, the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), and the pure mudrā. || 105 ||
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, beginning with the words "at the outset" (*ādau*) and so forth:
"Having been consecrated at the outset in the water-named first of the seven consecrations, one is called a lay devotee (*upāsaka*) because of the prophecy regarding the seven stages.
By that [consecration], one becomes a lay devotee; this is the rule."
The novice (śrāmaṇera) should be known as a "son of the Buddha" because of the prophecy at the stage of the Unwavering (acala), meaning a "prince.
Thereafter, through the secret initiation (guhyābhiṣeka), he becomes a monk (bhikṣu) due to the prophecy at the stage of Excellent Intelligence (sādhumatī);
he is thus called an "Elder" (sthavira).
Then, in the third higher consecration, the consecration of the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*), he is consecrated in the cause;
he becomes a teacher of the Dharma and a maker of disciples, for he has been prophesied in the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*). Thus, he is indeed a second Buddha.

Accordingly, the Blessed One said in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*: "Thus, his body is the unique youth of the three worlds, yet he is an elder, ancient, and the Lord of Creatures. He bears the thirty-two marks, is lovely, and is the beauty of the three worlds. (NS 8.5)
For he is the non-returner who does not fall back, the rhinoceros-like solitary leader; having emerged through various means of deliverance, he is the single cause of the great elements.

"The Arhat, the monk whose outflows are exhausted, free from passion, with senses conquered; he has attained security, attained fearlessness, become cooled, and is indeed free from turbidity" (Nāmasaṃgīti 6.10–11).

Likewise: "The bearer of the great vows, wearing the girdle of muñja grass, a celibate student, supreme in his vows; one of great austerity, established in penance, a bath-graduate, Gautama the leader; a knower of Brahman, a Brāhmaṇa, a Brahmā who has attained the nirvāṇa of Brahman; liberation, the state of being liberated, the limb of liberation, freedom, tranquility, and auspiciousness" (Nāmasaṃgīti 8.18–19). This is the consecration of the Ācārya.
Therefore, for the purpose of making the body, speech, and mind [into vajras], he gives the Vajrakāyamudrā.
And upon the turban, he bestows a crown for the purpose of making [the disciple] Viṣṇu, which means for the purpose of making the mind a vajra. [He also gives] the vajra-sacred thread.
He gives [the consort] made of gold or thread for the purpose of becoming the Body-Vajra-holder, that is, for the sake of becoming Brahmā.
To those [disciples], whether senior or junior, he gives the mudrā for the sake of the Ācārya, according to the power of their own Buddha-family and by the very force of the falling of the flower.
She is pure or consecrated for the purpose of purifying the Speech-Vajra, that is, for the sake of becoming Maheśvara.

Thus: "The bearer of the Body-Vajra is Brahmā; the bearer of the Speech-Vajra is Maheśvara; the bearer of the Mind-Vajra is the King, who is Viṣṇu of great power" (the one who gathers disciples). [In the chapter on] the Great Instruction on the Ritual of Consecration, the Gaṇacakra, and Yogic Conduct, it says: "He is the Vajrācārya. Likewise, the Blessed One said in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*: "He has a topknot, he has a crest, he has matted hair, he has locks, he is shaven-headed, he wears a crown; he is five-faced, he has five crests, and he has five rags as his head-ornament" (*Nāmasaṃgīti* 8.17). This is the rule for the Blessed One in all tantras.

In this regard, a monk, a novice, or a householder who has been consecrated in the Empowerment of the Lord of the Land (*deśakābhiṣeka*) must not perform worldly duties such as service and so forth, nor household occupations such as the wielding of weapons, trade, and the like.

If he performs them, it constitutes a violation of the command; from the violation of the command, one goes to the Avīci hell, because of the destruction of the teacher’s dharma. This is the rule for the ritual installation and empowerment of the Vajrācārya sovereignty.

Having spread a canopy above, one should draw three lines all around on the surface of the ground; at their corners, water-filled jars made of gems and gold, with mouths fashioned like lotuses, should be arranged. Then, having prepared fragrant water in vessels such as conch shells, or those made of gold or silver, and having placed a pedestal made of bright gold within the center, one should begin the ritual bath.

The deity should be anointed with fragrant oils prepared by heating them over the sun’s rays and fire; having rubbed the body with aromatic powders, one should bathe it with honey, ghee, curd, milk, and water. Then, having performed the *nirmāñcha* (waving) ritual here with white mustard seeds, lamps, and various excellent fruits, the image should be properly moved from that place while being covered with a red cloth.

Having constructed, within the center of the glorious maṇḍala on level ground, a five-lined grid according to the portions of the Jinas, one should place in its center an eight-petaled lotus adorned with the five symbols situated in the directions of one’s own family. In the middle of that, a deity or goddess with a face turned away, or a reliquary (caitya) and so forth, or a book, or a cloth painting (paṭa), should be installed; and likewise, the mantra-practitioner should stand facing it.

Having established the void nature together with the Supreme Victor, the Vajras of Body, Speech, and Mind, one should subsequently meditate upon Kālacakra—the seed-syllable of the Moon, Sun, and Rāhu—according to the previously mentioned yogas. One should meditate on the Knowledge Goddesses and the other Buddhas, born from their respective seed-syllables, according to their families: in the heart, throat, navel, secret place, and head; and at the crown wheel.

In other tantras, such as the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is said: "Furthermore, all the deities should indeed be meditated upon thus within the body of the [principal] deity. Having drawn the Jñānasattva, who is equal to the existence of the three worlds, into one's own body by means of the Wrathful Kings, the master should perform the entry, binding, pleasing, and the making of equal flavor with the deity. Therefore, the deity whose face is revealed should be saluted. (110)

That very seed-syllable of the male and female deities, which belongs to its own family and quality, situated within the heart and enclosed between the moon and the sun, conjoined with body, speech, and mind—divided by the thirty-two major marks and so forth present upon the entire body, and by its own eight letters—that same [syllable] should be visualized upon the petals of the manifest lotus, as well as upon the volumes of books. (111)

The Śrīcakra is in the interior of the Caitya; the discus, jewel, lotus, and sword are in the north. The syllable *hūṃ* is on the rosary, characterized by the counting of the jewels [the consonants]. The vowels are on the bell in the body; the ten consonant groups beginning with *ka*, tripled, are on the armor. Those same [consonants] are on the sacred thread; the eight consonants (*vasu*) multiplied by ten are on the upper garment. (112)

The consonant groups beginning with *ka*, each consisting of five measures (*mātrā*), numbering thirty-five (the sky [0] and the tastes [6] multiplied by the qualities [5]), are to be meditated upon as the yoga-band (*yogapaṭṭa*). For the two earrings, *haṃ* and *haḥ*; for the necklace and girdle, the pair *aṃ* and *aḥ*.

Thus, there is a pair of *ā* syllables for the two bracelets, and *ha* and *hā* for the anklets. Indeed, the fivefold void (*pañcākāra-śūnya*) residing in the entire body is to be meditated upon as the sacred ash (*bhasman*).

From one's own body, which is the form of gnosis, all the aggregates, elements, and so forth, together with the three vajras, should be sequentially deposited into the lotus of the heart of each deity by means of their respective seed-syllables. O Lord of Men, when the seed-syllable has been deposited, the consecration of stupas, plastering, and other works is accomplished; therefore, at the time of withdrawal, effect the entry of the seed-syllable into your own body by means of the hand-vajra. 114.

First, there should be a ceremonial bath with mirrors; thereafter, the deity should be worshipped with perfumes, songs, musical instruments, and fragrant flowers. Having performed the consecration with dances, various cloths, yak-tail fans, and white umbrellas, and having employed excellent and diverse flavors [in the offerings], a feast for the Saṅgha should be provided. 115.

In a well, a pond, or a tank, one should place the Vasus and the Nāga kings in every direction and intermediate direction. One should pour the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) mixed with honey and water, using the seed-syllables of the seven oceans. [From the *Paṭala*, verse 116: At the conclusion of the fire-offering (*homa*), having visualized Varuṇa, white and holding a noose, in the pond and other sites;
and in a garden, having sprinkled the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) which resides within all trees, as well as a single tree.

O King, a crown, a turban, a necklace, as well as bracelets, earrings, a girdle, and so forth, should be given to the noble one; and the donor, for the sake of merit, should offer a sacrificial fee according to his own capacity.
Indeed, the entire assembly of the Gaṇas should be entreated for the sake of others: "By this merit, may all beings dwelling in the three realms of existence attain unsurpassed enlightenment. (117)

Herein is the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of images and so forth. Beginning from the verse "Having offered a canopy above, and [a design] with three lines all around upon the surface of the earth," twelve verses are easy to understand.
Up until the point where the disciple performs the dedication of merit (puṇyapariṇāmanā), this constitutes the formal aspiration (praṇidhāna).
"By this merit, may beings in the three realms of existence attain unsurpassed enlightenment"—up to this point, the procedure for the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) is easy to understand;
therefore, no commentary has been provided here.

Now the procedure for the higher initiation (*uttarābhiṣeka*) is stated: Up to ten years of age, she is of one kind, being of ten types [of qualities], fit to be seen and touched; therefore, those who are to be embraced are the oceans of nectar, and those beginning with *Lā* are to be served.

Beyond twenty years of age, the mudrās are extremely terrifying, possessing the nature of wrathful deities, spirits (*bhūta*), and asuras; six and four are for the purpose of initiation, while the others grant the fruit of the bliss of peace and are for the purpose of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). (118)
Regarding the phrase "digvarṣam" and so forth:
here, for the purpose of the vase-consecration (*kalaśābhiṣeka*), one should avoid a girl as a mudrā until she is ten years of age (*digvarṣa*).
This is because the single Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) becomes tenfold.
Through the purification of generosity and the other perfections, she is renewed annually.

Here too, as long as the falling out of the teeth has not occurred, she remains due to the immutability of the element of gnosis (*jñānadhātu*); after that falling out of the teeth, there is the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).
Thus, by means of these two elements, the girl remains with an intact womb.

"She is to be seen, touched, and worshipped by him. Therefore, beginning from the tenth year up to the twenty years—starting from the eleventh year—she is to be embraced; she is like the oceans full of nectar. Together with the six [elements], the four beginning with *la* (the earth element) and those beginning with *va* (air and so forth) are to be cultivated.
Thus, the air element is in the eleventh year, fire in the twelfth, water in the thirteenth, and earth in the fourteenth; these are the four.
In the fifteenth [year] sound; in the sixteenth, touch; in the seventeenth, taste; in the eighteenth, form; in the nineteenth, smell; and in the twentieth, the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Thereafter, from above the twentieth year, the mudrās are extremely terrifying, consisting of the portions of the wrathful ones, spirits, and asuras.

Here, beginning from the twenty-first year after the twentieth, the ten wrathful goddesses correspond respectively to each year: Atinīlā, Atibalā, Jambhī, Mānī, Stambhī, Mārīcī, Cundā, Bhṛkuṭī, Vajraśṛṅkhalā, and Raudrākṣī.
From the thirty-first year, there are eight portions of the *bhūtas*: Carcikā, Vārāhī, Raudrī, Aindrī, Brahmāṇī, Mahālakṣmī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
From the thirty-ninth year, there are eight portions of the *asuras*: Śvānāsyā, Śūkarāsyā, Vyāghrāsyā, Jambukāsyā, Garuḍāsyā, Ulūkāsyā, Gṛdhrāsyā, and Kākāsyā.
These last forty-six years are for the purpose of meditating upon the *mudrās*.

Furthermore, for the sake of consecration (*sekārtha*), there are six and four [elements] which bestow the fruit of equal bliss, beginning from the fire element (*tejodhātu*) up to the phenomenon element (*dharmadhātu*).
It is a fixed rule that the wind element (*vāyudhātu*) is not to be grasped because it is devoid of dust (*arajastvāt*). || 118 ||

The touch of the venerable Prajñā’s breasts is the first [initiation]; that very pouring of the jar is the secret-of-secrets initiation through the tasting and gazing at the moon-bearer (the consort).

In the initiation of the knowledge of Prajñā, having purified the limbs and faces with all the Buddha-families, the Guru should give the mudrā to the disciple, having made even a Jina the witness in this matter. (119)

In this context, the higher initiation (*uttarābhiṣeka*) is twofold: one is for the purpose of introducing sentient beings [to the path], for the thorough knowledge of the path, and for the authority to hear the *tantra*; the other is for the purpose of conferring the rank of a great master (*mahācārya*) and making one a teacher.

Regarding the former initiation here: a girl of excellent character, twelve years of age or older, who is free from defects such as timidity or a distracted mind, should be sought out by the disciple and offered to the guru.
Then, having performed the request and so forth, the disciple requests the guru with the praise that is about to be described.
Then, being pleased, the Guru, in accordance with worldly convention, causes the student to touch his own mudrā’s breast;
by that, it is indeed the vase consecration (*kalaśābhiṣeka*).
Then, having performed the secret worship (*guhyapūjā*), he gives the nectar (*amṛta*) to the disciple.
And he causes her to behold the *mudrā*’s vulva.
By means of that tasting and beholding of the moon-bearer (*śaśadharā*), the secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*) occurs.

Then, in the initiation of the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*), having formed the five-family cluster (*pañcakulakalāpinī*) from the seed-syllables beginning with *oṃ*, the *mudrā* should then be given by the Guru to the disciple for the purpose of the embrace and the union of hands.
Having made the Jina Vajrasattva the witness:

"Just as this unfortunate being [is unfit], for his sake—regarding the practice of meditation and so forth, the hearing of the tantra, the teaching of the tantra to disciples, and the drawing of the mandala—this is first the rule for the initiation for the entry of disciples."

Thus, by the laughter of *āhū* the Master (*ācārya*) is of a twofold nature through the bliss of semen and the purity of the deity; by the kiss (*cumbana*), the Secret One (*guhya*) is of a threefold nature through the purity of the senses; by the embrace (*pāṇivyāpti*), he is of a fourfold nature through the purity of the [four] qualities; and by union (*dvandva*), he is of a fivefold nature through the bliss of semen and the purity of the deity. These points, beginning with "the purity of the deity," are to be explained in the fifth chapter, in the *Paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*.
Thus, according to worldly convention, this is the rule for the fourfold consecration (*abhiṣeka*) for the purpose of introducing sentient beings [to the path].

Then, once all the tantras have been heard and understood along with their commentaries, for the sake of attaining the status of a great sovereign, the ten vidyās as described in due order must be offered by the householder disciple to the guru.
Regarding this, the Blessed One said in the root mantra: "O! Six and three (ṣaṭ ca tisraḥ), tāvatastatrā, ca tāvattatrā;
ka! O you who are ripened by the dust of the elements!"
ca. by way of worldly convention;
ga. ca. ga. deity, bho. none; ca. touching.
O, [it is] for sentient beings (*sattvānām*).
O, there is no "āha. O, there is no "deva."

[To be stated in] the chapter on the Great Summary of the Ritual for the Gaṇacakra and Yogacaryā of Consecration (paṭala, verse): "The sister's daughter, the daughter, the sister, and likewise the mother."
The wife, the mother, and likewise the wife of one's maternal uncle.
Likewise, the wife of one's father’s brother,
a paternal aunt, a maternal aunt, and one’s own wife of excellent form— [these are not to be approached].
The ten vidyās, beginning with Tārā and ending with Dharmadhātviśvarī, are born of one’s own lineage;
they should be bestowed at the time of initiation by a householder who desires liberation.
For those living in households, [it is performed] with others.
If the Guru does not grant these sciences because of the protection of the family lineage,
then the consecration (seka) must not be given by other women of the Śūdra caste who have been initiated into the mandalas; rather,
O King, it should be granted by the Guru to the monks and novices.
The [energies] beginning with Vāyu are, in order: Śūdrī, Kṣatriṇī, Brāhmaṇī, Veśyā, Ḍombī, Kaivartī, Naṭikā, and Rajakī.
The leather-worker, the outcaste woman, and the ten born of the lowest strata of the dharma-realm—
these are declared to be the Great Vidyās, which bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus, by the sequence thus described, the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), the ten masteries (*vaśitā*), the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and the ten powers (*bala*) become completely purified.
Accordingly, the Blessed One said in the *Dharmadhātustava* of the *Nāmasaṃgīti*: "The Buddha Mahāvairocana, the Great Silent One, the Great Sage."
Arisen from the system of the Great Mantra, he is the very essence of the system of the Great Mantra.

He has attained the ten perfections, is pure in the ten perfections, is the method of the ten perfections, and is the foundation of the ten perfections. He is the Lord and Protector who rules over the ten stages, established in the ten stages; his self is purified by the ten knowledges, and he maintains the purity of the ten knowledges.
The Lord of Sages, possessing ten forms, whose purpose is the tenfold aim, the powerful one endowed with the ten powers;
he who effects the welfare of the entire universe, the great master of self-control appearing in ten forms.
Thus [it is said in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*]: "Ten mudrās should be given for the purpose of making one a presiding master;
this is the rule of the Tathāgatas regarding one who desires the rank of a Mahāmaṇḍalācārya."
Having thus offered the ten mudrās, the disciple then requests an instruction from the guru:
"Now what should I do, O Blessed One who has attained all the perfections?
Thereupon the ācārya says: "Take this wife of yours as your sovereign consort."
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, among the ten consecrations (*abhiṣeka*), together with her, perform my supplication.
Furthermore, for monks and novices, a Caṇḍālī must be made their own wife.

Then, having taken her according to the guru’s injunctions, he fashioned a maṇḍala with flowers such as *kanaka* and others; thereafter, he made this supplication to the two of them: "Salutations to you, Kālacakra, who destroys all obscurations!
Homage to you, the Gnosis Body (*jñānakāya*), filled with the bliss of the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara-sukha*)!"
O Protector, by means of that consecration which is the imperishable bodhicitta inseparable from emptiness and compassion,
grant me your grace now.
Together with my sons, wife, and others, I am forever your servant;
until I reach the seat of enlightenment, there is no other refuge for me.
Seeing his disciple together with his wife thus having made this request, the teacher removes all the ornaments from Śabdavajrā, makes her naked, and embraces her.
As for the householder, he embraces his wife’s mother.

Then: Tārā in the east, Pāṇḍarā in the south, Māmakī in the north, Locanā in the west; Sparśavajrā in the southeast, Rasavajrā in the southwest, Rūpavajrā in the northeast, and Gandhavajrā in the northwest.
One should fashion the circle of Yoginīs as naked, with disheveled hair, and holding a flaying knife and a skull-cup in their hands, according to the sequence of the nine Vidyās.
Thus is the sevenfold prior consecration by means of water and so forth;
after that follows the higher consecration (uttarābhiṣeka).
The successive consecration by means of the common action-seal (*karmamudrā*) is performed with the previously mentioned [women] beginning with the *śūdrī*.
For the offering of the seal, one should bathe the monk (*bhikṣu*) with ten nāgas, eight vases, and both the *jaya* and *vijaya* [vases].
For the novice (*śrāmaṇera*), one should bathe him among those [women] with six seals and four vases, as well as with the *jaya* and *vijaya* [vases].
Among those nine women, he should have the householder consecrated by one of them—his own wife—with one *vijaya* water-pot, according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Then, he should offer a seal (*mudrā*) for the purpose of bestowing the consecration from the jar.
[The text provided consists of two vertical bars (||), which in this context function as a section marker. [Section Break]

Having desired with his own vajra-jewel, which consists of wisdom and means, a beautiful maiden of twelve years—who is adorned with all ornaments, resembles molten gold, and is full of passion—the master, having ascertained the purification of the disciple, should place even his own vajra, together with the seed-syllable, into the disciple's mouth. Thereafter, he should give him his own mudrā; or else, another [mudrā] endowed with the path of smoke and so forth. (120)

In this context, having—by means of the deity-yoga consisting of wisdom and method as will be described—enjoyed with his own vajra-jewel a beautiful maiden who is twelve years old or up to twenty years of age, adorned with all ornaments, resembling molten gold, and possessing passion (being in her menses), [the master] should know the purification of the disciple through the successive empowerments. Then, having cast the vajra into the mouth [of the disciple], [he places it] in the flask.

[As stated in the section on the ritual for the installation and the gaṇacakra, and the yoga-conduct mahoddeśa, verses 119–120: "Thereafter, the master should give his own consort, who has been embraced [by him], together with the seed-syllable."
Alternatively, the preceptor himself approaches the wife of his son;

then, when the moment for the consecration (sekakṣaṇa) has arrived, he should hand over his own wife back to the disciple. In this regard, the means consists of the touching of the consort's breast; during the vase-consecration (kalaśābhiṣeka), the disciple should touch the breast of the preceptor’s wife.
In the secret initiation, one should cast the *vajra* into the mouth of the disciple’s wife.
Having bound the eyes of the disciple, the Guru should suck the nose of the *prajñā*.
Then, through the knowledge of the wife, the Master should offer his own consort (*mudrā*). This is the procedure for all initiations in the Great Sovereignty (*mahādhipatya*).
"If there are ten mudrās, then the teacher should offer whichever one the disciple is capable of desiring.
From two ghaṭikās after midnight until sunrise, he should then dismiss the gaṇacakra."
Having dismissed [the deities], one should bestow the vow (*saṃvara*) upon the disciple:
"That which has been described by me as the innate moment (*sahajakṣaṇa*) ending with the cessation (*virama*), up to the end of the three moments, does not exist in the ultimate sense (*vivṛtyā*).
In the ultimate sense, the bliss of yogins is unfallen (*acyuta*)."
Therefore, this great bliss must be protected by you.
Thus, the Blessed One said in the *Ādibuddha*: "Even when engaged with a karma-mudrā or in union with a jñāna-mudrā, the bodhicitta—the great bliss—must be protected by one firm in his vow."
Having established the *liṅga* in the *bhaga*, one should not emit the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).

One should, however, meditate upon the image of the Buddha; for by this very protection, the equipment of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃbhāra*) is fulfilled, and one attains the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*) throughout the entire realm of phenomena (*dhātu*) without exception.
In this very birth, may I attain Buddhahood,
endowed with merit and wisdom.
The perfectly awakened ones existing throughout the three times have set it in motion.

By this [mantra], the wheel of Dharma of all the perfectly awakened ones is turned; there is no knowledge superior to this, which is sovereign over the three realms and inseparable from emptiness and compassion, for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of oneself and others.
If you, my son, maintain the vow of all the Protectors,
then, empowered by all the Buddhas, you shall attain perfect awakening.
If, with your self overcome by passion, you do not maintain your vow,
then, having failed your husband, you shall go to the Raurava hell.
When the bodhicitta has been emitted into the womb due to a soft mind,
it should then be taken from outside the lotus by means of one's own tongue, having recognized the mudrā.
Thus.
Ka. Kha. Cha. read *savīryam*.
Ka. Kha. Cha. read *prajñayā*.

ka. kha. cha. *bhāryām karoti*, ga. *śiṣye*; ga. ca. *bhāryām*. Bho. "Then, in the initiation of the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*), one should offer one's own wife as the consort (*mudrā*)," refers to the master (*ācārya*). ga. *yadā*.
O. From the perspective of ultimate reality (*tatparamārthataḥ*).
Ga. Unimpaired.
Ga. Ca. Bho. The Blessed One said:
Ka.

Having bestowed the empowerment and the vows (*saṃvara*) upon the disciple, the preceptor (*ācārya*), and the disciple having likewise given the teacher’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*), should again construct the maṇḍala and pray: "May the Blessed One grant me the grace of the ritual procedure for empowerment.
Then the Guru should address the disciple.
Listen, my son!

Just as the bliss characterized by the sixteen joys—which is common to all sentient beings—has been extracted from the *Paramādibuddha* by Mañjuvajra in one hundred and twenty-two verses beginning with *kāmākṣobham* (Kālacakratantra 3.122), so too [is this bliss described] through conventional reality. || 120 ||

Terrified, mentally deranged, deceitful, under the sway of others, afflicted by disease, recently delivered, angry, rigid, fickle, addicted to falsehood and quarreling, physically deformed, or impure—these women, O King, must be avoided by a highly skilled master during the initiation of wisdom (*prajñābhiṣeka*). However, those previously mentioned who are devoted to the Buddha and uphold the master’s commitments (*gurusamaya*) are to be saluted and worshipped.
Sensual desire causes agitation in one's own mind; when full, it attains the fullness of the world. From that fullness, a flame with a drop flows forth, melting the moon from the head.

By its very nature, the drawing up of OṬṬĀ bestows supreme bliss at the end of the three releases of the drop: the bliss of light, touch, and union, as well as the bliss of emission, through the various stages of bliss beginning with *ānanda*. 122.
In this context, for the entire world, desire causes agitation in the mind; this is the first bliss (*ānanda*).
Thence it reaches fullness; because the *bodhicitta* is full at the forehead due to the embrace of wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth, this is the second, supreme bliss (*paramānanda*).

Thence, from the full head during sexual union, the state of the flame flows down as the drop (*bindu*), and having caused the moon-bearer to melt, it produces the third, the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*).

Therefore, at the stage of *oṭṭā*, at the time of the emission of the *bindu*, at the conclusion of the *bindus* of body, speech, and mind, and at the moment of the exit of the four *bindus*, it produces innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).

Thus, by means of the five sets of five digits (*kalā*) beginning with the first lunar day (*pratipad*), which correspond in nature to space, wind, fire, water, and earth, and which bear the names Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā, and possess the qualities of the vowels *a, i, ṛ, u, ḷ, k; a, e, ar, o, al, ra; ha, ya, ra, va, la, ḍ*—in this way, the fifth [digit] is full of bliss (*ānanda*), the tenth is full of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), and the full moon (*pūrṇimā*) is full of the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*).
Innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) is the sixteenth digit (*kalā*), the gathering (*samāhāra*), the union (*melāpaka*), the assembly (*samāja*), and the vow (*saṃvara*) of all elements (*dhātu*).
Thus, passion (*rāga*) is the white fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) of the bodhicitta, while dispassion (*virāga*) is the black fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).
As the Blessed One said in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*: "Dispassion and so forth is the great passion (*mahārāga*), possessing a brilliant radiance of universal colors."
The Perfectly Awakened One, seated in the vajra posture, upholds the Dharma of the Buddha’s assembly.
Thus: *ga* with twenty-one added; *cha* with thirty-two added; *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *cha*, *bho*;

then *ga*, *bho*, *oḍḍā*, *ca*, *uḍḍā*, *bho*, *ca*, *ga*, *vara*, *la*, *cha*. Beyond this, the phrase "he produces the bliss of desire" (*kāmānandaṃ karoti*) is additionally found in *cha*. [This concludes] the Great Chapter on the Yoga Practice and the Ritual for the Assembly Circle of the *Pratiṣṭhā* in the section on the Bliss of Cessation (*viramānanda*). Likewise—

"Having all forms yet formless, bearing the sixteen, the eight, and the four drops; partless, beyond calculation, he holds the pinnacle of the fourth dhyāna. (Nāmasaṃgīti 10.3)—such is the rule of the Blessed One.
Thus, it is stated that the knowledge of Mahāmudrā is to be explained in detail in the fifth chapter of the *Vivṛti*;
therefore, it has not been elaborated upon here. (121–122)
Now, the four yogas of the sixteen joys are described:

First, men produce the joy of desire (*kāmānanda*) by the mere sight with the eyes; afterwards, during the occasion of the full [emission], they produce supreme joy (*paramānanda*) once again within their own body.

When the flame flows as a drop, she delights with the vajra of the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*) in the lotus; at the end of the three drops, Oṭṭā, abiding in the immutable, produces the vajra of innate joy (*sahajānanda*). || 123 ||

The bliss of desire (kāmananda), trembling, and the syllable [Oṃ]—the union of these four is the first; the arising of power (śaktyudbhava) is indeed the supreme bliss (paramānanda), thus it is the second. The flame (jvālā), the drop (bindu), and dizziness (ghūrma)—again, this is the bliss of cessation (viramānanda), thus it is the third. Utterance (oṭṭā), sound (nāda), and sleep (nidrā)—this is the innate bliss (sahajānanda), thus it is the fourth. || 124 ||
By the words "desire" (*kāma*) and so forth:
here, for all sentient beings, there is the yoga of body, speech, mind, and gnosis (*jñāna*), distinguished by the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (*turya*).
These are sixteenfold through the distinctions of bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth.
In that context, "desires" refers to the bliss of the body;
"joy" refers to the bliss of speech;
and "trembling" refers to the bliss of the mind.
By the designation "syllable" (akṣara), there is the bliss of knowledge (jñānānanda).
Thus, by this group of four, the yoga of bliss (ānandayoga) is one.
Likewise, "fullness" (pūrṇā) refers to the supreme bliss of the body (kāyaparamānanda).

In this context, the triad beginning with *paramānanda* (supreme bliss) and ending with the final [element], or alternatively, speech (*vāk*), mind (*citta*), and knowledge (*jñāna*), are so designated by virtue of the meter.
Therefore, *paramānanda* is the supreme bliss of speech; *udbhava* is the supreme bliss of the mind; and *śakti* is the supreme bliss of knowledge.
This is the second yoga.

"Jvālā" is the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*) of the body; "viramānanda" is the bliss of cessation of speech; "ghūrma" is the bliss of cessation of the mind; and "bindu" is the bliss of cessation of gnosis (*jñāna*). This is the third yoga.
Likewise, "oṭṭā" is the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) of the body; "sahajānanda" is the innate bliss of speech; "nidrā" is the innate bliss of the mind; and "nāva" is the innate bliss of gnosis.
Thus, the body is fourfold, distinguished as the emanation, enjoyment, dharma, and essential bodies. Speech is likewise fourfold, and the mind is fourfold; knowledge is fourfold.
In this way, the sixteen divisions of bliss are to be explained in detail as they will be discussed further on.
Thus, the rule is that the innate (*sahaja*) extends to the end of the sixteen. [227a] 123–124.

By the words beginning with "kāma," there are three beloved ones (*kāntā*): *nāsti*, *ka*, and *ga*; *prasupta*, *ca*, and *ga*; and *cha*, *akṣara*, and *iti cha*. [The terms] *bho*, *ghūrṇa*, *ga*, *ghūrama*, *ka*, *ca*, *oddhā*, *ga*, *bho*, *oḍḍā*, *ga*, and *ca* will be explained in detail later. Now, the purification of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) is stated: the mother is to be contemplated by the mind; the sister by touching and embracing; the daughter-in-law (*bhāgineyā*) likewise during sexual union (*surata*) involving the entry of the vajra and its application.

The daughter, the wife, the one at the Bindu-fall, the one who has gone to another family, the Yoginī, and the one whose passion is destroyed—these six are the Yoga-mudrās, whose natures are earth, water, fire, air, space, and cessation. (125)
"By the words 'mother' and so forth:

here, in all the tantras, the mudrās such as the mother and others are described in general for the sake of inspiring passion in yogins. And that [mudrā] belongs to those who have stabilized their *bodhicitta*, not to other women who exist merely according to worldly convention."
They become the Mother and so forth through the differentiation of states.
Here, when a yogi contemplates a woman, she becomes the Mother as long as she is contemplated by the mind; she becomes the Sister through touch;
and she becomes the Daughter through the entry of the *vajra*.
When there is sexual union with effort, she becomes a sister's daughter;
when there is the falling of the drop, she becomes a wife;
and when passion has vanished, she who belongs to another family becomes a Caṇḍālī Yoginī through dispassion.

These six are the yoga-mudrās of the yoginīs, beginning with earth. Here, first there is the agitation of the earth element; likewise, there is the agitation of the water, fire, air, and space elements.
For those who are agitated, there is falling away (*cyavana*).
Therefore, there are six states consisting of the destruction of earth, water, fire, air, space, and consciousness.
Thus, at the time of falling away, the dissolution of the five mandalas on both the left and right [channels] should also be understood through the purification of the measures (*mātrā*).

The mudrās of the yogins consist of the wheel, the earring, the necklace, the armlet, the girdle, and the purity of ashes; likewise, they consist of the purity of the six perfections beginning with generosity—this is the rule. || 125 ||
Now the three seals (mudrās) of body and so forth are described:
the entry of the vajra into the lotus, the falling of the wind-bindu into the fire, and the third; this fixed triad of yogas is the seal of body, speech, and mind.

That which transcends passion and dispassion, the beginning of which is a treasury of supreme qualities, accessible through yoga—that is the fourth mother of the seals; she is tenfold and is the very mouth of the glorious Guru. (126)
By the words "abja" and so forth:

here, in all tantras, according to the provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), the body-seal (*kāyamudrā*) is at the forehead, the speech-seal (*vāṅmudrā*) at the throat, and the mind-seal (*cittamudrā*) at the heart.

According to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), however, the body-seal is the entry of the *vajra* into the lotus (*abja*) and the constant arising of the *vajra*; the speech-seal is the entry of the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*) into the central channel at the fire-center (*śikhin*).

Regarding "the falling of the drop" (*bindupāta*): by the words "O Mother," and so forth (*mātetyādinā*), [it is said] "O, regarding the knowledge of the mind" (*cittetyādinā*). In the versions *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, and *cha*, there is the word *rāgaṇāya*. In version *ga*, the word "of others" (*anyeṣām*) is added. In versions *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, and *cha*, there is the word *sparśanena*. In version *ga*, there is *satyavirā*. In version *bho*, there is *thig le mi lhung* (Sanskrit: *bindvapāta*). In the chapter on the ritual of the wheel of the assembly for consecration (*pratiṣṭhāgaṇacakravidhi*), within the section on the great instruction on yogic conduct (*yogacaryāmahoddeśa*), the "seal of the mind" (*cittamudrā*) is mentioned.
For this triad of yogas based upon the middle [channel], the seals of body, speech, and mind (*kāyavākcittamudrā*) occur respectively.
Above that, it says "that which goes to the end of passion and non-passion" (*rāgārāgāntagā*).
Passion (*rāga*) is the white fortnight, and she reaches its end; dispassion (*arāga*) is the black fortnight, and she is its beginning.

Thus, the sixteen digits (*kalā*), reaching from the end of passion to the beginning of dispassion, should be established. As long as she does not fall away, she bestows the supreme quality—the imperishable bliss of the *niṣkala* (partless).
She is accessible through yoga; the fourth [state] is accessible to yogins by means of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), but not to others.
She is the good mother, the progenitor of the nine mudrās—both preceding and succeeding—who exists from the time of conception until the end of death.

She is tenfold through the divisions of smoke and so forth, representing the perfections (pāramitās) such as generosity; she is the mouth of the glorious Guru Vajrasattva, meaning she is the fourth mouth, the mouth of gnosis (jñānavaktra).
She possesses the nature of the svābhāvikakāya; this is the rule.
Having thus explained the characteristics of the mudrās for the sake of the disciple’s consecration, the Guru gives the injunction for the *gaṇacakra*.
Therein, one should invite the thirty-six deities of the families (*kuladevatī*).
Then, during the day, having fed ten boys and girls with sweet food such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and the like, and having given them sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), one should dismiss them.

Then, having satisfied the community of monks and nuns with seven pots of non-material, sweet food, and having offered a ritual gift (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, one should enter a magnificent monastic residence (*saṅghavihāra*). From there, in a secluded house that is free from defects, one should contemplate the locations according to the procedure for the *gaṇacakra* of the heroes (*vīra*) and heroines (*vīreśvarī*).
Here, in accordance with one's wealth, the central leader is the Guru, whose nature consists of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*), while the four Yoginīs are situated in the four cardinal directions.
In the center is the Ḍombī, in the east the Śūdrī, in the south the Kṣatriṇī, in the north the Brāhmaṇī, and in the west the Vaiśyā; thus the leader of the group consists of five.
Their seats are human skin, dog skin, horse skin, cow skin, and elephant skin.

Then, secondly, in the intermediate directions: in the northeast is the vessel of urine, in the northwest the vessel of feces, in the southwest the vessel of blood, and in the southeast the vessel of marrow.

Then, in the second circle at the location of the mind-wheel (*cittacakra*), there is the group of eight yoginīs: in the east is Kaṃśakārī; in the south, Veṇunartakī; in the north, Maṇikārī; in the west, Raudrākṣī; in the southeast, Śālinī; in the southwest, Śauṇḍinī; in the northeast, Hemakārī; and in the northwest, Mālākārī. Their seats, in respective order, are: the skin of a ram, the skin of a wild horse, the skin of a camel, the skin of a rhinoceros, the skin of a goat, the skin of a deer, the skin of a donkey, and the skin of a boar.

Then, in the third circle, at the location of the Speech Wheel (*vākcakra*), there is the group of eight yoginīs: Khaṭṭinī in the east, Kumbhakārī in the southeast, Kandukī in the south, Gaṇikā in the southwest, Śibikā in the west, Kaivartī in the northwest, Naṭī in the north, and Rajakī in the northeast.

Their respective seats are, in numerical order: the skin of a *kumbhīra* crocodile, a heap of cowrie shells, a heap of crab shells, a dried fish, the skin of a *makara*, the skin of a *dardura* frog, the skull of a tortoise, and a conch shell.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, [regarding the consecration]: then, in the fourth circle, at the location of the body, there are eight [deities]: in the east, the iron-worker; in the south, the lac-maker; in the west, the silk-worm breeder; in the north, the oil-presser; in the southeast, the bamboo-worker; in the southwest, the wood-worker; in the northwest, the leather-worker; and in the northeast, the barber. Their seats are: the hide of a rhinoceros, tiger skin, bear skin, mongoose skin, yak-tail skin, jackal skin, otter skin, and cat skin.

Then, in the fifth circle, the cremation ground locations are as follows: in the east is Mlecchā; in the south, Haḍḍī; in the west, Mātaṅgī; in the north, Tāpinī; in the southeast, Varvarī; in the southwest, Pukkasī; in the northwest, Bhillī; and in the northeast, Śabarī—these are the eight Pracaṇḍās.
Their seats are the skins of a monitor lizard, a mouse, a śālījāta bird, a monkey, a hare, a porcupine, a *iskapa* animal, and a chameleon.

In the absence of these skins, one should provide seats as follows: a dog skin in the east, a horse skin in the southeast, an elephant skin in the west, a cow skin in the northeast, and a human skin in the center; having thus provided the seats, one should seat the Yoginīs.

One should have a small tray (*patulikā*) provided with these skins; likewise, skull-bowls (*karoṭaka*) are placed: in the east, a conch-shell cup (*śuktipuṭikā*); in the southeast, likewise; in the south, a coconut skull-bowl (*nārikelakaroṭaka*); in the west, a clay saucer (*aśarāva*); in the northwest, a human skull (*narakapāla*); in the north, [another] skull; and in the center, a wooden vessel.

Then, having offered liquor and so forth, as well as various foods and edibles together with lamps, and having offered the ten types of water-offerings (*toyārgha*) and so on to be described later, and having prepared the mandala, the disciple, together with the three ritual assistants (*karmavajrin*), should present the articles of worship.
Thus is the rule regarding the places and families in the *gaṇacakra*. || 126 ||

Prajñā is the mother, the good mother; Locanā and the others are the sisters, the mothers of the three worlds; the six Vajras are the nephews who cause fear to the ignorant; and Cakrikā and the others are the grandsons.

Residing in the wheels (*cakra*) at all times, having departed for their own family lands, they are to be served by yogins in the fields (*kṣetra*), seats (*pīṭha*), and cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*). They should never be released, whether in company or in solitude. 127.

Then, the movement [of the deities] should be performed according to the procedure taught in the fifth chapter, as well as sexual union. Regarding that movement: Prajñāmātā is in the center; she is the Leader of the Gaṇa, known as Sumātā. Furthermore, Ḍombī and Caṇḍālī are present everywhere in the circle of the Gaṇa among all the Yoginīs—namely, the four sisters beginning with Locanā, the six beginning with Śabdavajrā, and the two nieces, Nīlā and Raudrākṣī.

The eight Naptṛs, such as Caccikā and the others, who cause fear to common folk, arrive at all times through the movement of this Tārā-cakra; they are to be served by yogins when they have gone to their own family-sites (kulabhū).

They are to be served when present in the Pīṭhas, Kṣetras, Melāpakas, Śmaśānas, and the twelve Bhūmis. There is a rule that they must never be released in a populated area, in the midst of a village, in a communal feast (gaṇacakra), or in an external solitary place.
All of them wander about naked, unclothed, with disheveled hair, skull-bowls and flaying knives in their hands. || 127 ||
In the chapter [on] the Great Instruction on the Ritual for the Mandala Circle and the Practice of Yoga regarding Consecration:

Śrī-Vajrī, the glorious progenitor, the father of the three worlds; all the Buddhas, his brothers, beginning with Netra; and his many other various sons, nephews, and grandsons—those situated in the mandala who have gone to their own family lands with the Yoginīs, should be served with joy. In the field (*kṣetra*), the seat (*pīṭha*), and the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), they should never be released, whether among people or in solitude. 128.

Thus, the illustrious Śrīvatrī is the Ācārya, and the illustrious Janetā is the Ḍomba; he alone is the Caṇḍāla. Because of his leadership, the Ḍombī is the Caṇḍālī, due to her consuming leftovers and practicing sexual union with him.
In this way, through the purity of the *kula*, a yogin must not avoid his own mother and other female relatives who have come to his own domain, even if they are born of the same lineage.
In that regard, no sense of shame should be felt; rather, by yogins, Śrī Heruka—the progenitor of Śrī and father of the three worlds—should be viewed as Vajrasattva.

All Buddhas are his brothers; those of the *śūdra* caste and others, such as the *haḍḍika* (leather-workers) and so forth, are his paternal uncles; and those of the *netra* caste and others, such as the *kaṃsakāra* (bellows-makers) and so forth, are his nephews.
The eight grandsons, such as Haḍḍika and others, and the sons of the grandsons, such as the blacksmiths and others,
are not to be released by the Yoginīs either in a crowd or in solitude; this is the rule for the mutual purification of the minds [of the practitioners].

O King, whatever woman— moon-faced, with eyes like blue lotuses, and anointed with divine perfumes— offers vajra-worship to the Ācārya for the sake of merit with the threefold purity, she obtains all that merit which would otherwise result from the gift of elephants, horses, chariots, and many maidens; thus remains established the one who sits upon the moon and sun.

In that feast-circle (*gaṇacakra*) during the gift of land, whatever woman— possessing a moon-like face, lotus-eyes, and anointed with divine perfumes— offers a cloth-offering to the Ācārya together with the Vīras for the sake of merit, being pure in the three ways (*triśuddhi*), O Lord of Men,
all the merit that arises from the gift of land, elephants, horses, chariots, and many maidens belongs to that Yoginī; thus he addressed him.
