The meaning is that there is an inexhaustible sleep of the moon and sun while one remains in their natural state. || 129 ||

Now the families of Tārā and the others are described according to the castes of Śūdra and so forth: Tārā is a Śūdra woman of four kinds on the surface of the earth; Pāṇḍarā is a Kṣatriya; Kṣmā is a Vaiśya of three types; Māmakī, born of the family of the twice-born, is of seven kinds; Śabdavajrā is indeed a bell-metal worker (kāṃsyakārī); Rasavajrā is a female vintner (śauṇḍinī); Rūpavajrā is properly a goldsmith (hemakārī), O Lord of Men; and Gandhavajrā exists on the earth [as a caste]. (130)
The flower-seller is indeed well-known as Mālākārī; by the power of her natural qualities, she who works with garments of diamond-fiber becomes Vajrāntā, for she is the Dharmadhātu.
The butcher is well-known in the world as Cāmuṇḍā; by the power of her natural qualities, Vaiṣṇavī is the potter, Vārāhī is the ball-maker, and Gaṇikā is Ṣaṇmukhī; Sīvikendrī is the weaver. || 131 ||
According to the *Yajurveda* branch beginning with "Tāra," in this mortal world, one's family is determined by one's karma;
therein, the Śūdra woman is of four types: the cultivator of land, the cowherd, the worker in clay, and the architect of houses and the like.
Thus, Tārā becomes fourfold among Śūdras on the surface of the earth;
Pāṇḍarā is fourfold among Kṣatriyas according to the Kṣatriya dharma—as a foot-soldier, a horseman, an elephant-rider, and a charioteer;
and Locanā is threefold among Vaiśyas due to the Vaiśya dharma—as a merchant, a scribe, and a physician.

Born from a family of twice-born men, my mother is a Brāhmaṇī in seven ways according to the dharma of the twice-born: she is the branch of the Ṛgveda, the branch of the Sāmaveda, the branch of the Atharvaveda, the wife of a forest-dweller (vānaprastha), the wife of an ascetic (yati), and the wife of one who is liberated—thus she is sevenfold. Likewise, she is the diamond of sound (śabdavajrā), the maker of brass vessels, the diamond of taste (rasavajrā), and the female liquor-seller.
Rūpavajrā is the goldsmith,
Gandhavajrā is the garland-maker,
and Sparśavajrā is the weaver.
Dharmadhātuvajrā, Maṇikārī,
Raudrākṣī, Kūpakartrī, Atinīlā, Veṇu, and Nartakī.
Likewise, Dombanaṭī is Cāmuṇḍā, Khaṭṭikī is Vaiṣṇavī, and Kumbhakārī is [Vārāhī].
Vārāhī, Kandukī, Kaumārī, Veśyā, Aindrī, and Sīvikā. || 130–131 ||

Brahmāṇī shall be a fisherwoman; Īśvarī, in a dwelling on the surface of the earth, shall be a dancer; Lakṣmī becomes a washerwoman with a face like the full moon; and the eighth, Bhūtayoni, becomes a stage-maker and a Jambhinī.
O Lord of Men, Stambhakī is a silk-worm worker, Koṣakārī is known as a garland-maker, Subṛhatibalā is an oil-presser, and the fourth is a blacksmith. 132.
Brahmāṇī, Kaivartī, Raudrī, Naṭī, Lakṣmī, and Rajakī— these are the eight.
Likewise, Jambhī is the lac-maker,
Stambhī is the silkworm-reeler, Mālinī is the oil-presser.
Atibalā is a blacksmith woman. || 132 ||
Mārīcī is a leather-worker, Bhṛkuṭī likewise a woodworker; Śrībuddhā is a barber, and Śṛṅkhalā, residing in the world of the earth, is a bamboo-worker;
Vajrākṣī is a well-digger, and the tenth is Veṇunṛtyātinīlā. These ten women, born from the wrathful [deities] and being portions of the wrathful ones, are indeed to be worshipped by the yogin. 133.
Mārīcī, Carmakārī, Bhṛkuṭī, Kāṣṭhakārī, Cundā, Nāpitī, Vajraśṛṅkhalā, and Veṇukārī—these eight belong to the class of wrathful deities (krodhajātīya). || 133 ||

O King, the Mlecchā has the face of a dog; Haḍḍinī has the face of a boar; Mātaṅgī has the face of a jackal; Tāpinī, who dwells on the surface of the earth, has the face of a tiger; Varvarī has the face of a crow; Pukkasī is clearly established as having the face of a vulture; Śrībhillī has the face of a Tārkṣya (eagle); Śabarī has the face of a blue jay; and Aṣṭamī has the face of an owl. 134.
Śvānāsyā, Mlecchā, Śūkarāyā, Ahaḍḍinī, Jambukāsthā, and Mātaṅgī.
Vyāghrāsthā is Tāpinī;
Kākāsyā is Varvarī; Gṛdhrāsthā is Pukkasī.
Garuḍāsyā, Bhillī, Ulūkāsyā, and Śabarī—these are the eight Pracaṇḍās. || 134 ||

Through the thirty-six divisions of phonemes, the families (*kula*) of the Yoginīs are established upon the surface of the earth in sacred seats (*pīṭha*), fields (*kṣetra*), secondary fields (*upakṣetra*), excellent regions (*viṣaya*), cities (*pura*), and the glorious groves (*śrīvana*).
These are bonds for the foolish, yet on this most excellent ground, they bestow accomplishment (*siddhi*) upon yogins. They are four, six, eight, ten, and eight, and one by one, in sequence. (135)

Thus, by means of the thirty-six divisions of castes (*varṇa*), the families (*kula*) of yoginīs are established upon the surface of the earth in the sacred seats (*pīṭha*), fields (*kṣetra*), subsidiary fields (*upakṣetra*), excellent cities (*viṣayapuravara*), and hermitages (*dhīvana*).
These are bonds for the ignorant, yet on this supreme great ground, they grant accomplishment (*siddhi*) to yogins.

Furthermore, their subdivisions are fourfold: the Śūdras and so forth; the six, such as Śabdavajrā and others; likewise the eight, such as Carcikā and others; and the ten divisions of the Wrathful Ones (*krodha*). Among these, two have entered into the [groups] beginning with Sound (*śabda*).
The Vasus are of eight types, beginning with Śvānāsya. || 135 ||

Furthermore, there are four divisions of the Buddhas; indeed, the seasons are the divisions of the Bodhisattvas; the directions are the divisions of the Krodhas; likewise, there are eight divisions of Pretas in their dwellings upon the surface of the earth;
and the eight divisions of the Daityas residing in the world of the hooded serpents are to be known by the yogis as the pervasive lords of the Śrī-kulas within each of the three worlds. (136)
Thus, the eight Caṇḍas are in the netherworlds (pātāla), the Krodhas in the circle of the ten directions, and [the Lord] pervades the mortal world of the Śrīkulas. || 136 ||

In the seven netherworlds (pātāla) are the eight Caṇḍās; in the circle of the ten directions are the Krodhas; in the mortal world they are called Pretas; in the realm of the pretas [they are] the six beginning with Śabdavajrā in the abode of the best of gods;

in the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) are the four Śrīs; and in the supreme city of Śiva is the single Mother. With their faces enraged, they destroy the universe of the three realms, yet when pleased, they indeed protect it. (137)
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is stated: "Thus, in the netherworlds (*pātāla*) are the eight Caṇḍās, Śvānāsyā and the others;
in the circle of the ten directions within the mortal world are those born of the Krodhas;
and in the world of the Pretas are the eight known as Pretas."
In the abode of the excellent gods (the desire realm) is the group of six beginning with Śabdavajrā, belonging to the six classes of gods of the desire realm.

In the Egg of Brahmā (the form realm) are the four glorious goddesses, belonging to the form-realm gods such as the Brahmakāyikas; for those who have meditated on the "totality of earth" and so forth, and for the nameless formless beings, there is the element of emptiness.
In the supreme city of Śiva is the Sole Mother, the element of gnosis, Prajñāpāramitā.
When their faces are enraged, these [Yoginīs] withdraw the entire body; when satisfied, they indeed protect it.
Such is the rule of the Yoginī-kula. || 137 ||

Whether they be children, the elderly, or young women; whether their bodies are defiled, or they be Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, Śūdra, or even those of the lowest castes; or whether they have lost their eyes, hands, ears, lips, or noses—O King, all such persons should be honored with wisdom and skillful means by teachers whose hearts are compassionate, who are free from impurity, and who are established in the conduct of awakening for the sake of increasing [the lineage]. 138.
By the words "bālā" and so forth:

here, in this *gaṇacakra*, whether in solitude, at the time of meditation, or in a secluded place, [one may take] a girl, an old woman, or a young woman; one whose body is defiled, or a Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriṇī, a Vaiśyā, a Śūdrā, or an outcaste woman; or one who has lost her eyes or hands, or whose ears are severed, or whose nose is severed, or whose lips are severed.

Thus, all these [deities], even if deficient in some limbs, should be worshipped with supreme compassion for the sake of enlightenment by teachers or yogins who are free from defilement through the yoga consisting of wisdom and means, who are liberated from faults such as pride, who are established in the conduct of awakening, and who are freed from all attachments, external households, and dualities; such is the rule of the Blessed One. || 138 ||

Now, the designations of the four mudrās in the Vajra-pūjā are stated: first, the woman is the Guhyamudrā; indeed, in the Samaya, the Śrīnara is the Divyamudrā; the limb of play is the Karmamudrā; and by means of the two organs in equal bliss, she is the Dharmamudrā.

Regarding the messengers (dūtīs), there are five scents located in the lotus of the body, and their five types [of substances] are musk, lotus, urine, and so forth; due to the power of their natural qualities, they possess a fleshy odor and a putrid scent. (139)
By the words "at the beginning," and so forth:
here, in the *samayamelāpaka*, there are four types of designations.
That wisdom (*prajñā*) which is the woman at the beginning is called the secret seal (*guhyamudrā*).
The illustrious Nara is the yoga, and the consort (upāya) is the divine seal (divyamudrā) at the time of the commitment (samaya).
In their union, the acts such as embracing, limb-to-limb contact, and kissing are called the action seal (karmamudrā).
When there is the conjunction of the two organs, that which consists of the increase of equal bliss is called the great seal (mahāmudrā).
Thus, the fourfold symbolic language (*samaya-bhāṣā*) has been explained in the context of Vajra-worship.
Now, the characteristics of the scent in the bodies or the wombs of the female messengers (*dūtī*) are described, beginning with the words "of the messengers" (*dūtīnām*).
Here, five scents belonging to the messengers arise, residing either in their bodies or in their lotuses.
Thus, there are five types [of birth] among them;

in that regard, [the odors] are the scent of musk, the scent of a lotus, the scent of meat due to its qualities, and a putrid odor. (139) [This concludes] the Great Chapter on the Ritual of the Yoga of the Assembly-Wheel for Consecration.

The smell of urine; the natures are space and so forth. Of these, Śrī-Bhadrā is indeed the *padminī*, while the *jalacarī*, *citriṇī*, and *hastinī* are Śrī, Tārā, and she known as Pāṇḍarā, [respectively] according to their families, as well as Māmakī and Locanā.
The yogis are the lion, the deer, the horse, the bull, and the elephant due to the distinctions of their castes: Akṣobhya, Amoghasiddhi, Vimalamaṇikara, Padmapāṇi, and Cakrī.
Respectively, they are Śrībhadrā, Padminī, Śaṅkhinī, Citriṇī, and Hastinī. Their scents, such as musk and so forth, arise in this sequential order.
"Śrī" refers to Vajradhātvīśvarī, who is *śroḥ*.
Subhadrā is Tārā Padminī;
Pāṇḍarā is Śaṅkhinī; Māmaka is Citriṇī.
Locanā and Hastinī;
likewise, the yogin is also fivefold—lion, deer, horse, bull, and elephant—due to the distinction of their lineages.
Akṣobhya is the lion.
Amoghasiddhi is the deer;
Ratnasambhava is the horse;
Amitābha is the bull.
"Vairocana is the elephant.
From that, as before, there is the restriction of the fragrance and the restriction of the genus. || 140 ||

Now the characteristics of the body are described: Tanvaṅgī has slender limbs, fine hair, soft hands and feet, and is affectionate; Śrīsubhadrā is somewhat thin and tall, with steady eyes, and is a Padminī type with curly hair; Nirlajjā is shameless, possesses intense passion, and is prone to much quarreling; Śaṅkhinī has very little hair; Dīrghā is tall and indeed full in all her limbs; Laghuviṣayā is a Citriṇī type with long hair. || 141 ||
By the passage beginning with "tanvaṅgī" (slender-limbed) and so forth: here, Subhadrā—slender-limbed, with fine hair, having soft hands and feet, and affectionate by nature—is Vajradhātvīśvarī.
Likewise, she who is somewhat slender, tall, with steady eyes, a lotus-like form, and curly hair is Tārā.
Likewise, she who is shameless, possesses intense desire, is prone to much quarreling, and has thin hair is Śaṅkhinī; Pāṇḍarā has pale skin;
Citriṇī is tall, has all her limbs fully developed, is fond of trivial objects, and has long hair; and Māmakī is short. 141.
The *Hastinī* (Elephant-maiden) is stout, short, firm-limbed, possesses very hard organs, and has thick hair; she may sometimes here be of pure caste, but is always of mixed caste among messengers.

The *Siṃha* (Lion-maiden) dwells in solitude, is devoid of sensual objects, fearless, and generous by nature. The *Sāraṅga* (Deer-maiden) moves swiftly, has delicate and fleeting organs, and is timid-hearted and extremely afraid. || 142 ||
Thus, the *hastinī* has thick, short, firm-limbed, and very hard features, with coarse hair and eyes;

such is the pure caste (*śuddhajāti*) of the female messengers (*dūtī*), though here it may sometimes be mixed. This concludes the rule for the consecration (*abhiṣeka-niyama*) within the thirty-six [categories] in the *Vimalaprabhā*.
Now the characteristics of the yogins are described: Siṃha dwells in solitude, is free from sense objects, fearless, and disposed toward renunciation; he is Akṣobhya.
Sāraṅga moves swiftly, his senses are light and fleeting, his mind is agitated, and he is extremely fearful; he is Amoghasiddhi. || 142 ||

A horse indeed becomes lustful, dependent on others, smelling of urine, seeking the interests of another, with fixed eyes, slow-moving, dull by nature, and fish-scented; such is the bull. An elephant is indeed lustful, slow-moving, foul-smelling, and exceedingly foolish. Thus, there are thirty-six varieties distinguished by color, scent, and temperament in this world. (143)
The horse is indeed lustful, dependent on others, smelling of urine, and seeking the interests of another—thus is Ratnasambhava.
The bull has fixed eyes, moves slowly, is dull by nature, and smells of fish—thus is Amitābha.
The elephant is truly lustful, follows after others, and is foul-smelling and extremely foolish—thus is Vairocana.
Thus, in some cases there is a pure birth;
for yogins, however, there is everywhere a mixed birth.
In this way, within the abode of the earth's surface, the thirty-six varieties of the nature of color and fragrance, being mutually mixed, exist. || 143 ||

For the sake of worship, the science of desire (kāmaśāstra), which is the abode of many virtues, should be understood by the yogin; for a yoginī who is not satisfied does not grant accomplishment even when engaged in sexual union. A divine goddess becomes a piśācī, a human, a rākṣasī, or a nāginī; yet, by the power of her qualities, she becomes the divine Śrī Dharmadhātu and the goddess Chandravajrā.

O Lord of Men, the Piśācī is the one who possesses the vajra of smell; the Rākṣasī, who is indeed cruel, is the one who possesses the vajra of taste; the divine Nāginī is the one who possesses the vajra of touch. The goddess who delights in vows and observances, who is devoted to self-restraint, meditation, and virtue, and who is intent on providing aid to sentient beings, is the one who possesses the vajra of form. But she who is attached to sensual enjoyments and delights in filth, leftovers, and blood, is the Piśācī. 145.

Now, for the sake of worshipping those female messengers (*dūtīs*), the *Kāmaśāstra*—which is the abode of many virtues—must be known by the yogi. Why? Because a messenger who is not satisfied will not grant success (*siddhi*), even when sexual union (*surata*) has occurred, for both the yogi and the yoginī. Therefore, it is a rule that the *Kāmaśāstra* must be understood for the sake of worldly accomplishments (*laukikasiddhi*).
Now, the family of the dūtīs, beginning with Dharmadhātu, is described starting with the words "divyā" and so forth.

Here, the divine one (divyā) is Dharmadhātu; the goddess (devī) is Śabdavajrā; the piśācī is Gandhavajrā; the human woman (manujā) is Rūpavajrā; the rākṣasī is Rasavajrā; and the nāginī is Sparśavajrā. Among them, the divine one is one who benefits sentient beings, delights in vows and observances, and is characterized by self-restraint and meditation. The goddess is one who is attached to enjoyments. The piśācī is one who is fond of filth, leftovers, and blood. (144–145)
Mutually; and;
mixed;
and; therefore, of these.
*Rasavajrā* does not exist [here].
[From the *Rākṣasīpaṭala*, verses 142–148:

"The *Rākṣasī* who is passionately attached to desire, who delights in human blood, whose mind is intent on Māra, and the *Nāginī* who hopes for milk—these should be worshipped by the yogi upon the most excellent surface of the earth. [This concludes] the Great Chapter on the Ritual of the Gaṇacakra for Consecration and the Practice of Yoga.

In this way, other natures, divided into thirty-six varieties, belonging to the Khecarīs and Bhūcarīs dwelling upon the surface of the earth, are to be understood by the yogin according to the power of their innate qualities. 146.

A woman who is passionately attached to desire, who delights in human blood, whose mind is like that of a *rākṣasa*, and who is a serpent-like one (*nāginī*) with the hope for milk, should be worshipped by a yogi on this excellent surface of the earth.
This is the rule regarding all the *pīṭhas*, *upapīṭhas*, and so forth.

Likewise, other women of mixed nature should be understood by the yogi according to their natural qualities, through the disposition of desire or non-desire of Cāmuṇḍā and the others, by means of the method to be explained in the chapter on practice (*sādhanāpaṭala*).
Thus, there are thirty-six varieties of Khecarīs and Bhūcarīs residing upon the surface of the earth. (146)

Now, the rule for the drinking of the teacher is stated: If one who lacks the *mudrā* should drink liquor—which is of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) and produced from honey, molasses, grain, or trees—he becomes a worldly subject (*viṣayin*) enveloped by the hosts of Māra.

Therefore, for the sake of drinking, the practitioner (*mantrin*) should employ some *mudrā* belonging to this [system], even if she is devoid of the pledge (*samaya*), provided that liquor is dedicated to wisdom, removes the stains of defilement, and bestows accomplishment upon the practitioners. (147)
Regarding the passage beginning with "madyam": here, all intoxicants (*madya*)—whether produced from honey, molasses, grain, or trees, or even others—are of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Any master who drinks [an intoxicant] without the *mudrā* becomes an object of the senses; that is to say, he becomes a drunkard.
One does not become obscured by the hosts of Māra;
therefore, for practitioners of mantra, this [practice] which is devoted to wisdom, removes the stains of turbidity, and bestows accomplishment.
At the time of drinking this liquor in the maṇḍala, one may employ any mudrā whatsoever—even one devoid of the *samaya*—for the purpose of drinking, provided it is without a *gaṇacakra*.
This is the rule: [it is] for the purpose of the Vajra-worship. || 147 ||

The qualities of that fourth *samaya* which has been practiced by yogins are now described: O King, the single moon, when practiced at all times, removes the fear of death; it abides in the arising of the Dharma of wisdom (*prajñā*) together with the sun. How much more so when joined with yoga! Accompanied by Akṣobhya and Amoghasiddhi, the best of Jinas, and joined with dogs, horses, cows, and elephants, it is the vajra-staff of the afflictions, striking fear into common folk; and the eighth is another, exceedingly fierce. (148)
O King, the single moon, when served at all times with the bliss of the Infallible One (*acyuta*), removes the fear of death.

The element of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta-dhātu*), which abides in the source of wisdom and phenomena and is accompanied by the sun, removes the fear of death even when consumed externally; how much more so when practiced within the yogas!
0jamikṣu | kha. 0dhiyuktaṃ | in cooking.
ca. cha. The quality (*guṇa*) is mentioned.
kha. kha. "Served" (*sevitaḥ*) and "remover of fear" (*abhayaharaḥ*) do not exist.
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, [the phrase] "joined with consecration" (*abhiṣekayuktaḥ*) means "rendered immutable" (*acyutīkṛtaḥ*).
Akṣobhya is urine, Amoghasiddhi is marrow, and Vairocana, the best of Jinas, is [semen]; joined with these, it removes the fear of death.

Likewise, there is that which is joined with dog, horse, cow, and elephant; it is the adamantine staff of the afflictions (*kleśa*), a source of terror for base people, and the eighth is another, most fierce one, known as the *mahāmāṃsa-samaya*.
Thus, feces, urine, and marrow are the five lamps; together with the two, moon and sun, they constitute the eight pledges (*samaya*).

Thus, the tenfold worship consisting of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five lamps becomes the *gaṇacakra*. The fourfold commitment (*samaya*)—the consumption of liquor, meat, sexual union, and the nectar—must be performed by the master;
otherwise, one is seized by the hosts of Māra. Such is the rule of the Tathāgatas. (148)

Now, the thirty-six commitments (*samaya*) are described as the transformation of the forms of the Yoginīs: dog, horse, cow, elephant, ram, goat, deer, donkey, boar, rhinoceros, owl, these ten; crocodile, rat, crab, fish, shark, crocodile (*makara*), frog, tortoise, and conch; cheetah, tiger, bear, mongoose, yak, jackal, otter, cat, wild dog, and lion—these ten are the eight [groups] born of the elements and born of wrath. (149)
By the words "dog, horse," and so forth:
here, Tārā is the dog, and Pāṇḍarā is the horse.
Gaurī is Māmakī;
Hastinī is Locanā;
and Vajradhātvīśvarī is Sarvarūpadhāriṇī.
The ram is the thunderbolt of sound; the goat is the thunderbolt of touch;
the deer is the thunderbolt of taste.
The donkey is Rūpavajrā;
the pig is Gandhavajrā;
the camel is Dharmadhātuvajrā.
Know these ten according to the divisions of the families of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas:
likewise, Kumbhīra is Cakrī,
and Ākhu is Vaiṣṇavī.
The crab is Vārāhī;
the hare is Kaumārī;
the crocodile is Aindrī.
Darbura is Brahmāṇī,
Kūrma is Īśvarī,
and Śaṅkha is Mahālakṣmī; these are the eight Bhūtajās.
Gaṇḍa is Jambhī;
Vyāghra is Stambhī;
Ṛkṣa is Māninī.
Nakula is Atibalā;
Camarī is Vajraśṛṅkhalā;
Jambuka is Bhṛkuṭī.
Udara, Cundā, Viḍālā, Mārīcī, Āraṇyavāsinī, Atinīlā, and Siṃhī, Raudrākṣī—this is the group of ten born from Krodha. (149)

The lizard, the mouse, the monkey born of the *śāli* rice, the hare, the porcupine, the *kṛka* bird, the proud parrot, the one who has manifested the ocean, the cuckoo, the *śārikā*, the quail, the pigeon, the other crane, the sparrow, the ruddy goose, the swan, the *śrīkuñcā*, the *kokilākṣī*, the venerable washerwoman, the partridge, and the crane. (150)

The fallen ones: Tārā, Inā, Pañcatārā, Yoginī, Lug-mo (the Sheep Woman), Me-śi (the Goat Woman), Bon-mo (the Bon Woman), Kha-rī (the Donkey Woman), Phag-mo (the Sow Woman), Śūkarī, Kumbhīra, and Kumbhīrā—in the *pāṭha*, however, the sequence is "Gaṇḍo, Atibalā, Jambhī, Vyāghrī";
[then] Dom-mo (the Bear Woman), Ṛkṣī, Mānanī, and Māriṇī.
This female jackal (*jambukī*) is *uṭraḥ*; however, in the Tibetan recension, the sequence is "mārīcī, *uṭraḥ*, viḍālaḥ, *cundā*.
[The female] Mārīcī; the female lion (*siṃhī*)—the word "iti" is not present.

In the *Krodhavajra* chapter, [it is said]: "The great instruction on the yoga and ritual of the mandala for the assembly of consecration (*pratiṣṭhāgaṇacakra*)—namely, the cow is Kākāsyā; the mouse is Śūkarāsyā; the śālija bird is Jambukāsyā; the monkey is also Śvānāsyā; the porcupine is Gṛdhrāsyā; the arrow-maker (iṣuka) is Garuḍāsyā; and the chameleon is Ulūkāsyā—these eight are the pledges (*samaya*) of the asura classes, as well as their transformation of form.
Likewise, the tiger is the pledge-restriction (*samayaniyama*) for those moving on land and those moving in water, while the rabbit is [the restriction] for those moving in the air.
Now, the pledges of those moving in the air are stated, beginning with the word "mānī" and so forth.

In this context, just as there is a group of four beginning with the dog, so too there are four birds—the *mānī*, the *cātaka*, the parrot (*śuka*), and the cuckoo (*kokilā*)—which are the manifest seasons (*ṛtu*) such as Tārā and the rest.
Likewise, there are six beginning with Śabdavajrā.
The rule [of the remaining birds] is: the quail (*lāva*), the pigeon (*pārāvata*), the crane (*baka*), the sparrow (*caṭaka*), the ruddy goose (*cakravāka*), and the swan (*haṃsa*).
Likewise, there are eight [deities] born of the elements (bhūtajā) who are bound by the pledge (samaya):
Kucā, Kokilākṣī, Rajakī, Bhagavatī, Potakī, Tittirī, and Sārasā. 150.

One should know that the crane (balākā), along with the thousand Vasus, are possessed by Nīra; in sequence, the vulture, the wolf, the lion, the peacock, the cock, the sword, the sacrificer, the tree-enemy (elephant), and the others constitute the tenfold Krodhaja class. The blue-eyed one, the beautiful cakora bird, the wind, the anus-mouthed one, and the one who sleeps with feet upward are of the Krodha lineage. || 151 ||
"Norāviṣṭa" refers to the water-crow (*jalakāka*).
Regarding "balākā": the eight Vasus are to be understood [as the meaning].
"In the sequence of Cāmuṇḍā and the others" means as follows:
likewise, there are ten pledges (samaya) for those born of Wrath: the crow; and so forth.
The vulture, the owl,
and the "enemy of deer" (the lion), so says Mahāyājī.
*Śikhī* is a cock;
*bhedra* is a *saṃcāṇa*;
*ghāra* is a *cillā*.

The horse, the tree-rot, and the one born of anger—these belong to the class of those born of anger, such as Jambhya and so forth, respectively; likewise, there are eight *asurī* pledges, beginning with Śvānāsya:
Nīlākṣa, Cakora, Anila, Vāgbulikā, Gudamukha (known as Bukkī), Dātyūha, and the one who sleeps with its feet upward, the Ṭiṭṭibhaka. || 151 ||

O King, there is the Bheruṇḍa and the Ambarīka, and the eighth is the divine bird; these are the thirty-six varieties of species belonging to the land-dwelling and sky-dwelling [deities] throughout the world of earth.

At the time of worship, all those who have entered the Kula tradition must be consumed by the yogi according to the observance (samaya). O King, if a fool out of delusion ever abandons them, he quickly goes to his destruction.

The four [deities] with dog faces (Śvānāsyā) and bird faces (Kākāsyā) are not present in the *Ghaṭaka*. O Vajra, the word "iti" is not present. Among the wrathful ones, the Great Falcon (Mahāśyena), the Pājī, the Sañca, the Sañcana, the Pājī, and the King of Wrath (Krodharāja) are not present in the Bhoṭa [Tibetan] version. [The term] "cukkī" refers to the Bheruṇḍa; it is called Ambarīka.

O Lord of Men, for the asurīs such as Kākāsyā and the others, there is a divine group of eight birds. Thus, there are thirty varieties of species belonging to those who move on the earth and those who move in the sky.
At the time of worship, all these pledges (samaya) pertaining to the families must be consumed by the yogin when they are offered by the yoginīs.
If a fool, out of delusion, ever abandons the commitments (samaya) given at a feast-circle (gaṇacakra) and the like, he then swiftly goes to destruction through a mind of contempt. || 152 ||

Now the constituents of the body are described: O eminent lord of men, [the body] consists of teeth, hair, skin and so forth, along with flesh, sinews, bones, and the palate; lotuses, lice, and hair-insects; lungs, intestines, and the male organ; semen, the water drunk, the food eaten, the blood residing in the body, sweat, fat, tears, spittle, nasal mucus, water-like fluids, muscle-fat, color, smell, and excrement. (153)

The goddesses of the tongue, eyes, ears, and nose, together with the moon and sun, are to be worshipped; the thirty-six syllables, according to the influence of the qualities of *prakṛti*, are the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).

The thirty-six divisions of the elements, the castes belonging to all the qualities, the signs and mudrās, and the thirty-six Yoga Tantras residing upon the surface of the earth—all these belong here to the Yoginīs. (154)
By the words beginning with "with teeth," etc.:

[the body is filled] with teeth, hair, skins, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, pus, urine, lice, the tips of the body hairs, lungs, intestines, the penis, semen, bile, water, and even with pus—all these being located within the bodies of beings, belonging to the bodies of living creatures.

The deities are to be worshipped with the ritual substances (*samayadravya*) consisting of blood, one’s own semen, the two kinds of fat (*medas*), the two kinds of mucus (*kheṭaka*), nasal secretions (*siṃhāṇa*), glistening fluids, various kinds of marrow (*vasā*), various colors, various scents, tongues, eyes, ears, and noses; "moon" refers to the semen (*śukra*), and "sun" refers to the dust (*rajas*).
This is the rule for yogis regarding the *gaṇacakra*.
There are thirty syllables for them, according to the influence of the qualities of nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*), that is, according to the qualities beginning with space (*ākāśa*).
Ṅa gha gakha ka; ña jha ja cha ca; ṇa ḍha ḍa ṭha ṭa; ma bha ba pha pa; na dha da tha ta; — ka śa ṣa sa ha ya ra va la kṣa.
These are the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma), which together with the Bhagavatī constitute thirty-seven. Thus, there are thirty-six divisions of the elements (dhātu).
a ā i ī ṛ ṝ u ū ḷ ḹ aṃ aḥ | a ā e ai ar ār o au al āl aṃ aḥ | ha hā ya yā ra rā va vā la lā haṃ haḥ |
Thus are the thirty-six divisions of the elements (*dhātu*).
These are all the classes that pertain to the qualities (*guṇa*).
These are all the classes that pertain to the qualities.
The thirty-six marks [are indicated] by thirty-six mouths (ga) and two shields (ca). Bho. *Chu rgyus* (sinews); ka. *vaktraiḥ* (by mouths);
ga. ca. *kheṭābhyām* (by two shields).
O! With marrow and excrement;
with these powders.
kha. ga. ca. cha. bho, *dhātu*;
kha. ga. ca. cha. [the word] is not present; ga. *bhuvi*, ca. bho. *bhuvana*.

[The section on] the classification of elements (dhātubheda) [is found] in the chapter on the ritual procedure for the maṇḍala of the assembly of consecration (pratiṣṭhāgaṇacakra), verse [number]. This is the great instruction on the practice of yoga (yogacaryā). There are six mudrās.
Thus, by means of each individual syllable accompanied by a vowel, thirty-six Yoga Tantras are produced; likewise are the Yoginī Kula Tantras.
Together with the Bhagavatī, everything should be understood as consisting of thirty-seven [units]; this is the rule regarding those situated upon the surface of the earth.
The remaining ones are not pure families because they possess various secondary characteristics (*vyañjana*).
Thus there are thirty-six.
The procedure for the mandalas of the families and the worship of the yoginīs must be performed on the full moon; this is the rule of the Tathāgata.

Now, the offering of water and so forth in the *cakramelāpaka* is described: water for the feet, perfume, incense, flowers, fruit, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), a lamp, food offerings (*naivedya*), and clothing—this indeed constitutes the tenfold [offering] in the *cakramelāpaka*.
Semen, urine, marrow, fat, flesh, bile, blood, entrails, skin, and the "time-born" (flesh)—O King, this tenfold [offering] also occurs in the *cakramelāpaka*.
By the words beginning with "toyetyādinā":

the vessel for water, the vessel for the *arghya* offering, the vessel for fragrance, the vessel for incense, the vessel for flowers, the vessel for fruit, the vessel for unbroken rice (*akṣata*), the vessel for the lamp, the vessel for food offerings (*naivedya*), and the vessel for cloth—thus there are ten kinds of ritual substances (*pūjā-dravya*) for the purpose of worship during the assembly of the *gaṇacakra*, as well as in the *maṇḍalacakra*.
Likewise, the internal substances (*adhyātma-dravya*) are of ten kinds: semen, urine, marrow, feces, flesh, bile produced by time, blood, intestines, and skin.
There are eight kinds of wheels for the purpose of the ritual worship of the yoginīs during the *cakramelāpaka*.

"O King" is the form of address. Now, the thirty-six signs of those born of the families beginning with Tārā are described: the vajra, the sword, the arrow, the hundred-petaled lotus, and the fifth sign is the wheel; the lute, the mirror, and the vessel, O Lord of Men, as well as the flower garland and the garment;

the sixth is indeed the *dharmodaya* on the palm of the hand, which is the sign of Śabdavajrā and the others; likewise, there is the razor and so forth, the flask, and similarly the loincloth and the yellow garment.

In this regard, when yoginīs have entered a *gaṇacakra* or are staying in a village or a city, if a different color than their bodily complexion appears on their forehead, on both shoulders, or on the left or right hip region, that sign is to be understood by its color (*varṇa*).
Furthermore, that which appears on the palms of the hands or the soles of the feet is to be understood by means of lines (*rekhā*).
Therefore, one should train in the characteristics of women and men for the purpose of taking the hand of a yoginī.

By this means, even the wives of others will offer their own hands for the sake of a mark; under that pretext, one should recognize their identifying sign—whether located on the body, on the palms or soles of the feet, or inscribed in the house. This is the method. In this regard, [the word] *yasyāḥ* (of whom) [is used]; *ga.* reads "in the city" (*nagare*), while *ca.* reads "also" (*api*).
ga. "The two hides" | ga. and at the melāpaka | bho. Lha Mo rNams (of the goddesses) |
ga. For the purpose of performing [the ritual].
ga. Tārākula does not exist.
ga. and bho.: on the left or not; ca. and bho.: ‘vā’ is absent; [the word] is absent.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, the *Abhiṣekavajra* is seen in five places of birth according to its color; that Vajradhātvīśvarī is [seen] on the palm of the hand or on the foot by means of lines. (Note: *ka. kha. cha.* read *śarīrasthāṃ*; *ga.* reads *0stha*. *ka. kha. ca. cha.* do not have the word *vā*. *Vimalaprabhāyām*.)
Therefore, she belongs to the family of Ākāśadhātu. Likewise, the sword belongs to Tārā;
or the arrow or the jewel belongs to Pāṇḍarā.
The hundred-petaled lotus is the symbol of Māmakī;
the fifth, the wheel-sign, belongs to Locanā. These are the symbols of the families of Air, Fire, Water, and Earth. Likewise, the lute is the symbol of Śabdavajrā.
The mirror belongs to Rūpavajrā;
the bowl belongs to Rasavajrā;
the flower garland belongs to Gandhavajrā.

The garment belongs to Sparśavajrā; the *dharmodaya* (source of phenomena) belongs to Dharmadhātuvajrā. These are seen in the five places of birth, or in the hands and feet, for those born into the families of the sense objects.
Thus, the eightfold symbols of Śabdavajrā and the others consist of the knife and so forth.
Among those, the knife belongs to Cāmuṇḍā;
the water-pot to Vaiṣṇavī;
and the small shield to Vārāhī.
The yellow garment belongs to Kaumārī. O King, the needle or the mallet, the manifested and fixed fish-net, the trident, the mark of Lakṣmī, and the stone indeed belong to the eight Bhūtajās.

For Jambhyā and the others, there is the lac-vessel, the sun-like [object], the silkworm, the *kuśa* grass, the knife, the sandal, as well as the razor, the shoe, and the parasol. The needle or the mallet belongs to Aindrī;
the fish-net belongs to Brahmāṇī.
The trident is the emblem of Raudrī;
the square stone slab is that of Lakṣmī.
Thus are the emblems of the Bhūtas born from the families of the immortals and others.
Likewise, there is a group of ten born of anger (*krodha-jā*).
Among them: *Jambhyā* has a vessel of lac-dye that is circular and resembles the sun;
*Stambhyā* has a silkworm.
Kuśa [is the weapon] of Māninī;
a knife is [the weapon] of Atibalā;
a sandal is [the weapon] of Mārīcī; and a razor is [the weapon] of Cundā.

The sandal is the symbol of Bhṛkuṭī; the parasol is the symbol of Vajraśṛṅkhalā. The spade and the bamboo staff constitute the tenfold set of symbols arising from the Wrathful Ones (*krodha*). The cow-horn is the symbol of Mallā; the lute is on the palm of the hand; the meat-spear is Trākuṭī;

the *vīṇā* and the *upāṅga* are the bow; and the peacock feather is the eighth. These thirty-six distinct symbols are to be worshipped by the yogi upon this excellent surface of the earth. The spade is the symbol of Raudrākṣī.
The bamboo staff belongs to Balā.
Thus, there are ten [deities] among those born of wrath, each with their own specific emblem; likewise for the two types of organs of action.
Similarly, the emblems of the female deities (āsurī) are as follows: the cow-horn belongs to Śvānāsyā.
The *malla* is the bowl of Śukarāsyā;
the *tantrī* is that of Jambukāsyā;
the *śrākuṭī* is that of Vyāghrāsyā; and the *khaḍga* is that of Śvānāsyā.

11. [In] Ga, Ca, and Bho: *nīlāyāḥ*. 12. [In] Ca: *rājñām*. 13. [In] Bho: 14. [In] Ca: *śarāvam*, [in] Ga: *śarāvaḥ*.
15. *Tākuṭī*, [the practice] of *Syāyā*.
The great chapter on the yoga-conduct for the ritual of the *Pratiṣṭhā-gaṇacakra* is [the practice] of *Syāyā*.
*Māṃsaśūla* is [the practice] of *Kākāsyā*.
The lute (*vīṇā*) and its accessory (*upāṅga*) belong to Gṛdhrāsyā;
the arrow-shaft (*kāṇḍa*) and the peacock feather belong to Garuḍā and Ulūkāsyā.
Thus, by means of the purification of the eight gates beginning with the mouth, the eight signs of the eight families are seen;
likewise, those in whom the thirty-six signs are seen belong to those respective families.
"Having recognized [them] by that sign, they are to be worshipped; such is the rule for the yoginīs. || 158 ||

Furthermore, by the power of their qualities, the insignia of a Śūdra woman is either a lotus or a plough; that of a Kṣatriya woman is a jeweled band or a pen; and that of a Vaiśya woman is likewise a copper vessel accompanied by aquatic creatures. The insignia of the mother of the twice-born (Brahmin) is fourfold: a hand-drum, a large drum, a crown, and a rosary. || 159 ||
Furthermore, the signs of the Śūdra and other castes for the Tārās and so forth are now described here:
by virtue of the qualities of a Śūdra, the mark of a blue lotus or a plow is seen on those born of the Tārā family;
for one born of the Kṣatriṇī family, it is a white silk band; for one born of the Vaiśyā family, it is a pen and a jewel-garland; and for one born of the Locanā family, it is likewise [the same].
An aquatic creature, a conch,
and a copper vessel belong to a twice-born woman born of my own lineage;
thus, these four are the maternal signs, both preceding and following.
The hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*) and the skull-cup (*paṭala*) belong to the *Ḍombī*, who is born from the family of Vajradhātvīśvarī;
likewise, the crown or the rosary belong to the *Caṇḍālī*, who is born from the family of Prajñāpāramitā.
Thus, whichever sign is seen on the forehead, the shoulder, the hip, or the hands and feet, or is depicted in the home, that woman should be known by the yogi as belonging to that particular family.

Whatever *samaya-dravya* (sacramental substance) has been given by her must be consumed; when that reaches its conclusion after seven revolutions, then, by means of that *samaya-dravya*, the state of moving through the air (*khecaratva*) comes to be—this is the rule. || 159 ||

Now, the purification of the deities of earth and the other elements corresponding to the sacramental substances (samayadravya) such as excrement and so forth is described: Excrement, urine, blood, and flesh constitute the tetrad of goddesses; likewise, the ears, nose, eyes, tongue, anus, and vulva; the six beginning with sound and the vajra;

pus, phlegm, lice, worms, marrow, fat, hair on the body, and hair on the head; the eightfold [set]; the intestines, bile, bone, marrow, and the various bodily constituents, including the black [element] and the lungs. (160)
In this context, feces, urine, blood, and flesh constitute the fourfold group of the earth, water, fire, and air deities respectively.
Semen is Vajradhātvīśvarī, the space element (*ākāśadhātu*), even though it was not explicitly mentioned.
Likewise, the ears, nose, and eyes [are assigned to the other elements]. The *vīṇā* instrument belongs to Kinnarī; Gṛdhrāsyā [belongs to] the *kāṇḍa* (reed/flute). Garuḍāsyā [belongs to] the *kāṇḍa*.
2. ga. by means of purity;
3. kha.ga. [omitted] yogins; bho. does not exist; 4. bho. Ran Gi dBral Ba la (on one's own forehead); 2. ga. desire.
6. Kha, Ga, Ca, Bho: "that" is not present.
7. Bho: From this point onward, De bsten par bya ste (tat sevanīyam). 8. Bho: lHa rnams kyi (devānām).

3. ga. 0. The tongue is the one devoted to Vimalaprabhā; the anus is the *bhaga* [of the goddesses]. This is the group of six commitments (*samaya-ṣaṭka*) of the goddesses of the spheres of sound, smell, form, taste, touch, and mental phenomena, namely the group of six beginning with Śabdavajrā.

Likewise, pus, phlegm, lice, worms, nails, hair on the body, and head hair constitute the group of eight commitments (*samayāṣṭaka*), corresponding respectively to the elemental-born yoginīs: Cāmuṇḍā (Carcikā), Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Kaumārī, Aindrī, Brāhmaṇī, Raudrī, and Mahālakṣmī.

Likewise, the intestines, bile, bones, marrow, and the various bodily constituents located within the bodies of all sentient beings, as well as the lungs produced by time, are situated within their bodies. || 160 ||

The ten [limbs] consist of the channels, the skin, and the lungs, along with the fat, O Lord of Men; furthermore, the impurities located in the ears, nose, eyes, and mouth, as well as in the anus, the genitals, and the eight parts of the body beginning with the armpits, constitute the group of eight, O King.
Indeed, there are eight groups of eight Āsurī Yoginīs, who together with the nails, teeth, and skulls possess twelve limbs.

The ten [components] beginning with the channels and ending with the fat—namely, the channels, skin, lungs, and fat—are, respectively, Jambhī, Stambhī, Mānī, Atibalā, Vajraśṛṅkhalā, Bhṛkuṭī, Cundā, Mārīcī, Raudrākṣī, and Atinīlā; these constitute the ten pledges (*samaya*) of these wrathful goddesses.

Likewise, ear-wax, nose-mucus, eye-secretion, tongue-secretion, anus-secretion, vulva-secretion, penis-secretion, armpit-secretion, and body-secretion from all limbs constitute the eight pledges (*samaya*) for the Asurīs, corresponding respectively to Śvānāsyā, Śūkarāsyā, Jambukāsyā, Vyāghrāsyā, Kākāsyā, Gṛdhrāsyā, Garuḍāsyā, and Ulūkāsyā; these are the eight pledges of these [deities].

Likewise, regarding the sixty-four Yoginīs, such as Bhīmā and the others, their *samayas* are twenty nails and thirty-two teeth; these constitute the sixty-four *samayas* according to the division of the flow of the channels (*nāḍī*) within the skull into twelve segments.

Thus, by the division of the hundred families (*kula*), there are one hundred *samayas*, according to the scriptural statement: "The three families and the five families are indeed the single nature, the hundred families. [This includes] the thirty-six families and the sixty-four families.
The rule is that the oneness of the yoginīs is to be understood as the hundred families. || 169 ||

Now, the purification of the pledges (*samaya*) by means of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth is described: Feces, urine, blood, and flesh—these four located in various parts of the body correspond to the division of the *pīṭhas*. The ears, nose, eyes, tongue, anus, and vulva—these six correspond to the division of the *kṣetras*.

Pus and the rest, up to the hairline, correspond to the eight divisions of the *chandohas* in the abode of the earth-plane. And intestines and the rest, up to the fat, O King, correspond to the divisions of the *melāpakas* in the cardinal directions. (162)
Feces, urine, blood, and flesh— these four, located within the bodies of all various sentient beings, constitute the group of four in the division of the *pīṭhas*.
Ear, nose, eye, tongue, anus, and vulva— these six constitute the group of six in the division of the *kṣetras*.
Likewise, pus, phlegm, lice, and [in some versions] lymph; [in others] "bones."

6. In versions *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, and *cha*, the phrase "jihvāmalam" (tongue-impurity) does not exist.

9. ka. kha. bheditavyā.
3. Ga, Ca, Bheda, Kṛmilā, Śiva, and Sālomakeśā—these are the eight divisions of the *cchandoha*.
Likewise, the ten divisions of the *melāpaka* are: entrails, bile, bones, marrow, the black [organ], lungs, channels, skins, the heart, and fat. || 162 ||

Indeed, within the body consisting of the eight limbs beginning with the ears, there are various impurities which are the divisions of the cremation ground; Kālāgni, Indu, Arka, and Rāhu are the fixed quartet manifested in the division of the *pīṭhas*.

Furthermore, in the division of the fields (*kṣetra*), there is a hexad consisting of Bhauma, Saumya, Mantrī, Bhṛgu, Śani, and Phaṇin; and [the elements] Earth, Water, Fire, and Wind, as well as those born of Earth, born of Water, born of Wind, and born of Fire.
Furthermore, there are eight divisions of the *chandoha*s; likewise, there are six tastes, as well as smell, color, touch, and sound—these are the ten manifest divisions of the *melāpaka*.

Then there are earth, water, fire, air, and dissolution (*kṣaya*); these are the eight divisions of the cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*), located in front, on the left and right, and in the east, as well as in the intermediate directions for the four [elements] beginning with color. || 164 ||

Likewise, ear-wax, nasal mucus, eye-secretion, tongue-secretion, vaginal secretion, anal secretion, seminal secretion, and body-hair/underarm hair—these are the eight divisions of the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*).
Furthermore, in the external world-system, the *samayas* are spoken of through the purification of the *pīṭhas* and so forth;
here, Kālāgni, Indu, Arka, and Rāhu constitute the fourfold *samaya* of Locanā and the other goddesses within the division of the *pīṭhas*.
Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu—these are the pledges (*samaya*) regarding the division of fields for Rūpavajrā and the others.

Likewise, earth, water, fire, air, those born of earth, those born of water, those born of fire, and those born of air—these eight, consisting of both stationary and moving beings, are the pledges for those born of the elements (*bhūtajānām*) in the division of the *chandoha*. Furthermore, likewise, the "six substances" (*bar̤asā*)—smell, color, sound, and touch—are the divisions of the *melāpaka* for those born of the wrathful deities (*krodhajānām*).

The tetrad beginning with earth, as well as the destruction of color and the rest through inhalation and exhalation—these are the divisions of the cremation ground; these are the eight pledges (*samaya*) of the Āsurīs. This is the rule for the purification of the outer and inner pledges of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth. (163–164)

Now the locations such as the *pīṭhas* are described: the *pīṭha* is the abode of Tārā and others, clearly marked by the thunderbolt (*vajra*) and so forth; likewise, the *kṣetra* is said to be that of Caṇḍākṣī and others; the *chandoha* arises from Jambhikā and others, O King; the *melāpaka* is that of Śvānāsyā and others; the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*) is situated in the supreme realm; the root *pīṭha* is the most secret abode of the Mother; that is manifested on earth in two ways, for it belongs indeed to the outcaste (*antyaja*). || 165 ||

Regarding "fragrance, color, sound, and touch," in the *Vimalaprabhā* it is stated through the passage beginning with "the seat of consecration" (*abhiṣekapīṭha*) that the seats such as Jālandhara and so forth are mentioned here in a general sense for the purpose of leading the ignorant on a tour of the regions.

That very [principle] is not all-pervasive everywhere; for the thirty-six families (*kulāni*) reside even in a single city. Because of this, when supreme awakening is attained, the entire earth becomes pervasive; thus, sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth exist even in regions such as Bhotṭa and others. Those very same [seats] are taught through other minor tantras (*laghutantra*), and it is stated that the sacred seats and so forth are present in every city.
The *pīṭha* is the fourfold abode of Tārā and others;
likewise, the *kṣetra* is the sixfold abode beginning with Śabdavajrā;
and the *chandoha* is the eightfold abode beginning with Cakriṇī.
The meeting place (*melāpaka*) begins with yawning and so forth;
the tenfold house begins with the Dog-faced one (*śvānāsya*); the eightfold cemetery (*śmaśāna*) and so forth is situated in the supreme realm;
the root seat (*mūlapīṭha*) is the most secret Mother’s house, which is twofold. That is manifested on earth as the *antyaja*; for the *antyaja* house consists of the *ḍombī* and the *caṇḍālī*.
In this manner, a house belonging to a Śūdra and so forth should be understood by the yogin through its designation as a *pīṭha* and so on; such is the rule everywhere. || 165 ||

Now, the terminology of the internal seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth is stated: The seat (*pīṭha*) arises as the secret lotus of the woman; in this system, the *vajra* itself is the secondary seat (*upapīṭha*). The field (*kṣetra*), the grove (*chandoha*), the meeting place (*melāpaka*), and the cremation ground (*citibhuvana*) are likewise all [to be understood] in this same way.

The seat is the left limb first, and the secondary seat is likewise the right. In this manner, the entire [set of] fields and so forth resides in the hands and feet, extending to the tips of the fingers and toes. (166)

By the words "the seat" (*pīṭha*) and so forth: here, in the gathering of the commitments (*samayamelāpaka*), the seat everywhere is the lotus of the woman; by the term "subsidiary seat" (*upapīṭha*), the vajra of the man is meant.
Thus, the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) of women are the *kṣetra*, while those of men are the *upakṣetra*.
Likewise, the eightfold group of equal winds (*samānavāyu*) of women is the *chandoha*, while that of men is the *upachandoha*.

Similarly, the ten organs of action (*karmendriya*) of women—consisting of the tongue, the two hands, the two feet, the anus, the two channels on the left and right, and the two channels for urine and semen—are the *melāpaka*, while those of men are the *upamelāpaka*.

Thus, the two nostrils, the penis, the exit for excrement, the two ears, the two eyes, the mouth, and the anus constitute the eight cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*) for women, while for men they constitute the secondary cremation grounds (*upaśmaśāna*). Likewise, in both bodies, each *pīṭha* is located in the left limb first,
and the *upapīṭha* is in the right limb behind it.
Thus, the seat (pīṭha) is twofold:
likewise, the collection of the left-hand faculties is the field (kṣetra),
and the collection of the right-hand faculties is the secondary field (upakṣetra).

Thus, the quartet consisting of Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya is the *chanda*; the assembly of the *samāna*, *udāna*, *vyāna*, and *nāga* is the *upachandoha*. Furthermore, the assembly of the organs of action (*karmendriya*) on the left is the *melāpaka*. [From the *Pratiṣṭhāgaṇacakravidhiyogacaryāmahoddeśa*, Chapter on the Assembly of the *Nāgas*, Verse 238b.]

Likewise, on the right is the confluence (*upamelāpaka*), which is the collection of the organs of action; the exit of impurities from the openings of the left ear and so forth is the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*);
and the right [side] is the secondary cremation ground (*upaśmaśāna*).
Likewise, through another purification, the left side of the body beginning with the hands and feet is the *pīṭha*;
the right and the rear are the *upapīṭha*.
Similarly, the joint of the left arm and the joint of the left thigh and hip are the *kṣetra*.
The right secondary field (*upakṣetra*);
the left joint of the upper arm, the knee, and the joint of the thigh are the *chandoma*;
the right [thigh] is the secondary *chandoma* (*upachandoma*).
Likewise, the two joints of the hands and feet are the *melāpaka* on the left and the *upamelāpaka* on the right;
the nails of the fingers of the left hand are the *śmaśāna*, and those of the right are the *upaśmaśāna*.
Alternatively, the two joints of both arms are the *kṣetra*, and the two joints of the thighs are the *upakṣetra*.

In this way, the *chandoha* and so forth, extending even to the hands and feet as far as the tips of the fingers, are to be understood by the yogi as the designations for the *pīṭhas* and other sites according to the terminology of the *samayamelāpaka*. (166)

Now, the purification of the yoginīs by means of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) is described: The goddesses are the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), well-known in the Kālacakra; likewise, Prajñā is the mother who is the factor of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*). Furthermore, there is the group of six beginning with Śabdavajrā. The four oceans are the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*); the other oceans are the eight limbs of the two feet. The five wrathful deities are the powers (*bala*) as they are clearly manifested; the five [goddesses] are indeed the faculties (*indriya*). (167)

By the passage beginning with "The goddesses are Acirā," etc., it is established in the *Kālacakra* that here the four goddesses are, in their respective order: Locanā as the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyānusmṛtyupasthāna*), and Pāṇḍarā as the application of mindfulness to sensation (*vedanānusmṛtyupasthāna*)—these are in the west and south;

Māmakī as the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittānusmṛtyupasthāna*), and Tārā as the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmānusmṛtyupasthāna*)—these are in the north and east. These two pairs of seats (*pīṭha*) and secondary seats (*upapīṭha*) are distinguished according to the divisions of the body.
The meaning is that it is not established in another tantra, but is concealed by the Blessed One.

Likewise, among the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), one factor of enlightenment is the Mother Vajradhātvīśvarī, the family seat (*kulapīṭha*), namely the equanimity factor of enlightenment (*upekṣā-sambodhyaṅga*).
Furthermore, there is likewise the group of six beginning with Śabdavatra.
The factor of enlightenment of mindfulness is Śabdavajrā; the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena is Sparśavajrā;
the factor of enlightenment of energy is Rūpavajrā.
The secondary field (*upakṣetra*) is distinguished by the division of the body:
likewise, the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*) is Gandhavajrā;
the factor of enlightenment of tranquility (*praśrabdhisaṃbodhyaṅga*) is Rasavajrā.
The factor of enlightenment that is concentration is the locus of the *dharmadhātu*.
The field is twofold;
such are the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
The abandonment for the sake of the non-arising of unarisen evils is Cācikā; the abandonment of arisen evils is Vaiṣṇavī, which is the root of virtue;
and the abandonment of unarisen unwholesome states together with the production of the wholesome is Māheśvarī.
The non-abandonment of the dedication of arisen unwholesome states toward Buddhahood is Mahālakṣmī.
There are four secondary *chandohas*, which are the four goddesses who are the oceans of others; they become the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Among them, the base of psychic power of zeal (*chanda-ṛddhipāda*) is Brahmāṇī.
The base of psychic power of energy is Aindrī;
the base of psychic power of mind is Vārāhī;
the base of psychic power of investigation is Kaumārī—thus there would be an octad known as the division of the *chandoha*.
Likewise, there are the five powers of wrath:
here, the power of faith is Atinīlā,
and the power of vigor is Atibalā.
The power of mindfulness is Vajraśṛṅkhalā; the power of concentration is Mānī;
the power of wisdom is Cundā—this is the secondary assembly.
Likewise, she cooks the very sense-faculties that have been manifested as fixed:
the faculty of faith is Stambhī,
and the faculty of vigor is Mārīcī.
The faculty of mindfulness is Jambhī;
the faculty of concentration is Bhṛkuṭī;
the faculty of wisdom is Raudrākṣī—thus is the group of ten for the meeting place.

O Lord of Men, the perfect Eightfold Path corresponds to the eight classes of Daityas; and within the thirty-seven-fold division that abides in the three worlds, there are the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharmas).

All those Yoginīs are to be known by the yogi as residing upon the surface of the earth. Thus, O Lord of Men, everything beginning with the sacred seats (pīṭhas) exists externally as well as within the body. 168.
O Lord of Men, the eightfold noble path corresponds to the group of eight born of the Daityas;
here, Right View is Śvānāsyā (Dog-faced),
and Right Resolve is Kākāsyā (Crow-faced).
Right speech is Vyāghrāsyā; right action is Ulūkāsyā; right livelihood is Jambukāsyā.
Right effort is Garuḍāsyā;
right mindfulness is Śūkarāsyā;
and right concentration is Gṛdhrāsyā.

Thus, by means of the thirty-sevenfold divisions, those factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) which exist in the abode of the three worlds are to be known by the yogi as all the yoginīs—*ḍombī* and the others—in the abode of the surface of the earth.

O King, in this way, the *pīṭha*s and so forth, purified by the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment, become characterized as the *dharmakāya*; and likewise in the external body. This is the rule everywhere. (168)

Now, for the sake of propitiating these [deities], the conduct (*caryā-dharma*) of yogins is described: whether he be a Buddhist, a Śaiva, a naked ascetic, a Bhagavat, a *snātaka* Brahmin, a Kāpālika, one with shaven hair, a white-robed one, a protector of the field (*kṣetrapāla*), or a Kaula; whether he be silent, or even appearing like a madman—provided his heart is stainless, O King, such a wise student is indeed a yogi who, having attained the reality (*tattva*), is a treasury of all virtues and is capable of achieving perfection. 169.
With the words "Buddhist" and so forth:

here, one who has been consecrated in the mandala of the King of Tantras, the *Kālacakra*, is consecrated in all mandalas—even those of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). This applies to the practitioners of male and female deities such as Hari, Hara, and others, or Cāmuṇḍā and others, once their mandalas have been purified. Therefore, whether the yogi has received the consecration of reality and is a Buddhist for the sake of accomplishing worldly knowledge or the expansion of ritual action, or whether he is a Śaiva, or even a naked Paramahaṃsa, a Bhagavan, or a Snātaka—it makes no difference.
The Faculty of Mindfulness is Jambhī; the Faculty of Recollection is Mārīcī.

[In the chapter on] the Great Instruction on the Ritual of the Mandala Circle for the Assembly of Consecration and the Practice of Yoga: likewise, whether he be a Brahmin or a Kāpālika, one with shorn hair or a Kṣapaṇaka, a white-robed ascetic or a Kṣetrapāla, let him be pure;
or let him be one who observes silence.

Whether appearing as a madman, a Kaula, one of pure heart, a learned student, or a yogi— for the sake of attaining success and having realized the reality that is a treasury of all virtues— he may, O King, perform whatever conduct pleases his mind until success is achieved.
Therefore, by virtue of his power, let him transcend the worlds; such is the rule of the Tathāgata. || 169 ||

Thus ends the fifth great chapter on the ritual of consecration and the circle of the assembly (gaṇacakra) in the Vimalaprabhā, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the King of Tantras, the Short Kālacakra, which follows the Root Tantra.

(6) The Great Chapter on the Ritual for the Release of the Mandala, Seals, Gazes, and the Feast of Heroes: Having bowed to that Kālacakra by whom the lords of the Daityas were terrified with hand-seals and gazes, I shall explain the characteristics of the seals and so forth.
Just as it was extracted from the Great Tantra by the eloquent one using a short tantra, I shall expand upon all the mudrās, gazes, limbs, and secret signs (*chomaka*) with this commentary.
Thus:

here, for the purpose of binding the mudrās, the designations for the five fingers beginning with the thumb are as follows: the thumb, the forefinger, and likewise the middle finger, the ring finger, and at the end the little finger—this storehouse of all qualities is to be known by the yogins.

For the sake of the mudrās, there is a differentiation of names for the fingers according to their qualities; in the sequence described for binding, there is the *vajrabandha*, and likewise in the *muṣṭibandha*. (170)

The thumb is the eldest; then the second is the index finger (*tarjanī*), the third is the middle finger (*madhyamā*), and the fourth is the ring finger (*anāmikā*). At the end of that ring finger is the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*), which is a treasury of all qualities because it is of the nature of the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).
It is to be experienced by the yogi through the instruction of the teacher.
Thus, for the purpose of forming the mudrās, there is a distinction of names according to their qualities.
"By virtue of the qualities of smell, form, taste, touch, and sound," thus in sequence.
When the binding is thus described, it becomes the "vajra-binding.
When the fist is constrained and formed, it is the rule that it is the "vajra-fist-binding," because of the statement, "it is exactly like that. || 170 ||
8. cha. By means of the rite, [the element] space;
9. Bho. By way of restriction.
20 20 Now, the mudrā of the Lord of Jinas is described in the Vimalaprabhā:

In the case of the Lord of Jinas seated upon the vajra-throne during the consecration, there is the vajra-mudrā upon the thighs; the left hand is placed on the ground in the paryaṅka posture, while the right hand from the knee-region is in the earth-touching mudrā of Akṣobhya. For Ratnapāṇi, the right hand is above the left, with the palm facing upward and level; for Padmapāṇi, the right hand is likewise positioned above the left, with the palm facing upward and level. || 171 ||

Here, with both hands in the *vajra-muṣṭi-bandha* (vajra-fist gesture), the left thumb is pressed by the fist upon the left thigh; while seated in the *vajrāsana*, this is the *vajra-mudrā*. Now, the *Akṣobhya-mudrā* is described:

first, having assumed the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), the left hand is placed face upwards on that seat, while the right hand reaches from the region of the right knee down to the ground. This is the *bhūsparśa* (earth-touching) gesture.
In this way, the earth-touching gesture (*bhūsparśa*) is the mudrā of Akṣobhya;
furthermore, by that same sequence, however, the right hand turned upward is the boon-granting (*varada*) mudrā of Ratnapāṇi.

Likewise, when the left hand is above in the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*), the right hand placed level with it and turned upward is the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) mudrā of Amitābha, who holds a lotus. || 171 ||

With the left leg in the cross-legged posture upon the head, the other palm is held in the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) by the sword-handed one; on the right side, the left hand is indeed clenched in a fist, while another [hand] has the index finger extended in the fist-bind gesture.

This is the mudrā of Vairocana. Another is the wheel-mudrā (*cakramudrā*), which clearly resides at the heart; it consists of the joining of the index finger and thumb, while the middle fingers and the rest are spread out like bracelets here. || 172 ||

Thus, the left palm is turned upward at the top of the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*), while the other, the right palm, is placed upon the right knee in the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhayapradam*). This is the Abhaya-mudrā of Amoghasiddhi, who holds a sword in his hand. Likewise, with the right fist, the index finger of that right fist is extended; then, in the binding of the fist, that same index finger is drawn back inside. This is the Bodhyagrī-mudrā of Vairocana, clearly positioned at the heart.

Likewise, there is another *dharmacakra-mudrā*: the joining of the index finger and thumb on the left [hand], while here on the right hand there should be a bracelet; at the meeting of the nails of the left ring finger, by way of the yoga of teaching, there is the extension of the middle finger and so forth, and the ring finger is slightly raised above the little finger—this is the *dharmacakra-mudrā* in the region of the heart.
Such is the rule for the six Tathāgatas. || 172 ||

Now the divine mudrā is described: in the left hand is the perfectly full, stainless moon; in the right is the vajra-sun. Within the union of the sun and moon is the five-pronged, terrifying vajra born of wrath. Having formed a fist with the right and left [hands], [it is held] from the region of the forefinger.
And, having placed the left hand on the ground, [the right] hand... [ka.
kha. cha. bho. ...the right.

[In the section on] the Great Chapter concerning the Ritual for the Hero’s Feast, the Mudrās, Gazing, the Maṇḍala, and the Dismissal [in the *Ga*, *Ca*, and *Bho* recensions; in the *Ga* recension, this occurs in the Southern Paṭala]: "O King, having meditated upon the limbs to be touched, beginning from the head adorned with a crown down to the very ends of the feet—this is the glorious divine mudrā of Kālacakra, which removes the stains of impurity. (173)
133. Here, for the sake of the great armor (*mahākavaca*) within one's own body, it is said: "In the left hand is the perfectly full, stainless moon.
Here, the lunar mandala consisting of the fifteen vowels beginning with *a* is the perfectly full, stainless moon in the left hand, complete with its fifteen digits.
The vowels are: *a, i, ṛ, u, lṛ, a, e, ar, o, al, ha, ya, ra, va, la*.
Thus, in the right hand is Vajrasūrya, consisting of the fifteen vowels: *la, va, ra, ya, ha, ra, ā, au, ā, e, ā, lū, ū, ṛ, ī, ā*. This is the complete Sūrya.

Having meditated upon the Vajra produced from these two—the Sūrya and Indu—joined together as a "casket" (*sampuṭita*), which is terrifying, formidable, and born of wrath, namely the syllable *HŪṂ* arising from the five elements; one should touch every limb with that Vajra using the Vajra-mudrā to be described hereafter, starting from the head together with the crown (*samukuṭa*)—that is, including the *uṣṇīṣa*—down to the feet, even to the very tips of the toenails.
This is the glorious divine mudrā, O King, which provides all protection and removes the stains of defilement for Kālacakra. (173)

Whatever object is to be grasped—whether born from the earth, born from water, born from a womb, or born from sweat—and whether it be food, drink, potent substances, or even heavy items, it should be touched with the *mudrā*.

Whatever is suitable for a specific purpose should be employed according to its qualities, such as the elements of earth and so forth, for the sake of the mandala; likewise, the foot should be used by the yogi for movement and for striking. || 174 ||

Likewise, by means of this mudrā, whatever object is to be grasped—whether born of the earth, born of water, born of a womb, or born of sweat—the word "etc. including those born of moisture, as well as food and drink, along with potent meats, must be purified, awakened, and ignited according to the sequence to be described.

In this way, even the Guru is the foot; within the form of the deity, one's own foot is for the purpose of movement. Whatever object is suitable for a particular task, by virtue of its qualities—namely, under the influence of the objects such as the *guṇas* of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, or smell and so forth—one should touch that task with its corresponding *mudrā*. The earth and other elements, as well as the feet, which serve as the *maṇḍalas*, should also be struck by the yogin with this *mudrā* for the sake of movement; thus it is the Divine *Mudrā*. (174)

Now the mudrā of Krodhanātha is described: indeed, the mudrā of the Great Wrathful King arises from the two hands in the vajra-bind; the *tribhuvanavijayā* is the binding of the index fingers at the beginning and end; the Lord’s [mudrās] are in the form of his emblems through the fist-binding;
and the remaining [mudrās] of the gods and goddesses are manifest and fixed. When there is the vajra-bind with the two hands, the mudrā of the serpents takes the form of moving hoods. || 175 ||
[241b] . ga. ' evaṃ ' adhikaṃ . cha. huṃ . bho. Ses (miti) | ca. yāvanna . . ca. vam.
In versions ka, kha, and cha, the term "salilaja" (born of water) is absent.
In version ga, it reads "sarvavīryaṃ" (all-heroic), while in the Tibetan version (bho.), it reads "savīraṃ" (with heroism).
In version ga, it reads "bodhyam" (to be awakened), while in the Tibetan version (bho.), it reads "rGyas Pa" (to be increased, *vardhanīyaṃ*).

O friend, there are also two right hands in the form of moving hoods; thus, the mudrā in the form of moving hoods belongs to the serpents, and it should be understood in the same way for the leftward rotation as well. || 175 ||

Now the symbolic mudrās are described: with the thumbs joined and the little fingers like lotus petals, the middle fingers extended, the two index fingers half-curved and resting on the palms, and the ring fingers bent downwards—this is the five-pronged mudrā of the Vajra-holder, which is to be displayed; for the fingers beginning with the thumb are all [arranged] like spokes upon the palm that grants fearlessness. || 176 ||

With the words "joined" (*śliṣṭa*) and so forth, here, having formed the hollowed palms of the five-pronged vajra-mudrā, the two thumbs are joined, the two little fingers are joined like lotus petals, the two middle fingers are extended and equal, and the two index fingers are in the shape of half-moons at the middle of the [palms]. On the back part of the two middle fingers, the two ring fingers (*anāmikā*) are bent downward, resting upon one's own palms. Thus, this five-pronged mudrā indeed becomes that which is to be displayed by the Vajra-holder (*Vajrin*).

This divine mudrā is as previously described; likewise, another is the vajra-mudrā for embracing Prajñā, wherein all the fingers beginning with the thumbs, located on both hands, are held in the shape of a hook. || 176 ||

The two hands joined in the vajra-bind become the *kuliśa*; with the vajra-fist, together with the bell, it is below the fist; the sharp nails are like arrows, as are the index and middle fingers; the tridents begin with the index finger; furthermore, when spread apart, they form the half-fist for the trident; in the glorious *kartī*, there is a fist-binding; the terrifying and glorious little finger is the crescent moon. (177)
Likewise, the two hands are in the vajra-bind mudrā as before; indeed, with the right hand formed as a vajra-fist held upward, there is a thunderbolt,
and with the left hand held downward as a fist, there is a bell.
Likewise, with the middle finger forming a fist and the ring and little fingers within that fist, one recites "nāsti, nāsti, nāsti."
It is not, it is not.

In the wheel, the supreme [mudrā] is complete. Then, in the chapter [on the] Great Instruction on the Ritual for the Mudrās, Gaze, Maṇḍala Dismissal, and Hero’s Feast: the thumb itself serves as the fist for the sharp sword.
When the index and middle fingers are joined together like an arrow pointing upward, that is the Sword Mudrā (*khaḍgamudrā*).

Likewise, with the thumb forming a fist below and the index finger and others [extended], the index, middle, and ring fingers are in the shape of a trident and slightly separated; again, with the half-fist, this is the Trident Mudrā (*triśūlamudrā*) for the sake of the sense objects—the seventh [category]—in all cases.
Likewise, when the hands are joined in the form of a fist with the little fingers shaped like half-moons, it is terrifying to the unsubdued; this is the *kartikā-mudrā*. || 177 ||

O King, for the excellent arrow (varaśara), the fist-binding is at the ear; the thumb and middle finger are [raised], while the index finger is extremely bent. Likewise, in the goad (aṅkuśa), the fist-binding is at the base, with the index and ring fingers being like the arrow. In the spear (kunta), the middle finger is raised; in the staff (daṇḍa), it is a horizontal fist; and in the axe (kuṭhāra), the strength of the thumb rests upon the well-aligned palm.

In the *vara-śara-mudrā* (the mudrā of the excellent arrow), the fist is bound at the ear; the thumb is above the middle finger and the index finger is below it—this is the *śara-mudrā*. For the *aṅkuśa* (hook), there is the *vajra-muṣṭi-bandha* (vajra-fist binding); the index finger is raised from the fist, curved like a hook and not at all straight—this is the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*. Likewise, with the little finger and thumb forming a fist, the index finger and ring finger are below, closely joined like an arrow; above those two, the middle finger is like a spear—thus is the *kunta-mudrā*. Similarly, the fist is held crosswise with the arms extended—thus is the *daṇḍa-mudrā* (staff mudrā).

Likewise, with the palms well-joined, the thumbs are extended upward, while the four fingers beginning with the index finger are joined together in a horizontal position; thus the axe-mudrā (kuṭhāramudrā) is formed. || 178 ||

Above, there should be two fists; on the skin of the elephant of the Lord of Asuras, the index finger is placed at the fang, while the fist is bound and the palm is in the gesture of fearlessness (*abhayamudrā*). The little finger is like a half-moon; on the left, the arm is extended, the palm is turned upward, and there is a shield (*kheṭaka*). On the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), the fist is firmly clenched and without gaps, with the little finger resting firmly upon the shoulder. || 179 ||

Likewise, there should be two fists with the thumbs pointing upward; this is Vināyaka, the elephant of the Lord of Asuras. In his leather seal (*carmamudrā*), both fists have the index fingers pointing upward; this is the elephant-hide seal (*gajacarmamudrā*). Similarly, for the fang seal (*daṃṣṭrāmudrā*), one should form a fist and display the hand—the palm facing downward and shaped like a half-moon—with the little fingers bent and the right and left faces turned outward. Such is the fang seal. This is the rule for the seals of the hand-symbols: the elephant-hide seal and the fang seal.

Now, the hand-symbol mudrā of the left hand is described: here, there is an extension of the left arm with the palm facing upward like the palm of the "fearless" (abhaya) hand, as in the case of a shield or a wooden board; thus is the *phalaka* (shield/board) mudrā.

Likewise, for the *khaṭvāṅga*, the fist is held without gaps, with the index, middle, ring, and thumb fingers joined together at the position of the shoulder, while the little finger is extended downward; thus is the *khaṭvāṅga* mudrā. || 179 ||
He is indeed superior by this name.
Nyāmagha: the upward-pointing vajra between the two fists; Cakrātyanta.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the extension [of the limbs] such as "thus the staff": in the *Śrīkapāla* [tantra], the hand has fingers with no gaps like a lotus petal; when raised, it becomes an upward-facing fist in the bow [mudrā], while the left arm is indeed extended.

In the Vajrapāśa mudrā, the tongue rests upon the index finger and the middle finger is fixed; O King, in the Ratna mudrā there is a joining of the fingers, while in the Padma mudrā there is their opening.

The union of the index finger and the thumb occurs in the *jalacara* [mudrā]; in the *ādarśa*, there is a fist below the thumb, with the palms well-aligned and even, including the fingers, being indeed without gaps.

In the *śṛṅkhalā*, the path begins with the index finger and so forth, with the thumb arranged in sequence; the four fingers beginning with the thumb are level at the head, while the little finger is bent downward. || 189 ||

Likewise, the *kapāla-mudrā* is held with the palm facing upward like a skull-cup, with the fingers extended and the hand free of gaps, resembling a lotus petal; similarly, when the hand is extended and turned upward, it forms a fist [with the thumb inside], which is the *dhanu-mudrā*.
Likewise, the *vajrapāśa* is formed by placing the index finger upon the left fist, with the middle finger bent and a gap between the two.
This is the single-hand mudrā;
another is with three hands, wherein on the right side of Varuṇa and others, the thunderbolt-hook (vajrāṅkuśa) is not seen simultaneously,
but rather it is thus the noose-mudrā (pāśamudrā).
Likewise, the *dvandva* (union) is the *melāpaka*;
having placed the middle finger (*madhyamā*) between the five fingers upward in the hand, this is the *ratnamudrā*.

In the left hand, it is the *padmamudrā*: on the thumb (*aṅguṣṭha*) and on the index finger (*tarjanī*) and the others, there is thus the expansion of the fingers like a four-petaled lotus; with both hands, it becomes an eight-petaled [lotus].
Thus is the lotus mudrā; likewise, for the hand-drum (ḍamaruka), there is a fist-binding with the middle and ring fingers,
while the index finger is shaped like a hook over the nail of the thumb, and the little finger is turned downward.
Likewise, for the *mudgara* [mudrā], it is the clenching of the fist;
for the *cakra*, it is the spreading of all the fingers in the shape of spokes; for the single hand, it is the hollowing of the palms of both hands;
and likewise, the joining of the index finger and thumb with the little finger and others clenched beneath the thumb, while the thumb and index finger are extended, is the *śaṅkha-mudrā*.

Facing a mirror, with the palms well-joined, this is the mirror mudrā (*darpaṇamudrā*). Having likewise made the fingers from the index finger down to the little finger without gaps, with the thumb above [the palm], the index finger is bent in the shape of a ring; above that is the middle finger, above the middle finger is the ring finger, and above the ring finger is the little finger—this is the chain mudrā (*śṛṅkhalāmudrā*).
Likewise, the Brahmā mudrā is formed with the thumbs.
And on the thumb and the little finger.
In the directions beginning with the northeast, starting from the northeast and so on,
there is a lotus of petals.
And there is no [existence] by means of these two names.
She weaves the web.

In the Maṇḍala Chapter [of the Śloka], this is the great section on the procedure for the binding of the hand-gestures (mudrā), the gaze, the dismissal from the maṇḍala, and the heroic feast: "The binding formed by the successive arrangement of the fingers upon the back of the hands; the joining of three fingers together at the neck; the crooked joining of the two ends of both hands; and [the binding] at the girdle. (182)
