Likewise, when the two hands form the conch-mudrā (*śaṅkhamudrā*) joined at the crown of the head, there is the upward union of the pair of index fingers; with the palms of both hands turned outward and the five fingers behind the earrings, this is the earring-mudrā (*kuṇḍalamudrā*). Similarly, on the back of the hand, the sequential arrangement of the fingers in mutual binding constitutes the necklace-mudrā (*kaṇṭhikāmudrā*).

Likewise, for the girdle (*mekhalā*), the tips of the three fingers—the ring, middle, and index—of the left and right hands meet, while the little finger and thumb are clenched in a fist; this is the girdle-mudrā (*mekhalāmudrā*). || 182 ||

The thumb and the two middle fingers joined like a ring constitute the anklet; likewise, from the clenched fist, there arise the pair of armlets and the bracelets through the joining of the pair of index fingers.

The thumb belongs to the Ḍākinīs as their excellent family; the index finger belongs to the Guhyakas; and for the Gandharvas and the Serpents, the middle and ring fingers are arranged in succession. (183)

Likewise, when the two thumbs and the two middle fingers of both hands are joined and formed like a bracelet, while the remaining fingers form a fist, it is the *nūpura* (anklet) mudrā. Similarly, in the *keyūra* (armlet) or *kaṭaka* (bracelet), the joining of the thumbs and the joining of the index fingers forms a circle like a bracelet; these are the *cihna-mudrās* (symbolic mudrās) of the Blessed One.
Now, the *kula-mudrās* are described, beginning with the word "thumb" (*aṅguṣṭha*).
In this context, the common family mudrā for all ḍākinīs is the display of the thumbs upon the vajra-fist;
likewise, the index finger extended upward from the vajra-fist is the family mudrā of the Guhyakas and Yakṣas;
and for the Gandharvas, the middle finger is extended and displayed from the clenched fist, which constitutes their family [mudrā].
In this way, the ring finger becomes the lineage of the serpents. || 183 ||

For the Bhūtas, the auspicious little finger is the excellent hand-palm; for the Rākṣasas, it is the clenched fist; for the Siddhas, the joining of the joints of the fingers constitutes their noble family; for the Suras, it is the five fingers in the form of a half-triangle; the hand-palm with the fingers extended is the mudrā of the Jāti class; for the Nakhīs, it is the two index fingers; for the Śṛṅgis, it is indeed the two thumbs placed upon the head, arising from the clenched fist. || 184 ||

The Bhūtas are shown with the little finger extended; likewise, the family of the Rākṣasas is indicated by the fist being bound with four fingers while the palm is displayed. When the fist is bound and displayed, it becomes the family of the Siddhas.

Likewise, the joints of the upper arm and forearm of the Suras constitute the family of the Brahmarākṣasas; similarly, the back of the hand and the palm of the hand demonstrate the family of the Vyantaras.

Thus, these eight types of mudrās are to be displayed with the left hand by those born of the eight families. Now, the mudrā of the *nakhi* (claw-like) class is described, beginning with the word "five" (*pañca*). 1. O [Bhagavān], listen!
For the sake of Mekhalā.
For the sake of [it].
There is no space either.
And there is no manifest [state].
There is no "upabāhu" and there is no "parva" in [the manuscripts] kha and cha.
"O Lord, there is no end to the vetālas.
(kha)

Six mudrās of the clawed ones (nakhinī) are described here: the birth-mudrā (jātimudrā) consists of the five fingers bent halfway like the claws of a lion, performed with either one hand or both hands.
Likewise, when the two index fingers are bent at half-moon shape and displayed above the fists of both hands at the head, it is called the *śṛṅgiṇī-mudrā*, the "horned" fist-bindings. || 184 ||

When the little fingers are bound together and the palms are turned away from each other, it is the "Wing-union" (pakṣayoga); this is the distinguished birth-mark of birds, characterized by the tips of the five fingers being hollowed.

When the index fingers are extended and the others are joined below, it is the "Flame" (jvālā) mudrā; here, the two thumbs are joined and the other [fingers] are extended as index fingers. This is the specific seal of serpents. || 185 ||

Likewise, when the two little fingers are bound together with their palms facing away from each other, and the index, middle, ring, and thumb fingers are joined at their tips, this is the Garuḍa-mudrā;
similarly, when the five fingers are shown with their first joints bent, it becomes the Jāti-mudrā of serpents.

Likewise, in the *Jvālāmudrā*, the middle, ring, and little fingers are extended on both hands; the two index fingers are interlaced with one another; and the two thumbs are joined face-to-face above and below at the top of the head, in that same manner within the palms of the hands. However, the [other] index finger is extended; this is the *Jvālāmudrā*, a *jātimudrā* (birth-mudrā) which, according to the rule, is to be displayed with its faces turned sideways. || 185 ||

Now, the mudrās for the mutual conversation between the heroes and heroines are described: showing the index finger is said to signify "welcome" to the yogin; with two [fingers], the fortunate one proclaims "a very warm welcome"; from the binding of the thumbs, she says "well-being"; and from the snapping of the fingers, the excellent mantra-master certainly says, "You are here. With the thumb and ring finger, she says, "I offer you libation with the wine of the samaya. || 186 ||
By the words beginning with "tarjanyā" [it is meant]:
here, wherever it may be, having formed a fist by merely showing [the hand], one should display the index finger pointing upwards, joined with the thumb and facing towards it.
When that is shown, a welcome is expressed—whether by a yoginī to a yogin, or by a yogin to a yoginī.
By joining the two fingers—the index and the middle—back-to-back, a "welcome" is expressed. Likewise, the auspicious one proclaims "safety" by binding the left thumb in a fist.
Similarly, by snapping the fingers of the thumb and index finger, the excellent mantra-practitioner certainly says, "You are here."
Making a snapping sound with the thumb and ring finger, he says: "I offer you a libation with the wine of the samaya. || 186 ||
The first [syllable] of the middle [line] is *ca*. *Nāmitā*.
Of these:
[the reading] "of the hooded snakes" (phaṇinām) does not exist in manuscript Kha; in manuscript Bho, it is at the head [of the list].
O! [The one] with the finger shown by the mouth; Ca.
should show it.
O! Ca. O! [the one] with the hand extended.

[The section on] the Great Chapter concerning the Ritual for Mudrās, Gaze, Maṇḍala, Dismissal, and the Hero’s Feast: From the essence of the tips of all the fingers, the Fortunate One speaks; by touching the left limb, she always reveals, "O friend, you are my one [beloved].

Upon the touch of the vulva, or by scratching the pair of lips and breasts with the nails, or from the binding of the fingers against one another, she declares the *samaya* (pledge) through the essence of the middle finger and the thumb. (187)
Likewise, through the practice of salutation, the auspicious woman utters "Welcome" from the tips of all her fingers to the yogin;
likewise, by touching his left side, she always reveals, "You alone are my kinsman"; and likewise, upon the touch of the vulva, [she reveals], "You are my husband."
Likewise, when drawing upon the pair of her lower breasts, it is said that the husband has been mentioned.
Regarding "with the nails":

by the mutual binding of the fingers—meaning having formed a hollow with both hands such that the fingers from the little finger downwards are bound to one another—from this binding, specifically from the binding of the index finger to the ring finger and the extension of the thumb and middle finger, she indicates the meeting of the *samaya* (the assembly) through the *saṃbhāṣaṇa-mudrā* (the conversational gesture). || 187 ||
When the lips, brows, or eyes twitch, or when the head itches, one is extremely foolish; the little finger at the teeth reveals fear, as does the forefinger at the heart or the mouth.

By clenching the fist upon the thumb, by slapping the ground with hands and feet, or by touching the tongue, one says "I am eating"; however, when the belly or the teeth are struck, it means "it has not been eaten. (188)
Regarding the passage beginning with "the lips" (*oṣṭha*) and so forth:
here, when a practitioner sees a messenger girl (*dūtī*) anywhere and she, being virtuous, displays a crookedness of her lips and so on—

namely, when her lips are crooked, her eyebrows are crooked, her eyes are crooked, and likewise when she scratches her head— it signifies that she says, "You are a great fool, since you do not know the secret signs of the mudrās."
Likewise, if the little finger is placed between the fangs, then that little finger manifests fear;

or else, if the index finger is placed on the heart or the mouth, it indicates fear. Furthermore, having formed a fist around the thumb and then striking the ground with that very fist, or striking with both hands and feet, one says "I shall devour you" due to ignorance of the secret signs of the mudrās; these are the threatening mudrās.
Likewise, food is not eaten if it touches the tongue while one is not actually eating;
nor is it considered eaten if the stomach and face are struck with the left hand. || 188 ||

"Go! [she says] when her hands are on her back; "Stay! Stay! she certainly speaks when standing face-to-face; "O fortunate one, rest this very day," she says when pressing her knees against his thighs;
"No," [she says] with her feet.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*: "O crooked one, there is no union for me. O mother, grant me sleep by stretching out your feet; grant me sexual pleasure by stretching out the pair of your knees. When all my limbs are being touched and your hand has gone to my mouth, there is no union for me. (189)
Likewise, when the back of the hand is shown, she certainly says, "Go"; when the palm is shown facing her, she says, "Stay, stay.
Similarly, when the knee is pressed or the thigh is pressed, she says, "O fortunate one, rest today."
Likewise, she who sleeps by stretching out her feet gives [her favor] invariably;
likewise, the rule is that she grants me sexual union by stretching out both her knees.
Likewise, if she touches her own entire body with her left hand, or places her left hand upon her face [she gives].

When this is being done, she says, "There is no meeting with you for me," because she is protected by her master and others. (189) When there is a mutual joining of hands, she says, "Today there is a *cakra*-meeting in my house; from the tips of the thumbs and ring fingers, we shall satisfy ourselves in many ways according to our desire. When she scratches her foot, the meaning is likewise regarding the departure. And when there is a mutual joining of the index fingers during an external meeting, she says, "You are my friend Vajra; today [I] take away your fear. (190)

Likewise, when the hands are joined with one another and the thumb and index finger emerge from between them, she then speaks by means of this mudrā: "Today there will be a gathering of the *cakra* in my house; you too must remain," is the meaning.
When the thumb and ring finger are shown, she says according to various conventions: "We shall satisfy [the deities] as much as we desire.
Similarly, when she scratches her foot, she indicates departure for an external *cakramelāpaka*; the intention is: "You too should come."
Likewise, when the two index fingers are bound together in the shape of a *kuśa* grass blade, it removes fear [with the mantra]: "O Vajramitra, you are my friend today.
Such is the rule for the *samayamelāpaka-mudrā*. || 190 ||

When the hair is being cut, he says to the human-beast with his own teeth: "You are to be cast down here! When they gnaw at each other's teeth, he says: "This flesh of yours must be eaten by me today! When the tongue and lips are being caressed, he says: "I shall drink the blood from your body! And even while the lip is being bitten, he says: "We shall eat this intestine of yours from within our bellies! (191)
The rule:
"And in the mouth;
satisfy yourself, O venerable one! Offer it! (arpyatām).
He says to you:
"Outside," pointing with his index finger.

Mutual [regard], fear as well, [and so forth]. In the chapter, verse [number]: the great section on the procedure for the dismissal of the maṇḍala, the heroic feast, and the seals (mudrā) and gazes (dṛṣṭi), beginning with the word "hair" (keśa).

In this context, when a practitioner, out of false pride, shows contempt or displays a counter-seal (*pratimudrā*) without possessing the requisite power, then she, endowed with that very lack of power, cuts her own hair with her own teeth. When the cutting of her hair has been performed with her teeth, she says this regarding the seal: "O human-beast, you must be cast down here by me!
Likewise, she rubs her teeth against each other; when they have been rubbed there, she says: "O human-beast, this flesh of yours is to be eaten by me today!"
Likewise, when the tongue and lips are caressed, she says, "I shall drink your blood.

Similarly, even while her lip is being bitten by the teeth, she says, "We shall devour this entrail of yours that has entered our bellies; O beast of a man, where are you going? Thus, being enraged, she displays the mudrā.
Therefore, a counter-mudrā must not be shown by one who is devoid of such power.

Having performed a salutation to them, placing the palm of the left hand upon the heart, and having circled around one's own body by turning to the left, one should then depart after making a prostration upward with the left hand. One must not engage in conversation with them; this is the rule which the Lord gives for the beginner yogins, and it must be observed by him. Otherwise, the messenger (*dūtī*), being possessed of power, will lead one to death if she is provoked to anger—this is the rule of the Blessed One. Now, the characteristic of the counter-seal (*pratimudrā*) is described regarding the mutual display of seals.
In this context, the mudrās have the same form as the symbols held by the left and right arms of the Blessed One Kālacakra;
therefore, they are mutually mudrā and pratimudrā.

Of the vajra and vajra-bell; of the sword and shield; of the trident and *khaṭvāṅga*; of the flaying knife and skull-cup; of the arrow and bow; of the hook and noose; of the *ḍamaru* drum and jewel; of the mallet and lotus; of the wheel and conch; of the *kundī* vessel and mirror; of the staff and chain; of the animal skin and the face of Brahmā; of the elephant hide and the raised index finger; of the crown and earrings; of the necklace and breast-ornament (*rucaka*); of the girdle and anklets; of the horn and nose-ring; of the serpent and *garuḍa*; of the hands and feet; of the mouth and anus; of the vulva and phallus; of the breasts and lips; of the eyes and eyebrows; of the forehead mark (*tilaka*) and collyrium; of the wrathful tuft of hair and its loosening; of the knees and thighs; of the throat and forehead; of the navel and heart; of the parting of the hair and the line of vermilion (*sindūra*); of the fangs and the little finger; of the thumb and ring finger; and of the index finger and middle finger.

Thus, when many mudrās are shown, there are many counter-mudrās (pratimudrās); this is the rule that must be understood everywhere by the yogin through the principle of wisdom and means (prajñopāya) and according to the distinctions of the principles (tattva) such as earth and the rest. || 199 ||

O Lord of Men, through the yoga of Lāsyā she becomes Lāsyā; through the yoga of Hāsyā she becomes Hāsyā; through the yoga of Nṛtyā she becomes the manifold Nṛtyā; through the yoga of Vādyā she becomes Vādyā; through the yoga of Gītā she becomes Gītā, possessing excellent and diverse qualities; through the yoga of Gandhā she becomes Gandhā; through the yoga of Mālā she becomes Mālā by the power of her attributes; and through the yoga of Dhūpā she becomes Dhūpā. (192)
Now, there are infinite mudrās such as Lāsyā and the rest; having understood their intrinsic nature, all of them are to be known.

That is to say: through the yoga of Lāsyā one becomes Lāsyā, O Lord of Men; through the yoga of Hāsyā one becomes Hāsyā; through the yoga of Nṛtyā one becomes Nṛtyā in many ways; through the yoga of Vādya one becomes Vādya; through the yoga of Gītā one becomes Gītā, possessing excellent and diverse qualities; through the yoga of Gandha one becomes Gandhā; through the yoga of Mālā one becomes Mālā by virtue of its qualities; and through the yoga of Dhūpa one becomes Dhūpā. || 192 ||
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, lamps indeed have the form of a lamp and destroy darkness; the vessel-mudrā is the nectar. Thus all mudrās are further divided by five types.

Other mudrās are infinite and pervade all things; they should be understood by the yogi such that whatever the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an object on the surface of the earth may be, the mudrās possess that very same intrinsic nature. (193)

Indeed, lamps are those which have destroyed darkness by means of their circular form; the vessel-seal (*pātramudrā*) is nectar. Thus, all seals (*mudrās*) are further divided into five types. Furthermore, other seals that pervade the entire universe are to be known by the yogi as infinite. Whatever the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an object may be upon the surface of the earth, the seals possess that very same nature. Therefore: "As many as are the movements of the gaze, so many are the seals proclaimed. Who is capable of determining the seal within its counter-seal?"
As long as the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) have not arisen for yogins through meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
they should not display the counter-seal (*pratimudrā*) for the sake of worldly discourse.
Thus ends the rule for the conventions of the mudrās. || 193 ||

Now the convention of the gaze is explained: by means of a horizontal gaze, the messenger girl says, "O fortunate one, from where have you come? The yogin’s reply should be made by looking toward that direction with his hand placed upon his head. With an upward gaze he says, "May it be well with you"; with a gaze directed to the surface of the earth, "Stay; take rest"; with a sidelong gaze, "Go"; and with a gaze full of passion, the messenger girl speaks of sexual union.

By the words "diagonally" (*tiryak*) and so forth: here, when a Yoginī appears in the vision of a Yogin, she may show [him] with a diagonal gaze; by that gaze she speaks, asking the fortunate one—that is, the Yogin—"From which place have you come? Then, the reply of the Yogin would be: by looking at the left hand placed upon his head, he declares his arrival from the location in that very direction.
"Is it well with you? she asks with an upward glance; "Stay and rest," she says with a downward gaze.
"Go," she says with a sidelong look; "Make love," the female messenger says with a lustful glance. (194)

With a gentle gaze, she reveals herself as my friend; with a frowning, wrathful look, she declares, "I am cruel. Through her glance at the hair, she proclaims her auspicious nature through her gestures.

With a glance from the *ūrṇā* (the circle of hair between the eyebrows), the Yoginī reveals, "I am supreme"; with a glance at the nose, she indicates good fortune; and by looking at the pair of breasts, she says, "I am a beautiful seal (*sumudrā*)."
[Chapter 193–197, *Balo*]:

The Great Chapter on the Ritual for Seals (*mudrā*), Gazing (*dṛṣṭi*), the Mandala, the Dismissal (*visarjana*), and the Hero’s Feast (*vīrabhojya*). "The rule for the gaze of conversation is: 'You are my friend,' as one speaks with a gentle gaze.

Now, the fearful gazes are described: here, when one displays a wrathful gaze by knitting the brows, then by that wrathful gaze and the knitting of the brows, [the deity] manifests fear toward the yogin due to ignorance."

Likewise, by looking at the hair, he proclaims "I am fierce" to the fortunate yogi, [indicating] his own nature through these gestures. Similarly, by looking at the brow-tuft (ūrṇā), he reveals "I am supreme.
Likewise, he manifests his qualities by looking at the nose.
By the look of her lips, she reveals her own good fortune; likewise, by gazing at her pair of breasts, she says, "I am well-pleased. (195)

With the vision of the heart, she whose self is cultivated says: "I am Pracaṇḍā when looking at the pair of arms; I am Śaktā when looking at the shoulders; and I am Rākṣasī when looking at the palms of the hands along with the nails. When looking at the back, I am Bhujaṅgī; O King, I am Samayī when looking at the navel; I am Śuddhā when looking at the secret place; and I am Durjayā in sexual union when looking at the thighs. (196)
He says, "My self is cultivated by the vision of the heart.
Likewise, upon beholding the pair of arms, he says, "I am fierce. Likewise, by the vision of the shoulders, he says, "I am powerful."
Likewise, when her palms and nails are looked upon, she says, "I am a rākṣasī"; when her back is looked upon, she says, "I am a nāginī"; and when her navel is seen, she says, "I am a samayinī."
"Narendra" is the address.
Likewise, with a glance at the secret place, she says, "I am pure. Similarly, with a glance at the thighs, she declares, "In sexual union, I am invincible. || 196 ||

I am the Siddhā when seen at the knees; she certainly speaks when seen at the shins. When the big toe is observed, I too am the Sole Hero with a Vajra-body in this world. When seen at the tips of all the toes, I am the All-pervading Viśvamātā within the abode of the three worlds. This is the gaze of the Dūtīs that must be known by yogins upon the surface of the earth. || 197 ||
Likewise, by looking at her knee, she says, "I am accomplished. Likewise, by looking at her foot, she says, "I possess supernatural powers.
Likewise, when one gazes upon her big toe, by that very glance she also says, "In this world, I alone am the Hero with a Vajra-body."
Likewise, by looking at the tips of all the toes of both feet, she declares within the abode of the three worlds: "I am the All-pervading Mother of the Universe.

In this way, the adept also reveals his own qualities, which are endowed with power, to the female messengers (*dūtīs*). Thus, according to the sequence described, the gaze of the messengers alone should be understood as manifold again through their inherent natures; such is the rule for the convention of gazes (*dṛṣṭisaṃketa*).
Likewise, regarding signs (*chomaka*):
it should be understood that the apprehension of a particular entity occurs by means of the first syllable of its name, according to the context (*prastāva*).

For example, when it is said, "Bring the *saindhava*," it refers to a garment in the context of bathing, salt in the context of eating, a horse in the context of traveling, and a sword in the context of battle—according to this principle, it should be understood that every entity is characterized by its convention based on the first syllable.

In the *gaṇacakra* and other such assemblies, in the midst of those who have not yet attained the commitments (*asamayin*), it must be spoken by the yogin or the yoginī either through the language of symbolic discourse (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*) or by means of gestures (*chomma*). This is the rule everywhere. || 197 ||

Now, the rule for the distribution of one's own body and so forth for the sake of giving to disciples is stated: One should give a sixth part of the torso, as well as the hands, feet, and body; the head with speech and the organs of action; the mind along with the qualities (guṇas) among the sense organs; and a portion of the constituent elements (dhātu) among the elements. Having given the multitude of bipeds and cattle according to the division of the principles (tattva), and other things to the teacher, one proceeds to the state of bliss, permeated by the divine mudrā. (198)
Regarding the passage beginning with "a sixth part" (*ṣaḍbhāgam*):

here, when one who has been consecrated by a Vajrācārya—whether he be a householder, a celibate student (*celaka*), or a monk—must make this vow: "I shall at all times give a gift consisting of a sixth part of all my wealth.

In that regard, first of all, regarding "a sixth part in the middle of the body, [namely] the hands, feet, and body": among these five—the two hands, the two feet, and the body—the sixth part, which is the head, is to be offered to the Teacher, the Buddha, the Bodhisattva, and the Guru, for the purpose of prostration.

Having given that, pierced by the divine mudrā, one goes to the state of bliss as a "giver of gifts. Likewise, among the organs of action, speech—the sixth organ among the hands, feet, anus, genitals, and so forth—is to be given for the sake of truthful speech; this is the rule of the Blessed One regarding giving with speech.

Similarly, among the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body, the mind is the sixth; endowed with qualities and free from the proliferation of māyā, it is to be given for the sake of sentient beings—this is the rule of giving.
Likewise, there is the "portion of the elements."

A sixth part must be given from the elements that arrive after a long time; quadrupeds are to be given as a sixth part. These elements—insentient substances such as gold, jewels, grain, and so forth—are for the purpose of worshiping the Yoginīs and others. Likewise, sentient beings consisting of bipeds are to be set aside with five parts for the enjoyment of oneself and one's family.
Furthermore, by means of that same portion, other things such as beautiful wives are to be given as objects of desire five times within a month; such is the rule of the Tathāgata.
Otherwise, in the Mantra system, without the granting of desire, the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā does not occur even in infinite eons;
nor does the accomplishment of Karmamudrā or Jñānamudrā occur, because for one overcome by passion, there is the seizing of the *kula*.
Such is the rule regarding the gift of the six divisions. || 198 ||

Now the compassion empowerment is described: Having drawn in with the wisdom-vajra hook those sentient beings who have entered the three types of existence within the world-system, and having empowered them all around in the mandala with supreme compassion—[there is] none. [There is] the six-limbed [practice].

[This concludes] the six-limbed [practice]. Thus, there is an addition: "Those who have attained the path through the vajra-nectar of the Buddha—whose form is like the stainless moon—and who have sent forth [the winds] to their own places, being free from defilement and established in the conduct of awakening (bodhicaryā), [should be honored]. (199)
By the words "those beings," and so forth.

In this world-system, those beings within the six realms who have not received empowerment—those existing in the three states of existence—the Vajra Master, having drawn them forth with the hook of the wisdom of omniscience, should empower them in the mandala through mere meditation and supreme compassion by means of the Buddha’s feces, urine, blood, and marrow, as well as the vajra-amṛta which is the semen of the stainless lunar form. Then, having visualized that they have attained the path of the Vajra-holders, they should be sent back to their own places by the Vajra Master, all their defilements removed and established in the conduct of awakening; such is the rule for the Empowerment of Compassion. || 199 ||

Now, the rule for the initiation of the *avadhūta* disciple is stated: In the absence of material substances, the initiation must indeed be given to the *avadhūta* according to the word of the Lord of Jinas; likewise, the path of smoke and so forth, which is a treasury of all qualities, is joined with the yoga of the channels (*nāḍikā*).

For the sake of service, the hand-gesture (*hasta-mudrā*) is under the control of one’s own heart and is free from all defects. This heart of the Supreme Jina must not be given to others who are devoid of the worship of the Mother. (200)
By the words "absence of material goods" (*dravyābhāva*) and so forth:

here, when a disciple who has attained the state of an *avadhūta* lacks material goods, then the Guru must grant the consecration for the absence of material goods according to the words of the Lord of Jinas; that is, the seven consecrations should be given in their proper sequence, including the threefold [consecrations] beginning with the vase, and thus it should be explained and spoken that the fourth is to be given on the path of smoke and so forth.
Likewise, the treasury of all qualities, joined with the *nāḍikā* yoga, is the moment of great imperishable bliss (*mahākṣarasukha*), which must be described through speech.
For the sake of serving that [bliss], in the absence of a *karmamudrā*, the rule of the *hastamudrā* (hand-seal) is to be applied.
That *hastamudrā*, being under the control of one's own heart, is free from all defects; this is the rule for the stabilization of the *bodhicitta*.

Furthermore, the heart of the Supreme Victor, the vajra-word, must never be given to other householders who are devoid of the worship of the Mother; such is the rule of the Tathāgata’s secret. || 200 ||

Now, the dismissal of the mandala (maṇḍalavisarjana) is described: At the conclusion of the consecration (sekānta), a soft, fine, and pleasant bodice and a pair of garments should be given to the venerable Yoginīs;

likewise, another bodice and a pair of garments should be offered to those stationed at the door for the sake of the entire host of Gaṇas according to one’s own capacity. Then, having performed the fire-oblation (homa) at the end, one should cause the essence of gnosis (jñānasattva) to enter the lotus of one’s own heart.

Regarding the passage beginning with "at the conclusion of the initiation" (*sekānte*) and so forth: here, at the end of the initiation, the pair of garments together with the bodice that was upon the vase should be given to the yoginīs who acted as guardians of the vase.

Furthermore, another such golden [ornament] and a pair of garments should be given to each of the guardians stationed at the doors, as previously described; the rule is that crowns and other items should be given according to one's means.
Likewise, with one's own power, [offerings are made] to the entire assembly of the Gaṇas, and similarly to the other [deities] in the Gaṇacakra, beginning with the Vīras and Vīreśvarīs.

Then, having dismissed the Gaṇacakra, at the conclusion the Ācārya performs the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the rule; having performed the worship as before, he stands facing the Blessed One at the eastern gate, takes up the vajra and bell, and through the vajra-bind, causes the Jñānasattva to enter the lotus of his own heart. || 201 ||

In their own places, he should cause even all the worldly deities to carry away the dust to a pure river; having given betel, incense, perfumes, flowers, fruits, and fine garments to the maidens, the Preceptor, together with his disciples, having satisfied the entire host of Gaṇas as desired and having bestowed the command upon the disciple, should, out of supreme compassion, dismiss them to their respective abodes.

One should indeed dissolve the worldly deities, Indra and the others, into their own places; then, with an *aśvattha* leaf, one's own hand, or a *vajra*, one should dissolve the *mahāsukhacakra-vajra* via the path of the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) as far as possible. Then, having placed a particle of dust the size of a speck on one's own head, one should dissolve the lotus and so forth—this is the rule for the dismissal of the mandala.
Thereafter, one should take all the colored powders, together with the umbrella, fly-whisks, banner, and worship, and cast them into a pure river that flows toward the ocean.
Having filled with water that jar into which [the deity] was brought, one should place it again upon the neck of an elephant and lead it to the mandala house;
in the absence of an elephant, it should be led after placing it on a comfortable seat or a palanquin—this is the dismissal of the colored powders (*rajovisarjana*).

Then, having entered the maṇḍala-hall and smeared the maṇḍala-hall with cow-dung, the preceptor, together with his disciples, should satisfy ten young girls—ranging from five to ten years of age—in the forenoon with milk, ghee, milk-rice (pāyasa), sugar-candies, sweetmeats, and other sweet foods. Then, having given them betel, incense, perfumes, flowers, fruits, and fine cloth wrapped around the necks of their water-jars, the preceptor, along with his disciples and the entire assembly of gaṇas, should satisfy them with a heroic feast (vīrabhojana) as much as desired.

In that regard, this is the procedure for the Hero’s Feast (*vīrabhojya*): here, in the examination of the Master (*ācārya*), there are three types of Vajrācāryas—the superior, the middling, and the inferior.
As it is said: "Due to the thorough knowledge of the ten principles (*daśatattva*), the monk (*bhikṣu*) is the superior among the three;

the one called the *śrāvaka* is the middling; and the householder (*gṛhastha*) is the inferior of those two. According to this rule in the Tantra, among those monks, novices (*cellaka*), and householders, their status as senior or junior is generally determined by their consecration (*abhiṣeka*), even if they belong to a single mixed group.

Therefore, the row of monks and Vajradharas should be made to face east; the row of novices (cellakas) should face north; and the row of lay preceptors (gṛhasthācāryas) should face south. Likewise for the row of nuns (bhikṣuṇīs), each respective flask, flower, and fruit.
Or it does not exist;
[it is] facing east,
or facing south.
In this chapter, [verse]:
The Great Chapter on the Ritual for the Mudrās, Gaze, Mandala Dismissal, and Hero’s Feast. The row of the *mahallikās* and the row of the female lay practitioners (*upāsikās*) are separate;
seats should be assigned to them according to their seniority, whether elder or junior.

In that regard, among the monks, he who is the eldest may be a fool, whereas the junior one may be a great master and a teacher of the Tantra. Of these two, the one who is the teacher of the Tantra is the leader of the assembly at the *vīrabhojya* feast. The elder must be separately gratified in another house. The same applies to other elders who are teachers of the Dharma or instructors, because they are incapable of performing the welfare of sentient beings.

Furthermore, other cellakas or householders who have previously received initiation are not senior to a monk who is a Vajradhara, as long as [the latter] has not yet produced the superknowledges (*abhijñā*).
If someone then raises an objection, his capability is questioned;
if he demonstrates the superknowledges and so forth, then he is the leader of the *gaṇacakra*.
Now, if one who is conceited due to a false consecration initiates a quarrel by abandoning the conventional discipline (*saṃvṛti*), then he should be expelled from his own residence.
If, having been expelled, he accepts punishment, then food, drink, and so forth should be given as punishment by the master of punishments.
In this manner, food, drink, and so forth should be given to monks, novices, and householders respectively.

All of that should first be set aside. Having prepared a mandala in their midst and having offered food, drink, and so forth to the Blessed Kālacakra, one should then give [offerings] to the monks and other masters, as well as to the others who have been consecrated and are seated at those roots.

Having thus gratified the entire assembly of the Gaṇas as much as desired, the Ācārya, having then given his command to the disciple for the purpose of bestowing the Saṅgha, and having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Saṅgha according to his own capacity, should, out of supreme compassion, joyfully dismiss them to their respective abodes; such is the rule for the Vīrabhojana. || 202 ||

Now, the pacification of all fears and calamities is described: Enemies, lions, lordly elephants, fire, the king of serpents, thieves, bondage by noose, the agitated ocean, flesh-eating demons, diseases that cause fear of death, Indra’s afflictions, poverty, separation from one's wife, fear of an agitated king, the fall of a thunderbolt, and the loss of wealth—all these go to destruction for him who daily remembers the feet of the Yoginīs. (203)
By the words beginning with "enemy" (*śatru*), etc.:

here, some son of noble family, having drawn the mandala and received initiation, remembers daily the "practice" (*caraṇa*) of the aforementioned yoginīs—the practice within the inner self (*adhyātman*) of Avadhūtī and the others; for him, all fears go to destruction.

Fear of enemies, fear of lions, fear of elephants, fear of fire, fear of serpents, fear of thieves, fear of being bound by nooses, fear of the agitated ocean, fear of *piśācas*, fear of disease, fear of Indra’s affliction, fear of the suffering of poverty, fear of the suffering of separation from one's wife, fear of an agitated king, fear of the fall of a thunderbolt, and fear of the loss of wealth—thus these sixteen fears, as well as others, come to destruction. Their detailed explanation was given in the first chapter by way of praise; therefore, it has not been elucidated here in the *Vimalaprabhā*.
Thus, one who has been consecrated in the Kālacakra maṇḍala becomes consecrated in all the Yoginī and Yoga Tantras;
he is the teacher of all tantras, the authorizer of all mantras, and the achiever of all siddhis.

Just as the Lord Mañjuśrī, and just as Kālacakra the Ādibuddha, so too should the Vajrācārya be regarded by those seeking liberation as the teacher of the Kālacakra Tantra. Thus ends the commentary on the Consecration Chapter, written according to the Paramādibuddha. 203.

Thus ends the sixth major section, the procedure for the mudrās, gazes, dismissal of the maṇḍala, and the heroic feast (*vīrabhojya*), in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja*, which follows the *Śrī Mūlatantra*.
This commentary on the Chapter on Consecration is completed.
First, the mandala of the world-system is taught through the means of scriptural authority;
furthermore, it is taught within oneself through the yoga of personal realization.
One should indicate the pure *rajo-maṇḍala* based on the Guru as the authoritative source;

for the purpose of illuminating the profound meaning, the Blessed One has thus established the three authorities. How then is this sequence of the reality of the consecration (*sekārthatattvakrama*) not grasped by us through truth, having been taught both conventionally and ultimately?

That which is true is this: here, in the chapter on consecration, the fruit of passion—adorned with the splendors of the welfare that comes from the Tathāgatas—arises from this seed of liberation and bliss; from this seed of bliss, the mental wish-fulfilling tree grows, and through the sprinkling of great passion, it spreads across the ground of the three worlds;
thereafter, the fruit of bliss ripens again, pervading extensively throughout many eons for those whose intellects are marked by devotion to the feet of the Guru, transcending all conceptual time.

For one who is himself tossed about by the surging waves of the ocean of the bliss of consecration (*sekasukha*), what room is there for [worldly] agitation? Therefore, like the submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*) that never tires of the ocean, he remains unsatiated by the flames of the bliss of Great Passion (*mahārata*). Having caused this merit—which removes the fear of existence and is obtained through the consecration of the back [of the disciple] as it is struck by the first [sound] of the world and the self—to be written down by Avuka, [he attains his goal].

By whatever [merit] has been gained here through all those various [teachings] expounded in the *Sekoddeśa*, may the world be established in the firm-heartedness of the practice of the glorious *Vīryotsāha*;
may there be no [other goal]. Homage to the glorious Kālacakra!

Worthy people always behold the form of the Blessed One, fashioned from merit and wisdom, which is terrifying and formidable to those beings difficult to tame, yet free from pride; his speech consists of all sounds, reaching the ears of others and instructing them in the true path, according to the power of the resolute intentions of sentient beings— to him who is endowed with the excellence of all aspects, whose body appears through various inclinations, I pay homage.

That which manifests through beings by means of their own inherent nature is characterized as the *nirmāṇakāya*; this body, which appears according to the dispositions of sentient beings, is characterized as the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Neither impermanent nor permanent, neither characterized by unity nor multiplicity, neither an entity nor a non-entity—this is the supportless Dharmakāya.
It is perceived through the voices of all sentient beings as its own miraculous power; it is inseparable from emptiness and compassion, and is free from both passion and dispassion.

Having prostrated with my whole being before that auspicious one who consists of the four bodies, known as Kālacakra— the supreme natural body which is neither wisdom nor means— I, impelled by Mañjuśrī, [compose this work].
It is written by Puṇḍarīka, the Lord of the World, who holds a lotus.

In this *Sādhanāpaṭala*, the commentary was composed by me in my emanated body (*nirmitakāya*) here, in the glorious garden of Malaya to the south of the village of Kalāpa, within the jeweled pavilion at the end of the eastern door of the Śrī Kālacakra Maṇḍala house. Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, the Lord Mañjuśrī in his emanated body, Yaśonarendra, being entreated by Sūryaratha, proclaimed to the great assembly from the *Paramādibuddha*—the request of Sucandra regarding the *Sādhanāpaṭala* and the Blessed Buddha’s reply—in the first verse: "O Father of the Victors, I have obtained the seven initiations: the vase initiation, the secret initiation, the wisdom-knowledge initiation, and the fourth, which destroys the fear of existence and is to be realized through yoga."

Once again I ask correctly for the sādhana of the Lord of the Universe together with the Best of Jinas; the Lord of Jinas speaks the sādhana of the Wielder of the Thunderbolt according to the words of Sāucandra.

Having heard [the request], in the *Vimalaprabhā* commentary on the *Śrīkālacakra-bhagavat*, by means of the three words in this verse beginning with "ca," Sucandra’s entreaty for the teaching of the "Sādhana Chapter" is presented;
then, from the fourth word until the completion of the chapter, it constitutes the Blessed One’s reply.

Now, having heard the words of Sucandra, the Lord of Jinas, the Blessed Śākyamuni, absorbed in the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of Kālacakra, speaks the *sādhana* for the Vajra-holder, for the goddesses such as Vajradhātvīśvarī, for the goddesses of the sense objects such as Śabdavajrā, for the "Great" Wrathful Kings such as Uṣṇīṣa, for the wrathful goddesses such as Atinīlā, for the Mothers such as Cācikā, for the gods such as Viṣṇu, for the Naga Kings such as Jaya, and for the fierce goddesses such as Śvānāsyā; he speaks the *sādhana* for each of these and for others as well, for the sake of attaining worldly accomplishments (*laukika-siddhi*), by means of the meditation on forms extending up to the Akaniṣṭha realm—such is the rule of the Blessed One.

Now, the description of the form of the Blessed One through the purification of time for the Bodhisattvas such as Vajrapāṇi is stated: One should accomplish Kālacakra—the one who is equal to both non-existence and existence—who has sixteen limbs (the digits of the moon), twelve feet (the months), eighteen necks (the stars), four glorious faces (the oceans), universal colors, six shoulders (the aggregates), twelve arms (the sun), and hands like the lotuses of the Victors; whose joints are sixty-four (zero, six, and fire); who, with his two feet, terrifies Māra and Rudra within the mandalas of the Moon, Sun, and Fire; and who is trampled by the dancing [Goddess].

With the words "candrāṅgam" and so forth, the Blessed One said here regarding the unawakened: Day is the sun, passion (*rajas*), and the *vajra*; night is the moon, semen (*śukra*), and the *padma*. The union of these two is the *Kālacakra*, the Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*).
Thus, it has been stated by the Blessed One in a general sense in another *Paratantra* as well: "The Blessed Lord Vajrī is day, and Wisdom is proclaimed to be night;
for just as Rudra is the sun, so Umā is considered to be the moon."

Thus, time (*kāla*) is said to be the day and night distinguished by the sun and moon; its wheel (*cakra*) consists of twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths (*śvāsa*), characterized by the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and is the zodiacal wheel (*rāśicakra*) that serves as the cause for the arising and destruction of all sentient beings according to worldly convention (*laukika-saṃvṛti*). Accordingly, it is said: "Time creates all beings, and Time always destroys them;
for Time is the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, whose very nature is day and night."

Thus ends the great chapter on the protection of the site, the confession of sins, and so forth. In this manner, the practitioners of yoga must perform the sādhana of this Kālacakra for the purpose of generating, exhausting, and destroying [samsāra], according to the sequence to be described; this is the rule for the conceptualization of form, beginning with "the limbs of the moon," and so on.
A day and night, consisting of twelve zodiac signs, constitutes one limb; its six signs each constitute the left and right feet, which together form the pair of feet.

Then, the throat consisting of the four *lagnas*— namely the left, right, and middle [throat], as well as the "peacock-throat" (*śikhigala*)— is the "three-throated" (*trikaṇṭha*). Likewise, the four faces consisting of the three *lagnas* each— namely the east, south, west, and north— are the "four-faced" (*caturmukha*), which is the ocean and possesses the colors of the universe, as will be described.
Thus, consisting of two ascendants each on the left and the right, [divided into] front, back, and middle shoulders— making six shoulders—
and likewise twelve arms, each consisting of a month, with those arms being the "arms of the Sun" (*sūryabāhu*),
such is each half-ascendant.
The lotus-hand of the Victor has twenty-four fingers according to the division of the lunar fortnights.

Thus, by means of the sixty-six breaths that constitute each day, there are three hundred and sixty finger-joints on each hand; since each of the five fingers has three joints, there are fifteen joints per hand, and across twenty-four hands, this amounts to three hundred and sixty joints.
In this way, there are [the digits] zero, six, and fire (three) as joints.

With his two feet, he tramples upon Māra and Rudra—namely, the Māras of the aggregates (*skandha*), afflictions (*kleśa*), death (*mṛtyu*), and the son of a god (*devaputra*)—as well as Rudra, who consists of passion, hatred, delusion, and pride.

He is being offered oblations within the mandalas of the moon, sun, and fire; by that Kālacakra, who has overcome worldly attachment, he [the practitioner] becomes one with him, equalizing the state of non-becoming and becoming, merging them into a single unity with the state of nirvāṇa, through the removal of all obscurations.
"In this way one should accomplish Kālacakra"—this is the rule of the Blessed One.

Now, the locations for its accomplishment are stated: in a garden, on a mountain, in a temple of the Supreme Victor, in a deserted shrine, in a place of the Siddhas, in a cremation ground, at a lake, in a beautiful dwelling, or likewise in a secret place;
or wherever the mind finds satisfaction, O Lord of Men, there one should perform the practice, having indeed performed the previously mentioned protection, and having sat upon a soft bed or seat.
By the words "in a garden" and so forth, it is shown that here the location corresponds to the worldly rites to be accomplished;
the practitioner of mantras should perform the rite for the purpose of subjugation and attraction in a garden.
On a mountain for the purpose of immobilizing, deluding, or pinning;
in the temple of the Supreme Jina or at a great shrine (*mahācaitya*) possessing a presiding deity for the sake of the eight great supernatural powers (*mahāsiddhis*);
in an empty temple of a deity for the purpose of expulsion or inciting hatred; and by the word "or," on the shore of the great ocean.
In a place of accomplishment for the sake of attaining the *karmamudrā*;
in a cremation ground for the sake of slaying; and in a lake or a beautiful dwelling for the sake of pacifying and nourishing.

"In a secret place" means in a cave-dwelling or an underground chamber; for the sake of accomplishing the sovereignty over the three worlds, O King, one should perform the practice in whatever location brings satisfaction to the mind in accordance with the ritual action. Thus it is said: "Where the protector of the earth is righteous, and where the subjects are well-established..."
"There is no conflict for one who upholds the earth; there, one should undertake yoga.
Thus, having performed the protection previously mentioned—that is, the protection described in the Chapter on Consecration—in the *Vimalaprabhā*.
Indeed, one should sit upon a soft bed or seat; this is the rule regarding the place.

Now, the purification of the faces and so forth is described: First, one should meditate on the various rays of the *tattvas* within the moon at the heart, radiating in the ten directions. Having performed the purification of the faces and other parts, and having offered manifold and diverse worship to the Victors who have been projected into the sky, the practitioner should confess the accumulated impurities of many kinds and take refuge in the Three Jewels through the purification of body, speech, and mind.
With the words "At the beginning," and so forth, it is stated that here the yogin must first perform the previously mentioned protection and the expulsion of Māras.

Then, having instantaneously assumed the form of the deity according to the procedure taught in the *Sādhanapaṭala*, he should visualize within his own heart an eight-petalled red lotus transformed from the syllable *paṃ*. Above that, in the pericarp, is a moon-maṇḍala transformed from the syllable *aṃ*. In its center, conventionally, is a five-pronged vajra born from the syllable *hūṃ*. The yogin should contemplate its various rays of five colors.
Having first performed the purification of the mouth by placing a pill of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) in the mouth, the purification of the mouth is accomplished;
likewise, by means of the previously mentioned divine mudrā, one should touch oneself starting from the head down to the feet—
thus is the purification of the body.

Having performed the purification of the face and so forth in this manner, one should then awaken the Tathāgatas in the expanse of the sky by means of vajra-rays from the moon-maṇḍala. Having drawn back those rays—once they have been emanated—for the purpose of making offerings to those expanded Victors (Jinas), one should visualize them entering the moon-vajra within one’s own heart. Thereafter, one should meditate upon the seed-syllables of the twelve offering goddesses within the moon-maṇḍala.

Having performed worship to the Tathāgatas with these seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*)—namely *kkh g gh ṅa*, *kkh g gh ṅā*, *c ch j ñña*, *c ch jh j ñā*, *ṭ ṭh ūr ṇa*, *ṭ ṭh ūr ḍh ṇā*, *p ph bbhma*, *pph bbhmā*, *t th dh na*, *t th dh nā*, *s p ṣ ś ka*, and *spa ṣ kā*—which respectively produce dance, music, perfumes, garlands, incense, lamps, food offerings, unbroken rice, graceful gestures, laughter, song, and desire; and having performed the consecration according to the procedure taught in the Chapter on Consecration, the practitioner should then confess their various accumulated defilements in the sequence to be described hereafter. The rule is that the practitioner must first take refuge in the Three Jewels for the purification of body, speech, and mind.

Now, at the conclusion of the confession of misdeeds, one should rejoice in merit: Free from all defilement and established in the conduct of awakening, I rejoice in all the manifold roots of virtue performed by the Perfect Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, which removes the fear of existence, until the limit of awakening. For the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, I here make this aspiration: "May I become a Perfect Buddha.

The practitioner, free from defilement and established in the conduct of awakening, rejoices in all that has been done—by the Perfectly Awakened One, by the Bodhisattvas, and by the noble Saṅghas—consisting of manifold kinds of merit.
Then he goes for refuge to the Three Jewels: "I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, which removes the fear of existence, for the sake of the moon of awakening.

Having thus gone for refuge and performed the surrender of himself, he then makes a vow for the sake of sentient beings: "May I become a Perfectly Awakened One; I make this vow here for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings."

Thus, having performed the sevenfold worship—consisting of prostration, offering, confession of misdeeds, rejoicing in merit, entreaty to the Tathāgatas, supplication, and dedication of merit—one should there recall the three roots: the generation of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta), the purification of one's intention (āśaya), and the abandonment of the notions of "I" and "mine" (ahaṃkāra-mamakāra).
Thereafter, one should contemplate the ten perfections (pāramitās).

For the sake of the equipment of merit, knowledge, and ethical discipline, one should contemplate the perfection of generosity, and likewise the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, aspiration, power, and knowledge. Then, one should recollect the sublime abodes—namely, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Following that, one should contemplate the four means of attraction: generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful conduct, and consistency in purpose.

Then one should contemplate the abandonment of the ten unwholesome actions: killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, harsh speech, slanderous speech, frivolous chatter, covetousness, malice, and wrong view.

In this way, one should abandon the five hindrances—namely, remorse, lethargy and drowsiness, restlessness and regret, and doubt—and likewise abandon the afflictions of attachment, aversion, delusion, and pride.

In this way, having abandoned the influx of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the influx of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), the influx of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), and the influx of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*), one should then cultivate the four liberations (*catur-vimokṣa*). Having cultivated emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*), one should contemplate the realm of the moving and the unmoving with this verse: "In the absence of being, there is no cultivation of being; cultivation is not indeed cultivation.
Thus, being would not be being, and cultivation is not perceived.
Thus it is said.
The meaning of this shall be explained in what follows.

Now, the characteristic of emptiness for the sake of grasping a new existence is stated: This entire world is empty, devoid of the intrinsic nature of substantial form; therefore, there is neither Buddha nor enlightenment, nor compassion for the benefit of others—such is the vow of the signless (*animitta*).
Knowing all this, O King, one should meditate upon that very Vajra of Body, Speech, and Mind, the Bodhisattva of immeasurable qualities, the Lord of the Mandala within every mandala.

By the words beginning with "empty" (*śūnyam*), it is meant that this entire world is empty, being devoid of existence and having as its intrinsic nature the form of real entities. From that great emptiness (*mahāśūnya*), there is neither a Buddha nor enlightenment, nor altruistic compassion;
thus, with the vow of the signless (*animitta*), one thinks: "May I become a Buddha for the benefit of the world."

Knowing this in its entirety, O King, for the sake of Buddhahood, Bodhisattvas must meditate upon that which possesses immeasurable qualities—the Lord of the Mandala—within every mandala as the Vajra of Body, Speech, and Mind.

This is the Blessed One’s injunction: that the Leader, the Vajra of Body, Speech, and Mind, should be meditated upon within the mandala of Body, Speech, and Mind for the purpose of accomplishing worldly fruits and for the manifestation [of reality] to all sentient beings.

Now, for the sake of grasping the supramundane aggregates and abandoning the mundane aggregates of cyclic existence, meditative concentration is described: First, in this world, the yogi should effect the destruction of fire by means of water within the center of the body; afterwards, the water becomes earth, having entered into the midst of the water like salt.

Indeed, the wind undergoes disappearance after drying up that mass of water in the sky; then, at the end of darkness, he should place the mind, free from sense objects, in the middle ground within the fire. (7)
With the words beginning "By water," etc., it is meant that here in this mortal world, at the time of death for those born from a womb, the destruction of fire is brought about by water; therefore,
by that very same meditative absorption (samādhi), the yogi should first effect the destruction of fire by water within the body.
Subsequently, due to the absence of fire, the earth element abandons its hardness and, like salt, becomes liquefied and turns into water;
having entered into the midst of that water, the wind then dries up all that water, and the ether proceeds toward its internal dissolution.
Thus occurs the rapid destruction of the aggregate of the elements.

Then, one should place the mind—namely the *ālayavijñāna*—in the middle ground within the element of space (*ākāśadhātu*), which is at the end of darkness in the fire, appearing as a reflection in all its aspects yet devoid of objects.
Thereafter, one should recite this mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham;
oṃ animittajñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*.
Having recited, "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of wishlessness;

Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of non-conditioning," one should meditate upon the "image of emptiness," which transcends the elements and the nature of atoms; such is the rule of the Tathāgatas.

Thus ends the first major section, concerning the protection of the site, the confession of sins, and so forth, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja*, which follows the *Śrī-mūla-tantra*.
In this chapter, the great instruction on the accomplishment of the task through the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*).

Now, for the sake of fulfilling previous vows and for the purpose of setting the wheel of Dharma in motion, the means of accomplishment of the Blessed One through the stage of generation is described according to the manner of entering the womb: [The Great Instruction on the Accomplishment of the Task through the Stage of Generation] Now, for the sake of fulfilling previous vows and for the purpose of setting the wheel of Dharma in motion, the means of accomplishment of the Blessed One through the stage of generation is described according to the manner of entering the womb:
Empty are wind, fire, water, earth, gods, mountains, lotuses, moon, sun, and fires; and all around is the peaked pavilion, the cage born of vajras, radiating stainless light.

In its center, upon a vajra-ground, is a mandala shimmering with a multitude of jewel rays; from it arises the syllable Oṃ, born of primordial wisdom, the lotus of the supreme Jina, together with the seats of the moon and sun.

By the words "empty" (*śūnya*) and so forth, here, both externally and internally, the cause of origination is the infinite space-element (*ākāśadhātu*), the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) which is triangular;

externally it is circular and consists of ten-spoked vajras, while internally it is the body of the Mother. Therein, externally, is the wind-mandala in the middle, bow-shaped, measuring four hundred thousand *yojanas* in its transverse dimension, transformed from the seed-syllable *yaṃ*, black in color, and marked with banners at the top and bottom, accompanied by two double-vajras (*viśvavajra*) transformed from the syllable *hūṃ*.

Above that is the fire mandala, three hundred thousand yojanas in extent, transformed from the syllable *raṃ*, triangular in shape, red in color, marked with svastikas, and accompanied by two crossed vajras (*viśvavajra*) above and below, each transformed from the syllable *hūṃ*.

Above that is the water mandala, two hundred thousand yojanas in extent, transformed from the syllable *baṃ*, white in color, circular in shape, accompanied by two crossed vajras above and below, each transformed from the syllable *hūṃ*, and marked with a lotus.

Above that is the earth mandala, square and yellow in color, transformed from the syllable *laṃ*; it is sixteen thousand leagues in extent, marked with vajras, and accompanied by two double-vajras (viśvavajra) above and below, which are transformed from the syllable *hūṃ*. Above that is the great Mount Meru, consisting of vajra and transformed from the syllable *maṃ*; it is sixteen thousand [leagues] in width at its base and fifty thousand [leagues] in height. In its center is a universal lotus (*viśvājña*) of half the measure of Meru, transformed from the syllable *śaṃ*.
Its pericarp (*kaṇikā*) consists of three parts and measures twelve and a half thousand leagues; from that, [the stalk] is transformed from the syllable *kṣai*.
Above that is a moon mandala produced from the transformation of the syllable *haṃ*, equal in size to the pericarp;
above that is a sun mandala produced from the transformation of the visarga;
and above that is fire, which is the blue-colored Rāhu mandala produced from the transformation of the bindu.

Thus, having visualized the entire [universe] as a single unified mass in the form of the seed-syllable *ha kṣaṃ lava r ya~*, one should then contemplate the world-system as being fully accomplished. Thus, externally and internally, within the body of the Mother: by the previously mentioned method, there is the wind-maṇḍala at the forehead, the fire-maṇḍala at the throat, the water-maṇḍala at the heart, and the earth-maṇḍala at the navel;
from the navel down to the secret lotus is the Great Meru.
The secret lotus of the Blessed One is like a lotus; it consists of the three channels carrying feces, urine, and semen, which are the mandalas of the Moon, Sun, and Rāhu,
all of which are gathered together within the pericarp of the secret lotus.

Thus, above that, there is a gabled pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) which radiates stainless light on all sides; or else, a vajra-fence (*vajrapañjara*) born of the syllable *HŪṂ* and produced from vajras, according to the scriptural authority: "In the womb of the Mother is the lotus with the vajra" (*Kāyatrayastotra*). By that very [fence], there is a vajra-made enclosure. In its center, upon a vajra-ground, is a mandala shimmering with a multitude of jewel rays, transformed from the syllable *OṂ*. This *OṂ* is born of gnosis (*jñāna*), the lotus of the Supreme Victor (*jinavara*), and serves as the seats for the moon and sun. This is the mind-mandala (*cittamaṇḍala*), extending as far as the perimeter of the earth-circle.
And "bho"; "apūrva" does not exist in Ka, Kha, Ca, Cha; "daśākāra" in Ga;
"śukla" does not exist.
ga. ca. bho. "There is no equal"; bho. "There is no [state of] non-straightness"; ga. "yāma" [is not present].
And, O Venerable One, in my body (*nṛśarīre*). Ca bhagavat.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the external speech-maṇḍala: this eight-petalled lotus is indeed devoid of the moon and sun; on the outside, in the cardinal and intermediate directions, there are sun-lotuses and chariots at the middle of the gates.

O King, at the solar gates there are archways made of jewels and gold, and in the cremation grounds there are eight pillars. Within the womb [of the palace] is the wheel of perfect enjoyment of the Jina, consisting of vajras.

Outside of that, within the speech-maṇḍala (vāṅmaṇḍala) at the edge of the ocean-fence, is this eight-petaled lotus (*aṣṭakamala*), a group of eight lotuses devoid of moon and sun. Outside of that very [lotus], within the body-maṇḍala (kāyamaṇḍala) at the edge of the wind-fence, is the "day-maker" lotus (*dinakarakamala*), a twelve-petaled lotus likewise devoid of moon and sun.
Thus there are four gates and chariots.

In this way, the body-maṇḍala is four hundred thousand *yojanas* in extent; the speech-maṇḍala is half of that; the mind-maṇḍala (cittamaṇḍala) is half of that as well; and the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*) is half of that, being the lotus of the Blessed One.
The pericarp, resembling a lotus petal, contains the mandalas of the Moon, Sun, and Rāhu;

likewise, within the inner self, from the secret lotus downwards and upwards—from the heart to the secret lotus and up to the head—or alternatively, from the heart to the ends of the fingers, toes, and nails, [this is established] because of the presence of conceptualization within the body of the Mother; such is the rule.
Thus, there are four doors for each maṇḍala,
making twelve doors in total;
"at the solar doors, O King" is the address.
Outside the body-mandala, there are archways made of jewels and gold; within the interior, there are eight cremation grounds.

With sixteen pillars—divided into sixteen digits (kalās)—there is the well-enjoyment wheel (*sambhogacakra*) of the Victor, consisting of vajras and consisting of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
The purification of his body elements will be explained in the *Jñānapaṭala*;
here, according to the *Mūlatantra*, the purification of the aggregates of phenomena (*dharmaskandha*) is stated.

Regarding this, the Blessed One said: "By means of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Great Saṅgha, there is the maṇḍala of mind, speech, and body; and by means of the four sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*), there is the fourfold vajra-line."
It is symmetrical on all sides by means of the four foundations of mindfulness,
and it has twelve gates through the cessation of the twelve links [of dependent origination].
Likewise, the auspicious archways are formed by the twelve stages,
and the cremation grounds in the eight directions are formed by the Noble Eightfold Path.
The sixteen pillars are emptiness; the gabled chamber is formed by the [eighteen] elements; the porticos are the eight liberations; and the cornices are the eight qualities possessed of form.
The wings, moreover, are purified in five colors through the five aggregates beginning with ethical discipline, distinguished by mind, speech, and body.
In the threefold enclosure and the three vehicles, there are the five faculties beginning with faith;
likewise, there are the five powers beginning with faith within the mandalas of mind, speech, and body.
ca. bho. vasudala; ka. kha. pakṣaka; ca. cha.
prākāra.
ga. its half, and the maṇḍala, and raṃ.

In this chapter, [verse]: The great summary on the accomplishment of the effect through the stage of generation; the altar with the goddesses who uphold meditative concentration; and the variegated jeweled frieze, which fulfills the ten perfections, within the three mandalas.
By means of the eighteen unique qualities (*aveṇika-dharma*) and the masteries (*vaśitā*), Bakula has attained mastery over the wholesome roots.
It is filled with the sounds of bells and so forth through the liberations such as emptiness;
it is strewn with banners by means of the bases of psychic power, and it is radiant with mirrors through the [right] efforts.
It is inlaid with the factors of enlightenment, fanned by nine chowries, adorned with garlands of flowers,
its corners marked by the four means of attraction, and embellished with double-vajras.
It is adorned with the four jewels at the junctions of the gates and turrets,
and is perpetually encircled by the five great bracelets of the five superknowledges.
It is well-encircled by the vajra-garland of the limbs of enlightenment of the omniscient one,
as well as by the single wheel of bliss and the light-rays of the wisdom-vajra.
Through the division of wisdom and means, the moon and sun are ever-risen;
purified as mind, speech, and body, it is the Great Vase of the Wheel of Dharma.
The drum, the Bodhi tree, and that wish-fulfilling gem and so forth—
this is the Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala of Śrī Kālacakra.
Having meditated upon that which brings about all prosperity, one should then place the first letter of the alphabet;
this is the procedure for purifying the womb at the time of the Blessed One’s descent into the womb. || 9 ||
Now, the non-manifestation of the deity externally and the manifestation of the embryo internally are described:

One should meditate upon Kālacakra—the supreme Victor, whose body is adorned with vajras, who has a lotus-like form, twelve arms, four faces, three necks, twelve eyes, a blossoming face, and fangs that are half-visible and terrifying—emitting five rays of light from his first [hands], which hold the moon and sun together with the vajra, and from the others, the five [elements] beginning with the mirror (the earth element). (10)

By the words "the first" (*ādyā*) and so forth, it is meant that here, upon the center of the mandala, above the discs of the moon, sun, and Rāhu, the first [vowels] are to be placed in counter-clockwise and clockwise rotation upon the moon disc for the sake of the thirty-two marks (*lakṣaṇa*). These are the thirty-two: the thirty vowels, the nasal dot (*bindu*), and the visarga. Among them, *a, i, ṛ, u, la* constitute the first pentad of digits (*kalā*).
Then, by means of the differentiation of the qualities (*guṇa*), *a-e-ar-o* and *al* constitute the second group of five digits (*kalā*).
Then, by means of the substitution of *yaṇ*, *ha-ya-ra-va-la* constitute the third group of five digits.
At the end of the fifteen digits is the *bindu*.
The sixteen vowels are as follows: starting with *a*, they are assigned by moving counter-clockwise and then clockwise;

the sixteen vowels are *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, *ḹ*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, *au*, *am* (at the end of the new moon), and *visarga* (*aḥ*) as the sixteenth. These are the fifteen [vowels] ending with *lā*, *vā*, *rā*, *yā*, *hā*, *āl*, *au*, *ār*, *ai*, *āl*, *ū*, *ṝ*, *ī*, *ā*, and *aḥ* as the sixteenth vowel at the end of the new moon.
These thirty-two marks of a Great Being are established as being within the lunar portion at conception, in the seminal element (*śukradhātu*);
thereafter, in the solar mandala, there are forty single consonants beginning with *ka*,
and forty conjunct consonants.
In that regard, by means of *ya-ra-va-la*, there are thirty-six groups of six;

likewise, due to their twofold pronunciation, *la-va-ya-ḍa-ḍha* are included as *lla-vvva-yya-ḍḍa-ḍḍha*. [The sequence is: *lla vva yya haha ssappa śśa kka ta ththa dda dhdha nna ppa phpha bba bbha mma ṭṭa ṭhṭha ḍḍa ḍḍhḍha ṇṇa cca chcha jja ijha ñña kka khkha gga gha ṅṅa*. Thus, forty [letters] are joined with the divisions beginning with Earth (*pṛthivī*) in a clockwise direction.
Then, by way of counter-clockwise rotation: ṅa gha ga kha ka, na jha ja cha ca,
ṇa ḍha ḍa ṭha ṭa.
ma bha ba pha pa na dha da tha ta ka śa ṣa sa pa sa
Ha, ya, ra, va, la, ḍha, ḍa, ya, va, la—
these are the forty single-consonant entities.
Thus, there is the rule that the eighty secondary marks (*vyañjana*) are in the sun during conception (*garbhādhāna*), while the vowels (*araji*) are in the moon.
In this way, the consonants beginning with *ka* are likewise in the moon and the sun; these two are joined with the vajra.
Of those two, the moon is below the sun, and the sun is above the moon; in the center of the moon is the syllable *HŪṂ*, like the moon and sun.
Thus, semen is upon the dust;
within the semen is the *ālayavijñāna*, the *gandharva* being; from that [arise] the five forms by means of the seer and so forth.
Then, the Moon is Śukra, endowed with vowels,
the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), the progenitor of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), and Vairocana; the Sun is Rajas, endowed with consonants,
the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), the progenitor of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*), and Ratnasaṃbhava.
Discernment is the Gandharva-being accompanied by the syllable *HŪṂ*; Amitābha is the producer of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
The unity of these is the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*), accompanied by the syllable *HO* (or *HĪ*).
The knowledge of the performance of duties (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) is Amoghasiddhi, the progenitor of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).

Thereafter, consciousness (*vijñāna*), complete with all limbs and members, accompanied by the syllable *haṃ*, is the knowledge of the perfectly pure sphere of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*); this is Akṣobhya, the progenitor of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). Thus, consisting of these five knowledges, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is unified externally and internally: for the vowels it is the nasal drop (*bindu*), and for the consonants it is the visarga; for consciousness, it is the unobstructed.

The syllable *A* belongs to the vital breath (*prāṇa*); according to the sequence thus described, one should meditate upon the Blessed One Kālacakra as emitting five rays and possessing shimmering, stainless hands.
This is the rule for the accomplishment of the effect both externally and within the womb.
Now, the configuration [of the deity] according to the divisions of time within the body of the deity is stated, beginning with "on the garment," and so forth.
In this context, at the time of the deities' birth, they arise endowed with all ornaments; therefore, they are born with various limbs of the body, various colors, and various shapes.

Thus, [the deity] has a body adorned with vajras, hands like the lotuses of the Victors, twenty-four arms, twelve arms [in another form], four faces, three necks, twelve eyes, an open countenance, and half-bared fangs. Śukra.
O Me Lon and others, O Jñāna!
The nature of the self.
ca cha bhoḥ
And those others as well.

The Great Chapter on the Accomplishment of the Result through the Stage of Generation (*utpattikrama*). Regarding "Karāla," it refers to the characteristic of the sovereign of body-consciousness during the accomplishment of the result.
In the center, upon the pericarp of the mandala-lotus, the arrangement of deities contained within one's own body is said to be the form of the mandala. || 10 ||
I bow to the Lord of Jinas, born from the glorious syllable Oṃ, whose lotus-feet rest gracefully in the *ālīḍha* posture upon the hearts of Rudra and Anaṅga, who stand atop the moon, sun, and fire;
his right foot is red with Māra and his white left foot with Rudra, while the middle portion of both right and left sides resembles a bee and the sun, and his throat is the color of the moon.

In the glorious lotus born from the syllable *Oṃ*, the lotus of the heart, above the moon, sun, and fire, at the crown of the *lalanā*, *rasanā*, and *avadhūtī* channels—where Rudra resides within these two, the left and right flows that constitute the wings of Māra and the afflictions—in the heart is the Lord of Jinas with his feet beautifully poised in the *ālīḍha* stance. Therein, Māra, the god of desire, has five flower-arrows and a bow in his hands, holds a noose and an *aṅkuśa*, is four-armed and one-faced, red in color, and stands upon the sole of the [Buddha’s] right foot which is also red in color.

Likewise, Rudra has three eyes, one face, and four arms, bearing a trident, a *ḍamaru* drum, a skull-cup, and a *khaṭvāṅga*. On the sole of his left foot is the white [syllable] *Śukla*; thus he is blue-bodied. Furthermore, the middle neck is blue, the right [neck] is red like the sun, and the left or "non-right" [neck] is moon-colored, white; thus he has three necks according to the previously mentioned procedure.
The eastern face is black, fierce with bared fangs;
the southern is passionate and red; the northern is peaceful and white;
and the western, established in meditative absorption, is yellow.

He wears a crown of matted hair with a universal vajra and a half-moon; he bears the crown of Vajrasattva, as well as a vajra-jewel, earrings, a vajra necklace, a vajra breast-ornament, a vajra girdle, vajra anklets, a vajra fillet, a vajra garland, and a garment of tiger-skin. || 11 ||

The shoulders are blue, red, and white as the moon; on the right and left, there are two arms each, black in color like the sun’s body, while the others are the color of the moon. Likewise, by means of the twenty-four [arms], the hands are equipped with weapons in due order.
The five fingers have three joints each, and upon the moon-like lotuses [of the palms], the five-colored rays flash forth. (12)
Likewise, the right shoulder is first blue, second red, and third white; and so it is on the left.
Thus, there are two arms that are blue, two that are red, and two that are white, on both the right and the left.
Thus, four hands are black,
four are red,
and four are white.
On the right and on the left,
they are accompanied by the weapons that will be described; thus, on each hand there are five fingers, and each of these has three joints.
The thumb is yellow, the index finger is white,
and the middle finger is red.
The ring finger is black,
the little finger is green,
and the first row of joints on all the fingers from the palms is black.
The second is red and the third is white;
thus, within each moon, hand, and lotus, there are five colors, shimmering with those [five] seals.
Thus is the rule for the entry of ignorance, formative predispositions, and consciousness; this is the third month in the womb, the first measure.
And there is no "not" (a-vi).
What is it? Ka.
Furthermore, "self" does not exist.
ka kha ca
And also in color.
And what is exhausted?
Immediately after "O Akaniṣṭhas, you are green," the reading "tāḥ" occurs in manuscripts K, Kh, and Ca.
The first six.
And some say "ga."
O,
emanate in this very way!

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the "consciousnesses" (*vijñānāni*) as the Yakṣas, the collection of weapons is now described: the collection of weapons situated upon the excellent palm of the hand— whether black, red, or white— is the vajra, the sword, the trident, the razor-knife that causes fear to the world, and the fire-arrow.
Therefore, for the Wielder of the Vajra, in his right hands upon the solar lotuses, there are indeed a vajra, a hook, a bell, a *ḍamaru* drum, a mallet, a wheel, a spear, a staff, and an axe. (13)
