By the words "Kṛṣṇa" and so forth, in the four palms that are black, there is a vajra in the first, a sword in the second, a trident in the third, and a knife in the fourth; likewise, in the four palms that are red, there is a fire-arrow in the first, a vajra-goad in the second, a ḍamaru-drum in the third, and a mallet in the fourth.

In the third [section], on the four palms of the white [hands]: in the first palm is a discus, in the second a spear, in the third a staff, and in the fourth an axe; such is the collection of weapons in the right, and likewise for the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra) in the right lotus-hand of the Sun. || 13 ||

Now, the symbols on the four palms of the four black left hands are described: the bell, the shield, the skull-topped staff with its expanded head, the skull-cup filled with blood, the bow, the noose, the jewel, the lotus, the aquatic creature, the mirror, and the chain; as well as the four-faced head of Brahmā, which is the lotus-head of the Creator, and the head of Māra with its wretched face, and Rudra’s own goddess, all held in the left hands of the Jina, with their soles pressed against his feet. 14.
In the first [right hand] is a vajra-bell, in the second a shield, in the third a khaṭvāṅga with an open mouth, and in the fourth a skull-cup filled with blood;
likewise, in the four red palms of the left hands, there is in the first a bow, in the second a noose, in the third a jewel, and in the fourth a white lotus.

Likewise, in the four white palms of his hands: in the first palm is the "aquatic creature," which is the conch; in the second, a mirror; in the third, a vajra-chain; and in the fourth, the head of Brahmā.
Thus, the lotus-head of Brahmā—which is the ornament adorning the face of the Vedas—is held in the left hand of the Jina.
There, in the presence of Māra and Rudra, Rati, the consort of Māra, and Umā, the consort of Rudra, both making wretched faces and shaking the soles of their feet, enter into Akṣobhya. || 14 ||

Now the characteristics of Viśvamātā are described: golden-hued, with four faces, embraced by the eight-handed Kamalā; Viśvamātā holds in her right hands, in order, a knife, a goad, a rosary, and a *sarava* drum;

and likewise in her left hands, a conch, a noose, a hundred-petaled lotus, and a divine jewel. She stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, has three eyes, wears a crown of the Lord of Jinas, and is adorned with finger-rings. || 15 ||
In the left [hand], there is a bell and an axe.
In Kha, Cha, and Tale Ca, the word "ornament" (*bhūṣaṇa*) is absent;
[this concludes] the Great Chapter on the Accomplishment of the Result by means of the Stage of Generation (*utpattikrama*), beginning with the words "Having the luster of gold" (*hemābha*).

In that regard, from the single state of equal flavor (*ekasamarasa*), there is the arising of the Blessed One by way of the nature of the moon and semen (*candra-śukra*), and the arising of the Goddess by way of the nature of the sun and dust (*sūrya-rajas*).
Therein, the moon possesses the qualities of white and black, while the sun possesses the qualities of red and yellow.
Therefore, Viśvamātā—golden-hued, with four faces according to the Vedas, four mouths, and eight hands holding lotuses—is embraced in front [by the Blessed One].
In her first right hand is a knife, in the second a goad, in the third a *ḍamaru* drum with a staff, and in the fourth a rosary;
likewise, in the first left hand is a conch-shell, in the second a noose, in the third a white hundred-petaled lotus, and in the fourth a divine jewel.
Thus the Blessed One stands in the *ālīḍha* posture, while Viśvamātā stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture.
Having twelve eyes like the sun, crowned by the Lord of Jinas or by Vajrasattva, they are sealed with the five mudrās and abide in meditative union. 15.

There are eight goddesses on the eight petals, possessing the hands of Vasu, four faces, and twelve eyes; among them, four hold snakes and chowries in the intermediate corners. In the directions of Īśāna, Nairṛtya, Agni, and Vāyu, there are respectively the Dharma-conch, the Gaṇḍī-bell, the Cintāmaṇi-jewel, and likewise the Kalpavṛkṣa tree according to their sequence. || 16 ||
The other perfections, beginning with generosity (*dāna*), are included within that Perfection of Wisdom of the Mother of the Universe. On the eight petals are eight goddesses;
they possess the wealth-granting lotuses, have eight arms, four faces as prescribed by the Vedas, and twelve eyes like the sun.
Among them, four hold fly-whisks (*camara*); with their eight arms, they each hold eight fly-whisks.

Regarding the four corners according to the divisions of the faces of the Jina: [the goddess] in the southeast (Agni) is black, in the southwest (Nairṛtya) is red, in the northwest (Vāyavya) is yellow, and in the northeast (Īśāna) is white. Thus, behind them: in the northeast is the white Dharma-conch; in the southwest is the red Dharma-gong; in the southeast is the black Cintāmaṇi; and in the northwest is the yellow Kalpavṛkṣa. Likewise, on the eastern petal is the black [goddess], on the southern the red, on the northern the white, and on the western the yellow-shining one.

Just as the faces of the Bhagavat are divided according to the four directions, so too for the goddesses: the first face of Viśvamātā is golden-hued, the right is white, the left is red, and the western is blue. Likewise, for the yellow goddesses, the eastern face is white, the right is black, the western is red, and the left is yellow. For the white goddesses, the eastern face is white, the right is black, the western is red, and the left is yellow.
For the red [deities], the first [face] is red, the right yellow, the left blue, and the western white;
for the black [deities], the eastern is black, the left white, and the western yellow.
Just as the ornaments of the Blessed Lady consist of the five mudrās, so too should they be understood for the goddesses of the central lotus; such is the rule. || 16 ||

Now, the symbols in the right and left hands of Kṛṣṇadīptā and the others are described: in the palm of the first [right] hand of Kṛṣṇā is an incense burner; in the second, a vessel for cooling [drinks]; in the third, red flour; and in the fourth right hand, a full moon.

In the left hands, in sequence, are a bell, a lotus, a flower from the celestial tree (*surataru*), and a garland of flowers. For Raktā, there is a lamp and a necklace; in the right hand, a crown and a bracelet; and in the left hand, [the same]. (17)
"Kṛṣṇā" and so forth:

in the first right hand is a vessel of incense for Kṛṣṇā; in the second, a vessel of cold water and a vessel of sandalwood; in the third, red powder and a vessel of saffron; and in the fourth, camphor together with musk and a vessel [containing] sixteen moons—thus in the right hands.

In the left hands, there is a bell in the first, a lotus in the second, a flower of the celestial tree (surataru) in the third, and a garland of various flowers in the fourth, in sequence; thus on the eastern petal.
For Raktadīptā, in the right hands, there is a lamp in the first, a necklace in the second, a crown in the third, and a bracelet in the fourth; thus on the right. || 17 ||

In the hands of the Yellow Goddess (Pītā), there are, in order from right to left: a garment, a girdle, a sparkling, stainless hand, an earring, an anklet, a conch, a flute, a jewel, and a hand-drum (ḍamaruka);

in her left hands, a lute, a large drum (ḍhakkā), a resonant bell (kaṃsikā), a trumpet (kāhalā), and a vessel of milk-water with medicinal herbs; and in the hands of the White Goddess (Sitā), a vessel of food containing the fruit of the essence of nectar.
Likewise, in the left hand, there is a cloth in the first, a girdle in the second, a jeweled necklace in the third, and an anklet in the fourth;
similarly, for the radiant yellow [deity], there is a conch in the first right hand, a flute in the second, a jewel in the third, and a hand-drum (ḍamaruka) in the fourth;
and in the left hands, there is a lute in the first, a ḍhakkā drum in the second, a tinkling bell in the third, and a trumpet (kāhalā) in the fourth, respectively.
Likewise, for Śvetadīptā: in the first right hand a vessel of milk, in the second a vessel of water, in the third a divine herb, and in the fourth a vessel of wine;

in the first left hand a vessel of nectar (*amṛta*), in the second a vessel of *siddharasa*, in the third the fruit of immortality, and in the fourth a vessel of cooked rice—thus is the accomplishment of Vajrasattva together with his own mudrā. (18)

In the lotuses of the cardinal directions are indeed the four Buddhas, possessing nine eyes, three faces, and six arms; in the corners are the goddesses beginning with Tārā. Furthermore, in the eight chambers of those two [mandalas] are the eight vases.

The deities and goddesses are black, red, yellow, and white like the moon; and the male and female deities are black and white, while upon the head of the sun in the intermediate directions, they are red and yellow.

Now, having observed that the world is a fit vessel for the teaching of the Ādibuddha by the Great Passion (Mahārāga) in order to produce name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and so forth for those to be disciplined, [the practitioner] should cause the assembly of Victors such as Akṣobhya to enter his own body by means of the sound of *surata*. Then, through the process of generation (*utpattikrama*), he should bring about the completion of the task by causing the assembly of the elements such as space to emerge once again from his own body and dissolve them properly into Viśvamātā. That person—the Vidya—should be manifested in the nature of the deities whose essence consists of the sense organs such as the eyes and their objects such as forms; having thus emerged from his own body, he should again dissolve it into Viśvamātā in the correct manner.

Then, having emitted [the deities] in that same manner once more, one should cause the Tathāgatas, together with their relics, to enter one’s own body in the form of a maṇḍala-circle. Having caused them to become like liquid moon and emitted them through one’s own vajra, one should meditate upon the maṇḍala of the assembly of gods and goddesses—which has been transformed therein, characterized by the relationship of support and supported, and presided over by Akṣobhya—within the interior of the lotus of one’s own vidyā; then, one should first cause them to enter the body of the Blessed One. Thereafter, in the cardinal and intermediate directions, the four oceans of Buddhas should indeed be emanated: they have nine eyes, fire-like faces, three faces, six arms, and six hands.

There, upon the sun disk of the eastern lotus is Amoghasiddhi, black, with a clockwise sequence of black, red, and white faces; in the south is Ratnasaṃbhava, red in color, with a clockwise sequence of red, white, and black faces; in the north is Amitābha, white, with a clockwise sequence of white, black, and red faces; and in the west is Vairocana, yellow, with a clockwise sequence of yellow, white, and black faces—these are the four [Buddhas] on the sun disks, according to the scriptural authority stating, "The Lord Vajrī is indeed the day."

In the southeast is Tārā, like Amoghasiddhi; in the southwest is Pāṇḍarā, like Ratnasaṃbhava; in the northeast is Māmakī, like Amitābha; and in the northwest is Locanā, like Vairocana. Thus, these four [deities] reside upon moon-maṇḍalas.
Furthermore, based on the scriptural indication that "wisdom is proclaimed as being at night," there are eight jars of nectar in the eight bays between those two deities and goddesses.
Thus, Kṛṣṇā, Raktā, Pītā, Śaśadharadhavalā, Devatā, and Devatī [are situated];

and at the eastern gate, Atibala-krodha is black in color, face, and arms, like Amoghasiddhi; at the southern gate, Jambhaka is red in color, face, and arms, like Ratnasaṃbhava; at the western gate, Stambhaka is yellow in color, face, and arms, like Vairocana; at the north, Mānaka is white in color, face, and arms, like Amitābha; and above, Uṣṇīṣa is dark blue (śyāma) in color, face, and arms, like Akṣobhya.
However, these wrathful deities are in the *ālīḍha* posture and the wrathful goddesses are in the *pratyālīḍha* posture;

thus, in the fourth month, at the time of the arising of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), form—which consists of the four great elements and the nature of the wind, fire, water, and earth constituents—is [manifested], and by that, there is the emission of the aggregates, elements, and wrathful deities. || 19 ||

Then, in the fifth month, at the time of the arising of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), one should emanate Khagarbha and the others: Vaigarbha and the rest are on the wall, situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions; and Sparśavajra and the others are in the eastern, right, left, and rear petals. Likewise, the glorious Viśvabhadra, Vajrapāṇi, Rava, Kuliśa, Dharmadhātu, Jambha, Stambha, Māna, and Atibala—whichever is the gatekeeper, he is in the east. (20)
Regarding the phrase "and Vaigarbha and others on the wall":
here, the nose born of wind is Vaigarbha; in terms of its configuration, it is like Amoghasiddhi and is located on the wall of the eastern enclosure to the right of the eastern gate.
In the intermediate direction of the southeast corner, the touch-vajrā born of wind is Tārā in terms of its configuration.
Thus, on the left of the southern gate, the eye produced from fire is Kṣitigarbha, [who is] like Ratnasaṃbhava in terms of shape;

likewise, in the south-western corner, the tongue produced from the fire element is Pāṇḍarā, [who is] like [Pāṇḍarā]; and on the left of the western gate, the body-faculty produced from earth is Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhī, [who is] like Vairocana.
Thus:
"O Earth-born one! O Essence of the Elements! O Khagarbha!"
O, there is no "abhittoṃ. O, there is no "kāyendriya evaṃ pṛthvī.
O, [the term] "Sa Khams Las" refers to the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*).
In the Vimalaprabhā, Gandhavatrā is in the wind-corner; like Locanā, she is on the right of the northern gate. Jihvā, born from water, is like Lokeśvara Amitābha.
In the northeast is Udakajanyā, who possesses the form of Vajrā and is like Māmakī.

Below is the mind (*manas*) produced from the element of ignorance; Samantabhadra is blue in color, with three faces and six arms, and in terms of color he is like Kālacakra. On the wall of the enclosure to the left of the eastern gate is Śabdavajrā, produced from the element of gnosis (*jñāna*), who in her configuration is like Samantabhadra on the left of the northern gate.
Above, the ear is produced from the space element (*ākāśadhātu*); it is dark blue like Vajrapāṇi-Akṣobhya and is located on the left of the southern gate.
Likewise, Dharmadhātuvajrā, produced from the space element, is located on the left of the western gate; she is identical in form to Vajrapāṇi.

Thus, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) [are formed] in the fifth month. Based on the scriptural authority stating, "In the sixth [month], contact (*sparśa*)," the objects such as contact and so forth [arise].
Thus, regarding the abandonment of the twelve sense-bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), this is the second measure of the Body-Vajra (*kāyavajra*).

Here, the black and white deities and goddesses—situated in the east, north, and above—are to be placed upon the moon-mandala, because the elements of space, wind, and water possess the nature of semen (*śukra*).
Furthermore, according to the statement: "The goddesses situated in the intermediate directions are Prajñā at night on the moon" (*Viṣamapadabhañjikā*, p. 150).

Thus, the deities and goddesses of the south and west, as well as those below, are red and yellow respectively. This is because the solar mandala consists of the elements of fire (*tejas*) and earth (*pṛthivī*), which possess the nature of *rajas*.

Now, regarding the deities situated in the cardinal directions: according to the statement, "The sun is day, and the Lord Vajrī [is night]" (*Viṣayaprajñaptiprakaraṇa*, folio 150), he who faces the Blessed One is the leader (*nāyaka*) in the cardinal directions, while in the intermediate directions, the deity facing the Blessed One is the female leader (*nāyikā*).
The one who turns his face away is the secondary hero (anunāyaka). || 20 ||

In the lap of Prajñā (Wisdom) is Apāya; and in the moon-lotus are the deities and their goddesses. The two are mutually embraced with their own hands, which bear lotuses marked by their respective symbols.

Whichever symbol is on the palm of one's first right hand, that is his mudrā, excluding the lotus. Through Prajñā and Upāya, the wheel has attained supreme bliss, enriched by the lotus and vajra seats. ||21||

Therefore, the consort is on the lap of Wisdom (Prajñā) in the moon-lotus at the corner, specifically in the intermediate directions; likewise, the goddess is on the lap of the male deities (Upāyas) in the solar mandala in the cardinal directions.

The two are mutually embraced, each with their own hands joined like lotuses, marked by their respective symbols to be described hereafter. Whichever symbol is on the palm of the first right hand is his mudrā, excluding the lotus.
The lotus symbol is on the left, while the jewel and sword are common to both the right and left;

thus, from front to back and left to right, below and above, there is the wheel situated in supreme bliss through wisdom and means. It is the rule that it is enriched with the vajra-throne as the leader of the means, and enriched with the lotus-throne as the leader of the host of goddesses. ||21||

Now the insignia are described: for those who are black, there is a sword and a cleaver in the [right] hands, a trident causing fear to the world in the right hand, and a shield and a skull-cup in the left; in the palm of the hand is a white *khaṭvāṅga*, and likewise in the right hands in sequence are an arrow, a vajra, a goad, and a *ḍamaru* drum with a skull; in the left hands are a bow and a noose, all shining and adorned with spotless gems. || 22 ||
(From the *Nāyikāmīmāṃsā*): The great chapter on the accomplishment of the effect through the process of generation (*utpattikrama*) begins with the words "of the black ones" (*kṛṣṇānām*), etc.,
wherein the six symbols [are established] through the purification of the six aggregates of the families (*kulaskandha*).
Among those who are black and born of the Saṃskāra family, in the first right hand is a sword, in the second a dagger, and in the third a trident;

in the left, in the first is a shield, in the second a skull-cup, and in the third, upon the palm of the hand, a white khaṭvāṅga. This applies to Amoghasiddhi, Tārā, Atibala, Khagarbha, and Sparśavajrā. Likewise, for those who are red, in the first right hand is a fire-arrow, in the second a vajrāṅkuśa, and in the third a ḍamaruka with a staff.

"In sequence" means: in the left [hands], in the first is a bow; in the second, a vajra-noose; in the third, a jewel with shimmering, stainless gems. [These are] for Ratnasaṃbhava, Pāṇḍarā, Jambhaka, Kṣitigarbha, and Rasavajra—[the lords] of those born from the family of Feeling (vedanā), who possess nine-pronged [vajras]. ||22||
For the yellow ones, there is a discus, a staff, and a terrifying vajra in the right hands in sequence; the glorious conch, a chain, and a bell with a *sara* are in the left hands.
For the white ones, as bright as the moon, there is a glorious mallet and a spear in the right hands; in the left hands, a white lotus with a hundred petals, a mirror, and a rosary.

Thus, for those born of the *rūpa*-family, there is a wheel in the first right hand, a staff in the second, and a terrifying vajra in the third; in the first left hand a conch, a vajra-chain in the second, and a bell with a handle (*saravā*) in the third. Likewise, [the deities] are yellow: Vairocana, Locanā, Stambhaka, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, and Gandhavajrā.
Likewise, for those born of the Saṃjñākula who are white: in the first right hand is a mallet, in the second a spear, and in the third a trident;
in the first left hand is a white hundred-petalled lotus, in the second a mirror, and in the third a rosary. This is the form of the Vajras of Amitābha, Māmakī, Padmāntaka, and Lokeśvara. || 23 ||

The vajra, the knife, and the axe appear in sequence on the right of those who are green; on the left are the bell and the skull-cup. That which is the treasury of all qualities, the face of Brahmā, should be understood as belonging to those who are blue.
Likewise, for the goddesses, according to the influence of their natural qualities, they are black, red, white, and resembling molten gold—the goddesses of the eastern earth and the other directions.
Likewise, for those born of the *Vijñānakula* who are green: in the first right hand is a garment, in the second a knife, and in the third an animal;

in the first left hand is a bell, in the second a skull-cup, and in the third the head of Brahmā. This is the rule for the emblems of Akṣobhya, Vajradhātvīśvarī, Uṣṇīṣa, Vajrapāṇi, and Dharmadhātuvajrā.
Similarly, for those born of the *Jñānakula* who are blue: [the emblems] of Vajrasattva, Viśvamātā, Sumbharāja, Samantabhadra, and Śabdavajrā are as follows. This is the rule for the emblems.
Alternatively, for Tārā, there is an utpala lotus in place of the khaṭvāṅga, and for Samantabhadra, there is a human head (brahmaśiras) in place of the khaṭvāṅga. ||24||

O King, having excluded the eight goddesses beginning with Dhūmā and the Lord of the Jinas from the lotus, the Śrīcakra sometimes occurs within the center of the womb, consisting of twenty-five [deities],
and here in the south there are six.

Having known the power within one's own mind, this Blessed One should also be meditated upon by yogins; or else, for the sake of initiation, there is a mandala according to the family lineage, which is devoid of an external wheel. ||25||

Excluding the eight goddesses beginning with Dhūmā, the eight vases, and the Dharma-conch and so forth, the Śrī-cakra—the maṇḍala of the mind—sometimes resides within the center of the womb of the Jina-lotus, O Lord of Men, consisting of twenty-five aspects.
Even when seated there, the Blessed One becomes like the glorious *Samāja*;
there is no fault here, because of the absence of a [substantial] lineage (*niranvayatvāt*).
Having understood this, the power within one's own mind should be meditated upon by practitioners as the Blessed One;
or else, for the sake of consecration (*sekā*), there is the mandala, which, according to the family (*kula*), is devoid of the external wheel.

Herein, the innate bliss (*sahajasukha*) is Vajrasattva, the semen that has entered the womb: in the first month it is ignorance (*avidyā*); in the second, formative forces (*saṃskāra*); in the third, consciousness (*vijñāna*); in the fourth, form (*rūpa*); and in the fifth, the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) associated with form.
From the [sense of] touch until the sixth month, according to the family (kula), such is the rule of the Blessed One.
Thus, in the heart, the mind-maṇḍala consists of five sets of five elements.
Then, in the seventh month, at the time of the arising of sensation, the third measure is the emission of the goddesses of the time-channel in the speech-maṇḍala.

In that context, the mandala of speech should be understood as square, extending up to the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*) at the throat. Within that emanation wheel, there are four types of channels: four in the first inner circle, eight in the second, and twelve in the third, by way of being the nature of mind, speech, and body;
thereafter, in the fourth circle, there are sixty-four channels common to the three vajras.
In that regard, the four channels carrying sixty [breaths] at the throat are indeed empty;
thus there are three hundred channels carrying [the breath] for one *muhūrta*, and two are empty.

Likewise, at the *nirmāṇacakra*, the channels of speech carry [the breath] according to the division of eight watches (*prahara*), together with the sixty-four situated in the second circle; this is the rule for exhaling from the throat downward. 25.

Now the emanation of the deities of the speech-mandala is described: On the outside, on the eight petals of the lotus by means of eight groups of eight, there are the Yoginīs beginning with Cāmuṇḍā, who are the deities of the eight directions; they are devoid of moon and sun, hold four hands, and have three eyes.

On the eastern lotus is Cāmuṇḍā; in the southeast is Śyenī (Khagapatigamanā); in the south is Śūkarī; and in the southwest is Ṣaṇmukhī. In the northwest, along with Varuṇa and Vāyu, is Vajrahastā, who has four faces.
Regarding the passage beginning with "bāhya" (external):

here, outside the mind-mandala, in the speech-mandala, and further outside that, upon the eight petals of the lotus by means of groups of eight [deities] in each of the eight directions, there are the yoginīs, Cakrī and the rest, together with the eight direction-yoginīs. They are devoid of the moon and sun, seated upon their respective vehicles, possessing four arms, three eyes, and various faces, with the Vedas in their hands.
There, in the eastern lotus, is Cacihā, who has one face, is black,
and whose movement is like that of a bird in the southeast; she is Vaiṣṇavī.
Śūkarī and Ṣaṇmukhī are red-colored; Aindrī is yellow in the south, the southwest, and the west; and Abdhivaktrā and Brahmāṇī are yellow in the northwest. || 26 ||
O! Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
[In some versions] "and" (*ca*) is absent;
[in others] "five" (*pañca*) is absent.
ka. kha. cha. read "sahitāśca"; tye ca ca.
[is] in the Vāruṇa [recension], while kha. cha. read "varuṇe".

In the chapter [on] the Great Summary of the Accomplishment of the Task by means of the Process of Generation: Raudrī, Lakṣmī, and the others, along with the eight groups of eight Yoginīs, reside upon the petals of the lotus; they embrace the bodies of the Means (upāya) and possess the colors of their respective leaders.

Starting from the east, the first hand holds a curved knife (kartikā), followed by a trident, a discus, a mace, a staff, a sword, and a spear; and in the right lotus-hand of Yama, there is indeed a goad (aṅkuśa).

In the north is Raudrī, white and one-faced; in the northeast is Lakṣmī, also white; thus, just as the principal goddess resides in the pericarp, so too are they [the others] according to their respective colors and forms.
The goddesses situated upon their petals are likewise the Yoginīs, numbering sixty-four and so forth, who reside on the lotus petals and possess the colors corresponding to the [presiding] Nāyikās.
Now, the emblems held in the two right arms of Cāmuṇḍā and the others are described in their proper order, beginning with the words "In the east," and so on.
In this [mandala], in the first hand of Cāmuṇḍā (Cacikā) is a curved knife; in the second, a trident;
for Vaiṣṇavī, a discus and a mace; for Vārāhī, a staff and a sword.
The power of Kaumāryā is the goad. ||27||
In his [right] hands are a vajra, an arrow, a lotus, a trident resembling lightning and fire, a Brahma-staff bound with various jewels, a bell, a *ḍamaru* drum, a lotus, and a rosary;
in the left hands are a conch shell, a *khaṭvāṅga*, a lotus, a conch-trumpet, a chain, a shield, a jewel-noose, and a bow with a straight-sounding, jingling vajra-bell. || 28 ||
With the Aindrī [mudrā] comes the thunderbolt;
with the Bāṇa [mudrā], the Brahmāṇī [mudrās]; with the Raudrī [mudrā], the trident and the hand-drum.
For Mahālakṣmī, there is a lotus and a rosary in her two right hands;
likewise for the goddesses on the petals.
Then, in the two left hands, starting from the east in due order: in the first left hand of Cāmuṇḍā is a skull-cup, and in the second is a khaṭvāṅga staff.
The lotus belongs to Vaiṣṇavī, the conch to Vārāhī, the chain and shield to Kaumārī, and the jewel and noose [to Māheśvarī].
With the [mantra] addressed to Indra, the bell and the bow. || 28 ||

[There are] a water-pot, a mendicant’s bowl, a skull-topped staff, and likewise a serpent, as well as a jewel born of water; these belong to the sixty-four Yoginīs who, with weapons in their hands, reside upon the petals of the lotus of the earth.
Likewise, Bhīmogrā, Kāladaṃṣṭrā, Jvaladanalamukhā, Vāyuvegā, Pracaṇḍā, Raudrākṣī, and Sthūlanāsā [reside] upon the petals of the lotus of the earth in their own respective directions of Carcikā.
The water-pot (kuṇḍikā) belongs to Brahmāṇī, the skull-topped staff and serpent to Raudrī,
and the lotus and jewel to Mahālakṣmī.
Thus, there are eight groups of eight yoginīs on the petals of the lotus of the earth, with weapons in their hands just like that;
the rule is that they are exactly as the principal goddesses (nāyikās) are. In the Vimalaprabhā [Sādhanā-paṭala], their names are now given:

In that regard, the goddesses beginning with Cāmuṇḍā (Carcikā) are to be understood as being on the lotus petals starting from the east and proceeding clockwise; among them, Bhīmā is on the first petal, and likewise Ugrā, Kālavaktrā, Jvaladanalamukhā, Vāyuvegā, Pracaṇḍā, Raudrākṣī, and Sthūlanāsā are on the second and subsequent petals, located in their respective directions upon the eight petals of the lotus of Cāmuṇḍā. || 29 ||
Śrī, Māyā, Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Suparamavijayā, Śrījayā, Śrījayantī, and Śrīcakrī as the eighth—these indeed reside on the eight petals of the lotus in the Vaiṣṇava directions.
Kaṅkālī, Kālarātrī, Prakupitavadanā, Kālajihvā, Karālī, Kālī, Ghorā, and Virūpā—these are the petal-deities on the petals of the lotus, along with Śūkarī. (30)

On the first petal and so forth of the Vaiṣṇavī lotus, there are Śrī, Māyā, Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Vijayā, Śrījayā, Śrījayantī, and Śrīcakrī as the eighth; these reside on the eight petals of the lotus in the direction of Vaiṣṇavī, starting from the southeast (Agni).

Then, on the first petal and so forth of the Vārāhī lotus, there are Kaṅkālī, Kālarātrī, Prakupitavadanā, Kālajihvā, Karālī, Kālī, Ghorā, and Virūpā; these are the petal-deities of the sow (Śūkarī) on the eight petals in the southern direction. ||30||

O King, where the heroine is Padmānaṅgā, Kumārī, Mṛgapatigamanā, Ratnamālā, Sunetrā, Klīnā, Bhadrābjapatre, Varaśikhigamanā, Vajrābhā, Vajragātrā, Varakanakavatī, Vaṃśī, Citralekhā, Rambhā, Ahalyā, Sutārā, Kamala, Vasudale, and Vajrahastādhidevā; || 31 ||

Likewise, O King, on the eastern petal and the others of Kaumāryā’s lotus are Padmā, Anaṅgā, Kumārī, Mṛgapatigamanā, Ratnamālā, Sunetrā, Klīnā, and Bhadrā; and where the heroine Varashikhigamanā is on the western petal of the lotus, so too, on the eastern petal and the others of Aindrī’s lotus—presided over by Vajrahasta in the west—are Vajrābhā, Vajragātrā, Kanakavatī, Urvaśī, Citralekhā, Rambhā, Ahalyā, and Sutārā. || 31 ||

Sāvitrī, Padmanetrā, Jalajavatī, Buddhi, Vāgīśvarī, the two Gāyatrīs, Vidyut, Smṛti, Kamalā, Vedavaktrā, Adhidevī, Gaurī, Gaṅgā, Nityā, Suparā, Turitā, Totalā, Lakṣmaṇā, Piṅgā, and Kṛṣṇā—these eight are the presiding goddesses upon the petals of the lotus-wealth [of the heart], where Raudrī is the central mistress. (32)

Then, in the Brahmāṇī [mandala], starting from the eastern petal, are Sāvitrī, Padmanetrā, Jalajavatī, Buddhi, Vāgīśvarī, Gāyatrī, Vidyut, and Smṛti; likewise, in the lotus of the eight petals (aṣṭadala), which has the Vedas as its face and the presiding deity Vāyu in the northwest, there are the eight heroines of the Raudrī [mandala] starting from the eastern petal: Gaurī, Gaṅgā, Nityā, Turitā, Totalā, Lakṣmaṇā, Piṅgalā, and Kṛṣṇā. Thus, the heroines of the Raudrī [mandala] are in the north within the eight-petaled lotus. || 32 ||
Chapter [X], Verses 29–35:

The Great Summary on the Accomplishment of the Task through the Stage of Generation (utpattikrama). The venerable Śvetā, Candralekhā, Śaśadharavadanā, Haṃsavarṇā, Dhṛti, Padmeśā, Tāranetrā, Vimalaśaśadharā, and Īśapadma—these are the goddesses with their respective emblems.
Outside of them, upon the solar lotus, are Danuka, Cala, Yama, Pāvaka, Ṣaṇmukha, Yakṣa, Śakra, Abdhivaktra, Paśupati, Udadhi, Śrīgaṇendra, and Viṣṇu.

Then, starting from the eastern petal of Lakṣmī, there are the sixty-four yoginīs: Śrīśvetā, Candralekhā, Śaśadharavadanā, Haṃsavarṇā, Dhṛti, Padmeśā, Tāranetrā, and Vimalaśaśadharā, each with their respective emblems. These are the leaders in the Vāṅmaṇḍala upon the petals of the lotuses of Ciccikā and the others. Thus, the accomplishment of the Sarvakāyavajra is to be understood as occurring within the limb of sensation and also the limb of craving; it should be known that this occurs during the accomplishment of the body, from the forehead down to the secret lotus. Therein, those which are the twelve [petals] on the hands and feet are the twelve joints and lotuses.
In the wheel of action (karmacakra) and the wheel of ritual activity (kriyācakra),
one should emit twenty-eight petals as the forms of the deities of the channels during the eighth month;
outside of that is the sun-lotus (sūryapadma).

On the outer body-maṇḍala of that [palace], within the twelve lotuses beginning from the right side of the eastern gate on the wall of the enclosure, Nairṛtya and the others are described in their respective order, like Khagarbha and the rest:
Danuka is Nairṛtya at the right of the eastern gate, and Acala is Vāyu in the southeast (Āgneyī).
Yama is on the left of the southern gate,
Pāvaka on the right, and Ṣaṇmukha in the southwest.
On the left of the western gate is Yakṣa,
on the right is Śakra,
and in the northwest is Brahmā.
To the left of the northern gate is Rudra,
to the right is Samudra, and in the northeast is Gaṇapati.
On the eastern side is Viṣṇu; thus all [the deities] are four-armed. || 33 ||

In the [right] hands there appear a sword, a knife, the king of trees (the *kalpavṛkṣa*), the flower of the celestial tree, a staff-sword, a spear-staff, a spear, a lance, a jewel, a mace, a thunderbolt, a fire-arrow, a needle, a rosary, a trident-arrow, a noose, a gem, an axe, and a thunderbolt; and in the left hand there appears a discus-staff. //34//
The symbols for these twelve [deities] appear respectively on their two left hands:
for Nairṛtya, a sword in the first and a knife in the second;
for Vāyu, the lord of trees, the *kalpavṛkṣa*, in the first and the *pārijātaka* flower in the second.
In the first [hand] of Yama is a staff, in the second a sword;
in the first of Vaiśvānara is a spear, in the second a staff;
in the first of Ṣaṇmukha is a spear, in the second a lance.
In the first [hand] of Dhanada is a jewel-gem; in the second, a mace.
In the first [hand] of Indra is a thunderbolt; in the second, a fire-arrow.
In the first [hand] of Brahmā is a needle; in the second, a rosary.

In the first [hand] of Rudra is a trident; in the second, an arrow. In the first [hand] of Varuṇa is a noose; in the second, a jewel. In the first [hand] of Vināyaka is a battle-axe; in the second, a thunderbolt.
In the first [wheel] of Viṣṇu is the discus; in the second is the movement.
O Lord of Men, in the left hands, in sequence, there is a shield, a skull-cup, a dark-blue jewel, a blue lotus, a chain, a noose, a lotus, and a water-pot;
likewise, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, there is a mirror, a *nakula* flower, a lotus, a vajra-bell, a bow, a lotus, a water-pot, a double bow, and a snake-noose, as well as a jewel. (35)
Then, in the left [hands]: in the first hand of Nairṛti is a shield, in the second a skull-cup;
in the first of Vāyu is a sapphire, in the second a blue lotus;
in the first of Yama is a chain, in the second a noose.
In the first [hand] of Agni is a lotus; in the second, a water-pot. In the first [hand] of Kārttikeya is a jewel; in the second, a mirror.
In the first [hand] of the Yakṣa is a mongoose; in the second, a lotus.
In the first [hand] of Indra is a bell, in the second a bow;
in the first of Brahmā is a lotus, in the second a water-pot;
in the first of Rudra is a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) accompanied by a serpent, in the second a bow.
In the first [section] of the ocean is the serpent-noose; in the second is the moonstone jewel. || 35 ||
The noose, the jewel, and the lotus belong to the Enemy of Danu (Viṣṇu), as does the conch Pāñcajanya.
On the petals of the lotus are the lunar days beginning with Caitra, numbering eight and ten; in the pericarp are all the [remaining] days, numbering two, zero, six, and three.

These should be known as the supreme digits of the moon arising from the conjunction of the years. At the gates are the goddesses mounted on chariots, bearing swords and vajras, holding goads and arrows in their hands.
For Vināyaka, there is a noose in the first [hand] and a jewel in the second; for Vāsudeva, there is a lotus in the first and the Pāñcajanya conch in the second—
thus are the emblems of all [the deities] in their respective order upon the two left hands.

In the twenty-eight petals of those [lotuses] located at the pericarp-sites of Nairṛti and the others, which are arranged in three concentric circles with a clockwise rotation— four petals in the first circle, eight in the second, and sixteen in the third— the lunar dates of the months beginning with Caitra,
including the full moon and new moon days of both the bright and dark fortnights, reside as the presiding deities within the pericarps.

In this manner, the lunar days (tithis) of Caitra are on the lotus petal of Nairṛtya; those of Vaiśākha, of Vāyu; those of Jyeṣṭha, of Pāvaka; those of Āṣāḍha, of Ṣaṇmukha; those of Śrāvaṇa, of Samudra; those of Bhādra, of Vināyaka; those of Āśvina, of Indra; those of Kārttika, of Brahmā; those of Mārgaśīrṣa, of Hara; those of Pauṣa, of Yakṣa; those of Māgha, of Viṣṇu; and those of Phālguna, of Yama.
Likewise, the goddesses possess the same colors, weapons, and postures as their respective deities.

In this way, Caitra and the other months are to be known as the sixty-three supreme lunar digits (kalās) of the moon: eight, two, and fifteen on the lotus petals; two and zero in the pericarp; and all the zeros of the world [in the center], totaling three hundred and sixty. These are established through their conjunction with the year.
The rule is that by means of the seed-syllable to be mentioned later, which serves as the initial element, their names end in "Vajra."

Now, through the purification of the radiation from the hands, feet, soles, uṣṇīṣa, anus, and channels, the goddesses Mārīcī and the others stand upon chariots at the gates; they have one face and four arms.

Because they have gone to the stations of others, they possess the quality of being "followers" (anunāyikā), while Nīladaṇḍa and the others possess the quality of being "leaders" (nāyaka) by virtue of their own original positions.
Therefore, the family of these [goddesses] is the East and so forth, while Vajraśṛṅkhalā and the others move to the positions facing them.

By virtue of that family lineage, on the first left arm of Śṛṅkhalā there is a sword, and on the second a vajra; this is by virtue of the Amoghasiddhi family, and likewise by virtue of the Ratna family.
In the first hand of Bhṛkuṭī there is an arrow, and in the second, "with a goad," there is a goad. || 36 ||
In the chapter [on the] Great Summary of the Accomplishment of the Task through the Stage of Generation:

By the power of the qualities of nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*), she holds a discus and a staff in her hands; she holds a mallet and a spear; indeed, she holds a glorious knife and a vajra; she holds an axe and a trident in her right hands, while in her left hands she holds a shield and a sword by the power of the qualities of nature; she holds a noose and a bow; likewise, she holds a glorious conch, a jewel, a lotus, the moon, and a mirror in her hands.
By the power of the Vairocana family, Mārīcī has a wheel in her right hand and a staff in the second;

by the power of the Padma family and the qualities of nature, Cundā has a mallet in her first hand and a spear in the second; and by the power of the Jñāna family, Atinīlā has a knife in her first hand and a vajra in the second.
Due to the influence of the space family (*ākāśakula*), Raudrākṣī holds a scimitar in her first [left] hand and a trident in the second;
likewise, in her left hands, Bhṛkuṭī holds a chain and a shield, and in her first [right] hand a bow, and in the second a noose.
The conch is the jewel of Mārīcī, and the lotus mirror is that of Cundā. ||37||
Śrīghaṇṭā should indeed be known as having a conch and a snake in her hands, while Mārīcī and the others have one face and four lotus-like hands; they are to be understood in sequence.

Below the pillars are the eight nāgas, who hold jars and vajras, or lotuses and rubies in their hands; in the mandala starting from the northwest (Vāyu), Padma, Karkoṭaka, and the others likewise have four lotus-like hands.
The skull of Atinīlā is the bell; that of Raudrākṣī is the snake-noose and the *khaṭvāṅga*.
This is the rule for Nīladaṇḍa, Ṭakkirāja, Mahābala, and Acala, who are stationed at the eastern, southern, western, and northern gates respectively.

Then, in the ninth month, during the stage of grasping (*upādāna*) within the wheel of action (*kriyācakra*), one should emanate the ten Nāgas and the ten Pracaṇḍās through the purification of the twenty finger-breadth channels.
On the exterior body-maṇḍala, at the base of the eight pillars of the four gateways, there are eight nāgas; Jayā and Vijayā are below and above [respectively], and all have four arms,
with an amṛta-pitcher in the first right hand and a vajra in the second.

In the left [hands], in the first is a lotus, in the second a jewel; therefore, those with a water-pot and a vajra in their hands, or with a lotus and a ruby in their hands, are in the wind and water mandalas respectively— thus,
Padma and Karkoṭaka are in the two wind mandalas in the east.
In the south, on the fire-mandala, are Vāsuki and Śaṅkhapāla;
in the west, on the earth-mandala, are Takṣaka and Mahāpadma; and in the north, on the water-mandala, are Ananta and Kulika.
"Victory in space and triumph in knowledge"—thus are the ten toes of the feet. || 38 ||

Śvānāsyā with a dog’s face, Śūkarāsyā with a sow’s face, Jambukāsyā with a jackal’s face, and Vyāghrāsyā with a tiger’s face stand in the cardinal directions; situated in the northern quarter, Citibhuvanagatā holds a knife and a shell in her hands;

Kākāsyā with a crow’s face, Gṛdhravaktrā with a vulture’s face, Khagapativadanā with a garuḍa’s face, and Ulūkavaktrā with an owl’s face are in the intermediate corners; and Vajrākṣī, who is intensely blue, is in the sky when it has become dark, at the end of the world where all beings originate and remain motionless. (39)
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the purification of the fingers of the hands: Śvānāsyā is in the east,
Śūkarāsyā in the south, and Jambukāsyā in the west.
In the north, in the great cremation ground situated between the circles of wind and fire, upon a tiger-skin seat, she has two arms, holds a curved knife and a scalpel in her hands, and has one face.
Thus, Kākāsyā is in the southeast fire [direction], Gṛdhrāsyā in the southwest, Garuḍāsyā in the northwest, Ulūkāsyā in the northeast, Vajrākṣī in the underworld, and Nīlā in the sky;
all of these have skull-cups and flaying knives in their hands, are naked, adorned with the five mudrās, and wear hanging garlands of severed heads.

Thus, through the purification of body hair and head hair, [the hair] extends from the end of the immobile source of beings (bhūtayoni), which consists of three and a half crores, to the edge of the wind-circle, and finally to the skin as the hair.
The mantra-practitioner should thus emit [the deities] externally; in this way, within the limit of nine months, the accomplishment of the assembly of body-deities is achieved. ||39||

Now, the lotus-seats of Cāmuṇḍā and the others are described: a red corpse, the king of birds (eagle), a buffalo, a peacock, an elephant, a swan, a cow, and a five-faced one (lion) arise in sequence as the lotus-seats for Cāmuṇḍā and the rest in the cardinal and intermediate directions.

And likewise for the [other] goddesses, starting with Detyā: for the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) and Agni, for Varuṇa and Vāyu, for Gaṇeśa, for Mātaṅgeśa, for Meṣa, Makara, Mṛga, and Mūṣaka, they arise in sequence. (40)

With the words "the red preta" and so forth, here in the east, Cāmuṇḍā has a seat upon a great red preta; on the pericarp of the lotus are the goddesses beginning with Cāmuṇḍā, and on the eight petals likewise: for Vaiṣṇavī, Garuḍa; for Vārāhī, a buffalo; for Kaumārī, a peacock; for Aindrī, an elephant; for Brahmāṇī, a swan; for Raudrī, a bull; and for Mahālakṣmī, a lion—these are the seats in sequence upon the lotus in the cardinal and intermediate directions.

And because of the statement "and likewise for the Daityas and others," there is a fixed rule for the south-western [direction] and those following: a red *preta* is the seat of Viṣṇu, his vehicle Garuḍa; a buffalo is that of Yama; a peacock is that of Kumāra; an elephant is that of Indra; a swan is that of Brahmā; and a bull is that of Rudra. Similarly, for the five [deities] beginning with Dhanapati (Kubera) and Śikhin (Agni), and for the Ocean and Vāyu, as well as for Gaṇeśa, [the vehicles are assigned] according to their respective order.
The elephant belongs to Dhanapati, the ram to Agni, the crocodile to the Ocean, the deer to Vāyu, and the rat to Gaṇapati. || 40 ||

Bheruṇḍa has the face of a jackal, blue eyes, and a rear-facing mouth; Khaḍgī, Ṛkṣa, and Siṃha arise in the corners starting from the direction of Kākavaktra. Camarī has the face of a dog and others in the cardinal directions.
The eight-legged Vajrākṣī is on the ground, while Nīlāratha is in the sky. Anila is cruel, five-colored, a bird with a massive body and three eyes.
Likewise, on the surface of the wheel of Kākāsyā is Bheruṇḍa; on that of Gṛdhrāsyā, Kruñca; on that of Garuḍāsyā, Nīlākṣa; and on that of Ulūkāsyā, Vāgvali—thus in the corners.

Likewise, in the cardinal directions, on the surface of the wheel of Śvānāsyā is Khaḍgī; on that of Śūkarāsyā, Ṛkṣa; on that of Jambukāsyā, Siṃha; and on that of Vyāghrāsyā, Camara—according to the *Śvānavaktrādi-paṭala*. [In the verse concerning] the Great Chapter on the Accomplishment of the Task through the Process of Generation (*utpattikrama*), in the cardinal directions, on the surface of the wheel of Vajrākṣī is Aṣṭapāda, mounted upon a subterranean chariot (*pātālaratha*).
In the sky, there is the bird Nīlāratha, whose wind is five-colored and accompanied by Śakra; and there is the one with three eyes, whose body is vast. || 41 ||

The boars of Mārīcī, the horses, elephants, and lions of Cundā—these seven are upon her chariots. Śṛṅkhalā [is in the north], while in the east are Gandhā and Mālā; Dhūpā and Dīpā are situated toward Yama and Varuṇa. Lāsyā, Hāsyā, Vādyā, and Nṛtyā are on the ground of Kubera, and Gītā and Kāmā are in the sky.
Thus, on Mārīcī’s chariot there are seven boars at the eastern gate;
on Cundā’s chariot at the south, seven horses;
and on Śṛṅkhalā’s chariot at the west, seven elephants.
In the north, on the chariot of Bhṛkuṭī, there are seven lions;

likewise, from that [state], by way of the nature of the heart-channel, the worship goddesses should be emitted into the mind-maṇḍala, upon the right and left balconies of the four gates: Gandhā and Mālā.
In the southeast are Dhūpā and Dīpā;
in the west are Lāsyā and Hāsyā; in the north are Vādyā and Nṛtyā.
In the sky are the songs of desire;
below, by the nature of the channels of feces and urine, they are the offerings of the fruit of immortality. || 42 ||

In the womb [of the maṇḍala], on the pedestal, beneath the archway in the expanse of the sky, one should employ [the deities]; on the fillet, the supporting goddesses together with the family of hoods; on the pedestal, those who receive [the offerings].

O King, there is the desire for hatred, as well as the desire for paralyzing (stobhana) and nourishing (pauṣṭika); likewise, the desire for immobilizing (stambhana) through the purification of Tārā-devī and others; and the desire for killing and causing upheaval, which gives birth to the three worlds. ||43||

Whichever goddesses from the sky-realm are present in the dust-mandala, they should be visualized beneath the eastern and western archways; however, in the meditative visualization (*bhāvanā*), the guardians of the directions and others are to be placed exactly as previously described in their respective locations.
Furthermore, it is a fixed rule that Samantabhadra and the other four are to be at the left side of the door.
Thus, just as there are the Pūjā goddesses, so too are there infinite Dhāriṇīs upon the frieze and the altar.
Likewise, on the outer body-maṇḍala, the Pratīcchās together with the serpent family are located on the altar;
therefore, on the speech-maṇḍala, the Icchās are on the altar.

In that regard, the desire for enmity in the east is born from Tārā; the desire for paralyzing (stobhana) in the south is born from Pāṇḍaravāsī; the desire for nourishment (pauṣṭika) in the north is born from Māmakī; and the desire for immobilizing (stambhana) in the west is born from Locanā. Thus, through the purification of the goddess Tārā, the desire for killing is born from Vajradhātvīśvarī, the mother of the three worlds; and the desire for creation is born from Viśvamātṛ. || 43 ||

O Lord of Men, there arises a desire for musical instruments, a desire for ornaments, and thirdly, a desire for food; a desire for fragrance, a desire for garments, and the sixth is the manifest and fixed desire for sexual union.

There is a desire to scratch the body, a desire to discharge phlegm from the mouth, a desire for filth on the limbs, a desire for dancing, a desire for a seat, a desire for water, a desire for lying down, and a desire for bathing and immersion. (44)

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is stated: "Thus, the desire for musical instruments is produced by sound; the desire for ornaments is produced by form; the desire for food is produced by taste; the desire for fragrance is produced by smell; the desire for clothing is produced by touch; and the desire for sexual union is produced by the *dharmadhātu*. These are located on the eastern and other altars. According to the divisions of their respective families, the desire to scratch the body is produced by Cāmuṇḍā;
the desire to discharge phlegm from the mouth is produced by Vaiṣṇavī."
The desire for limbs is born from Vārāhī;
the desire for dancing is born from Kaumārī;
the desire for a seat is born from Raudrī.
The desire to float in water is produced by Brahmāṇī; the desire to immerse oneself in sleep is produced by Aindrī;
and the desire for sovereignty is produced by Lakṣmī. || 44 ||

On this earth, there are also the eight rites beginning with Cāmuṇḍā; indeed, for those born of anger, there is the desire for torment and imprisonment through mild words, as well as the desire for withering, eradication, and the extraction of urine. ||45||

O King, when there is the desire to attract through touch, to bind, to pin down, or to run, as well as the desire to crush all limbs, these are the eight activities of Cāmuṇḍā and the others, which are the manifest and fixed desires of those born of Wrath on the surface of the earth.
Among these, the desire for torment arises from Atinīlā;
the desire to bind arises from Stambhanī.
The desire for gentle speech arises from Māninī;
the desire for withering arises from Jambhanī;
the desire for eradication arises from Atibalā.
Likewise, the desire for non-contact is produced by Vajraśṛṅkhalā;
the desire for attraction is produced by Bhṛkuṭī;
and the desire for binding is produced by Cundā.
The desire to pierge is produced by Mārīcī;
the desire to run is produced by Raudrākṣī.
Likewise are the desires of those born in the lineage of Danu.
The desire to agitate all limbs is produced by the dog-faced [deity];
the desire to discharge urine is produced by the boar-faced [deity]. || 45 ||

Indeed, in the fifth [segment], characterized by much strife and leftover food, there is the desire to deceive sentient beings; in the snake-bond, there is the desire for battle; and in the family of Danu, there is the desire to revile children.

Furthermore, there are thirty-seven pledges (pratīcchā); moreover, within the mandala on the outer cloth, whatever task is to be performed for sentient beings is here the task of the Yoginīs at every daily occasion. 46.
The desire to deceive sentient beings is born from the jackal-mouth; the desire for much quarreling is born from the tiger-mouth; the desire to consume leftovers is born from the crow-mouth.
The *gṛdhrāsyājanyā* is characterized by a desire for battle; the *garuḍāsyājanyā* by a desire to bind snakes;
and the *ulūkāsyājanyā* by a desire to revile children.
The thirty-seven *icchās* (desires) are located in the *vāṅmaṇḍala* (speech mandala) according to the divisions of their respective families in their own directions.

Likewise, there are thirty-seven *pratīcchās* (counter-desires); *pratīcchā* is the turning back of the *icchās*. This is called the "Great Chapter on the Accomplishment of the Task" (*kāryaniṣpattimahoddeśa*) by way of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*). These [deities] are located on the altar of the *kāyamaṇḍala* (body mandala) according to the power of their respective families in their own directions; this is the rule everywhere.

Thus, whatever other external activity there may be within the Brahma-maṇḍala, performed according to one's desire at the time of each day, all that is the activity of the Yoginīs here; such is the rule, by virtue of the [five] elements. || 46 ||

Now, the eternal and the non-eternal are explained: Thus, the entire three worlds of the Vajrī are said to have the form of a maṇḍala; externally, within the body, and in the supreme [reality], they abide as the emanation and dissolution of all things.

Within that, the Space-Vajra (khavajra) is eternal and does not undergo impermanence throughout the three types of existence; yet the multitude of elements is not eternal, O Lord of Men, for the multitude of elements is just like a magician’s illusion (śakrajāla). ||47||
With the words "In this way," and so forth:

thus, by means of the seven months and so on, the entire three worlds of the external Vajrī—the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth—are said to be in the form of a mandala for the sake of stabilizing the minds of ordinary people.

Here, in the external world-system (*lokadhātu*), within the body (*adhyātma*), and in the supreme imagined mandala, there is radiation (*spharaṇa*) and reabsorption (*nidhanatā*); these two, radiation and reabsorption, are established as the nature of all things.
In this context, the "substance" (*vastu*) refers to the material atoms (*paramāṇudravya*), namely the four elements: earth, water, fire, and air.
The space element (*ākāśadhātu*) is the moon, the anusvāra, semen, or likewise the menstrual blood; it is also the two dots (*bindudvaya*) and the sun.
Rāhu is the consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*).

Thus, the Great Being, the preeminent person, consists of the six elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*). Of that class of entities (*vastujāti*), there is arising, which is expansion, and destruction, which is dissolution; these two are established as the nature of all beings. Thus, the class of earth consists of stationary things such as trees; the class of water consists of those born from moisture; the class of fire consists of those born from a womb; the class of wind consists of those born from an egg; the class of the moon consists of *nāgas* and *asuras*; and the class of the sun consists of spirits and deities.
The Rāhujāti are formless; the Kālāgnijāti are hell-beings.
Thus, the eightfold birth is the birth of entities possessing form;
therein resides the eternal Khavaṃtra.
Here, "kha" refers to the ninth element, the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*). It is devoid of substantial atoms (*paramāṇudravya*) and is indivisible.
Because it is indivisible and impenetrable, the space-vajra—the space-element—is eternal due to the absence of substantiality.
That is the space-element (ākāśadhātu);
because it is all-pervading,
it does not undergo impermanence throughout the three realms of existence.
O King, the aforementioned collection of elements is not eternal; it is just like a magician’s illusion, according to the principle that "what is seen perishes. || 47 ||

Having perceived both the eternal and the non-eternal, that [practice] must indeed be taught as a means for the purification of the minds of those of dull intellect; for no one here is established as the goal within the heart.

Whatever is to be accomplished is the practitioner himself—this entire process of accomplishment belongs to the Wielder of the Thunderbolt (Vajrin). Therefore, O King, one should make one's own mind free from defilement the Lord of the Mandala.
In the mandala;
on the altar;
there is none.
In that which is imagined,
there is no "gods."
And,
O Bhagavan, it is of eight kinds.
There is not.
There is not. Khavajra.
O,
there is no relic of the Blessed One.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*: "Thus, having seen and analyzed the eternal great emptiness, or the impermanent aggregation and disintegration of atoms—having seen both of these, there would be no means for attaining Buddhahood.
Nevertheless, O Sucandra, King of Men, you must explain this means for the sake of introducing the dull-witted and the ignorant, and as a cause for the purification of the mind;
however, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), not a single entity, whether eternal or impermanent, is established here within the heart."
Therefore, there is this rule: that which is to be accomplished for the sake of Buddhahood is the practitioner himself.
In this context, whatever conceptualization serves as a means is delusion.
O King, all such means belong to the Vajrī.
One should make one's own mind free from defilement and devoid of conceptual construction the Lord of the Mandala; such is the rule. || 48 ||

Now the support and the supported are described: O Lord of Men, the mind here becomes Śrī Heruka; the body-vajra is the mandala, and the speech-vajra is the deities born from the lineages of the *ali* and *kali*.

Above the moon and sun are the bulb (*kanda*), the stalk (*nāla*), the letter *a*, as well as the petals and the filaments, which are the letter *u*; in the center is the glorious pericarp (*kaṇikā*), and the moon and sun situated on the two paths are the letter *ma*. (49)
By the words beginning with "Śrī," etc.:
in the mandala of body, speech, and mind, Śrīvajrī is the leader and becomes Cittavajra; O Lord of Men!
the mandala is Kāyavajra, characterized by body, speech, and mind.
The Vāgvajra of the deities born from the *mala* and *kali* families is the wheel atop the moon and sun;
likewise, in the mandalas of speech and body as well, there is the assembly of deities as Vāgvajra.

Thus, the threefold mind is in the form of the body and in the form of the mandala, while the body is threefold and speech is also threefold by means of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*); this is the rule everywhere.
In this context, the bulb and the stalk of the lotuses arise from the syllable *a*; the petals and filaments are produced from the syllable *u*;
in the center, the pericarp is the moon-seat from the syllable *m*, or the sun-seat from the syllable *ra*.
Thus, the syllable *oṃ* is the *praṇava*.
The heart is called the lotus.
It is a rule that for those born from a womb, the formation of the body of the first deity occurs here in this birth.

Having thus meditated upon the Blessed One Kālacakra, who consists of the five wisdoms and is crowned with Vajrasattva, as being of the nature of the utterly pure *dharmadhātu*, one should then visualize all sentient beings dwelling in the six realms of existence drawn into that very maṇḍala. Then, having caused the Tathāgatas, Vairocana and the others, along with their relics, to enter one’s own heart, they become liquefied as the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*); one should then emit them by means of one’s own secret vajra and meditate that all those sentient beings are consecrated by that *bodhicitta*.

Then, one should visualize all those sentient beings touched by the rays of the *bodhicitta* as having three faces, various faces, and various colors, possessing the forms of deities, consisting of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*), and filled with the bliss of supreme joy. Then, one should suddenly perceive their own bodies as having become the nature of the mandala circle,
wherein are the seed-syllables of the mantras, joined with various consonants and accompanied by vowels.
In this context, the letter *kṣa* is the aggregate of all consonants;
by that indicator, whatever is the first name [of a mantra], its consonant is used to perform all of that.
Here, *kṣa* and *kṣi* are added.
The vowels and consonants do not exist apart from the letter *ga*.
Enlightenment is wisdom; it has various gateways and is not devoid of garments,
being filled with happiness.
The great chapter on the accomplishment of the task through the generation stage of one's own assembly: *Śr̥ kṣu la* refers to the five Tathāgatas, beginning with Vajrasattva.
Likewise, *kṣā*, *kṣo*, *kṣa*, *kṣū*, and *la* are the five elements beginning with space (*ākāśa*).
Similarly, *kṣa*, *kṣa*, *kṣa*, *kṣa*, *kṣa*, and *kṣaṃ* are the six Bodhisattvas beginning with the ear.
Likewise, *kṣā*, *kṣe*, *kṣār*, *kṣau*, *kṣāl*, and *kṣāḥ* are the six objects (*viṣaya*).
*Lṛ, kṣya, kṣa, va, la* are the five organs of action (*karmendriya*).
Here, *kṣ*, *kṣyā*, *kṣā*, *kṣvā*, *kṣlā* are the five objects of the organs of action.
Thus [are established] the five aggregates (*skandha*), the five elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the five organs of action, and the five objects of the organs of action.

In this way, one should visualize all sentient beings as having the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*dvātriṃśanmahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*) and appearing in the form of a mandala circle, either instantaneously or, in detail, by generating each individual deity within the secret place of the Goddess from their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*) and then emitting them. Regarding these, the Blessed One said in the Root Tantra: "Those sentient beings in the Buddha-fields who [are sustained] by the nectar of the pledge of the three bodies..."
All those Tathāgatas born there were touched by the splendor of the vajra.
The Perfect Buddhas, who have attained the three vajra-knowledges, have appeared here;
having meditated upon them, one should then cause them to enter their respective fields.
Thus,
the rule is that the bestowing of consecration is for the sake of compassion toward sentient beings.
Now, regarding the tenth limb of existence, the "emission" (*prasṛti*) is described for the purpose of relinquishing the vital breath and generating the speech-vajra.

Externally as well, there is the accomplishment of the second measure: there is the syllable *ho* at the navel and also at the crown (*uṣṇīṣa*). Between these two, interlaced, is the Body-Vajra *oṃ* at the forehead, the Speech-Vajra *āḥ* at the throat, and the Mind-Vajra *hūṃ* at the heart—thus the three syllables characterized by body, speech, and mind. This is the source of the three channels. At the navel is the syllable *ho*, held by the rays of gnosis; within the lotus of equal bliss, the Body-Speech-Mind Vajra is melted by the passion of wisdom (*prajñārāga*). That Lord Vajrin is like the moon.

By virtue of the word "and" (*cakāra*), having observed together with wisdom (*prajñā*), the goddesses—whose natures are loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—sing a song for the sake of the internal flow of the five maṇḍalas, for the sake of enjoying all external objects, for the sake of the manifestation of the deities externally, and for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of the entire world; these are Tārā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, and Locanā.

"O Blessed One, you who benefit all sentient beings, protect us, O Vajra-holder, Teacher of the gods and men! Thus Tārā, the destroyer of desire, urges on the Mind-Vajra in the form of loving-kindness (*maitrī*); Māmakī, in the form of compassion (*karuṇā*), [urges on] the Body-Vajra; Pāṇḍarā, in the form of sympathetic joy (*muditā*), [urges on] the Speech-Vajra; and Locanā, in the form of equanimity (*upekṣā*), urges on the Wisdom-Vajra.

Thus, the Blessed One, whose nature consists of mind, body, speech, and gnosis, having heard their song, that Vajrin beheld the entire triple world characterized by the form of desire, which is like a magical illusion (*indrajāla*). There, within the lunar fluid, he saw a blue-colored *hūṃ* syllable; from that, a vajra was produced, radiant and pure-handed. By means of that, he expanded himself as the perfected [deity]. The yogin, the Blessed One, is adorned with vajras, wears the crown of the Lord of Jinas, and is embraced by Prajñā as before.
Furthermore, [he is] composed of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya-ātmaka*), and likewise—thus [it is said]—the syllable *kṣū*.
And so it is, O venerable one. Likewise, kṣlā.
O friend, there is no "Indrajāla" by means of the seed-syllable *kṣā*;
there is no "deity."
O, birth (prasūti);
O, origination (utpattiḥ) in Kanakā; the effect (kārya).
O, he objects: "There is no form (rūpa) in the Formless (ārūpya) realm by way of physical shape (mūrti)."

In the *Sarvālaṅkāravimalaprabhā*, it is stated that one should perform the emanation of the maṇḍala through the phenomena of mind, body, and speech, beginning from the awakening and crying of the newborn infant;
for here, in this Mantra system, the formation of the infant’s body occurs over nine months according to the process of birth from a womb.
The first limb of service (*sevāṅga*) here is the accomplishment of the task characterized by the fivefold awakening of the deities.

For the sake of the divine pride (*devatāhaṅkāra*), the practitioner should utter the mantra-word: *oṃ suviśuddhadharmadhātusvabhāvo ’ham* ("I am of the nature of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena"). Then, for the sake of the arising of speech, the yogi should cultivate the second limb of service.

"Within the womb of that which begins and ends with *hoḥ*," thus [ends] the second great chapter on the accomplishment of the task through the stage of generation in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja* following the *Mūlatantra*.
Having beheld the Lord Vajrin—the Vajra of Body, Speech, and Mind who bestows the fruit of equal bliss, who is melted by the passion of Wisdom, and who is like the moon—[one should proceed].

The goddesses sing this song: "O Blessed One, you who benefit all sentient beings, O Wielder of the Vajra, Teacher of the thirty-three gods and of men, protect us from those who torment us with lustful desires."

The Vajra of Speech, consisting of ten mandalas, abiding here in five locations through the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and by nature of the vowels due to the divisions of emptiness and so forth, always exists for sentient beings according to their inclinations; it is the instructor of the true path from the fear of cyclic existence. Its arising is now extensively set forth as explained by Mañjuśrī in this commentary.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Ho: Kāra," and so forth:

here, just as in this mortal world the elements such as earth, which circulate within one's own mandala, impel the consciousness for the sake of generating the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*) of those born from a womb in order to attain the waking state—once that [consciousness] has entered the dream state—so too should the goddesses Locanā and the others be understood for the sake of sentient beings.

Here, having placed the syllable *hoḥ* at the beginning and end of the deity upon the path of the *nābhāvadhūtī* and the *uṣṇīṣa*, one then places the Body-Vajra *oṃ* on the forehead, the Speech-Vajra *āḥ* on the throat, and the Mind-Vajra *hūṃ* on the heart. Thus, that which has arisen from body, speech, and mind—characterized by the moon, sun, and Rāhu—is melted from below and above by the fire of time (*kālāgni*) and by the rays of wisdom (*prajñā*). "Melted by the passion of wisdom" means it is melted by the *caṇḍālī* who is wisdom.
Here, there is a twofold impelling: the first for the accomplishment of the vital wind (*prāṇa*), and the second for the accomplishment of bliss up to the age of sixteen.

By that [means], having quickly perceived both the Moon-like [Vajrasattva] and the Thunderbolt-wielder (Indra) through the syllable *ca*, he also [perceived] wisdom (*prajñā*). The mind, together with wisdom, resting upon the *avadhūtī* and *śaṅkhinī*, is the blazing Wisdom-Vajra.
O, for the child, it is the awakening and the realization.
O venerable one, it is of the nature of intrinsic being;
O venerable one, it is the Vajra of Speech (vāgvajra).
In the *Śrīmūla*, it is not present in the "Chapter on Means" (*asādhana-paṭala*); having examined [the manuscripts], [this is] from M. (Mu.).
And, O Bhava, O Subala, in the word "adrutam" occurring everywhere, the reading there is "dravam."
Having looked upon the chapter,
[the section] titled "The Great Chapter on the Generation of the Life-Breath Deities" (prāṇadevatotpādamahoddeśaḥ),
the goddesses sing: "O Blessed One, you who benefit all sentient beings, O Vajrī, teacher of gods and men, protect us who desire our desires and seek prosperity."

Here, the goddesses Tārā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, and Locanā—whose natures are loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—exhort the Blessed One for the sake of the world and for the benefit of the ignorant, so that they may practice the flow of the five mandalas. This is the rule regarding the exhortation by the goddesses through vajra songs.
Thus, it is said in the *Mūlatantra*: "I am Locanā, the mother of the world; I abide as the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) for yogins.
O Kālacakra, arise from desire and unite with me, whose nature is the mandala!"
I am Māmakī and a sister; I abide as the fruition for yogins.
O Kālacaja, arise from my nature as the maṇḍala and desire me!
I am Pāṇḍarā, the daughter, abiding as a woman within the nature of the maṇḍala for yogins; O Kālacakra, arouse desire for me!
I am Tāriṇī, the sister’s daughter, established in stainlessness for the yogins; O Kālacakra, arise from my maṇḍala-nature and desire me!
Having taken up the mandala of emptiness, emanate the mandala of body, speech, and mind for the sake of the world; O you whose intention is to uplift the world!

Thus, in this way, the deities awaken the consciousness that has entered into a state of fainting within the secret lotus of the navel and other centers—which bestows the fruit of equal bliss—residing within the body of the practitioner, just as they do for ordinary beings; such is the definitive meaning (nītārtha). || 50 ||

Now the emergence of the deity is described: Having heard the song and seeing all the three worlds as indeed like a magical illusion, that Vajrin brings about his own manifestation, having expanded his own emblem with quivering, stainless hands.
Adorned with vajra ornaments, crowned by the Lord of Jinas, and embraced by Prajñā, O King, he performs once again the complete emission of the mandala through the union of Prajñā and Upāya. ||51||
By means of the passage beginning with "Having heard the song," and so forth:

here, the Blessed One, having entered into emptiness (*śūnyatā*), was awakened by the songs. Having perceived the entire world as being like an illusion (*māyopama*), he brings about rebirth for the sake of sentient beings. Having expanded his own insignia—the five-pronged vajra—which has transformed from the syllable *HŪṂ* and possesses shimmering, stainless rays; and being adorned with vajras and wearing the crown of the Lord of Jinas, which is the crown of Akṣobhya; he is embraced by Prajñā, who is Viśvamātā, the sovereign of the Vajradhātu, who flows through the mandala of emptiness.

In that heart, as with children, by means of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*), [the practitioner] addresses [the King], O King. Through the meditative union (*samāpatti*) of wisdom and skillful means, having caused the Buddhas— who abide in space and possess the nature of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), and who are the essence of the five mandalas for the sake of the pledge-mandala (*samaya-maṇḍala*)— to enter one’s own body, one should then emit them from the lotus of wisdom (*prajñā-padma*) as before, characterized by faces, arms, emblems, and postures, and possessing the nature of the individual syllables of mantra within the mandalas of gnosis, mind, speech, and body.
Thus is the dismissal of the mandala;
by the word "and" (ca), it is as before.
At the time of the child's emergence from the womb, there is the arising of the ten winds, beginning with prāṇa.
At the time of the disciples’ entry into the maṇḍala, there is the casting of flowers.

Through the purification of the deity as a naked infant wearing the membrane of the womb, the awakening of the sense faculties and the entry of the *jñānasattva*—just as it occurs for an infant—is to be meditated upon by yogins within the deity, characterized by the twenty modes of awakening (*viṃśatyākārasaṃbodhi*).

Thus, in the fivefold awakening (*pañcākārābhisaṃbodhi*), the limb of service (*sevāṅga*) pertains to the accomplishment of the body; in the twentyfold awakening, the near-accomplishment (*upasādhana*) pertains to the accomplishment of speech. In this way, the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) is twofold: one is the womb-born (*jarāyuja*), and the second is the egg-born (*aṇḍaja*).
That which is egg-born is the origin of the world-system; this is expressed by the term "born from the cosmic egg" (brahmāṇḍaja). That which is womb-born is the origin of human beings.
That which is instantaneous is birth by spontaneous generation (*upapāduka*);
that is the single stage of arising for sentient beings.

The stage of completion (*utpannakrama*) was taught by the Blessed One according to the disposition of sentient beings in its instantaneous form, and it is furthermore free from conceptual construction.
Born from space, self-arisen, the great fire of the wisdom of insight;
Vairocana of great radiance, shining with the light of gnosis.
This is to be understood through the fivefold awakening (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*), beginning with these [verses]. || 51 ||

Now, the summoning of the wheel of gnosis (jñānacakra) is described: One should dispatch Vajravega—who has the luster of blue, a terrifying body, a smiling face made formidable by bared fangs, who roars, whose eye is the sun, who has twenty-four hands, four faces, and two feet; who arises from wisdom and means, is equipped with weapons, and emerges from wisdom and means—mounted upon an eight-wheeled chariot, the crusher of the enemies of the Victors, for the sake of the wheel of gnosis. (52)
By the passage beginning with "blue-colored" (*nīlābha*) and so forth:

here, for a newborn infant, the exit of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through the central channel (*madhyamā*) is blue-colored. With its exit, there occurs the awakening of the sense faculties and the engagement of the six consciousnesses with external objects within the internal self.

Therefore, for the manifestation of the external deity, one should visualize the blue-colored vital breath—purified by the central channel—as Vajravega, of earthy body, with a laughing face, formidable with half-bared fangs, roaring, possessing twelve eyes, twenty-two Jina hands, and twenty-six arms.

One should dispatch that Vajravega—who has four faces and two feet, who arises from wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), who is like a lord accompanied by his weapons, who wears an elephant hide as a garment, who is adorned with the five mudrās, who bears Akṣobhya on his crown, who wears a garland of skulls and severed heads, and who is decorated with snake ornaments, being an emanation of the *hūṃ*-syllable vajra—thinking of him as the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).

He stands upon a chariot with eight wheels, situated amidst sound, touch, taste, form, and smell, and the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; he is the crusher of the enemy of the Victors, the destroyer of the Māras and the afflictions (*kleśa*).
For the sake of the wheel of knowledge, it is for the cessation of the cognition of the five sense objects. || 52 ||

Having struck the navel with the goad, having bound the Lord of the Knowledge Wheel—who possesses shimmering, stainless hands—by the very hands, and having terrified him with his own weapon, the thunderbolt-serpent;

having rendered the entire object of practice [subservient], he departs again after setting the excellent wheel in motion. The Jambhakas and others perform entry, binding, pleasing, and the creation of equanimity. 53.
Then the vital breath (*prāṇa*), having emerged from the navel-lotus, draws in external objects and returns again.

Therefore, having struck [the deity] with the pure [breath] at the navel, one binds the Lord of the Wisdom-Wheel (*jñānacakra*)—who possesses shimmering stainless rays—with the vajra-hook in his hands; having bound him in twenty-four hands, one terrifies him with the naga-nooses together with the thunderbolts and with one's own weapons.

Having thus made the Wisdom-Wheel the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*), one proceeds again to one's own place, having set in motion the entire Wheel of the Universe (*viśvacakra*) characterized by all phenomena.
Then Jambhaka effects the "disguise," which is the store-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) produced by the visual faculty;
Stambhaka effects the "bondage," which is the body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) produced by the tactile faculty;
and Mānaka effects the "satisfaction," which is the tongue-consciousness (*jihvāvijñāna*) produced by the gustatory faculty.
The extremely powerful one effects the equalization of flavor (*samarasī-karaṇa*) by means of the olfactory consciousness produced by the sense of smell.

Thus, the fivefold [process] is: drawn in by the syllable *jaḥ*, entered by the syllable *hūṃ*, bound by the syllable *vaṃ*, gratified by the syllable *hoḥ*, and made of equal flavor by the syllable *hīḥ*.
This is accomplished by means of the vajra-hook, the vajra, the vajra-noose, the vajra-bell, and the vajra-staff.

Having thus worshipped the wheel of gnosis (jñānacakra), one should meditate upon the wheel of commitment (samayacakra) as having become of one flavor (samarasībhūta), just as before; such is the rule. || 53 ||

He is liberated—now, through the yoga of accomplishment (*niṣpatti-yoga*), the mind of oneness with the wisdom-deities (*jñāna-devatā*) together with the commitment-deities (*samaya-devatā*) arises in each respective place. [The goddess] is red and blazing atop the fire in the womb-lotus within the sky. In the east, she is glorious and blackly blazing; in the excellent lotus-petal of the south and the north, she becomes glorious and white by virtue of her family (*kula*). In the west, she is yellow and blazing; in the southeast, smoke-colored; likewise in the southwest, the direction of the Marīcis, and in the region of the radiant hair-tuft (*dyotakeśa*). (54)
"By the words beginning with *citta* [it is meant]:
