here, in the yoga of completion (*niṣpattiyoga*) within the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) together with Vajradhātvīśvarī in the sky resides in the lotus of the womb (*garbhapadma*) within great bliss (*mahāsukha*). Above the fire, upon the mandalas of the moon, sun, Rāhu, and Kālāgni, there is the state of equal flavor (*samarasatva*) of the gnosis-being (*jñānasattva*) with the commitment-being (*samayasattva*).
Likewise, on the eastern petal, Kṛṣṇadīptā is of equal flavor."

On the petal of the excellent lotus, she is red-radiant in the south, white-radiant in the north, and yellow-radiant in the west, according to the family and the power of the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*).
Likewise, Dhūmā is in the southeast,
and Marīci is in the southwest.
There are ten million confectioners in the northeast. || 54 ||
In the northwest are Śrīpradīpā and Maṇi, as well as Taru, Dharmagaṇḍī, and Śaṅkha; in the southeast, northwest, southwest, and northeast, likewise in the inner corner regions.

In the east is the earth of formative predispositions (saṃskāra) situated in a lotus; in the south is the water of sensation (vedanā); in the north is perception (saṃjñā), and fire is in the west, while wind and form are in the other [northeast].
In the northwest is the lamp, which is of equal flavor (*samarasa*).

Likewise, in the southeast is the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), in the southwest is the Dharma-gong, in the northeast is the Dharma-conch, and in the northwest is the wish-granting tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*).
These are located within the corner regions between the vajra-fence and the lotus petals.

Thus, in the previous lotus-seat, within the pericarp upon the sun, the two—formative predisposition (*saṃskāra*) and earth (*pṛthivī*)—are of one flavor together with the two pledge-beings (*samayasattva*).
To the south, feeling (*vedanā*) and the water element; to the north, perception (*saṃjñā*) and the fire element; to the west, form (*rūpa*) together with wind (*pavana*) becomes of one flavor.
Herein, the means (*upāya*) are the leaders. (55)

In the southeast, there is the form of Vāyu; in the southwest, the designation of Fire; and in the northeast, both Water and Feeling (vedanā). In the northwest, Earth is conjoined with the aggregates (skandha) of Formations (saṃskāra).

Between the deities, there are jars of nectar-essence in the region of the eight petals. Furthermore, in the eastern enclosure, there is the Nose and Odor; in the southern enclosure, the Eye and Form.

Thus, in the southeast, wind and form are of equal flavor (*samarasa*); in the southwest, fire and the element of sensation (*vedanā*); in the northeast, water and the element of perception (*saṃjñā*); and in the northwest, earth and the element of mental formations (*saṃskāra*) are of equal flavor—these are the presiding goddesses of the corners.
Likewise, in the intermediate spaces between the goddesses and the Buddhas, the jars of nectar-flavor are of equal flavor in the eight chamber-regions; such is the rule.
Then, in the enclosure of the Tathāgatas and subsequently in the enclosure of the Bodhisattvas, the nose and odor are of equal flavor on the eastern lotus.
In the south is the eye, whose object is visible form. || 56 ||

On the left [side] there is the tongue and taste; for on the side of Varuṇa there is touch and the body. Likewise, in Pātāla, there are sound and the ear, according to the family system, on the left of the southern gate. Mind and the element of phenomena (dharmadhātu), together with space, are on all sides on the left of the gates. First, there is the group of six skillful means (upāya) as the presiding deities of the maṇḍala, according to the power of the Jinas. (57)

In the [relevant] chapter, verse: This is the great section on the generation of the life-force deities (*prāṇadevatā*). In the North is the tongue and taste; in Varuṇa (West) is the body-faculty of touch; in Pātāla (South) are sound and the ears; and in the South Gate, to the East and West, there is indeed the mind and the dharma-element together with space in the left of the East Gate.
Thus, first, there is the group of six means (*upāya*);
according to the lineage of the Tathāgata family, these are the presiding deities (*adhidaiva*) of the maṇḍala. ||57||

Afterwards, the group of six beginning with Prajñā is manifest, each as a presiding deity upon their respective lotus seats. At the eastern gate is Pracaṇḍa, holding a sword and possessing great strength; Stambhakī is his mudrā. To the right is Jambha, and at the gate of Dhanada (the north) is Mānaka; Mānakī is his mudrā. Stambha is Anantavīryā, and she resides at Varuṇa (the west); the lotus is situated in the middle of the gates. (58)
Subsequently, there is the group of six beginning with wisdom (*prajñā*), starting with the *dharmadhātu*.
Here, in the southeast is Sparśavajrā, the tactile faculty; and in the netherworld (*pātāla*) is Śabdavajrā, the auditory faculty.
To the left of the northern gate is the *dharmadhātu*, and to the left of the western gate is the mind (*manas*); thus are the twelve sense bases (*āyatana*).

In the *bodhisattva* enclosure, the equalization of flavor (*samarasīkaraṇa*) of the *jñānasattva* occurs upon their respective lotus seats on the moon at the summit. Now, the state of equal flavor of the wrathful kings (*krodharāja*) is described: at the eastern gate is Pracaṇḍa, whose consort is Sidhūgatibala; his mudrā is Stambhakī. At the southern gate is Jambhaka, whose consort is Mānī; his mudrā is [the corresponding one]. At the northern gate is Mānaka, whose consort is Jambhakī; his mudrā is [the corresponding one].

At the western gate is the pillar Anantavīryā; her mudrā is the state of equal flavor (samarasa). "The lotus situated in the middle of the door" refers to the creation of the state of equal flavor within the mind-maṇḍala.
This is the rule concerning that which is born in the navel-cakra and the heart-lotus. ||58||
Mārīcī, Nīladaṇḍa, Acala, Bhṛkuṭī, Śṛṅkhalā, Anantavīrya, Aṭṭahāsā, and Cundā—these eight, together with Ratnapāṇi and Dhanada, are in the southern gate in the middle of the doorway.
Sumbha is below Raudrekṣaṇā, and Uṣṇīṣa is in the sky; Atinīlā is at the eastern gate, and above her, between the two, is the chariot (Syandana) as a certainty.

Thus, incidentally regarding the wrathful deities: Mārīcī and Nīladaṇḍa are the gatekeepers in the outer body-maṇḍala; they are in a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) in the east. To the south are Ṭakkirāja and Cundā on a chariot. In the north are Acala and Bhṛkuṭī. In the west are Śṛṅkhalā and Anantavīrya Mahābala—these are in a state of equal flavor. Sumbharāja and Raudrākṣa are in the netherworld (*pātāla*).
Atinīlā and Uṣṇīṣa are above in the dust-maṇḍala; Uṣṇīṣa is above the eastern gate.

In the west is Sumbha, and there is a chariot (*syandana*) at both [ends]; this is the rule. Furthermore, in the visualization, there is a chariot below and above as well. In the central mandala, there are the gates of the mouth, the organ, the anus, and the *uṣṇīṣa*.
"Organ" refers to the gate of urine and semen.
"Externally, in the body-maṇḍala, there are the nose, eyes, tongue, body, and ears;
as they are in the body of a child, so they are in the maṇḍala—this is the rule. (59)

In the mandala born of Speech, there is for the Bhūtas a seat consisting of eight directions and eight weapons; Cāmuṇḍā and Indra are in the east, and Vaiṣṇavī, who has four faces, is in the southeast (Śikhin).

In the south (Yāma), Rudra and Varāhī are present; in the direction of Danupati (the west), Ṣaṇmukhī and Vighnanātha are located. To the right of the outer gate of Indra (the northeast), and in the west (Danupati), Vāyavī and Indra are situated. (60)
Vāyu, Brahmā, and Vidyut are indeed in the north; Sāgara and Śūkarī are in the northeast; Gaṇendra is in the northwest;
and Rudra, Kāla, Viṣṇu, and Dhanada are on the left side of the door of the other deity. Among them, the mudrās of Girijā, Yāminī, Śrī, and Dhaneśā are well known.

In the Yakṣa [direction] is Raudrī; Yama is in the direction of Bhava (Nairṛta), and likewise Ṣaṇmukha is in the direction of Paśupati (Vāyu). Lakṣmī is at the right side of the eastern door; Danupatī and Rākṣasī are his mudrās.

In the southeast is Vāyu; Pracaṇḍā and Hari are also there. Varuṇā is at the right side of the southern door; Lakṣmī and Śrī are indeed there. Ṣaṇmukha is in the southwest; Danupatī, Vāyavī, and Indrā are in the west.
Externally, all the nāgas are on the western altar of the gods, Yama, and Kubera: Padma, Karkoṭaka, and Vāsuki situated in the circle of the ocean, along with Śaṅkhapāla;

Kulika, the well-known Ananta-nāga, prevails in the fire situated at the head of the water; likewise, by the power of the family, Takṣaka indeed becomes the great lotus situated on the earth mandala. (63)

Their wisdom-consorts (prajñās) are Pracaṇḍā and the others, such as Śvānavaktrā, who reside in the worlds of the cremation grounds. Their skillful means (upāyas), by virtue of the other family (kula), become lotuses and so forth for the sake of true bliss.
Śvānāsyā is indeed in the eastern wheel, situated in the moving circle; Śūkarāsyā is in the southern cremation ground at Śūlabheda; and Vyāghravaktrā is in the north at the place of corpse-burning.

When there is moisture and a putrid odor in the northwest (Varuṇa), there is likewise the Jambukāsyā; when there is filth and a terrible battle in the southeast (Śikhin), there is the Kākavaktrā along with the Gṛdhra;
and in the north (Vāyavya), when one is bitten by a snake.

On Īśvara, the face of the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) is to be visualized; on Bālamṛtyu, the face of an owl situated upon a wheel; and the Moon and Sun are to be visualized as residing within the circle of the earth. ||65||

For the mother’s stance is indeed *pratyālīḍha*, while that of the host of goddesses is *samapada*; the *viśākha* is for [the father], and the *maṇḍala* is for the hosts of the ten Vasus and the Asuras.

Indeed, for those standing in *pratyālīḍha*, there is the attainment of *samāpatti*; for those in *ālīḍha*, it is called *vaiśākha*; and for those in *viśākha*, it is certainly *maṇḍala*, and likewise for those in *maṇḍala*.

The remaining deities in the mandala are seated upon vajra-thrones, while the goddesses are seated upon lotus-thrones, positioned in the directions of their respective families atop their own lotuses and moons.

The gods are seated upon vajra-thrones together with the naga-family, stationed upon their own directional mounts; likewise, the goddesses of the gods and those born of spirits (bhūta) stand in graceful postures upon the petals.
O King, when the left feet are extended and the right are bent and placed upon the ground, that is the *pratyālīḍha* stance, measuring two and a half cubits.

From the engagement of the left [foot] it becomes *ālīḍha*; when both feet are even, it is *samapada*; and when there is an extension of the pair of knees according to the requirements of the [ritual] qualities, it becomes the *vaiśākha* circle (*maṇḍala*). (68)
Indeed, when the face is slightly raised, it becomes graceful; the rest is well known and should be understood by the yogin for the purpose of the Vajra-dance in the Bharata tradition.
Thus are the five doors of speech due to the articulation from the five locations. Likewise, below and above are the three doors of emptiness.
Excluding the door of semen (*śukradvāra*), which is characterized by the locations of the body and the throat, there are twelve doors within the three mandalas.

Thus, according to the division of the solar *lagnas*, there are twelve doors; according to the division of the lunar digits (*kalā*), there are fifteen, by way of the phenomena of body, speech, and mind for all sentient beings—this is the rule.
Here, the state of equal flavor (*samarasatva*) of the mandala of speech and so forth, as well as the *pratyālīḍha* stance and other such postures, are easily understood.
Beginning with “In the mandala born of speech” and ending with “for the sake of vajra-dance,” these nine and a half verses are easy to understand.

Now, the family mudrās of the deities are described: for Vajra, there is the mutual-vajra; indeed, the five Buddhas are on the crown. Sometimes Akṣobhya is above Rūpa, and for the one clearly holding a lotus, Vairocana should be [above]. (69)
24 5 10 15 20 T 25 END_OF_PDF_PAGE_213 5 10 15 20 20 25 186 *Vimalaprabhā* [Sādhana-chapter]: "Of the Vajra," and so forth.
Here, in this Maṇḍala of the Paramādibuddha, there is indeed a mutual vajra upon the crown.
For what reason?
"From the mutual conjunction of knowledge and consciousness.
Therefore, by means of ignorance one attains consciousness, and by means of consciousness one attains knowledge.
For both, the Mind-Vajras wear the monastic robe and the turban; they are seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture upon their heads with the earth-touching mudrā (*bhūsparśamudrā*).
There is the sealing by the five families through the consolation of the Tathāgatas, and the exclusion of the Svābhāvika family, because it is the progenitor of the Buddhas.
Now, according to the principle of gnosis and consciousness (*jñānavijñāna*), the crown consisting of the essence of the five Buddhas may sometimes be fashioned; such is the rule of the Tathāgatas.
Ākṣobhya is above form, because of the statement: "mind [appears] in the form of the body.
Vairocana would belong to him alone who holds the clear lotus, because of the statement: "the body [is expressed] by the utterance of speech. (69)

The bearer of the lotus belongs to Ratneśa; the one with the excellent jewel in his hand belongs to Amoghasiddhi; and the crown of the six [deities] is known as having matted hair (jaṭā) due to the influence of the qualities (guṇas), while the remaining wheel belongs to the others.

Indeed, the production of the wheel occurs on earth, that of the lotus in water, that of the jewel in fire, that of the sword in wind, that of the thunderbolt in space, and that of the knife in the syllable (akṣara).
Ratneśa holds a lotus because of his nature as *rajas* (passion);
and Amoghasiddhi has a crest-jewel (*pravaramaṇi*) on his head because of the redness arising from *māṃsa* (flesh).
The crest of the six [deities] is called "matted hair" (*jaṭā*) due to the influence of the *guṇas*.
The qualities [of these forms] are for the sake of converting the followers of other sects.
Through the purity of the mouth of Īśvara, there are six faces or five faces characterized by the five Brahmās, bearing matted hair and crowns.
Herein, Sadyojāta is Vairocana, Vāmadeva is Amitābha, Aghora is Ratnasaṃbhava, Tatpuruṣa is Amoghasiddhi, Īśāna is Akṣobhya, and Kālāgni is Vajrasattva.

The primordial aggregates (*prākṛtaskandha*), whose natures are earth, water, fire, air, space, and consciousness, are sealed by the pure aggregates (*śuddhaskandha*)—namely, fire, wind, water, and earth.
Thus, the crowns of the six are called "matted locks" (*maulijaṭā*).

As for the deities of the remaining wheel, the crowns of the goddesses consist of various jewels and are sealed by their respective families (*kula*); the sealing of each deity by that [deity] from which they were born will be explained below.
Now, the generation of the symbols, such as the wheel and so forth, is described—beginning with the words "on the earth" and so on.
Here, the generation of the wheel occurs from the letter *la*, which is the seed-syllable of the earth;
that of the lotus occurs from the letter *u*, which is [the seed-syllable] of water.
In fire, the letter *ṛ* of the jewel;
in wind, the letter *i* of the sword;
in the void, the letter *a* of the thunderbolt.
The connection with the action is that the knowledge of the syllable *Aṃ* becomes the knife. || 70 ||

Indeed, there arise a garment, a vessel of nectar, a mirror, a garland, and a lute; the sixth is the source of Dharma (dharmodaya), arising from earth, water, fire, air, ether, and the peaceful [unmanifest].
Likewise, there are five emblems: a shield, a spear, an arrow, an axe, and a hand-drum (ḍamaruka); and similarly, there are indeed a staff, a noose, a goad, a mallet, and a trident.

In the chapter [on the Great Summary of the Generation of the Life-God], verses 69–73: thus, the garment arises from the syllable *la*; the vessel of nectar from *u*; the mirror from *a*; the perfume from *ī*; the lute from *ā*; and the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) from the visarga, which is the form *ā*. These are the symbols according to the distinction of the qualities of earth and the other elements.
Likewise, the shield from *al*; the spear from *o*; the arrow from *a*; the axe from *e*; and the hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*) from *a*.
Thus are the five signs according to the distinction of the qualities (*guṇa*).

Likewise, the staff (*daṇḍa*) is in the vowel *ā*, the noose (*pāśa*) in *au*, the goad (*aṅkuśa*) in *ār*, the mallet (*mudgara*) in *ai*, and the trident (*triśūla*) in *āl*; these are the five signs according to the increase of the vowels (*svaravṛddhi*).

The bow, the blue lotus, and again likewise the face, the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), and the bell—these, as well as the chain and so forth, the aquatic creature, the cup, the leopard skin, and the elephant hide;

the remaining secondary emblems here, born of earth, water, fire, wind, and space, are to be known according to the influence of the qualities of nature (guṇas) for the male deities and female goddesses.

"The bow is by the letter *la*, the lotus by the letter *va*, the face by the letter *ra*, the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) by the letter *ya*, and the bell by the letter *ha*. Likewise, the chain is by the letter *lā*, the conch by the letter *vā*, the skull-cup by the letter *rā*, the leopard skin by the letter *yā*, and the tusk by the letter *hā*. Thus, according to the long vowels and the *yaṇ*-substitutions, this is the rule for the vowels of the thirty-two symbols.
The remaining secondary symbols here should be known as those born from earth, water, fire, wind, and space; they belong to the deities and goddesses by virtue of their natural qualities."
The signs of all [the goddesses], beginning with Cāmuṇḍā, are to be understood according to the distinctions of wind and the other elements. || 72 ||

The three hundred vowels beginning with *la* and so forth, born from earth, water, fire, air, and space, are the respective mantras of the signs; they are arranged in sequence through the divisions of short and long. All of them indeed reside within the lotuses of the wheels (*cakras*) and so on, seated upon the thrones of the moon and the sun. Wherever the sixth sign occurs according to the influence of the qualities (*guṇas*), there the Unstruck (*anāhata*) sound shall be.

The three hundred vowels beginning with *a* mentioned here, born of earth, water, fire, air, and space, are the respective mantras of the symbols arranged in their proper order through the distinctions of short and long [vowels].
All of these indeed reside within the lotuses of the wheels (*cakras*) and so forth, seated upon the thrones of the moon and sun.
Wherever there is a sixth symbol, by virtue of its qualities, there the Unstruck (*anāhata*) sound occurs.
Thus, the generation of the sign from the seed-syllable, and the generation of the deity from the sign, is to be understood by the yogin in all cases; this is the rule of the Tantra. || 73 ||

Now, the seed-syllables of the birth [of] Vajrasattva and the others are stated: O Lord of Men, Nāda is Śrīvajrasattva; Akāra is Cittavajra; Hrasvekāra is Khaḍgī (Khadiravaṇī); and furthermore, Ṛkāra is Ratnapāṇi. Hrasvakāra is Amitābha; and furthermore, Lṛkāra here is Vairocana. Through the distinctions of the long vowels, the entire host of gods belongs to the six Jinas in sequence—the entire host of gods belonging to the six Jinas in sequence. (74)
By the words "Nāda," and so forth:
Nāda is the unstruck sound (anāhata); Śrīvajrasattva is the aggregate of consciousness (jñānaskandha).
In this manner, everywhere there is a relationship between the designation and the designated.
Thus: A is Akṣobhya;
I is Amoghasiddhi;
Ṛ is Ratnasaṃbhava.
U is Amitābha;
Lū is Vairocana;
Lṛ is Locanā.
Ū is Māmakī;
Ṛ is Pāṇḍarā; Ī is Tārā.
To Vajradhātvīśvarī. ||74||

The venerable Mother is indeed known as Anāhatā; likewise, the space element born from the letter Ā consists of the sequence I, Ṛ, Ū, and LṚ, which reside respectively in wind, fire, water, and earth.

Through their mutual transformation into the body, she becomes Viśvamātā, the supreme consort of the Lord of Jinas, for the sake of bliss. Akṣobhya is the space element, while Locanā is the one whose lotus-like hands hold a sword. (75)
The venerable Mother Prajñāpāramitā is known as Anāhata.
Thus, by way of the distinction between body and essence, there is the birth of the short and long vowels.
In this manner, body and essence are mutually related.
The supreme Lord of Victors is the aggregate of gnosis;
Viśvamātā is the element of gnosis;
consciousness is the space element.
Veneration is the water element. ||75||

Ratneśa and Māmakī are you; likewise, Kamaladhara and Pāṇḍarā constitute the body-form. Similarly, Cakrī and Tārā arise from the influence of their inherent qualities through short and long vowels. The syllable *Aṃ* becomes Viśvabhadra by virtue of its form; the syllable *Akāra* is Vajrapāṇi, and likewise, the syllable *Ha* is Khagarbha, and correctly so is Bhūmigarbha.
Perception is the fire element;
form is the wind element.
Thus, the syllable AṂ is Samantabhadra.
A is Vajrapāṇi;
E is Khagarbha;
Ar is Kṣitigarbha. || 76 ||

The letter *o* is the Lord of the World (*lokanātha*), and likewise, here in the case of Viṣkambhin, the letter *ā* is the Dharmadhātu; indeed, from the letter *ka* is born Śabdavajrā. From the letter *ai* is born Sparśavajrā; from the letter *a*, due to the division of the bodies, is born Rasakuliśā. O King, likewise, from the letter *au* is born Rūpavajrā, and from the letter *at* is born Gandhavajrā. (77)
O Lokeśvara! Al Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhī!
Thus, Ā Dharmadhātu!
Māḥ is the sound-vajrā; Ai is the touch-vajrā; Bār is the taste-vajrā.
Au is Rūpavajrā;
Ālū is Gandhavajrā. || 77 ||
Śrībhadra and Dharmadhātu, Rava and Vajra, and Vajrapāṇi form a pair; Vairambha and Gandhavajrā, Vararasa and Vajra, and Lokanātha form a pair;
Bhūgarbha and Rūpavajrā, and likewise Sparśaviṣkambhin—thus indeed the six families are to be correctly understood according to the power of the qualities of nature. (78)
Samantabhadra is the dharmadhātu;
they are mutually embodied.
Śabdavajrā is Vajrapāṇi.
The couple consists of body and nature. The embryo is Gandhavajrā; Rasavajrā is Lokeśvara.
Kṣitigarbha is Rūpavajrā;
Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin is Sparśavajrā.
Thus, the six families are to be understood by the authentic yogin according to the power of their natural qualities; this is the rule. (78)

Now the seed-syllables of the five families of the wrathful deities are taught: the syllable *haṃ* is the uṣṇīṣa-cakra; here, by the power of the body, there is *ha*, and by the power of the body, *atinīlā*. *Sumbha* is the short *ha*; likewise, the long one is *raudranetrā*. By the sequence of pairs, *yaṃ* and *lā* are Prakaṭamati and Stambhakī; the pair *raṃ* and *vā* are Jambha and Mānī; and *vaṃ* and *pi* are *ra* and *ve*, which are Māna and Jambhakī. (79)
By the words "haṃ" and so forth:
here, the syllable *haṃ* becomes the *uṣṇīṣa* [cakra] due to the body, that is, from the division of the physical form;
and so it is for the others as well.
Haḥ and Atinīlā; Sumbha, ha; Raudrākṣī, hā.
Yaṃ is Atibala;
Lāḥ is Stambhaka;
Raṃ is Jambha.
Vāḥ is Amānakī;
va is Mānaka;
rāḥ is Jambhaka. || 79 ||

*Laṃ*, *yāḥ*, *stambhaḥ*, and *ativīryā* constitute [the first group]; *ya*, *va*, *ra*, *laṃ*, *nīladaṇḍaḥ*, *acalaḥ*, and *ṭakkikaḥ* constitute *anantavīrya* according to the body-parts (*tanuvaśāt*) of the goddesses, and these letters are long.

*Yā*, *vā*, *rā*, and *lā* likewise correspond to the elephant, horse, lion-vehicle, and boar; and *mārīcī*, *nīladaṇḍaḥ*, *acalaḥ*, *bhṛkuṭī*, *śṛṅkhalā*, and *anantavīryaḥ* [correspond to the remaining deities]. (80)
Laṃ is the immobilizer;
yāḥ is the one of extreme potency.
Thus, it occurs according to their respective order.
Ya, va, ra, laṃ:
Nīladaṇḍa, Acala, Ṭakki, and Mahābala.
And due to the influence of their respective bodies, the [syllables] of the goddesses are long.
She who is Vajraśṛṅkhalā on the elephant chariot, Cundā on the horse-drawn chariot,
and Bhṛkuṭī on the lion-drawn chariot.
Mārīcī is on the chariot of a boar.
Thus: "Mārīcī and Nīladaṇḍa form a pair; body and nature are mutually [united].
Acala and Bhṛkuṭī [form a pair]."
Vajraśṛṅkhalā is Atibala. || 80 ||
O King, in the mandala for the sake of true bliss, Ṭakkirāja and Cundā form a pair; the eight Śaktis are born from the syllables Ā, KĀRA, VAṂ, the Visarga, HAM, API, HA, and HĀKĀRA.
In these jars, the syllable HA is divided by the vowels of air, fire, water, and earth—namely OṂ, HŪṂ, HOḤ, and ĀŚAṄKHA—the stainless jewel of qualities, the foot, and the section on Dharma. (81)
Ṭakkī and Cundā form a pair in the maṇḍala for the sake of true bliss through the embrace of the other's family;
such are the powers (śakti) and the seeds (bīja).
The powers, such as Dhūmā and the others, have the causal deities (nimitta-daivata) as their presiding deities.
In that regard, the vowels *a*, *ā*, *aṃ*,
and *aḥ* are [the seed-syllables]. Respectively, they are Black Radiance (*kṛṣṇadīptā*), Yellow Radiance (*pīṭadīptā*), White Radiance (*śvetadīptā*), and Red Radiance (*raktadīptā*).
"Thus am I also, indeed"—this is "ha ha. "Haṃ" is a firefly; "haḥ" is a ray of light.
Ha Dhūmā; Hā Pradīpā.
Thus, there are eight powers born from the eight syllables.
In this manner, the letter *ha* in the jars is divided by the vowels of air (*ma*), fire (*ra*), water (*la*), and earth (*ṣma*).
Thus: in the eastern jars, *hi* and *hī*; in the southern jars, *hṛ* and *ha*; in the northern jars, *hū* and *hū*; and in the western jars, *hḷ* and *hal*.
Thus ends the classification of the winds and so forth.

Likewise, Oṃ is the conch of Dharma, Hūṃ is the wish-fulfilling gem, Hoḥ is the wish-granting tree, and Āḥ is the drum of Dharma; these are the seed-syllables of the deities in the mind-maṇḍala. || 81 ||

Now, the seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*) of Cāmuṇḍā and the others in the circle of speech (*vāṅmaṇḍala*) are stated: Cāmuṇḍā is indeed the syllable *ha*; *ham* and also *ha* are [for] Īśvarī and Śūkarī; *hā*, *kṣa*, *kṣa*, *kṣa*, *kṣa* are for Aindrī, Khagapatigamanā, Brahmikā, and Śrī-Kumārī.

*Hī*, *hr̥*, *hū*, *ha*, and *lū* are on the back of the excellent lotus-petal, with short vowels (*hrasvamātrā*) in front; likewise, *kṣī*, *kṣa*, *kṣa*, *kṣū*, *la* are manifested as fixed, and the short vowels are likewise [applied]. (82)
Cāmuṇḍā is indeed the syllable *ha*; *haṃ* is Māheśvarī;
*haḥ* is Vārāhī.
Hā! O Aindrī!
Kṣa! O Vaiṣṇavī! Kṣā! O Brahmāṇī!
*Kṣaṃ* is Mahālakṣmī;
*kṣaḥ* is Kaumārī—these are the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the goddesses.
Likewise, where the goddesses are situated in due order in the eight directions starting from the east upon the petals at the back of the lotus: *ho*, *ha*, *ha*, *halṛ*.
*Kṣa kṣa kṣa kṣū la* followed by a short vowel measure (*hrasvamātrā*) at the front; thus, on the eight petals are *hi hṛ hu ha*, *lakṣi kṣu kṣu la*. || 82 ||

In the eastern, left, and right [petals], as well as those of Varuṇa, Havi, Anādi, Īśa, and Vāyu, there are six lotuses on the six-petaled [wheel], distinguished by six measures and arranged in sequence, consisting of short and long vowels.

[In this] chapter, in the "Great Chapter on the Generation of the Vital Deities" (prāṇadevatotpāda-mahoddeśa), all [the letters] beginning with *hi* and *kṣi* and ending with *la*, multiplied by eight (the Vasus) and nine (the serpents/Phaṇis), serve as the means for the goddesses beginning with Cāmuṇḍā upon the petals; according to the Kula system, they face forward through the various divisions of mantra.
In the two northern [corners],
in the two western [corners], and in the two southeastern [corners].
In the two eastern lotus petals;
in the two southern ones; in the two southwestern ones.
In the two [petals] of Īśāna;
in the two of Vāyu and Agni;

in the remaining six petals, the six vowels—distinguished by their six measures and arranged according to the sequence—are placed in the petals of the lotus in the cardinal and intermediate directions, both short and long.
There, on the eastern lotus petal of Cāmuṇḍā, the syllable *hi* was previously placed.

Then, proceeding clockwise, on the second petal is *ya*, on the third *yi*, on the fourth *yū*, on the fifth the previously placed *ho*, on the sixth *yu*, on the seventh *yūla*, and on the eighth *yaṃ*. Thus, for Vaiṣṇavī: *kṣi yā yī yū kṣī yū yūlu yaḥ*. Likewise, for Vārāhī, on the eastern petal is *hai*, followed by *ra ri raha ṝ ru raṃ*.
For Kaumārī: kṣa rā rī dhṛrū raḷ raḥ.
For Raudrī: hu va vivṛ hū' vu vḷ vaṃ.
Likewise for Mahālakṣmī: kṣu vā vī vṛkṣa vū valu vaḥ.
Of Aindrī: *lū la lila halu lla laṃ*.
Of Brahmāṇī: *kṣūla lālī lu lū llū laḥ*.

Thus, indeed, all those beginning with *kṣy* and ending with *lo*, multiplied by eight—the number of Vasus and the number of hoods—are the rule for the petals of the goddesses Bhīmā and the others, respectively, being multiplied by eight.
For in the cardinal directions are those beginning with Ādi, and in the intermediate directions are those beginning with Padma;
and here, by virtue of the *kula*, the means for Cāmuṇḍā and the others becomes face-to-face through the various divisions of mantras.
In this context, Cāmuṇḍā is Vaiṣṇavī, who possesses the lineage of purification (*saṃskārakulinī*).
Facing her is the Means belonging to the Form family, characterized by the division of mantras and the letter *la*;
he belongs to the Vārāhī and Kaumārī families and is of the nature of sensation (*vedanā*).
Facing him is the Means belonging to the Perception family, born from the letter *u*.

Aindrī is Brahmāṇī, belonging to the lineage of form (rūpakulinī). Facing her is the Means (upāya), born from the letter *i*, belonging to the lineage of purification (saṃskārakulī). Raudrī is Mahālakṣmī, belonging to the lineage of designation (saṃjñākulinī).
Facing her is the family of sensation (vedanā), the method (upāya) born from the syllable Ṛ.
Thus is the arrangement of the four families in the mandala of speech.

Now, the seed-syllables of Śakra and the others in the body-maṇḍala are described: *taṃ* for Śakra with four faces; *paṃ* for Sāgara; *maḥ* for the glorious Gaṇendra; *ṭaṃ* for Vahni; *ṇo* for Kumāra; *caṃ* for Rākṣasendra; and *ñaḥ* for Vāyu. *Kaṃ* for Viṣṇu; *kālaḥ* for Hara; and *ha* for Dhanada. Thus, the initial letters of the consonant groups (*ka*, etc. together with their vowels become the [seeds] of the deities upon the petals of the divine lotus. (84)
Śakra is that; Brahmā is us; the ocean is *paṃ*.
Maḥ is Gaṇendra;
ṭaṃ is Vahni;
ṇaḥ is Kumāra.
Ca is the lord of the Rākṣasas; Ña is Vāyu; Kaṃ is Viṣṇu.
I am Yama; Saṃhara is Ka, the Yakṣa;
there is none other.
There is none;
there is none.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the *sādhana*: thus, by means of the divisions of short and long vowels for the six groups beginning with *ca*, the seed-syllable of the new moon (*amāvāsī*) of Caitra and the other months is to be grasped through *caṃ*, *ñaḥ*, and so forth, starting from the new moon of Caitra up to the new moon of Vaiśākha.
Thus, the first groups of consonants, consisting of three morae each, belong to the goddesses on the petals of the divine lotus. (84)

By virtue of the seasonal rule of the lunar days beginning with Caitra, the number sixty-four (64) is mounted upon the principles (*tattva*); the letter *ha* resides among air, fire, water, and earth, starting from the east and so forth.

The seven immutable groups (*kūṭastha*) consist of the consonant classes joined with *kṣa*, *ya*, *ra*, and *la*, belonging to the Asuras in the cremation ground. By virtue of the family (*kula*), he who faces [the center] here in the middle becomes the embodiment of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*).
By virtue of the seasonal regulation of the lunar days beginning with Caitra, there are three hundred and sixty lunar days in a year, corresponding to the numbers zero, six, and fire (three).
Here, the goddesses of Caitra reside on the fourteen petals of the first circle.
Among them, Trivajrā is on the first petal, Trivajrā on the second, and likewise Nṛvajrā, Juvajrā, Vajrā, and Vajrā.
Likewise, Jhavatrā, Jhivā, Jhavatrā, Jhuvajrā, Jhalavajrā, and Jhaṃvajrā;
Javajrā, and Jivitā—these fourteen goddesses are on the lotus petals of the southwest.
Vajrā is the wisdom consort (prajñā) of Saṃmukha, because she is the most excellent [like] the full moon.

Thus, in the second circle, beginning with the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapratipad*), there are *juvajrā* on the first petal; likewise, *jalavajrā*, *jaṃvajrā*, *chavajrā*, *chivatrā*, *chvajjā*, *chuvajrā*, *chlavajrā*, *chaṃvatrā*;
*cavajrā*, *civajrā*, *cṛvajrā*, *cuvajrā*, *clavajrā*, and *caṃvac*—this is the seed-syllable of the new moon (*amāvāsī*).
And here, [the sequence follows] the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*).
"Ña" is in reverse order, according to the sequence of emanation.
On the petal in the northwest is Cāvajrā;
in this manner, all the mantras end with "vajra."
Cā cī cu cū cūla caḥ;
chā chī chu chū chlū chaḥ;
jā jī jū—thus the full set of words is as before.
In the second circle, [the letters] beginning with the first day of the dark fortnight are: jū jlū jaḥ;
jhā jhī jhu jhū jhlū jhaḥ;
trā ñī ñū ñū ñlṛ ñaḥ.

The seed-syllable of the New Moon (*amāvāsī*) belongs to the center of the wind; likewise, the *ṭa*-group [belongs] to Jyeṣṭha and Āṣāḍha; the *pa*-group to Śrāvaṇa and Bhādra; the *ta*-group to Āśvina and Kārtika; the *sa*-group to Mārgaśīrṣa and Pauṣa; and the *ka*-group to Māgha and Phālguna.
Such is the rule for the seed-syllables of the lunar days and deities of the year.
Now, the seed-syllables of the *Nāgas* are stated, beginning with "the letter *ha* mounted upon the principles" (*tattvārūḍho hakāraḥ*), and so forth.
Here, the *tattvas* are *ya-ra-la-va*. One who has ascended to these is "one who has ascended to the *tattvas*.

*Hyā* and *hyā* belong to Karkoṭaka and Padma respectively in the wind-maṇḍala; *hnya* and *hlā* belong to Takṣaka and Mahāpadma respectively in the earth-maṇḍala; *ha* and *hrā* belong to Vāsuki and Śaṅkhapāla in the fire-maṇḍala;
*hvā* and *hvā* belong to Ananta and Kulika in the water-maṇḍala. Thus, in the maṇḍalas of air, forest, water, and earth, the letters beginning with *ha* are situated starting from the east.

Now the seed-syllables (bījas) of Śvānāsyā and the others are stated. "Kūṭa" refers to a peak consisting of five syllables; by means of each individual syllable, those seven groups situated at the peak become eight when joined with *kṣaya*, *ra*, *va*, and *la*—thus [are the seeds] of the Asurīs.

In the eight cremation grounds there, in the eastern cremation ground are *k, kh, g, gh, ṅa*; in the south, *h, y, r, v, la*; in the west, *—k, ś, ṣ—p, sa*; in the north, *h, y, r, v, la*; and in the corners, in the southeast, *ñ, jh, j, ch, ca*; in the southwest, *ṇ, ḍh*. [Note: The Tibetan commentary specifies *la-ra-va* for the southwest and *ya-ra-la-va* for the northwest. In the [sixth] chapter, *ilo*.

9. The Great Chapter on the Generation of the Life-God (*prāṇadevatotpāda*). 10. *ṭha*, *ṭha*; in the northwest (*vāyavya*) are *ṇa*, *dha*, *tha*, *ta*; in the northeast (*īśāna*) are *ma*, *bha*, *ba*, *pa*.

Thus, everywhere, by means of the states of the limbs of wisdom (*prajñā*) and method (*upāya*), [the deity] arises according to the family (*kula*). He who is here in the center should be understood by the yogin through the distinction between the Leader (*nāyaka*) and the Sub-leader (*upanāyaka*). 11. This is the rule of the Tantra (*tantraniyama*). (85)

13. Śrīvatrī becomes Viśvabhadra by virtue of his family; Vajradhṛk is Vajrapāṇi. 14. Bhūmigarbha is correctly [Amoghasiddhi]; Garbha is Amoghasiddhi, the one who makes the jewel stainless. 16. Viṣkambhī is Vajrapāṇi by virtue of his family; Lokanātha is Amitābha. 17. Śrīmātā is the Dharmadhātu; moreover, she is the excellent Vajra and Vajradhātvīśvarī. (86)

18. Śrītārā is indeed Sparśavajrā, and Pāṇḍarā is Rasakuliśā due to the distinction of their castes (jāti). 19. She who is called Rūpa is Māmakī, while Locanā arises by virtue of the family (kula), as Gandhavajrā. 20. Vajravega is the Lord of Wrath (Krodhendro), and he himself is Viśvabhadra, the Lord of Jinas. 21. Here, Uṣṇīṣa is Akṣobhya; furthermore, Atibala is well-known as Amoghasiddhi. ||87||

22. Jambha is indeed Ratnapāṇi by virtue of his family; and Mānaka is Amitābha. 23. Stambha becomes Vairocana, and the powerful Sumbha is Vajrapāṇi. 24. Vegarbha is Nīladaṇḍa by force of his natural qualities; and Bhūmigarbha is Ṭakki. 25. Viṣkambhin is Ativīrya by virtue of his family; and the Lord of the World is Acala. ||88||

26. The Mother is the Mudrā of Wrathful Indra by the power of the family (kula), and likewise the Dharmadhātu. 27. She is called Śūnyā, exceedingly blue; and Marut, Anala, Jala, Kṣmā, and the others possess infinite valor. 28. Jambhī and Mānī are manifested in sequence as the well-known Stambhakī. 29. By the power of the family, Raudrākṣī becomes Śabdavajrā, and Śṛṅkhalā becomes Sparśavajrā.
30. Mārīcī, Gandhavajrā, Bhṛkuṭī, and the well-known Cundā; 31. O Lord of Men, they are to be known according to their distinct classes as Rasavajrā and Rūpavajrā.
32. Herein, Stambha, Kālāntaka, and likewise the famous Atibala, the enemy of obstacles; 33. Jambha, Prajñāntaka, and similarly Mānaka, the enemy of Padma, arise. || 90 ||
34. Cāmuṇḍā, Śūkarīśā, Marut, Anala, Jala, Kṣmā, and likewise Indrī as the fourth; 35. Gandha, Rūpa, Rasa, and Sparśa—these reside in the moving-harmer (Vāyu), the Daitya (Rākṣasa), and Vahni (Agni).

36. Brahmā indeed becomes Vairocana by the power of the family (*kula*); and Sāgara becomes Amitābha. 37. Vahni becomes Śrī Ratnapāṇi; and Pavana likewise becomes Amoghasiddhi. 91. 52. Akṣobhya becomes the enemy of the Daityas (Viṣṇu); and the Lord of Jinas (the Buddha) is well-known as Śaṅkara. 54. He who is Viṣkambhin becomes Śakra; and Gaṇapati likewise becomes the Lord of the World (Lokanātha).
38. Bhūgarbha shall be Ṣaṇmukha, and Śrīkhagarbha is well known as Danupati. 56. Kāla becomes Śrīvajrapāṇi, and Viśvabhadra is the sixth Danupati. 92.

39. There are six sciences (*vidyā*) and six non-vajras, according to the power of their natural qualities (*prakṛti-guṇa*), and they have their respective seals (*mudrā*). 58. The seals, the sciences, and so forth, are the suns, the lords of the best of gods, white and black, and full. 40. Those which are on the lotus petals are the lunar days (*karatithi*) starting from the month of Māgha. 60. In six months, there is the first group of six, and another [group] of the goddesses according to the family (*kula*). 93.

41. Those eight jars which are the *nāgas* are the powers (*śaktis*) on the petals of the lotus; they are the Pracaṇḍās. 62. By virtue of their family lineage, Śrīdhūmā has the face of a crow, and Marīci has the face of a vulture.

42. Khadyotā is renowned for having the face of an owl, and Śrīpradīpā has the face of a bird-king (eagle). 64. Kṛṣṇadīptā has the face of a dog and a very deformed countenance, while Śūkarāsyā is exceedingly radiant with the face of a boar. || 14 ||

43. Vyāghrāsyā is white and radiant; by the power of her *kula*, Jambukī is yellow and radiant. 66. Thus, all [the goddesses] beginning with Lāsyā are the ten manifest forms of Viśvamātā without exception. Now, regarding the relationship between the produced (*janya*) and the producer (*janaka*), from "Śrīvajrī Viśvabhadra" ( ) up to "Viśvamātā without exception" ( ), ending at verse 68, there is the relationship between the *kula* and the *kulīna*. 86–943.

Now, the purity of the speaker’s body is described: 70. The divine ones, the Buddhas, and the Vidyās; the *sataru* and the *kalaśas*; the pure body of the Jina; those mounted on excellent chariots in the body-maṇḍala, such as Amārīcī and others; the well-known solar deities; the twelve [deities] beginning with Nairṛtya;
and the eight *nāgas* beginning with Karkoṭaka.
The fierce ones such as Śvānāsya and others—
these deities and so forth, together with their retinues and the deities upon the lotus petals— are the emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Buddha.
Thus, the body of the Victor is further twofold, being both external and internal;

just as the birth from the womb occurs with certainty, so it is likewise in the mandala. The Teacher, the divine jars, and so forth, are the innate body (*sahajakāya*) within the center of the mandala; the Buddhas and others are indeed the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); and the [deities] such as Rasakuliśa are the Enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

The wrathful deities are the *nirmāṇakāya* according to their respective families, situated within the womb of the maṇḍala; the eight goddesses beginning with Cāmuṇḍā, together with their retinues, are indeed the *śuddhakāya* on the outside. Here, in the womb, just as the consciousness (*vijñāna*) and gnosis (*jñāna*) of a child in the womb—consisting of semen and blood—is the *śuddhakāya*, so too are the Teacher, the Blessed One, the divine [goddesses] such as Dhūmā, and by the word "etcetera," the Dharma-conch and so forth, the eight vases; these are the *sahajakāya* within the womb of the maṇḍala.
Likewise, just as the arising of the aggregates and elements (*skandhadhātu*) of a child is the *dharmakāya*, so too are the Buddhas and others in the maṇḍala.
Then, just as for the child there is the arising of the sense bases (*āyatana*) which is the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*), so too in the mandala are Śabdavajrā and the others;

and just as for the child there is the arising of hands, feet, hair, and so forth, along with the time of birth, which is the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), so too are Yamāntaka and the other four wrathful deities. Thus, by virtue of their families, they are situated within the womb in the mandala—specifically in the mind-mandala by virtue of the mind-family—and this is the fourfold rule regarding the womb.

Now, the external [manifestation] is described in four ways, beginning with Cāmuṇḍā: here, just as for a newborn infant there is the exit of the vital breath from the navel-cakra which is the Sahaja-kāya, so too in the external Vāṅ-maṇḍala are the eight goddesses beginning with Cāmuṇḍā, together with their retinues and accompanied by the sixty-four Yoginīs. In the *Vimalaprabhā*: "O King, the gods and so forth are the Dharma-kāya; the entire family of serpents (*phaṇikula*) here is the Saṃbhoga-kāya; and Caṇḍā is the Nirmāṇa-kāya, for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings."

The pair is the Body-Vajra (*kāyavajra*), for the sake of the accomplishment of the image of the body of the co-emergent Victor; and the Speech-Vajra (*vāgvajra*) becomes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), as a pair, for the purpose of teaching the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). In this context, just as the contraction of a child’s hands, feet, and so forth, and their indistinct speech, is the Dharma-body, so too are the twelve deities;
by the word "and so forth," it is meant that there are six goddesses seated upon chariots.
Here, just as when a child’s teeth have emerged and their speech has become distinct, that is the Enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), so too in the mandala is the entire family of hooded serpents.

In this context, just as for a child there is the *nirmāṇakāya* from the falling out of the teeth until their re-emergence up to the end of life, so too in the mandala, Caṇḍā, Śvānāsyā, and the others, together with their retinues and accompanied by three and a half million spirits, constitute the *nirmāṇakāya*, O Lord of Men, for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings. This is the rule regarding the purification of the four external activities.
Now, the mutual union of the four bodies and the four vajras is described, beginning with the words "the pair," and so forth.

Just as here, for the sake of producing the reflection of a child, the innate body (*sahajakāya*) and the body-vajra (*kāyavajra*), which consists of the four elements, form a couple; so it is also in the mandala. Likewise, the mind (*citta*) and the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) also become a couple, performing the welfare of all sentient beings; and wisdom (*jñāna*) and the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) indeed become a couple, bestowing liberation upon living beings.

The yogi should understand the state of the limbs of wisdom and means through the even and uneven families, by means of the divisions of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), beginning with the moon, sun, and so forth, as they exist within the threefold existence. (99) Thus, the Vajra of Speech is the Dharmakāya; just as the pair [of speech] exists for the sake of speaking for a child, so too does it exist for the sake of teaching the Dharma in the mandala.
Here, the Bodhicitta of the child is the Saṃbhogakāya, which performs the welfare of all sentient beings as a pair; likewise, it is so in the mandala as well.

In this context, just as for a child at the time of death there is "knowledge," and at the age of sixteen there is the "emanation body" (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the state of a perfected constituent (*paripūrṇadhātutva*), so indeed for living beings there is a pair that bestows liberation.

Here, "liberation" (*mokṣa*) refers to the moment of the emission of the drops of bodhicitta; that which bestows this is the "pair that bestows liberation. This pair, characterized by knowledge and the emanation body, belongs to living beings.
Likewise, by way of its dissimilarity [to that], it bestows liberation within the mandala as the cessation of the twelvefold causes and effects; this is the Buddha’s rule.
Furthermore, these four bodies and four speech-aspects constitute the state of being limbs of wisdom and method through the even and uneven families.

By means of the families of elements arising from *rajas* within the equal families (*samakula*), by the unequal families (*viṣamakula*) arising from the element of *śukra*, by the divisions of gnosis belonging to the three types of existence beginning with the Moon and Sun, by the divisions of consciousness beginning with bliss (*ānanda*), and by the divisions of the twelve sense bases (*āyatana*), the yogi should understand the entire [process] as it was taught for the child in the "Inner Chapter" (*adhyātmapaṭala*), so too in the "Deity Sadhana" regarding the generation stage (*utpattikrama*).
Thus is the accomplishment of the deity’s form. || 99 ||

• The Great Chapter on the Arising of the Life-God (*prāṇadeva*). Now, the empowerment of body, speech, and mind is described: The Vajra, accompanied by *svāhā*, is at the head, throat, heart, navel, secret place, and crown. With these [mantras], one should bathe the limbs empowered by the supreme Lord of Jinas with the goddesses.

In the emptiness of the *dharmadhātu*, during the commitment (*samaya*) of the three vajras and the passion for the worship of gnosis (*jñāna*), the practitioner should say: "Through taking the three refuges, I am of the nature of that [reality]. (100)
"By the Vajrīs," and so forth:

for the child who has been born according to the [natural] order, there occurs the blessing (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of body, speech, and mind, characterized by the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. Just as mothers bathe the child whose limbs are blessed with these—*oṃ*, *āḥ*, *hūṃ*, *hoḥ*, *svāhā*—placed on the forehead, throat, heart, navel, secret place, and crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*), so too should one bathe the supreme Lord of Victors (*jinapati*) with the deities and yoginīs.

At this location, the forehead, there is a moon mandala transformed from the syllable *A*. Above that is an eight-spoked wheel transformed from the syllable *Oṃ*, and from its transformation arises the white-colored Kāyavajra, with three faces: the central face white, the left red, and the right black; he has six arms, holding a wheel, a vajra, and a lotus in his right hands, and a sword, a bell, and a jewel in his left hands. Having thus generated him together with his consort (*saprajña*), one should then emanate him from the forehead and visualize the entire expanse of space completely filled by him. After performing the teaching of the Dharma for those beings who are to be disciplined by Kāyavajra, he returns and stands before oneself, whereupon one should entreat him for empowerment (*abhiṣeka*).
"May the holders of the Body-Vajra consecrate me.
Then, the goddesses of the Body family consecrate him with jars of nectar.

When the consecration has been performed, one should cause the empowerment to take place: one should cause the Body-Vajra to enter a moon-maṇḍala on one's own forehead and recite this: "The glorious Holder of the Body-Vajra is realized as the indivisibility of the three vajras."
May the Body-Vajra today grant me the state of empowerment.
May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, who are meditated upon as indivisible from the three vajras,
grant me today the state of empowerment, O Vajra-Body holders!

Thus is the empowerment of the body. Likewise, at the throat is a sun-maṇḍala transformed from the syllable *repha* (*ra*). Above that is a red eight-petalled lotus transformed from the syllable *āḥ*. From that is emanated Vāgvajra with Prajñā, red in color, with faces that are red, white, and black. He holds a lotus, a vajra, and a wheel in his right hands, and a jewel, a bell, and a sword in his left. Having visualized the space-element as being completely filled by him after he has been emanated, and having performed the teaching of the Dharma for those beings to be disciplined by Vāgvajra, one should again establish him in front of oneself and request the consecration with this mantra: "May the Vāgvajras consecrate me."

Then, having visualized oneself being consecrated by the goddesses of the Vākkula with jars of nectar, one should perform the empowerment of speech (*vāgadhiṣṭhāna*). Having placed the Speech-Vajra (*vāgvajra*) within the solar mandala, one should utter this: "May the glorious Holder of the Speech-Vajra, who is meditated upon as the indivisible nature of the three vajras, grant me today the state of empowerment of the Speech-Vajra."
May the Buddhas situated in the [four] directions, meditated upon as inseparable from the three garments,
grant me today the state of empowerment, O Vajra of Speech!
Thus, O goddess, there is nothing more.
Having sprinkled [it] in the Vimalaprabhā, this is the consecration of speech.

In the practice of the empowerment of the mind (*cittādhiṣṭhāna*), one should visualize a blue lunar disc of Rāhu at the heart. Upon that, one visualizes a drop (*bindu*), which transforms into a five-pronged vajra, which in turn transforms into the Mind-Vajra (*cittavajra*) together with his consort. He is black in color, with faces that are black, white, and red; he holds a vajra, a wheel, and a lotus in his right hands, and a bell, a jewel, and a sword in his left hands. Having emanated him, one visualizes the entire expanse of space filled by him. After teaching the Dharma to those beings who are to be disciplined by the Mind-Vajra, one should re-establish him in front of oneself and request the empowerment.
"May all the Mind-Vajra deities consecrate me.
Then, having visualized oneself being consecrated by the goddesses of the Mind-Vajra family, one should perform the empowerment.
Having placed the Mind-Vajra within the mandala of Rāhu, one should utter this: "The glorious Holder of the Mind-Vajra is meditated upon as inseparable from the three vajras."
May the Vajra-Mind today perform the empowerment for me.
May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, who are meditated upon as indivisible from the three vajras,
grant me today the state of empowerment, O holders of the mind-vajra.

Having thus performed the empowerment of the mind, the yogi should then maintain the ego-identification (*ahaṅkāra*) as a single unity with the thought: "I am of the nature of the body, speech, and mind of all the Tathāgatas. This is the rule.

Likewise, for the Prajñā, there is the syllable *ho* at the navel, the syllable *svā* at the secret place, and the syllable *ha* at the location of the uṣṇīṣa; this is the method (*upāya*) of the three families by way of the nature of the seminal essence (*śukra*).

"The six families are the nature (*dharmatā*) of the seminal essence (*śukra*) of the wisdom-consorts (*prajñā-rajas*). Thus, the subsequent supplication and consecration must be performed according to the procedure taught in the "Chapter on Consecration" (*Abhiṣeka-paṭala*).
The rule is that whatever was not mentioned therein must all be performed by this present method.
Now, the locations of the *ahaṃkāra* (ego-sense) starting with "void" (*śūnya*) are described by the words beginning with "void":

just as here, at the end of death for all sentient beings, the aggregates (*skandha*) of the time of death become void, so too are the locations of the human aggregates and *ahaṃkāra* of the yogins described, for the purpose of relinquishing them and for the purpose of accomplishing the aggregates of the deity.
The rule is: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the diamond of the wisdom of emptiness."

Now, just as the body of the embryo and the infant is produced through the five aggregates (*skandhas*) according to their respective origins, so too is the production of the body of the deity in the form of the five aspects—the mirror and so forth—within the mandala.

Regarding that, the rule for the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the pure *dharmadhātu*. Thus, in the state of the *dharmadhātu* within emptiness, during the occasion of the triple-vajra.

Thus, regarding the passion for the worship of knowledge (jñānapūjānurāga) which is about to be described, it should be stated here that—just as for a child there is the piercing of the ears and so forth, and at marriage the taking of the hand—there is the cultivation of passion for the worship of knowledge up to the limit of sixteen years; likewise, at that time, one should say, "I am of the nature of that [reality]. This is the Lord's rule concerning the stage of generation (utpattikrama).

Now, all the channels (*nāḍikā*) of the wheels are described according to the purity of the deities: the Dharma wheel arises in the heart by means of the eight vases and [the goddesses] beginning with Dhūmā; and the sixteen-spoked Sahaja wheel is established on the head of the Buddha by means of the Vidyās.
[The deities are] red and white, [holding] a sword and a jewel.
There is no "non-existence" of beings; thus it is not so.
In that regard,
there are no aggregates of name or consecration.
"The bases are being stated"; there is no [term] ending in -tya here.
Oṃ,
excellent purity,
O pledge of the family!

In the [relevant] chapter, verse: The great section on the generation of the life-force deity; at the throat is the enjoyment wheel with thirty-two [petals] occupied by the bodhisattvas and others; and at the navel is the emanation wheel with sixty-four [petals] occupied by Bhīmā and the other goddesses.
Regarding the passage beginning with "In the throat by the jars," and so forth:
here, the heart-cakra, which has eight spokes, is purified together with the eight jars [representing] smoke and the other [substances]; that itself is the Dharma-cakra.

By means of these eight—the four vidyās, Locanā and the others, and the four Buddhas, Vairocana and the others—there are sixteen through the division of body and nature; thus, the sixteen-spoked cakra on the head is purified. That itself is established as the innate (*sahaja*). This is because it was not explicitly mentioned [previously].
The pure *uṣṇīṣa*-cakra is purified by the four— the Dharma-conch, the Dharma-cintāmaṇi, the Dharma-gaṇḍī, and the Kalpa-tree;
the *saṃbhoga*-cakra has thirty-two spokes and is purified by the thirty-two Bodhisattvas and others,
namely the twelve sense-bases (*āyatana*) and the four Wrathful Ones, totaling thirty-two through the division of wisdom and method.

At the navel is the Nirmāṇacakra with sixty-four spokes, purified by the sixty-four [deities] beginning with Bhīma, multiplied by the eight serpents (vasu), as well as by the eight beginning with Cāmuṇḍā; and the Guhyacakra is purified by the eight beginning with Glāsya.

The wheel of karma at the joints of the arms and legs consists of ninety times sixty-four [units] and is presided over by the gods and the Cūḍā-nāgas; that which is called the wheel of action (*kriyā*) belongs to the kings, while the joints of the fingers and toes belong to Śrī Vajrī.

O Lord of Men, through the purification of time (*kālaśuddhi*), there is the division of years, months, and so forth; the form of the mind is not the sun, for the Mother of the Universe (*Viśvamātā*) is pure by virtue of her daily power.
In the twelve joints of the arms and legs, the *karmacakra* is purified by three hundred and sixty deities;

it is purified by these sixteen *nāgas* and *cundās* through the division of bodily parts in the joints of the finger-phalanges, which is called the *kriyācakra*. This is the rule for the purification of the cakras.
Now, the further purification of the central figures (*nāyaka*) and others is stated, beginning with "The glorious vajra," and so forth.
Here, "time" refers to the external and internal wheel of the zodiac signs beginning with Capricorn (*makara*), consisting of twelve parts and comprising cause and effect.

Among these, five are causal factors (*hetu-dharma*), seven are both resultant and causal factors (*phala-hetu-dharma*), and those consisting of afflictive factors (*kleśa-dharma*) are resultant factors (*phala-dharma*) characterized by suffering; these are as described in the chapter on the world-system (*lokadhātu-paṭala*).

Through the purity of those causal and resultant phenomena, through the purity of the purity of time, and through the purity of the cessation of cause and effect, the Vajrī, the Lord of the Maṇḍala, is the Kālacakra who is completely pure.
This shall be explained in what follows regarding the distinctions of years, months, and so forth:

he is the form of the mind, the completely pure mind; he is not the sun, which has the characteristic of the saṃsāric mind, nor is he the aggregate of consciousness mounted upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Because of the influence of each day, the Mother of the Universe is pure;
for just as there are twelve zodiac signs in a year through the division of months, so too there are twelve zodiac signs in each individual day through the division of risings.
In this way, Wisdom (Prajñā) is also purified by the cessation of the twelve links [of dependent origination].

Herein, those dharmas of the three vehicles constitute the seal; the eighty-four thousand aggregates of dharma and the deities are sealed by the Buddha-seal; and the fourfold Saṅgha, together with its attendants, [is likewise sealed].
The six-syllable [mantra] is threefold; there is no [mantra] consisting of eight [syllables] such as *lāsya* and so forth.
O fierce one, there is no wheel in the junctions of the fierce states of being.
The body is black;
there is no cause, nor are there the seven fruits, nor is there karma.
There is no "wheel of cessation" through divisions of months;
there is no "purification day by day."
And because wisdom is pure, that which is there becomes pure here; therefore, regarding the three vehicles, within these three vehicles,
there is no [existence] of his aggregates.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the sealing of the monk in the ritual of accomplishment (*sādhanā*): thus, the Saṅgha has the monk as its precursor; just as the Dharma has the Dharma as its precursor, so too the assembly of Bodhisattvas and wrathful deities has the Buddha as its precursor.
Thus, in the maṇḍala, the rule is that the leader is the inconceivable Cittavajra, and the female leader is Viśvamātā, whose nature is the gnosis of emptiness. || 102 ||

[2812] Now, the purification of smoke and the others is described: Smoke and the rest are purified by wind and reside in the lotus of one’s own heart and at the navel-cakra. Rudra, together with his wife and the hosts of Māras, resides at the soles of the feet of the Lord; likewise, Māra, Śaṅkha, Gaṇḍī, Maṇi, and Druma, as well as the Kumbhas with the Kāyavajra and others, and the jars of the eight nectars, along with the Jaya and Vijaya jars, are purified by the bodhicitta and so forth. || 103 ||
Regarding the passage beginning with "smoke" (*dhūma*) and so forth:

here, within the heart-lotus, there are eight channels (*nāḍī*) that serve as the support for the *samāna* and other vital winds. Through these, the divine [channels] beginning with smoke—ranging from black to radiant—are purified.
By means of the *avadhūtī* and *śaṅkhinī*, which consist of the digits (*kalā*) and the point (*bindu*), they are purified through the restraint of the ten winds.
Rudra is pure on the sole of the left foot through the destruction of the four afflictions; Māra is pure on the sole of the right foot through the destruction of the host of Māras;
Śaṅkha is pure through the destruction of the obscurations of the body.
The gong is pure through the destruction of the obscuration of speech;
the jewel is pure through the destruction of the obscuration of mind;
the wish-fulfilling tree is pure through the destruction of the obscuration of knowledge.

And by means of the body-vajra and so forth, as well as the two jars with the limbs of the eight nectars; here, through the cessation of marrow, the two jars are purified according to the division of left and right,
and thus it should be understood everywhere according to the division of left and right.
Likewise, by the cessation of blood, there are two jars;
similarly, by the flow of urine, there are two jars;
and likewise, by the flow of excrement, there are two jars.
Thus, the *jayaghaṭa* is [filled] with the emission of semen and the *vijayaghaṭa* with the emission of menses;
these are the eight vessels, or alternatively, the pure skull-bowls. 103.

Now, the purification of the Buddhas is described: Amoghasiddhi is the formative factor (*saṃskāra*); Vimalamaṇikara is sensation (*vedanā*); Amitābha is perception (*saṃjñā*); and Cakrī is indeed form (*rūpa*). They are purified by blood, urine, and feces. The six goddesses are purified by the [six] elements; the Bodhisattvas by the objects and subjects of the senses; the five seals (*mudrās*) by the [five] powers; and furthermore, the other five wrathful deities (*krodhas*) by the [five] faculties (*indriyas*). ||104||
Here, when the conventional phenomenon has ceased, those other [factors] such as formations (saṃskāra) and so forth remain;
thus, through the purification of formations, Amoghasiddhi is the Vimalamaṇikara, and Ratnasaṃbhava is feeling (vedanā) through the destruction of the obscuration of formations.
The word "ca" has the sense of conjunction;
thus, Amitābha is the designation for the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha),
and "Cakrī" refers to Vairocana.
Furthermore, these [deities] beginning with Akṣobhya are as follows:

"Śaśī" refers to semen (*śukra*); "Bala" refers to flesh, blood, urine, and feces. Through these being purified and free from obscuration, the five aggregates (*skandha*) beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) become purified.
Thus, there are six goddesses: Viśvamātā, Vajradhātvīśvarī, Tārā, and Acittā.
The moon is composed of the measures (mātrās) of black, white, and blind.
There is no "and," nor is there "thus," nor is there "duality," nor is there "flesh."
In this chapter [of the Śrīparamādya],
the great summary on the generation of the deities of the vital breaths (prāṇadevatā): Pāṇḍarā, Māmakī, and Locanā.
"By the elements" means that by the elements of gnosis, space, wind, fire, water, and earth, when they are restrained, the other elements become purified; thus,
"by those who have consumed the poison of sense objects."

Regarding the objects such as form and so forth, through the purification of the subjects—the eyes and so forth—those objects such as form are distinct, and those subjects—the eyes and so forth—are purified. Together with the Form-Vajras and others, there are the Bodhisattvas Kṣitigarbha and the rest, who are "pure seals. Regarding the statement "the five Wrathful Ones are pure by means of the powers" (*balaiḥ*):

the powers of faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom arise through the destruction of the obscurations of lack of faith, lack of vigor, lack of mindfulness, lack of concentration, and lack of wisdom; they are pure by means of those powers.

Furthermore, the wrathful kings Uṣṇīṣa, Vighnāntaka, Prajñāntaka, Padmāntaka, and Yamāntaka are indeed pure; likewise, Sumbharāja, Nīladaṇḍa, Ṭakkirāja, Acala, and Mahābala are the five [deities] associated with the organs of action— the Blessed One’s speech, hands, feet, and anus— by way of the activities of the organs of action.
Together with Raudrākṣī and the others, they are completely pure. || 104 ||

Situated upon the lotus petals: by means of the *ghaṭīs* of the Sun at the ascendant, Cāmuṇḍā and the others [arise] from the eight [petals]; the Daityas and the rest [arise] from the months of the Sun; the *nāḍīs* situated on the lotus petals are equal in number to the breaths (*śvāsa*).

The *Nāgas* and *Caṇḍas* are in the secret place (*guhya*), purified by twice the number of kings (*nṛpati*, i.e., sixteen) *nāḍīs*. Thus, these [deities], beginning with Icchā, are purified through their bodily functions according to the influence of the qualities of *prakṛti*. || 105 ||

Cāmuṇḍā is purified by the eight watches (*yāmas*); those situated on the lotus petals are purified by the solar ascendants (*lagnas*); the four beginning with Bhīmā are purified by the sixty jars; and the others, beginning with Cakrī and the Bhīmās, are purified by the exhaustion of the coverings of the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*) through the purification of the void-leaves. The deities beginning with Daitya—namely Nairṛti, Vāyu, Agni, Ṣaṇmukha, Samudra, Gaṇendra, Dākṣa, Brahmā, Rudra, Yakṣa, Viṣṇu, and Yama—are twelve in number; they are purified by the exhaustion of the coverings named after the months of Caitra, Vaiśākha, Jyeṣṭha, Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, Bhādra, Āśvina, Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, Pauṣa, Māgha, and Phālguna.

Of those [deities], the three hundred and sixty residing on the lotus petals—endowed with dance (*lāsya*) and so forth—are purified through the exhaustion of the enclosure of three hundred and sixty days, which corresponds to the number of breaths in a *nāḍī*.
Those others are the deities and those others are the goddesses of the petals; thus they are pure.

The *nāgas* and *caṇḍas* in the secret place are purified by the *nāḍīs* multiplied by twice the number of kings (thirty-two); their twofold nature arises from the distinction between wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*).
Regarding the phrase "thus, the desires and so forth":
here, there are thirty-six desires (*icchā*) and thirty-six counter-desires (*pratīcchā*), as previously stated. By virtue of the qualities of *prakṛti*, they are purified through bodily actions;
through the exhaustion of the obscurations of bodily action, those other desires and so forth become pure. || 105 ||

By means of his hair, all the Siddhas are present; by his body hairs, the multitude of spirits residing in the realms of existence; by his principles (tattvas), the weapons of the Lord; by the elements (dhātus) under the influence of the qualities of nature, the external mudrās; and by the adamantine internal mudrās, which reside in the heart and upon the moon-crested head of the glorious Vajrin—the Mother of the Universe, who pervades the threefold states of existence through the yoga of imperishable gnosis. || 106 ||
"O sir, [it is] the month of Bhādrapada," thus [he says], adding this further.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is said: "Those others are perfected by means of the hair; all are without obscuration by means of the body hairs numbering three and a half crores. In the cremation ground, the state of being the elements is thus purified. Likewise, those others are perfected;

'others' refers to the elements, which are pure by virtue of the twenty-four principles (*tattva*) being free from obscuration. The weapons, such as the vajra and so forth, belonging to the Lord are pure due to the absence of the twenty-fourfold primordial nature (*prakṛti*)."
Regarding the phrase "by the power of the qualities of nature" (*prakṛtiguṇavaśāt*):

"nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to the collection of elements beginning with earth; their "qualities" (*guṇa*) are the six objects. Through the destruction of the obscurations of these [objects], the other six external mudrās are purified by the six elements beginning with smell.

"By means of words" refers to the purification through the removal of obscurations by the body, speech, mind, and gnosis-vajras, characterized by the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (turyā).
Thus, the four internal mudrās—the pure body-mudrā and so forth—are purified; this is the "six-fold heart."
Abiding within the heart of the Maṇḍala Lord upon the moon is the glorious Vajrī,
the innate bliss, the supreme immutable;
she is Viśvamātā, the gnosis of emptiness in all its aspects, and the vision of the three times.
"Because of the destruction of the veil of conceptualization regarding the bliss of cessation"— thus,

the aggregates and so forth, as they exist within the three realms of existence, are pure in every way and at all times; this is the Blessed One’s rule that they are purified through the destruction of all veils.
Thus, the thorough knowledge of existence (*bhava*) is here called *nirvāṇa*.

In this context, the thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*) is the vision of the three realms of existence (*tribhava*) as they truly are throughout the three times—past, future, and present. That very [knowledge] occurs simultaneously for the perfectly awakened ones (*saṃbuddha*) through the destruction of the obscurations of the three realms and the cessation of cause and fruit, by means of the power of the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of the aspects of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*).

Neither Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, nor Bodhisattvas possess a simultaneous and thorough knowledge of the three realms of existence as they truly are throughout the three times within the *sopadhi-nirvāṇadhātu*, in the manner that Bodhisattvas do due to their possession of only a minute residue of obscurations; likewise, it is established that the Lords of Wrath (Krodhendras) also possess mastery over the ten stages (*daśabhūmīśvaratva*). || 106 ||

Now, the arising of the pure *dharmakāya* and so forth is described: From the glorious *śuddha* [body] indeed arises the *dharmakāya*; from the *dharma* [body] arises the *sambhogakāya*; and from the *bhoga* [body], the *nirmāṇakāya* arises for the Lord of Jinas who acts for the benefit of all sentient beings.

The fourth state is deep sleep; moreover, another is the waking state due to the division of the bodies. Thus, the mind dwells in four ways within the limbs of living beings according to the divisions of the bodies. (107)
O Śrī Śuddhāditya and others,

here in the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), dependently arisen phenomena are momentary and characterized by arising and ceasing; due to the non-comprehension of existence and the latencies of ignorance, the four states beginning with the fourth (*turyā*) occur for those in cyclic existence.
Among those, the mind dwells in four ways through the divisions of the body; it dwells in four ways within the limbs of living beings.

Here, at the time of conception during the entry into the womb, there is the state of the emission of semen, which is the fourth; and that, according to conventional truth, is called "great bliss" (*mahāsukha*).
That very non-dual gnosis arising from the syllable Śrī is, conventionally, the Pure Body (śuddhakāya), meaning the Innate Body (sahajakāya);
from that comes the Dharma Body (dharmakāya), characterized by the state of deep sleep;
and from that, the Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya), characterized by dreaming.
Therefore, the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is characterized by the state of being awake.
Due to the completion of its activity, or from the time of the departure of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it is further said to be fourfold externally.
In this way, the division of bodies occurs within the mandala.

Because the Lord of Jinas acts for the benefit of all sentient beings through the destruction of the obscurations of conventional reality, his mind dwells upon the knowledge of others' minds within the three realms; and because he has fully understood existence, his mind dwells upon the recollection of former abodes. || 107 ||
Sro mudrā; Ga. lacks "viśuddhā"; Bho. reads "tathā pūrvavāsā."

[Chapter, verses 106–109] The Great Chapter on the Generation of the Life-Wind Deities (prāṇadevatotpāda). Now, the activity of the four bodies is described: The mind indeed has the power to produce emanation and enjoyment through the faculties of body and speech; in the [body of] perfect enjoyment (saṃbhoga), it enters into unperceived thought by the force of its qualities; and in the dharma-body, it enters into sleep.

Here, at the time of day and night, it attains bliss in the pure [body] at the end of the three emissions of the drop (bindu). Therefore, that must be meditated upon daily by the yogi for the sake of the imperishable meaning. (108)
"Regarding the passage beginning with *nirmāṇa* (emanation) and so forth:

here, for transmigrating beings, in the state of emanation—that is, during the waking state—the agent of experience prevails with respect to objects by means of the body, speech, and sense organs acting as instruments.

In the state of enjoyment—that is, during the dream state—it "enters into thought under the influence of qualities," which means under the influence of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of objects, directed toward non-material [mental] objects not previously perceived."

In the *dharmakāya*, during the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), one enters into sleep; the meaning is that the mind becomes devoid of the sensory faculties. In the pure *turya* state, one attains bliss—at this time, whether by day or by night.

*Samaya* means time; at that time, when sexual union (*maithuna*) is performed, at one single moment—at the end of the three emissions of the *bindu*, in the instant of the innate (*sahaja*)—one attains great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

Since reality (*tattva*) is [attained] through the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), therefore it must be meditated upon day and night by the yogi for the sake of the "unfallen" meaning—that is, for the sake of the non-emission instant—as will be explained by the rule of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*).
Thus, when the obscured phenomenon (*sāvaraṇadharma*) is restrained, the unobscured phenomenon (*nirāvaraṇadharma*) arises; this is the principle, being devoid of arising and passing away. || 108 ||

Now, the purification of the *pratyālīḍha* posture and so forth is described: the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) occurs in the left, and likewise contraction in the right; that which is the *pratyālīḍha* posture, as well as the *samapada* and the other *ālīḍha*, arise from the movement of the fire-constituent (*agni*).

The *vaiśākha* stance, the circle (*maṇḍala*), the excellent *lalita* posture, the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), and the vajra posture (*vajrāsana*)—these are the movements in space and so forth, occurring in five ways according to the even and uneven courses of the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*). || 109 ||
"Vāma," and so forth.
Here, when the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) occurs in the left channel (*vāmanāḍī*) for those transmigrating in *saṃsāra*, then contraction occurs in the right.
The vital breath itself is also the deity of the mantra.

By that extension of the left and contraction of the right, the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) occurs in the left; likewise, the contraction on the right is called the *pratyālīḍha* stance of the mantra-deity. The other, the *samapada* stance, is the *ālīḍha* stance respectively, according to the movement of fire—that is, according to the movement of the central channel (*madhyamā*).
Simultaneously, there is the equal step in both channels.
From the movement of the sun—that is, from the movement through the right channel—there is the contraction of the left, whereby the *ālīḍha* stance arises.

In this way, the *vaiśākha* stance, the *maṇḍala*, the *lalitapada*, the *padmāsana*, and the *vajrāsana* occur respectively in the left channel, the right channel, or in space and so forth, that is, in the sphere of space (*ākāśamaṇḍala*), as the mind.
There is contraction,
due to its activity.
That maṇḍala is the *khyapada*;
"and the vajrāsana" is not present.
In the *Vimalaprabhā*, the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇasañcāra*) is the *vaiśākhapada*.
Movement within the wind mandala is the maṇḍala step;
movement within the fire mandala is the graceful step;
movement within the water mandala is the lotus posture.
The movement upon the circle of the earth is the "vajra-seat.

Thus, the fivefold movement of the vital wind (prāṇavāyu) in both even and uneven courses—when purified by that—results in the purification of the seats and positions of the deities through the absence of trembling; this is the rule.
Such is the second [chapter], concerning the accomplishment of the speech of one born [in this way]. 109.

Thus ends the third major section, "The Generation of the Life-Wind Deities," in the Vimalaprabhā, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja*, which follows the root tantra, within the chapter on the Means of Achievement (*sādhana*).
The Great Chapter on the Sadhana of the Arising Stage: Having prostrated to the Imperishable One who holds the sixteenfold half-and-half drops, his means—the perfect Binduyoga—is now proclaimed.
The Caṇḍālī, resembling lightning and fire, resides within the navel-cakra, which has slain the nine serpents and contains the wisdom-essence of the syllable *Ho*.

Awakened by the splendor of gnosis in the presiding deity of Cācikā and the others, Locanā burns Vairocana and the rest at the navel, O Lord of Men; having burned all [the senses] beginning with the eyes, she flows from Sucandra as the one who is the Vajrin in the form of a drop at the head. (110)
By the words "the Caṇḍāla," and so forth:
here, in the entire generation stage (*utpattikrama*), the perfection of the effect is the *maṇḍalarājāgrī*;
the perfection of speech is the *karmarājāgrī*, because it sets in motion the activity of the action-faculties (*karmendriya*).
The yoga of the drop produced from the drop of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*):
