Having first well-trained a girl of noble family, sixteen years of age, adorned with beauty and youth, and having consecrated her, one should begin the practice.
One should place the passion-elements of body, speech, and mind on the forehead and other locations;
then, with "Svāhā," one should purify the lotus at the secret place and the great uṣṇīṣa.
The syllable *hūṃ* is endowed with a vajra;
by means of the syllable *āḥ*, there is an eight-petaled lotus. Thus, the lotus together with the vajra arises from the cause of the movement of wisdom (*prajñā*).
The reading "consisting of the channels of the twelve zodiac signs" does not exist; nor is the word "he said" present. [End of chapter, verses 109–110.

In the section on the Great Summary of the Sādhana of the Utpannakrama: one should visualize one's own five-pronged vajra by means of the syllable *HŪṂ*, and in its center, an eight-petaled lotus by means of the syllable *ĀḤ*.
One should arrange.
Having thus formed the vajra together with its lotus,
the yogi should place the lotus while uttering "hūṃ phaṭ," thereby bearing the pride of Vajradhara.
Having established the linga in the bhaga, one should not emit the bodhicitta;
rather, one should meditate upon the image of the Buddha throughout the entire threefold world without exception.
The blazing Caṇḍālī at the navel burns the five Tathāgatas;
Locanā and the others [the sense organs] such as the eyes are also burned, and then the moon, "I," flows forth.
Nectar in the form of semen flows in the form of drops;
this is known as Binduyoga, which sustains the half of a half of the sixteen drops.
Akala is beyond time, the holder of the pinnacle of the fourth dhyāna;
he is renowned as Sūkṣmayoga, having ascended from the state of immobility and so forth.
This Śaṅkhinī is the Mahāmudrā; she is celebrated as Caṇḍālī.
That which is Ḍombinī at the path of the navel is Avadhūtī, the nose of man.
The vital breath consists of five rays and carries the five mandalas;
it is known as a mustard seed at the tip of the nose, and that is remembered as prāṇāyāma.

The thorough knowledge of the three realms of existence is understood when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is mastered; that [knowledge] occurs through the withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*) upon a mustard seed, the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), in space, in the nose, and in its region, wherein the entire collection of elements—including all that is moving and unmoving—is seen in its entirety as having the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyalakṣaṇa*), wherever the mind is fixed.
At the end of the *nimitta*, upon that line, the yogi should contemplate the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings, as well as meditation and the rest, within it.

Thus is the rule in the Root Tantra; here, however, it is stated in brief. Therefore, it should be understood in accordance with the Root Tantra—this is the rule of the Blessed Mañjuśrī. Regarding "Caṇḍālī in the navel-cakra is the nine-slaying serpent":

here, at the navel, the wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) consists of the "nine-slaying serpent," which is composed of seventy-two channels, composed of the channels of the twelve zodiac signs (*rāśi*), and composed of the channels of the sixty mandalas.

In that [state] where the nine-fold serpent has been slain, which has Cācikā and others as its presiding deities, which has the syllable *HŪṂ* as its core of gnosis (*jñāna*), and which is presided over by the Gnosis-Vajra—the Caṇḍālī, resembling lightning and fire, is awakened by the light of gnosis.

Conventionally, "gnosis" is desire; its "light" is the fire of desire. Being awakened by that fire of desire, she burns Vairocana and the others who reside in the five mandalas within the *nirmāṇacakra* at the navel. On the left and right, she burns Locanā and the others, as well as the eyes and other sense organs, and even the objects such as form; because the mind grasps the *dharmadhātu*, there is the non-functioning of all [senses], which is what is meant by "burning."

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is said: "Having thus burned all [the elements] down to Sucandra, that which flows from the seed of birth and awakening (*janmabodhibīja*) at the head is the syllable *haṃ*, in the form of a drop (*bindu*), the adventitious semen; this is the Vajrin, meaning the *bodhicitta*.
[It flows] from the head to the throat, from the throat to the heart, from the heart to the navel, and from the navel to the secret lotus. (110)

Furthermore, the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū), having emanated the entire wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*)—which resides within the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) of wisdom and is endowed with various ornaments like [the reflection] in a mirror—by means of the drop (*bindu*), purifies the threefold existence (*bhava*) consisting of desire, form, and formlessness in succession; thereafter, by the flame of gnosis, he should draw forth the entirety of the three worlds all at once. 111.
That very lotus is called the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Likewise, the lotuses of the navel, heart, throat, forehead, and crown are called the source of phenomena of wisdom.
Thus, being in a state of melting, it becomes the *kāyabindu* at the secret place, the *vāgbindu* at the navel, the *cittabindu* at the heart, and the *jñānabindu* at the throat.
Thus, the *bodhicitta* situated in the *prajñā-dharmodayā* is again said to have "spread" (*sphārita*) in the manner it came, that is, as it was gone.

Just as it came from the forehead through the distinctions of *ānanda* and so forth, or through the distinctions of *vicitra* and so forth, until it was filled with the fifteen digits of the moon; likewise, having gone upward to the forehead through the distinctions of *niḥspanda* and so forth, its stainlessness (*vaimalya*) becomes spread. By means of that drop (*bindu*), which is stainless, the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*)—endowed with various ornaments, like a reflection in a mirror, equal to a *pratisenā*, and pertaining to the three times—is the Self-Arisen One (*svayambhū*). Through this yoga of the drop, the subtle yoga (*sūkṣmayoga*) arose.

Thus, having purified the threefold existence— namely desire, form, and the formless— in due order, that is, by means of the sequence of the arising of the drops (*bindu*) of body, speech, and mind; afterwards,
"by the flame of gnosis" indeed means by the rays of immutable bliss.
"Entirety of the three worlds" means that the three realms (*traidhātuka*) are to be drawn forth at once; this is simultaneous knowledge of the three times (*traikālyajñāna*).

In the yoga of the deity, there is the radiation of the form of the mandala-circle of the deity, and for those in cyclic existence (*saṃsārin*), there is the radiation of sons and daughters from the *bodhicitta*.

Thus, for those born from a womb, the perfection of body, speech, mind, and gnosis occurs through the sixteen-year ritual procedure; for deities, by the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*); and for Buddhas, by the power of the four liberations (*vimokṣa*). This is according to both the conventional and ultimate truths. || 111 ||

Now, the recitation of mantras and so forth within the inner self is described: The recitation of the Body-Vajra and the others proceeds through the threefold movement beginning with the moon, the sun, and so forth; through the six [limbs] beginning with withdrawal (pratyāhāra), there is the yoga of body, speech, and mind in the well-golden lotus. Through the [four] joys (ānanda) and so forth, this meditation on the equal flavor within the hollow of the vajra-lotus is the Three-Vajras. In the lotus of wisdom, the meditation on the mind-drop by the power of innate bliss shall be the Unstruck (anāhata). || 112 ||
By the words "Candra" and so forth:
here in this body, "Candra" refers to the left channel (*nāḍī*), and "Āditya" refers to the right channel.
"Ādi" refers to the collection of vowels beginning with *a*, which is the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the left [channel].

The group of consonants beginning with *ka* is in the right channel-petal [as stated in verses 110–113]. This is the great chapter on the means for the practice of the completion stage (*utpannakrama*), concerning the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇasaṃcāra*).
Regarding the phrase "having gone to the threefold course":
"The vital breath that has gone to the left course is called the recitation of the body-vajra (*kāyavajrajāpa*)."
The vital breath (prāṇa) moving through the right channel is called the recitation of speech (vāgjāpa);
the vital breath moving through the middle channel is called the recitation of mind (cittajāpa).
Through the cessation of these, the unstruck sound (anāhata), the speech of the Omniscient One, arises.

Therefore, this six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga) should be cultivated by means of withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) and the others, according to the statement: "Withdrawal of the senses, as well as meditation (dhyāna), breath control (prāṇāyāma), concentration (dhāraṇā), recollection (anusmṛti), and meditative absorption (samādhi)— this is held to be the six-limbed yoga."

The meaning is that by practicing these [previously mentioned methods] and those to be described—namely, "the beautiful golden lotus" (in the navel-lotus) and the "union of body, speech, and mind"—there occurs the cessation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) which has moved through the three types of courses.

Then, from that cessation, by means of bliss and so forth—namely, bliss (*ānanda*), supreme bliss (*parama*), the special bliss (*virama*), and innate bliss (*sahaja*)—this meditation on the "three vajras," which consists of the union in equal flavor within the vajra and lotus due to non-emission, is the cessation of semen, feces, and urine.

Likewise, in the *Mūlatantra*: "One should always worship the *Kulikā* with the supreme central breath (*madhyamottamaśvāsa*) and scented water; one should worship the *Dūtīs* according to the specific times. This is the rule.

Then, when the mind-drop (*cittavindu*) is situated within the lotus of wisdom—the secret lotus—there arises, by virtue of innate bliss (*sahajasukha*), that is, by virtue of imperishable bliss (*akṣarasukha*), the unstruck meditation (*anāhatā bhāvanā*) for those whose vital essence flows upward (*ūrdhvaretas*). || 112 ||

Now, service (*sevā*) and the other stages are described: Service is performed by means of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth, by the oceans and the vajra, by the recitation of mantras (*jāpa*) and so forth, and by withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*) and so forth. Accomplishment (*upasiddhi*) occurs through the nectar born from the vajra-lotus. Meditation (*bhāvanā*) is the practice (*sādhana*) wherein one attains the state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) within the three vajras and the lotus, by means of bliss (*ānanda*) and the rest. Indeed, the great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*) arises when there is non-emission (*acyuta*) during union with wisdom (*prajñā*), through the subtle yoga (*sūkṣmayoga*). || 113 ||
"Sevā," and so forth.
Here, the beginner must first perform the *sevā* according to the "method of the means" (*sādhanavidhi*).
Regarding this, it is said: "The *sevā* [is performed] with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth."
Externally, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) consist of feces and so forth;

by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), cow's urine and the rest are included. By consuming these, service (*sevā*) is performed for the purpose of pleasing the deity. Internally, the five nectars are the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the five sense-faculties are meant as the five lamps. Their independent service consists in the renunciation of craving for the body and material things.
Through that service, the deities become bestowers of boons; it is not by consuming excrement and the like.

"By the vajras of the ocean-treasury" means indifference toward the enjoyment of body, indifference toward the enjoyment of speech, indifference toward the enjoyment of mind, and service characterized by indifference toward the bliss of emission; the meaning is the restraint of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) of body, speech, and mind.
"The deities become granters of boons through no effort, not through longing for the enjoyments of existence.
[This is stated] in the *Vimalaprabhā* regarding "by the recitation of mantras and so forth."
In this context, what is called "mantra-recitation" (japa) is the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇasaṃyama).

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the term "sādhanā," the yoga of exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*) is meant; through this constant service, the deities become granters of boons. This is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*): it is not by means of unrestrained breath or idle chatter that results are achieved. According to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), however, practices such as recitation with a rosary and the like should be performed for the sake of ordinary accomplishments (*sāmānyasiddhi*).
Now the *upasādhana* is described, beginning with "pratyāhāra" and so forth.

Here, "pratyāhāra" means this: for those wandering in saṃsāra, *āhāra* is the grasping of objects such as form by means of the senses, such as the eyes; the abandonment of that is called *pratyāhāra*.

In the empty image (*śūnyatābimba*), the grasping of other objects such as form by means of other [senses] such as the eye and flesh, etc., is the *upasādhana*. Likewise, meditation (*dhyāna*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and concentration (*dhāraṇā*) constitute the *upasādhana* through the non-emission of the nectar born from the vajra-lotus according to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*); and through the external emission of the deity according to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*). This is the accomplishment of the *upasādhana*.
Now, the *sādhana* is described, beginning with "Bliss" (*ānanda*), and so forth.

In this context, Ānanda, the practice of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) consists of the three drops (*bindu*) of body, speech, and mind reaching a state of flavor-unity (*samarasa*) within the lotus; this is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
The meaning is that the abiding of the drops occurs at the *hṛt* (heart), *nābhi* (navel), and *guhya* (secret place).
Such is the means of accomplishment.
Then, when the unchanging bliss arises through union with wisdom (*prajñā*), that indeed is the "great accomplishment" (*mahāsādhana*) by means of subtle yoga.
According to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), the "great accomplishment" is said to be the union of the semen above the *suṣumnā* channel.

Furthermore, according to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), the rule is that it is [visualized] as a mustard seed or the like at the tip of the nose within the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) of wisdom.
Thus is the great accomplishment (mahāsādhana). || 113 ||

Now, the service (*sevā*) and so forth are described according to the distinction of degrees such as "mild" (*mṛdu*) and so on: First, indeed, is the awakening to emptiness (*śūnyatābodhi*); then follows the gathering (*saṃgraha*) of the lunar drop (*candrabindu*); from that, the arising of the image (*bimba*); and thereafter, the placement of the protective syllables (*rakṣaranyāsa*) within the family of the supreme essence (*pravararasakula*). This is the common service (*sāmānyasevā*). The middling practice (*madhyama-sādhana*) consists of the ocean and the vajra; likewise, the means (*upāya*) here becomes fourfold, being mild or firm according to the limbs of the practice. (114)
"First," and so forth.

Here, in the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*), "first" refers to the realization of emptiness (*śūnyatābodhi*). At the end of death for living beings, due to the relinquishing of the aggregates (*skandha*) and the subsequent grasping of the aggregates belonging to the portion of rebirth, there is an intermediate interval; that single moment of emptiness in which the three realms of existence are seen as empty is what is called "emptiness."
"Khalu" means certainly;

"then, after that moment, the gathering of the moon-drop" (saṃgrahaścandrabindoḥ) refers here to the gathering, which is the taking up of the drops of semen by the *ālayavijñāna* within the mother's womb.

Then, from the grasping of semen (*śukra*) and so forth, there is what is called "the arising of the image" (*bimbotpatti*), which means the completion of the embryo after seven months, that is to say, the completion of the body.

Then, by the "families of excellent essences"—meaning the six aggregates (*ṣaṭskandha*)—there is the "arrangement of the letters" for the eyes and so forth, and the engagement with objects such as form (*rūpa*).
In this way, even in the practice of the deity (*devatāsādhana*), the beginner should meditate on that which consists of conceptual construction (*kalpanātmaka*).

This is the general service by means of the ocean and the vajras; it is the middling sādhana through the perfection of the vajras of body, speech, mind, and gnosis, and herein lies the means for the perfection of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
And both internally and externally,
O Bhagavan.
ka kha cha
Then,
by means of the concentration on the breath.
Because of its retention, [it is] by means of the *ga*, *ṇ*, *ḍ*, *r*, *d*, *g*, *b*, and so forth (*ihānandādyaṃ*).
And what is above?
Food.
And [the distinction between] weak and intense.
That is six.
There is no accomplishment of the body of the abode.
Thus ends the great chapter on the means of accomplishment of the stage of generation in the [third] chapter, verse—
It becomes fourfold:

in the limb of service (*sevāṅga*) and the limb of near-attainment (*upasādhanāṅga*), [the practitioner is] neither soft nor firm; likewise, in the limb of attainment (*sādhanāṅga*), there is the rule [of practice] until the limit of sixteen years.

In this context, one who has just developed hair is a *mṛdu* (tender) child; from the eruption of teeth until their falling out, one is a *madhyama* (middle) child; and from the falling out of the teeth, one is a *kumāra* (youth).
Furthermore, from the eruption of the teeth until the age of sixteen, one is "adolescent" (*prauḍha*), because of the capacity to produce sons and daughters;
thus, the yogin should meditate upon the fourfold limb of all deities according to this rule of worldly truth (*laukikasatya*).

Now, the accomplishment of the Buddha-image by means of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is described: here, first is the realization of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wherein nothing at all should be conceptualized in the darkness.

Then, "the gathering of the moon and the drop" refers to the perception of the signs beginning with smoke up to the point of the drop (*bindu*), as well as the arising of the *bimba* from that [drop].
From that drop, there is the vision of the universe and the arising of the *bimba*.
"By the families of the excellent flavors" means by the six unobscured aggregates (*skandhas*).
The "arrangement of syllables" (*akṣaranyāsa*) is the cessation of the limited aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth;
therefore, the distinction between the "mild" and other stages occurs through the attainment of the levels (*bhūmi*), until one becomes a master of the twelve levels.
Then: [one is] the knower of the meaning of the truths in twelve aspects and the knower of reality in sixteen aspects.
He who has awakened to the twentyfold aspects of enlightenment is the supreme omniscient one; such is the rule.

Now the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) is described: (from the *Nāmasaṃgīti*): Withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) is the Lord of Jinas (*jinendra*), which is tenfold; meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is Akṣobhya himself; breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is Khaḍgin, who is likewise tenfold; retention (*dhāraṇā*) is Ratnapāṇi;

mindfulness (*anusmṛti*) occurs in the *ḍombī* [mudrā] and is Kamaladhara; and the glorious absorption (*samādhi*) is Cakrin. Each one of these is further divided into five varieties, according to how they are differentiated by the vowels (*ādi*) and consonants (*kādi*).

By the words "withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*) and so forth, here "withdrawal" refers to the initial action; "Jinendra" (Lord of the Victors) is the aggregate of gnosis (*jñānaskandha*), and that aggregate of gnosis is tenfold according to the distinctions of its signs (*nimitta*): it is conceived through the distinctions of seeing smoke, mirage, fireflies, lamp, flame, moon, sun, Rāhu, the digit (*kalā*), and the point (*bindu*).

Dhyāna is indeed Akṣobhya; it is the tenfold aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), the unification of the ten [factors] consisting of objects and subjects within the Universal Image (*viśvabimba*).

Prāṇāyāma is also tenfold, known as Khaḍgī; it is the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), because of the state of being unified (*lolībhūta*) within the single [central channel] of the ten mandalas of the left and right [sides].
Furthermore, there are nine types of *dhāraṇā*, namely "Ratnapāṇi";

this refers to the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), which consists of ten types of *prāṇa-dhāraṇā* according to the distinction between the going and returning [of the breath] through the lotuses of the navel, heart, throat, forehead, and crown.
Likewise, in the *ḍombī* [mudrā], there is *anusmṛti*; and "Kamaladhara" refers to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), which is also tenfold.
And that recollection (*anusmṛti*) occurs in the *ḍombī* [cakra] within the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*) through the differentiation of the ten states of passion; thus,
the glorious Samāja is the "Wheel-Bearer" (*cakrī*), namely Vairocana, who is tenfold as the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) resulting from the cessation of the ten winds.
Thus said the Blessed One in the *Vimalaprabhā*: "Established in nirvāṇa, he is not carried away by the wind" means that each one is of five types;
here, each individual yoga is the carrier of the five maṇḍalas.
By means of cessations.

"By means of the vowels and consonants beginning with A and Ka," refers to the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through the left and right channels. Now, the characteristics of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the other [limbs] are described: Withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) is the non-engagement of the ten objects and their perceivers within the body. Wisdom (*prajñā*), reasoning (*tarka*), deliberation (*vicāra*), and passion (*rati*) constitute unwavering bliss; meditation (*dhyāna*) is also one-pointedness of mind. Breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is the two paths; it becomes the stumbling [of the breath] when the vital breath enters the middle channel. The entry of the breath into the *bindu* is indeed the cessation of both movements; retention (*dhāraṇā*) is one-pointedness of mind.
Regarding "pratyetyādi" and so forth:

here, "withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*) refers to the non-engagement of consciousness with the ten objects and subjects within the body through their connection, while the engagement with objects occurs by means of the other five types [of faculties], such as the eye;
likewise, "wisdom" (*prajñā*) is the illumination within that very same image.
"Reasoning" (tarka) refers to the apprehension of the object;
"investigation" (vicāra) refers to the purpose of determining it;
and "delight" (rati) refers to attachment to the image.
"Immovable bliss" (acalasukha) is the unification of the mind with the *bimba* (the reflection).
Thus, meditation (*dhyāna*) is tenfold here according to the distinction between the perceived and the perceiver.
"Breath control" (*prāṇāyāma*) refers to the two paths, namely the left and right channels.

Stumbling is the cessation [of the breath] and entry into the middle path; and that is tenfold due to the obstruction of the ten circles (*maṇḍala*). Here, "in the drop" means the entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into the forehead;
"struck down in both movements" means being devoid of going and coming.
The retention of the vital breath at the forehead is called "one-pointedness of mind."

Indeed, when there is the vision of the Caṇḍālī within the body and in the sky, there is *anusmṛti*; and by virtue of the non-emission of bliss consisting of wisdom and means, there is *samādhi* in the gnosis-image (*jñānabimba*).

This practice of the Lord of the Universe may be threefold according to the divisions of "mild" and so forth. There are three *mudrās*, each having three measures, according to the three types of movement: the *karmamudrā*, the *saṃkalpamudrā*, and the *divyamudrā*.

The vision of the Caṇḍālī in the expanse of the three worlds is said to be the tenfold *anusmṛti*; it should be understood as consisting of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), through which the object of knowledge and the knowing consciousness become unified.
Due to the power of immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*), this is *samādhi* within the image of gnosis (*jñānabimba*).
That [non-violence] is also tenfold due to the absence of [killing] living beings and so forth;

thus, this practice of the six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga) for the sake of Kālacakra, the Sustainer of the Universe, may be threefold according to the distinctions of "soft" (mṛdu) and so on, consisting of the three mudrās and the three measures (trimātra).

"By way of the three types of movement" means that here, the immovable movement (*akṣara-gati*) of the *bodhicitta* is the soft degree, while the vibrating movement (*spanda-gati*) is the middling degree. "By the fivefold division" means that here each conjunction results in five mandalas. "Of the *a*-group and *ka*-group" means by the cessation of the perfectly circulating vital breath (*prāṇa*) of the vowels and consonants on the left and right [channels].
O, as previously stated in the chapter [of] the verse...

The Great Chapter on the Means for Accomplishing the Arisen Stage (*utpannakrama-sādhanamahoddeśa*): The movement of the non-pulsating (*niḥspanda*) is the superior; thus, the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) bestows the bliss of the unchanging (*akṣara*), the wisdom-seal (*jñānamudrā*) bestows the bliss of pulsation (*spanda*), and the great seal (*mahāmudrā*) bestows the bliss of the non-pulsating. Thus, the meditation on the three seals has been taught by the Blessed One within the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*). Therefore, the six-limbed yoga should be meditated upon by the yogi for the sake of attaining Buddhahood. || 117 ||

Now the fruit of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the other [limbs] is stated: By withdrawal, O Lord of Men, the yogi becomes devoid of sense objects and is empowered by all mantras; he attains the five superknowledges (*abhijñāna*). Purified by the yoga of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and purified by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*)—being freed from the moon and sun—he is honored as a Bodhisattva. Through the power of retention (*dhāraṇā*), he enters the One Possessing Ten Powers (*daśabala*), which destroys the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth. (118)

"Having returned," and so forth: here, when the yoga is purified through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) by means of the stable image (*bimba*), then he is empowered by all mantras; he grants boons and so forth with his speech, and becomes a possessor of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñāna*), O Lord of Men, "purified by the yoga of meditation. Here, when one becomes one whose eyes do not blink, then one possesses the divine eye; likewise, one becomes possessed of the divine ear, purified by meditation. "Purified by breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*)" means: here, when the yogi is devoid of the paths of the sun and moon and always causes the flow through the central channel (*madhyamā*), then, being purified by breath-control, he is worshipped as a Bodhisattva—meaning he is praised. He enters the "Ten-Powered One" (*daśabala*), which is the image of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bimba*); here, the mind of subject and object enters by the power of retention (*dhāraṇā*), and through the cessation of the coming and going of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it becomes unified as a single mass. || 118 ||

Through recollection (*anusmṛti*), one becomes completely purified; from that reflection of gnosis (*jñānabimba*), the stainless halo of light also arises. Thereafter, through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the other [limbs of yoga], the pure body of gnosis (*jñānadeha*) is accomplished in a few days within meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

If this desired perfection is not attained by the practitioners of mantra, then by the forceful practice of the *nāda* and the obstruction of the *bindu*, one should accomplish the jewel of the lotus and the thunderbolt (*vajra*). || 119 ||

"Pure through recollection (*anusmṛti*). Here, "recollection" refers to the mind’s embrace of the image (*bimba*), which is its state of being free from all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). When it is pure because of that, then the stainless circle of light (*prabhāmaṇḍala*) arises. Furthermore, by the word "also," it is implied that five-colored rays radiate and issue forth from the pores of the skin, from the image of gnosis (*jñāna-bimba*) and other images. Therefore, "pure in meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Here, when the imperishable bliss (*akṣara-sukha*) arises through the oneness of the mind of the apprehended and the apprehender, that bliss is called "meditative absorption. Because of that, being pure in absorption and having attained stainlessness, one succeeds in the "body of gnosis" (*jñānadeha*) within a few days—specifically, three years and three fortnights. Thus, having attained the ten masteries (*vaśitā*) and so forth, one becomes a Bodhisattva. This is the rule for withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the subsequent stages. (Section Kha)

Ga. Cha. Bho. And when, for these [practitioners], O Ga. Ca. Bho., the yogi—[the word] *miṣat* is not present here in Cha. and Bho.—in the course of days, the moment of the imperishable (*akṣarakṣaṇa*) does not arise in the reflected image (*bimba*) due to the unrestrained state of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), even though it has been seen through withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*) and so forth; then, by means of the practice of *nāda* to be described, having forcibly (*haṭhena*) caused the vital breath to flow through the central channel (*madhyamā*), he should accomplish the moment of the imperishable through the immobilization (*niḥspandena*) of the drop of bodhicitta within the vajra-jewel situated in the lotus of wisdom (*prajñā*). This is Haṭhayoga. || 119 ||

Now, the gaze for the purpose of accomplishing the image of emptiness is described: In the stage of service (*sevā*), there is the initial yoga (*ādiyoga*) of ten kinds in the sky by means of the wrathful gaze of the Wheel-Bearer (*cakrin*); and in the stage of near-accomplishment (*upasādhana*), there is the six-limbed yoga by means of the gaze of Vighnāntaka directed toward the path of nectar.

In the stage of accomplishment (*sādhana*), it should be the three-syllabled [mantra] at the tip of the vajra-jewel from the moon-drop emitted by Prajñā; and in this great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*), when bliss is not lost, the innate (*sahaja*) yoga of gnosis (*jñānayoga*) is that which ends with *ka* (the letter *kṣa*).

"Service," and so forth. Here, "service" (*sevā*) refers to the meditation on the signs such as smoke (*dhūmādi*). In that service, the "initial yoga" (*ādiyoga*) is the grasping of the signs such as smoke by the mind; this is of ten kinds, being the cognition (*pratyaya*) together with smoke and the other signs. It is "tenfold" because it belongs to the "Wielder of the Wheel" (*cakrin*), namely the *Uṣṇīṣa*, by means of the "wrathful gaze"—that is, the upward gaze without blinking—which constitutes the sign through the yoga of night. Through the yoga of day, it is sixfold. Thus, up to the "image" (*bimba*), it constitutes the limb of service (*sevāṅga*) by means of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and meditation (*dhyāna*). "By the gaze of Vighnāntaka": here, Vighnāntaka is Mṛtakundalī. His gaze is directed toward the place of nectar, located in the forehead. By that gaze of Vighnāntaka, who has entered the path of nectar, there is the "six-limbed" (*ṣaḍaṅga*) practice during the "near-attainment" (*upasādhana*). From the word "and" (*ca*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and retention (*dhāraṇā*) must be performed. When the image of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is seen, there is near-attainment. "Of the moon-drop created by wisdom" (*prajñāsṛṣṭendubindu*): here, that which is created by the passion of wisdom (*prajñārāga*) is the "moon-drop" (*indubindu*), thus "the drop created by wisdom. Of that drop of enlightened mind (*bodhicitta*) created by wisdom, which has reached the tip of the vajra, there is the "three-syllabled yoga" in the secret place, the navel, and the heart. That constitutes the "attainment" (*sādhana*); thus it occurs in the third limb, the attainment. In this way, the limb of attainment is to be performed. "In bliss, unperished, the single peace": here, the single moment of the enlightened mind (*bodhicitta*) when bliss is not lost is called "peace" (*śānta*); it is the "innate" (*sahaja*). Here, in the great attainment (*mahāsādhana*), it is the "yoga of gnosis" (*jñānayoga*), meaning the oneness of the mind with immutable bliss. This is the fourth limb, the great attainment. Thus, the four-limbed attainment of gnosis is the mundane deity-attainment according to the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) as previously described; the supramundane attainment of reality is according to the completion stage (*utpannakrama*). For it is said: "The teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas relies upon the two truths."
By means of the truth of worldly convention and by means of the truth of ultimate reality.
Thus is the rule of the Blessed One: furthermore, "My teaching as the Vajra-holder relies upon two stages:
one is by way of the generation stage, and the other is by way of the completion stage."

O friend, there is no "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) or "vital breath" (*prāṇa*). [The reading] *nirodhakṣaṇarakṣaṇam* is found in Ka, Kha, Ga, and Bho. From this point onward, the additional reading *bimbamevam* is found in Ga. [The reading] *dṛṣṭyā* is not present in Bho; [the reading] *kasyeti* is not present in Ga; [the word] *yoga* is not present in Ca; [the word] *nāṅge* is not present in Bho. As it has been said (*tathāha*): "Furthermore," [the word] *punaḥ* is not present in Ga.

In the chapter on the Great Summary of the Means for Accomplishing the Arisen Stage (*utpannakramasādhanamahoddeśa*), such is the rule: in the accomplishment of a deity, there is meditation involving conceptual construction (*vikalpa-bhāvanā*); in the accomplishment of reality (*tattva-sādhana*), it is by means of the four limbs free from conceptual construction. || 120 ||

Now the definition of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is stated: Breath control is desired as far as the crown of the head, for it bestows the fruit of equal bliss on all sides; beyond that, however, it is undesirable, causing fear of death and being the cause of the destruction of the aggregates (*skandhas*).

Having pierced the *uṣṇīṣa*, the yogi, while proceeding toward the state of supreme bliss, attains equal bliss even in the absence of the aggregates; yet, this is not well-known in the world. || 121 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "prāṇa" and so forth: here, when the image of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bimba*) has been seen, the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) which must be performed by the yogin should continue as long as it does not cause pain in the head—that is, until it produces the fruit of bliss. Beyond that, namely, once the headache occurs, it becomes undesirable, causing the fear of death and becoming the cause for the destruction of the aggregates (*skandha*). Now, having pierced the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) by the power of yoga, the yogin must certainly join the moving breath exclusively to the state of supreme bliss within the image of emptiness.
Thus, even in the absence of the aggregates (*skandha*), the yogi proceeds to the "Buddha-image" which is equal bliss; "the yogi proceeds" means that the yogic mind proceeds.
However, because this is not well-known in the world, [people say] "this yogi is dead"—such is the rule for breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). || 121 ||

The entry of the vital breath into the center, the embrace devoid of objects, the penetration into the lotus of the Mother of the Universe, and likewise the radiation of one's own vajra into the midst of the moon and sun;

this bliss, which reaches the climax of union when the seed does not fall—this is the yoga of yogins, the most supreme secret even among secrets of the Lord, for the sake of attaining the perfection of the mudrā. (122)
The subsequent verse is easily understood. || 122 ||

Now the dismissal of the deities is described: At the uṣṇīṣa there is indeed a five-pronged [vajra]; at the outer [uṣṇīṣa] the vajra has double the prongs. At the dharma-cakra it is doubled again; another is twice that;

yet another is twice that as well, in the sahaaja-, sambhoga-, and nirmāṇa-cakras. Within its center is a single-pronged [vajra] located in the interior of the secret lotus, which bestows the fruit of equal bliss.
"Uṣṇīṣa," and so forth.

Here, having meditated upon the *binduyoga* and *sūkṣmayoga* of the *maṇḍalarājāgrī* and *karmarājāgrī*, and having performed worship and praise with "Homage to you, O supreme speech of the Granter of Boons" (*namaste varadavacāgra*) and so on, as stated in the *Vimalaprabhā* [in the section on the *sādhana*], one should then, for the purpose of dismissing the deities of the maṇḍala, visualize a five-pronged vajra at the *uṣṇīṣa*.
Within its central hub (*varaṭaka*), one should dismiss the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*).
Its outer prongs are doubled, making eight prongs; together with the middle prong, it becomes a nine-pronged vajra at the heart, which is the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).
Upon its central hub (*varaṭaka*), one should emanate the [deities] beginning with Dhūmā.
The other is doubled, making sixteen prongs; together with the middle prong, it becomes a seventeen-pronged [vajra] at the Sahaja, the forehead.
Upon its pericarp, one should dismiss the deities of the aggregates and elements.
Its other [petals] are double that number; thus, there are thirty-two stamens, and together with the central stamen, there are thirty-three stamens in the throat, which is the *saṃbhoga* [cakra].
Upon its pericarp, one should dismiss the twelve sense bases and the four wrathful deities.
Twice that [number] again makes sixty-four; thus, a vajra with sixty-five prongs—including the central prong—is to be fashioned at the navel-cakra of emanation (*nirmāṇa*).
In its hub (*varaṭaka*) are Cācikā and the others, as well as Bhīmā and the others—the sixty-four who carry the maṇḍalas and the four belonging to the family of emptiness (*śūnyakulikā*).
Thus, one should dismiss seventy-two.

"Even within its interior, there is a single-stamen" means that within the interior of those [lotuses], the previously mentioned single-stamen lotus— which bestows equal happiness— is situated in the belly of the secret lotus (*guhyapadma*).
Therein also, the number of stamens is thirty-two, corresponding to the number of petals.
One should dismiss those [deities] such as Mārīcī who are upon its pericarp.
In this way, having formed the action-wheels (*karmacakra*) and the vajras of the twelve deities together with their retinues, one should dismiss them upon their respective pericarps.
And the nāgas, such as Śvānāsya and the others, are in the activity-wheels (*kriyācakra*).
Having performed the dismissal (*visarjana*) in this manner, one should then offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) at the three junctions of the day according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having purified the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) according to the former method, one should satisfy oneself with them.
Thus has the practice of Kālacakra been taught by the Blessed Lord Mañjuśrī through both the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) and the completion stage (*utpannakrama*). || 123 ||

Now the practice of yoga is described: the yogi commits the taking of life day and night; that which is called the destruction of breath is said to be the sound that arises in the heart devoid of speech. Furthermore, the seizing of the ground of omniscient wisdom by the yogi is declared to be theft; and bliss arising from the non-falling of the *bindu* is the service of another’s wife due to the absence of passion. (124)
"Yogī," and so forth.
Here, the yogic practice of yogins is twofold: one is external, and the second is internal.
Of these, that which is external is for the sake of worldly results.
And that which is internal must be performed by the yogin for the sake of the supramundane fruit.
Here, whatever killing of living beings the yogin performs day and night is said to be the destruction of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within his own body;
it is not external killing of living beings, [performed] for the sake of attaining the state of omniscience.

In this context, regarding the external "killing" mentioned for the purpose of taming those who are difficult to tame: the yogin must draw their life-force (*prāṇa*) by means of the power of yoga and cause it to re-enter that very same body;
in this way, he becomes a tamer of the difficult to tame.
It is established that the word "one who is not the ender of the unsubdued" is devoid of a speaker;

here, the speech of the Omniscient One is every sound, which exists within the hearts of all sentient beings through their respective individual languages. That very speech is called "unfounded" because it is the nature of the sounds of all sentient beings, and because it is unfounded, it is said to be "false speech."
Furthermore, regarding the external [world], statements such as "Mahāmāyā is greatly fierce and effects the destruction of beings" are for the purpose of training sentient beings.
Likewise, from the *Sukha-dvīndriya-ja-tattva-buddhatva-phaladāyaka* section of the *Utpannakrama-sādhanamahoddeśa*:
"Men are the forms of Vajradhara; women are Vajra-women."

Statements such as these are not false speech, nor are they deceptive words intended to mislead sentient beings; rather, for the sake of establishing the state of Buddhist yogins, when this body has become free from obscurations, the yogin’s grasping of the twelve stages of the Omniscient One is here called "the grasping of theft. Furthermore, in the external world, for the benefit of sentient beings, treasures and the like must be extracted in order to liberate the guardians of those treasures from miserable rebirths.
The bliss that arises from the non-falling of the seminal drop (*śukrabindu*) is the service to the "wife of another" (*paradāra*).

The "wife of another" is the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), who has gone to the further shore of *saṃsāra*. The "Supreme One" (*para*) is Vajrasattva, who has gone to the further shore of *saṃsāra*; his wife is the "wife of another," and the service to her—by virtue of non-detachment and immutable bliss—is the service to the wife of another for yogins.

Furthermore, externally, at the time of initiation (*sekādi*) and so forth, when one's own wife or others are given by the donor, the service to her is the service to the wife of another, by virtue of non-detachment.
The meaning is that for those who observe their own commitments (*samaya*), there is no dispassion, nor is there a violation of the commitment. || 124 ||

By the fire of *prāṇāyāma*, even the liquid drink of the Moon—the drinking of wine—descends from the crown (*uṣṇīṣa*) through the joint of the thumb according to the lunar days until the end of the full moon; then one's own mind descends from the crown to the fingers at the conclusion of the dark fortnight. This is the practice of the yogi which, performed at every daily moment, bestows the desired accomplishment. 125.
Regarding the phrase "by the fire of breath-control" (*prāṇāyāmānalena*):

here, the *caṇḍālī* that is ignited by the restraint of the vital winds (*prāṇa*) is called the "fire of breath-control. By means of that fire of breath-control, the "moon"—that is, the melted *bodhicitta*—is in a state of liquefaction. That which is the drink in the form of a drop (*bindu*), drawn upward from the mouth of the *vajra*, is said to be the "drinking of wine" for yogins, as it generates innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). Furthermore, externally, this is said to be for the purpose of an offering (*bali*) to the external deities at the time of initiation (*seka*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "from the big toe to the crown of the head," it is heard here in the *Kāmaśāstra*: here, during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), from the big toe of the left foot, the bodhicitta—meaning one's own mind—proceeds to the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) by the increase of the lunar digits (*candrakalā*) starting from the first day (*pratipadā*) until the end of the full moon, according to the sequence of the lunar days (*tithi*). Then, again from the crown of the head, it proceeds to the toes of the right foot; this occurs again by the power of the lunar days of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), until the conclusion of the dark fortnight, which is the new moon (*amānta*).

Thus, at the end of the dark fortnight, the bodhicitta should be known to be in the big toe of the right foot; furthermore, in the following month, during the bright fortnight, it is in the big toe of the left foot, as before.

Regarding this, it is said: the first lunar day (*tithi*) is on the first joint of the [left] finger; the second on the second; the third on the third; the fourth at the joint of the left foot; the fifth at the joint of the knee; the sixth at the joint of the waist; the seventh at the joint of the first phalanx of the fingers of the left hand; the eighth at the middle joint; the ninth at the third joint; the tenth at the joint of the forearm; the eleventh at the joint of the upper arm; the twelfth at the joint of the shoulder and upper arm; the thirteenth at the heart; the fourteenth at the throat; the full moon (*pūrṇā*) at the forehead; and the end of the full moon (*pūrṇānta*) at the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*)—this is for the bright fortnight (*śukla*).
Again, on the forehead during the *kṛṣṇapakṣa* (dark fortnight), the second [digit] is at the throat, the third at the heart, and the fourth at the joint of the right shoulder and arm;

the remainder proceeds in reverse order as on the left, up to the nails of the toes of the right foot, until the end of the month. That practice of the *bodhicitta* bestows the desired accomplishment upon the yogin at every daily occasion.

Here, by virtue of the flow through the left and right channels (*nāḍī*), when the *bodhicitta* has moved through the left and right, it always flows through the central channel (*madhyamā*) into the six lotuses beginning with the secret place, moving both downward and upward.
And service.
And the middle finger.

And the third is the practice called "attainment" (*sādhanāgamana*); that is the accomplishment of the desired goal, the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā. Because it is the supreme bestower of that, it is established as "the giver of the desired."

Furthermore, externally, the "conduct of women" (*nārīcaryā*) consists in the taking up of the women belonging to the families of the five Tathāgatas; within those conducts of women, "churning" (*manthāna*) is celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and it is by means of this that the yogin must act.
Likewise, as for what that movement of the *nāḍīs* of the bodhicitta is, the rule in the Root Tantra is that one must effect its upward movement as one whose semen is drawn up (*ūrdhvaretas*).
Thus ends the rule for the conduct of women. || 125 ||

Anxiety, longing, fever in the limbs, the inability to consume dry food, trembling, madness, dizziness, mental confusion, intense fainting, and the sensation of smoke—these ten manifest states of the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra) appear within the bodies of living beings in this world; yet these same states are clearly and invariably manifested by the God of Love (Manmatha). Who then is the Conqueror (Jina), and who is that Kāma? || 126 ||

That white stream which falls from the drop day and night is my consort Māmakī; it is not wine. The daily vibration of the eyes and other senses is the meat of cow and so forth, never the flesh of another.

Service to the five nectars consists of making them of one flavor through the entry of the mind into the empty body purified by the deities residing in the sites of one’s own family; that is not sexual union in a womb.

Generosity is the renunciation of wealth; ethical discipline is the non-falling away of the mind from attachment to women; patience is the lack of obsession with sounds and other sense objects; and vigor is indeed like the wind, which destroys both states of existence. Meditation and wisdom are the mind that has attained innate bliss; she is all-pervading and speaks all languages. Her miraculous power for the sake of sentient beings consists of the destruction of cyclic existence, the attainment of the unborn, and the other four [miraculous powers]. (128)

When this primordial [mantra], consisting of twenty-five parts, endowed with power in its single limb and joined with nine words, is meditated upon, the mudrās and other accomplishments indeed arise within a few days.

Abiding in the maṇḍala and being fully realized, you bring about paralysis, pacification, subjugation, and even the destruction of worlds through the various faces; you shall subdue the hosts of Dānavas and serpents. 129.
Here, four verses out of the one hundred and twenty-five have been easily understood;
therefore, they have not been elaborated upon here. (126–129)
The reading "bho iṣṭapradeti siddham" does not exist in manuscript Ga.
The six bestow accomplishment (siddhi). Ga.
Come to your own seat,
O Śāriputra!
What is that? Ka kha.
Six krośas, sir.
Regarding the "Conduct of the Root" (*mūlacaryā*),
it is said: "There is nothing here that has been performed by him."
In this chapter, the Great Summary on the Sādhana of the Utpannakrama:

Now, the meditation on the deity for the purpose of pacification and so forth is described: White [in color], one effects pacification and nourishment within one’s own mind; red, attraction and subjugation; yellow, immobilization and delusion; and that which resembles a dark cloud, killing and expulsion—meditated upon or recited, it likewise effects these within one’s own mind. One should accomplish the Vajras of Body, Speech, and Mind, situated in the mandala of the elements within the abode of the three worlds, by means of the various ritual actions. (130)
Regarding the passage beginning with "white" (*śveta*) and so forth:

here, the Lord Kālacakra—whether as the Sole Hero (*ekavīra*), or consisting of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*), or consisting of five aspects—becomes [the deity] Śāntika and so on through the distinctions of faces and other features.
When the yogi performs pacification (*śānti*), then the yogi, having made the body and face the leader, should meditate on him as white in color, situated upon a moon mandala at the forehead.
White, he brings about peace and nourishment;

red, he brings about attraction and subjugation, O Leader of the Vajra of Speech. When meditated upon in the mind as residing in the throat within a solar mandala, yellow, he brings about paralysis and delusion, O Leader of the Vajra of Gnosis, when meditated upon at the navel within a mandala of the fire of time.
Kṛṣṇa performs killing (*māraṇa*), expulsion (*uccāṭana*), and creates enmity (*vidveṣa*) within the heart in the mandala of Rāhu; he is the leader of the mind-mantras (*cittavajra*).

Thus, one situated in the mandala of these beings should accomplish the clan of the *danu* and snake-demons (*bhujaga*). Since he has been meditated upon, one should accomplish that very eightfold clan of the *daityas* and snakes as described in the *Gāruḍa*; it is not elaborated here.

"Meditate and recite likewise within your own mind"—[this means that] one meditates upon the deity with one face and two arms according to the distinctions of color for the body and so forth; such a deity, through the sequence to be described, performs pacification and other rites.

"Of those who have become thus, situated in the mandala" refers to the fourfold vajra situated in the mandalas of water and the other elements. "One should accomplish it in the abode of the three worlds by means of numerous types of ritual actions" means by various methods. || 130 ||

Now, the meditation on the one whose garment is the moist hide of an elephant for the sake of taming those who are difficult to tame is described: With his right and left [hands], which arise from the excess of the wings and resemble a jewel and gold respectively, having torn apart the entire elephant-hide drawn from the shoulders and neck; with the palms of his hands holding the excellent skull-cup of the blood of the Lord of Daityas; with a hand that has the face of Death and Māra; treading upon the feet of the enemies that are the afflictions (*kleśa*); and possessing two hands more than the Victor (Jina)—he should be meditated upon for the sake of others. (131)
Regarding the passage beginning with "pakṣa" and so forth:

here, through the purification of time, it is established that by means of the twenty-four fortnights of a year, the glorious one who holds the vajra-garland possesses twenty-four arms. Furthermore, for this [deity] who wears a moist elephant-hide garment, the purification of the arms is achieved by means of the twenty-six fortnights of a year consisting of thirteen months, which includes the intercalary month (adhikamāsa).
Therefore, arising from the excess of the wings, there are two arms; by those two arms, which resemble jewels and gold— that is, black and yellow— on the right and left sides, [kakha].
Or it is as stated in the *Cāṣṭamaka* and other [texts].
O yogin, there is no "cha."
Having formed the "Vajra of Speech," there is no *ka* or *cha*.
Vajra Ga Cakra Cha
And delusion and greed.
There is neither "this person acts" nor "this person causes [another] to act," and there is no mutual hostility.
ka kha ga
One should cultivate the six.
There is no [difference] between the black and the yellow,
nor between the left and the right.
In the *Vimalaprabhā*:

"The elephant of the Māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*)—like an elephant—is reduced to a mere fragment through its destruction; that very hide is the 'ocean' (*ogha*), which, having been torn entirely, constitutes the elephant-hide garment held from the pair of feet of the Māra of the aggregates, with the pair of feet hanging down. Thus, it is held as an elephant-hide garment.
With the left [hand], the head on the left side and the foot,
O Lord of Daityas; thus is the onset of ignorance of that son of the gods,
[expressed by] "blood."

Due to the destruction of that [blood], there was a mere drop of blood on his skull; thus, he whose excellent palm held that blood-stained skull was called "He whose excellent palm holds the skull of the life-blood of the lord of demons.

Furthermore, because of the destruction of Mṛtyumāra, there was a covering of a mere drop [of blood] on the face in his hand; thus, he whose hand had a face [marked by] Mṛtyumāra was called "Mṛtyumāra-āsyahasta" (He whose hand has a face of Mṛtyumāra).

Because he has fallen at the feet of the enemy of the afflictions (*kleśāri*), that is, due to the destruction of the Māra of the afflictions, the afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*)—which remains as a mere fragment (*lava*) and has not yet been completely incinerated—is like a *preta*; having fallen at his feet, he is thus "one who has fallen at the feet of the enemy of the afflictions.
Likewise, because he has destroyed two and a half parts of the obscurations consisting of a mere fragment, he is "the Victor with twenty-six hands," possessing twenty-six arms.
His weapons are like those of Kālacakra; he wears a garland of severed heads and skull-cups, is clothed in a tiger skin, and is to be meditated upon as adorned with bone seals and lordly serpents.
"For the sake of others" means for the sake of those to be trained who are difficult to subdue; this is the rule.

Now, the characteristic of that wisdom (*prajñā*) is stated: there, the Mother has one face, two hands, a lotus, a flaying knife (*kartikā*), and a glorious skull-cup (*kapāla*). From the sun, the moon moves by its own course according to the power of its motion; it is one [day] with twelve additional [hours].

Therefore, from the divisions of the body, the Lord of Jinas likewise becomes the Universal Mother (*viśvamātā*); such is the state of the limbs of wisdom and method (*prajñopāya*), which bestow the fruit of equal bliss through the movements of the moon and sun.
Regarding the passage beginning with "of the mother" and so forth:
here, by way of the division of the body, the sun is wisdom (*prajñā*) and the moon is method (*upāya*).

And that moon, due to its movement relative to the sun, performs one additional movement of twelve [days] until it completes its course; thus, month by month, it moves through thirteen zodiac signs (*rāśi*).
The sun moves through one zodiac sign;
by virtue of that solar movement, there is a single face for the mother therein, and by means of the purification of the month,
there is a pair of lotus-hands in the form of twin lotuses.
In that right lotus-hand there is a water-pot (*karakamala*), and in the left, a knife and a skull-cup (*naraka-pāla*).
From that, by means of the divisions of the body—namely, the twenty-six divisions of the lunar zodiac—the Lord of Jinas becomes twenty-six-armed;
likewise, Viśvamātā [becomes so] by means of the divisions of the body, as the single zodiacal sign of the sun.
According to the different systems of tenets, she is two-armed and naked with loose hair as Viśvamātā; the rest [of the deities] are adorned with ornaments just like the Blessed One.
Thus it is said regarding the states of the limbs of wisdom and means.

The rule is that [the practice] should be cultivated by means of the movements of the moon and sun, through the restraint of inhalation and exhalation, which grant the fruit of equal bliss and the fruit of imperishable bliss.

Now, the meditation on the Universal Form (*viśvarūpa*) is described: Having one face and so forth up to infinite faces, with many hands and feet and many colors, he consists of wisdom and means at the end of darkness; indeed, through the obstruction of the channels, moon, and sun, he bestows equal bliss. The single Void (*śūnya*), which is without beginning, middle, or end, the piercer of all things from earth upwards like a stainless jewel, the objectless object that has been realized as Kālacakra.
"Single," and so forth: here, he may have one face; by the word "or" (*ādi*), [it implies] three faces, four, five, or even infinite faces; many hands and feet, or many hands and feet;

bearing many weapons; possessing many colors and many forms. As it is said in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*: "The Great King who holds the illusion of the universe, the great holder of the Buddha-vidyā, the Blessed One who holds the syllable of emptiness, whose nature is wisdom and means."

He who perceives the yoga of the *prajñāpāramitā* at the end of darkness during the night through the conjunction with night, or during the day through the conjunction with day, sees it in the sky at night and sees it in the open space during the day. Thus visualized, it extends as far as the reflected image (*bimba*). Then, from the obstruction of the channels of the moon and sun—that is, from the obstruction of the left and right vital breaths—it bestows "blazing equal bliss," which is the supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*).
Regarding "of the earth and so forth," this refers to the elements such as earth;

"the piercer resembling a stainless gem" means that here, just as a stainless gem transforms stone and the like into a precious mineral by mere touch, it is not a "piercer" (bhedaka) in the sense of piercing through or boring into.

Likewise, the one void, the stainless, which pierces through all the bodily elements such as the earth and so forth, is that whose form is emptiness; it has no beginning, no end, and no middle; it is beyond the reach of objects, yet it is the appearance of objects even without objects—like a magical illusion, a dream, or a reflected image.

The rule is that the accomplished Kālacakra bestows equal bliss; thus has been stated the sādhanā of the glorious Ādibuddha according to the utpannakrama, and its detailed exposition shall be explained in the Jñānapaṭala.

Thus, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the twelve-thousand-verse commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja* following the *Śrīmūlatantra*, the twelfth chapter, the Great Chapter on Various Sadhanas, is concluded; and the fourth [chapter], the Great Chapter on the Sadhana of the Arising Stage (*utpannakrama*), follows.
Having paid homage to Vajravega, the Lord who holds the universal vajra, the leader of the wrathful kings, the various sādhanas are now described.
The Lord of Wrath, Vajravega, who has twenty-two hands, four faces, and two feet; who is tawny-eyed and tawny-haired, wearing a crown of the Victors;

whose fangs are fierce and formidable; adorned with snakes and clad in a supreme garment of tiger skin; holding weapons in his hands like his Master; with a garland bound upon his head consisting of skulls from all the families of the Victors in five colors.

With the words "Krodhendram" and so forth, here [one should visualize] Krodhendra Vajravega, produced from the syllable *HŪṂ* and the vajra, according to the previously mentioned method of accomplishment, possessing twenty-six arms— two more than the number of Jinas— and wearing an elephant-hide garment.

"Vevavaktra" means four-faced; "dvipāda" means two-legged; "piṅgākṣa" means tawny-eyed; "piṅgakeśa" means tawny-haired; "jinapatimukuṭa" means having Akṣobhya as a crown, that is, a crown of Akṣobhya; "tīkṣṇadaṃṣṭrākarāla" means fierce with sharp fangs;
"sarpāla" means adorned with snakes; and "vyāghracarma-pravaranivasana" means wearing a tiger skin as a supreme garment.
Like a master, with a weapon in hand, and like the Wheel of Time,
he is bound upon his head with a garland of five-colored skulls for the sake of purification within the entire family of the Victors.

Meditating upon the Lord of Beings (Bhairava) as he stands in the *ālīḍha* posture with his feet powerfully treading upon the lords of beings within a multicolored mandala on a universal lotus atop the sun, his stainless hands flashing, terrifying the spirits, gods, and serpents, the sole embodiment of the essence of knowledge— by meditating thus for one month, one shall accomplish the host of spirits residing in the realm of the cremation ground.

Thus, within the *viśvājña* [mandala], upon the solar disc, is the pure, radiant, stainless-handed *ekavīra* in the center of the *viśvavarṇa* circular chamber. Having placed, in sequence, the vajrāṅkuśa, vajra-vajrapāśa, and vajra-vajraghaṇṭā at the four gates, he stands with great power in the *ālīḍha* posture, treading with his two feet upon Bhūtanātha and Aparājita-Pretanātha. Terrifying the hosts of spirits (*bhūtāvī*), he wears an elephant hide and strikes terror into the asuras, *phaṇis* (serpents), and gods with the threatening fingers of his hands; such is he, the sole embodiment of the *jñānasattva*.

With these mantra-syllables—*jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*—the yogi, while meditating, shall accomplish the host of spirits (*bhūta*) residing in the city of the cremation ground or situated on the ground of the charnel ground for one month. That leader of the spirits and so forth, having been cast down at his feet by that [yogic] form, attains accomplishment along with his retinue, whether he be a *preta*, a *rākṣasa*, or the like; such is the rule for the accomplishment of spirits and so forth. || 135 ||

Now, the sādhana of the Nāga King for the purpose of causing rain from the clouds is described: Having placed the Nāgas upon the eight petals of a lotus, and having pinned Jayā and Vijayā beneath the sun with his two feet, one should meditate on the pair of serpent-lords situated on the lotus petals, their entire tails and tips emitting a mass of clouds from their bellies in every direction; thus, the Lord of Wrath (Krodhendrarāja), when meditated upon in this way, shall accomplish the gathering of clouds within a few days.
"Regarding 'the nāgas' and so forth:
here, that very Vajravega, the Lord of Wrath, when meditated upon, shall accomplish the host of clouds within a few days— that is, within days of a month— by this method."
"The nāgas [are placed] upon eight-petaled lotuses."

On the petal preceding the lotus (the east) is Karkoṭaka; in the southeast is Padma; in the south is Vāsuki; in the southwest is Śaṅkhapāla; in the north is Ananta; in the northeast is Kulika; in the west is Takṣaka; and in the northwest is Mahāpadma. Furthermore, having placed the two Nāga kings Jaya and Vijaya—black and blue respectively—in the east and southeast, which are black; in the south and southwest, which are red; in the north and northeast, which are white; and in the west and northwest, which are yellow; one should place them upon the sun-disk atop the sun with their left and right soles [respectively], in human form from the waist down and serpent-like below that, with seven hoods and a circular canopy above their heads, shimmering with great jewels, and lying face upwards. Having thus placed the other Nāga kings, the tip of each of their tails should be positioned respectively above Jaya for those in the east and north, and above Vijaya for those in the south and west.

Having thus restrained the entire tip of the tail with both feet, [one should visualize] the pair of serpent-lords in the chapter [on the] various great methods (śloka 134–139). For those situated upon the lotus petals, the entire tip of the tail and so forth— thus,
the five hooded serpent-kings of the Ghanakula family, emitting a mass of clouds from their bellies on all sides.
Thus, having meditated upon Krodhendrarāja in a cremation ground for a number of days and months, one should accomplish a mass of clouds;
thereafter, at whatever time one desires, one causes it to rain, and by means of the rite of dismissal (visarjana), one restrains it.
This is the rule for the sādhanā of the Nāga King. || 136 ||
Now, the accomplishment of the deities through various ritual actions is described:

"O Lord of Men, this is the primary means of accomplishing the male deities; for each of the female deities within this mandala, according to the power of their own Jina-family, there are all the various ritual actions—stambhana, śānti, vaśya, seizing the wealth of others, māraṇa, uccāṭana, and so forth. Furthermore, for the thirty-six yoginīs, there is indeed recitation and fire-offering with their own seed-syllables. (137)
"Thus, the first," and so forth.

Here, O Lord of Men, the aforementioned and other deities constitute the *sādhana* for the [other] deities within this mandala; in each case within this mandala, by the wise, according to their own Jina-family—that is, according to the family of Vairocana and the others—there is a *sādhana* through all the various types of rites:

for paralyzing (*stambhana*), pacifying (*śānti*), subjugating (*vaśya*), seizing the wealth of others, killing (*māraṇa*), and expelling (*uccāṭana*). Furthermore, the *sādhana* of the thirty-six Yoginīs and the others up to the cremation grounds is indeed performed, as well as the recitation (*japa*) and fire-offering (*homa*), by means of their respective mantra-seeds. ||137||
Now, the meditations for pacification and the other rites are described:

For pacification, the meditation is peaceful; the deity is white as the moon and possesses a peaceful form. For the fierce rite, the meditation is fierce; the deity resembles a dark cloud and possesses a fierce form. For subjugation, the meditation is passionate; the deity has the body of the sun and is the embodiment of passion. For paralyzing, the meditation is stupefied; the deity resembles fine gold and possesses a paralyzed form. || 138 ||
Regarding "for pacification" and so forth:

here, for pacification, the meditation is peaceful; one should meditate on the deity as being white like the moon and possessing a peaceful form. For the fierce [rites], such as killing and the like, the meditation is fierce; the deity is black in color and possesses a fierce appearance.
In the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*), meditation is passionate; the deity is red in color and has a form of passion.
In the rite of paralyzing (*stambhana*), meditation is deluded; the deity is yellow in color and has a rigid form.
As it is in the case of pacification (*śānti*), so it is in the case of nourishment (*puṣṭi*), the alleviation of fever, and the removal of poison.

The rule is as follows: as it is for killing, so it is for expulsion, inciting enmity, and the transmission of fever; as it is for subjugation, so it is for attraction, paralyzing, and the production of fever; and as it is for immobilization, so it is for deluding and pinning down. || 138 ||
Now, the accomplishment of pacification and so forth within the Gaṇa family is described:

O King, peace and nourishment are accomplished by the goddesses in the family of the Victors together with their sons; hatred and eradication are accomplished by those born of Wrath through the power of the qualities of nature; subjugation and the like are accomplished by those born of Spirits; and in the manifestly favorable family, piercing is accomplished by the Asuras, while all rites—both killing and reviving—are accomplished by the Mothers in the family of the two pavakas (fire-gods). || 139 ||

Regarding "peace," and so forth: here, "peace and prosperity along with the families of the Victors and their sons" refers to form, feeling, perception, and mental formations; these four are the families of the Victors together with their sons.
Viṣkambha, Kṣitigarbha, Lokeśvara, and Khagarbha—these are the families of the Bodhisattvas.
Likewise, Locanā, Pāṇḍarā, Māmakī, and Tārā are the families of the Victors (Jinas).
Gandhavajrā, Rasavajrā, Rūpavajrā, and Sparśavajrā are the families of the Bodhisattvas.

O King, when these white-colored families are meditated upon individually within a moon-maṇḍala on the forehead in the lotus posture— with the male deities [representing] skillful means holding white lotuses and displaying the boon-granting gesture, and the female deities [representing] wisdom holding white utpalas and displaying the gesture of fearlessness— peace and nourishment are accomplished; the address "O King" implies,
by the force of the word "and," the neutralization of poison and the subsiding of fever as well.

He performed acts of inciting hatred, expulsion, killing, and the transmission of poison by the power of the qualities of one's nature—that is, by the power of the quality of the wrathful nature. It is accomplished through those born of wrath:

the ten wrathful deities born from the *hūṃ* syllable and the vajra; the ten wrathful consorts born from the *phreṃ* syllable and the flaying knife (*kartī*). Killing is accomplished in the heart within the mandala of Rāhu by the Wrathful Lord, who has feet that trample down and holds a vajra-noose in his hand.

With goddesses who have swords and chains in their hands, who are black in color, cruel, and accompanied by threatening gestures, subjugation and other rites are accomplished; with goddesses born of the elements (*bhūtajā*) who hold flaying knives and skull-cups in their hands, and who are surrounded by those holding swords and nooses, [subjugation and other rites] are likewise accomplished.

In this system, subjugation (*vaśya*) is accomplished by means of the eight goddesses beginning with Carcikā, who are red in color, possess feet like those of a *viśākha* plant, and hold bows and arrows in their hands within the solar mandala at the throat; likewise, attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*) and so forth are accomplished by those holding nooses and goads.
This is the secret method for bringing [the deity] under control, while the "closing" (*kolana*) is performed by the Asura goddesses.

Here, by means of the eight goddesses beginning with Śvānāsyā, who are yellow in color, stationed at the navel within the yellow mandala of the fire of time (kālāgni), with their hands holding wheels and mountains, the rite of immobilization (stambhana) is accomplished;
with their hands holding hammers and spikes, the rite of pinning down (kīlana) is accomplished; and with their hands holding tridents and serpents, the rite of delusion (mohana) is accomplished.

"By the two mothers" means that all rites are accomplished within the secret lotus by means of Vajradhātvīśvarī or Prajñāpāramitā, according to the divisions of the maṇḍalas such as water and so forth, with colors such as white and so forth, and with the individual symbols and words previously mentioned. Killing and reviving are accomplished:

by means of the vajra-posture, the deity together with bliss within the center of the drop (*bindu*) brings about revival; by drawing in the vital breaths through the power of yoga, the detached [deity] effects killing by means of the fallen drop. Furthermore, there is no returning to life for the one who has been killed.

Therefore, that means of accomplishment should not be performed by a Buddhist yogin, for there is a rule in all ritual actions that when the vital breath (prāṇa) of the object to be accomplished is drawn in, the emission of semen occurs. || 139 ||
Now, the primary cause for accomplishing all ritual activities (*karma*) is stated:

First, the illustrious Kālacakra and the Mother of the Three Worlds must be diligently accomplished; afterwards, those activities such as pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth are to be accomplished in this world.

For a son who is deprived of both mother and father never exists, as is well known in the world; therefore, these two must be accomplished, for they grant the fruit of equal bliss, and otherwise there is no success in ritual activity. (140)
The Great Chapter on the Various Sadhanas of Lhamo: "At the beginning," and so forth.
Here, at the outset, the yogi must diligently practice according to the guru’s instruction; that is, the glorious Kālacakra—the vital wind—must be made to enter the central channel.
"Always the mother who gives birth to the three worlds" refers to the image of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bimba*).
Those two, which are the very life of the *bimba*, must be accomplished with effort;
thereafter, all the rites previously mentioned—such as those for pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth—become achievable within the abode of the earth’s surface.
Herein lies the illustration: a son who is devoid of both mother and father never exists, as is well known in the world.

Therefore, both the form (bimba) and the vital breath (prāṇa) must be accomplished, as they grant the fruit of equal bliss; otherwise, there is no accomplishment of the ritual action. This is the rule: [it cannot be achieved] without the form and the vital breath being accomplished. || 140 ||
Now, the initial meditation for the sake of accomplishing pacification and so forth is described:

One should place a five-pronged vajra, born of gnosis, resembling a cloud at the time of dissolution, and possessing rays of light, upon the moon, sun, and fire within the center of the lotus of the Lord’s heart;

therein, having filled the entire three worlds with the hooks of light and drawn it in, one should cause the Gnosis-Wheel (jñānacakra) residing in the threefold existence to enter through the path of the vajra. || 141 ||

One should emit everything, appearing like molten moon, from the mouth of one’s own vajra into the lotus of the Mother; having entered that sun, it becomes of equal flavor (samarasa) when joined with the initial vowels and consonants.

In its center is the seed-syllable of gnosis (jñānabīja), which arises according to the family (kula) and the ritual action such as pacification (śāntika). From that, the Goddess is born, who indeed bestows the fruit—the deity of the yogin. || 142 ||
Regarding the passage beginning with "of the Lord" (*bhartuḥ*) and so forth:

here, when the yogi perceives the image (*bimba*) clearly situated within the *avadhūtī* as having entered the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he then perceives that image exactly as he conceives it. That image is the "Lord," namely the previously mentioned *Kālacakra*, which is to be accomplished. Then, in the center of his heart-lotus, upon the pericarp, is the triadic mandala of the planets consisting of the moon, sun, and fire—namely, the conjunction of the moon, sun, and Rāhu. In the inner self (*adhyātman*), this occurs within the fire-lotus where the *lalanā*, *rasanā*, and *avadhūtī* have become unified into one.

Therein, the Sage should place a five-pronged vajra transformed from the syllable *HŪṂ*, resembling a cloud at the time of dissolution and black in color; it emits rays, meaning it radiates five-colored rays. "In its center" means that in the central hub of that vajra, one should meditate upon a vajra-hook transformed from the syllable *JAḤ*.

Then, by the rays of that hook, having filled the entire threefold realm—the triple world—with the form of a vajra-hook, one draws in the pure wheel of gnosis (jñānacakra) which has the appearance of the triple existence through those vajra-hooks; and having caused that which pervades the three types of existence to enter, by way of the avadhūtī, through the paths of the crown, forehead, throat, heart, navel, and secret place.

"Everything" (*sarvam*) refers to that which possesses all aspects and has the appearance of molten moon; this is the characteristic of the *bodhicitta*. "One should emit it from the mouth of one's own *vajra* into the lotus of the Mother" means that just as a man would cast the blissful *bodhicitta* into the woman’s lotus through his own garment or mouth, so too, through the yoga of the deity, one should emit it into the lotus of the goddess.
"Mother" (*mātṛ*) refers to the progenitor of those who will be described hereafter, just as she is for those born from a womb; likewise, [the *bodhicitta*] enters into that sun.

In this context, just as the semen, having entered the female womb, becomes of equal flavor with the blood, so too the moon, having entered the center of the sun, becomes of equal flavor within the mother’s lotus.

The lunar fluid is joined with *Ā* (the letter A), and the solar dust is joined with *Kā* (the letter Ka). Joined with the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, in their midst—that is, between the *prāṇa* and *apāna*—there arises the seed of gnosis (*jñānabīja*), characterized by the *ālayavijñāna*.
"By the power of the lineage" means that by the power of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the five aggregates,
the consciousness of sentient beings arises;
likewise, from the pacifying rite of karma, the seed of knowledge arises.
