Just as a girl or a boy is born from that seed, so indeed, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, [the deity] becomes a bestower of fruit within the limit of twelve years or sixteen years; likewise, the Goddess, the deity, or the Means (*upāya*) is meditated upon by the yogin—this is the rule. Therefore, the Goddess, when meditated upon, becomes a bestower of boons after twelve years, and the God becomes a bestower of boons after sixteen years.
Thereafter, all activities, all accomplishments, and all pleasures of the yogin are perfected.

Otherwise, affliction remains absolute; thus, in all other tantras, there is a restriction of time for those who possess vigor and whose selves have been cultivated day and night, but not for others until the end of a hundred years—this is the rule regarding accomplishment. || 141-142 ||
Now, the seed-syllables of gnosis for the production of the [mudrā] symbols are stated:

*jaḥ*, *hūṃ*, *vaṃ*, *hoḥ*—in this order, these are the hook, the thunderbolt, the vajra-noose, and the bell; *oṃ*, *āḥ*, *hūṃ*, *hoḥ*—so it has been said; likewise, the moon, sun, and thunderbolt, as well as the syllable; and similarly, *ī*, *ṛ*, *ū*, *lṛ*; and likewise, *pra*, *ka*, *ṭa*, *ya*, *ra*, *va*, *la*, which are wind, fire, water, and earth.
Haḥ, huṃ, haṃ, phreṃ; as it has been stated, the sun is the vajra and the moon is the kartikā.
"Ja," and so forth.
Here, "jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ" occurs in sequence; by the syllable *jaḥ*, there arises a vajra-hook (*vajrāṅkuśa*). Through its transformation, one becomes a goddess or a god holding a vajra-hook in hand.
Likewise, by the syllable *hūṃ*, there arises a vajra; through that, one becomes [a deity] holding a vajra in hand.
By means of the syllable *vaṃ*, she becomes one with a noose in her hand;
by means of the syllable *hoḥ*, she holds a bell, and thus she becomes one with a bell in her hand. It is stated as: *oṃ āḥ hūṃ hoḥ*.
"So be it" means in sequence as before.
With the syllable *oṃ*, there is the moon-maṇḍala, which is the moon (*śaśin*). With the syllable *āḥ*, there is the sun-maṇḍala, which is the sun (*ravi*).
By the syllable *huṃ* is the lunar disc, which is the vajra;
by the syllable *hoḥ* is the solar disc of the fire of time (*kālāgni*), which is likewise imperishable (*akṣara*). *Ī*, *ṛ*, *ū*, and *lṛ* are exactly the same.
In due order, the letter *ī* transforms into a sword; the deity fully manifested by that is a goddess holding a sword in her hand.
Likewise, by the letter *ṛ*, there is a jewel or an arrow; the deity of fire manifested by that is a goddess holding a jewel or an arrow in her hand.
By the letter *ū*, there is a lotus; the deity of water manifested by that is a goddess holding a lotus or an *utpala* lily in her hand.

By the letter *lṛ* is the wheel; by the wheel is the Earth goddess, the deity who holds a wheel in her hand. In this same manner, *ya*, *ra*, *va*, and *la* are also the deities of air, fire, water, and earth, respectively.
Likewise, *haḥ* is the solar disc;
*hūṃ* is the vajra of the Leader upon the head of the sun;
and *ham* is the lunar disc.
Thus, above the lunar disc is the *phatkārī*.
This is the rule for the symbols of the Heroines (*nāyikā*).
So it has been said. || 143 ||

It is said: Now, when the deity has been accomplished, for the performance of rites such as pacification (*śānti*) and so forth, one should meditate on the deity’s samādhi; then, having visualized a lotus consisting of the seed-syllable of water (*toyabīja*) between the moon and sun accompanied by the vowels (*ali*) and consonants (*kali*), from that [lotus] one should dispatch the goddess—who has one face, two hands holding a lotus, the color of the moon, mounted upon a white serpent, with hands holding a white lotus and displaying the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), clad in white garments, adorned with white ornaments, and possessing a smiling countenance—to the house of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*). || 144 ||
The Great Chapter on Various Means of Accomplishment (*Nānāsādhanamahoddeśa*), beginning with "having meditated" (*dhyātvā*) and so forth:

here, within the previously mentioned secret lotus of the Mother, between the moon and sun and accompanied by the vowels and so forth, is a white lotus consisting of the seed-syllable of water, transformed from the syllable *va*. From that is born the deity with one face and two arms, moon-colored.
"Mounted upon a white serpent" means she is mounted upon Airāvata.

The goddess, whose hands hold white lotuses (*sitajalaja*), is a deity with a white lotus in her hand; she grants fearlessness (*abhayā*) with her right hand, holding the gesture of fearlessness (*abhayahasta*). She is to be visualized as wearing white garments, adorned with white ornaments and pearl jewelry, and possessing a smiling countenance.
And she should send her to the house of the person to be converted. || 144 ||

Therefore, having taken hold of the *sādhya* and having entered again into the circle (*maṇḍala*) of the Lord, and having received the command of their husband, Locanā and the others—exceedingly joyful—are the ten excellent Śaktis who bathe that *sādhya* with jars of nectar; Rūpā and the others worship him; Lāsyā and the others nourish him with the ten manifest [Śaktis] and satisfy him. || 145 ||
The ten classes of *krodha* born of wrath, known as the *bhūtas*, protect; the *nāginīs* kiss; the twelve celestial maidens embrace;

and the fierce ones provide protection upon the entire surface of the earth for the sake of peace and nourishment. Thus, the yogi should meditate upon everything that brings supreme bliss to the practitioner (*sādhya*). (146)
The two subsequent verses are easy to understand.

From the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) onwards, up to the conclusion that "thus the yogi should meditate upon the all-pervasiveness of the object of proof (*sādhya*), which brings about supreme bliss," [the meaning is established]. (145–146)

Visualizing the bow as a stalk of sugarcane with arrows that are blue-lily buds, and the syllable *hrīṃ* within the orb of the sun and moon, she is born from it with the luster of the sun; with her two hands drawing the bow to her ear and releasing an arrow, she stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture upon a lotus and the moon.
Having struck the target with the arrow at the heart, navel, secret place, head, and mouth, she shall dispatch the target to the house of the one to be acted upon (*sādhya*).
Bound by a noose around the neck and led into the mandala even while agitated, though stripped of clothes by fierce women, he is surely encircled by serpent-women;

being reviled by goddesses, struck with clubs and pestles, threatened by those possessed by wrathful spirits, and pinned down by sharp claws, he is likewise subjected to the *lāsya* and other dance movements. || 148 ||

With the *vajra* [mantras] one destroys the intellect; with those born of earth, water, fire, and wind, one binds [the target]. Stripped of clothes and humbled by all pride, they are cast down by the *śakti* [mantras].

Having thus brought them under control, the powerful master should then satisfy the object of the rite (*sādhya*) there. Likewise, through the noose (*pāśa*) and the hook (*aṅkuśa*), the various types of summoning rites (*ākarṣaṇa-karma*) are performed in three ways. || 149 ||

Likewise, beginning with "Hnīṃ, within the womb of the moon and sun," and so forth, up until "thus, by means of the noose and goad, there occurs manifold work of attraction within the three realms," the three circles for the rites of subjugation and attraction are easily understood. || 147 – 149 ||

Having meditated upon the syllable *HŪṂ*, long and resembling a dark cloud, in the center of the sun and moon, from its radiance is born a pale goddess with a sword in her lotus-hand and a noose in her hand holding the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*).

Standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture upon the head of a camel, with a wrathful countenance, she is dispatched to the house of the victim; having bound the victim with the noose, she brings him, with her angry face, to the gate of the maṇḍala. (150)

If one mounts a camel of noble breed that has been driven by its master’s command into a strong wind, and while mounted, should naturally cause it to move with its tail and legs flickering like fire, then even the Lord of the Gods would be driven away; how much more so a mere human? Furthermore, for the purpose of inciting enmity, two camels devoid of strength and prone to constant quarreling should be led to the left and the right.

Likewise, for the rites of inciting hatred (*vidveṣa*) and eradication (*uccāṭana*), one should meditate on [the weapon] within the womb of the sun and moon as being like a whetstone, beginning with the words "long, having the form of a sword," and so forth; these two verses are easy to understand. (150–151)

Having meditated upon a yellow-colored, excellent wheel transformed from the syllable *la* within the womb of the sun and moon, one arises as [Cakravegā], who has one face and resembles fine gold; she holds a chain and a wheel in her hands.

Seated upon the tortoise, the seat of the Daityas, she moves with an exceedingly gentle gait. When impelled, she goes to the house of the victim, causing the victim to fall to the ground by means of the wheel, his feet bound by the chain. (152)

Having brought [the enemy] into the mandala according to the word of the Lord of Victors, one should cast him upon the ground; then, on his head, a pillar made of excellent gold should be placed for the purpose of immobilization (stambhana) within the body of the victim.

Furthermore, for the purpose of pinning, he should be pinned with spikes made of vajra at the six joints. In the rite of delusion (mohana), he should be meditated upon as falling here while being crushed by all [the spikes]. || 153 ||

Having meditated on [the seed-syllable] *ila* transformed into a yellow-colored, excellent wheel (*sucakra*) within the womb of the sun and moon, and so forth—the two verses concerning *stambhana*, *kīlana*, and *mohana* are easy to understand. || 152–153 ||

Having meditated upon a curved knife (kartikā) resembling lightning and fire within the womb of the sun and moon, having the nature of the syllable *Phreṃ*, from that is born Pracaṇḍā, who resembles a cloud at the time of universal dissolution, holding a curved knife and a conch-shell in her hands. This is the Great Chapter on Various Means (*Nānāsādhanamahoddeśa*). She stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, naked, positioned above the enemy of Hari (Viṣṇu), and dispatched to the house of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*); she quickly seizes the *sādhya* by the hair and brings him, stripped of clothes, into the mandala. (154)

Brought by vultures, crows, and jackals to the illustrious cremation ground at the command of the Lord of Jinas, the flesh—blood-red in all its limbs—and likewise all the bodily constituents (*sarvadhātu*) of the victim are eaten. Thus, on this excellent surface of the earth, everything belonging to the one to be slain (*sādhya*) should be meditated upon for the purpose of killing. By means of this meditation, even Śakra goes to the city of Yama; how much more so when one has meditated upon a knife within the womb of the sun and moon, resembling lightning and fire, [and visualizes] the victim born again from that womb? (155)
The two verses beginning with "svabhāvām" regarding killing are easy to understand.
Likewise, the nine verses concerning subjugation (*vaśya*) and so forth are easy to understand; therefore, they have not been written [commented upon] here.

(154–155) Now, another meditation for pacification (*śānti*) is described: In pacification and nourishment (*puṣṭi*), the meditation is white due to the influence of the *kula*, arising from the water-seed (*am*). For subjugation and attraction, it is red, and for the burning of the body, it consists of the fire-seed (*ra*).

For causing enmity and eradication, [the form] resembles a cloud at the time of universal dissolution and possesses the nature of the seed-syllable of air; for paralyzing, pinning, and similar rites, it resembles excellent gold and consists of the seed-syllable of earth. (156)
Regarding the passage beginning with "In pacification" (*śāntau*) and so forth:

here, first of all, for the rites of pacification, subjugation, and the like, one should meditate upon oneself as the Solitary Hero Kālacakra with twenty-four arms; for the rites of killing, paralyzing, and the like, [one should meditate on him] with twenty-six arms.
Then, by way of instantaneous appearance, [one meditates] in pacification and nourishment.

Here, in the heart of Kālacakra, on the water-maṇḍala and from the water-seed-syllable, the deity born is of the nature of water and white in color; she is white by virtue of her *kula*, specifically by virtue of the *ukāra-kula*.
Her meditation is white meditation (*śukladhyāna*), which, arising from the water-seed-syllable, serves for both pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*).
Likewise, for subjugation and attraction, it is red;
moreover, the subtle vehicle (tanuvahana) consisting of the seed-syllable of fire is in the throat within the fire-mandala by virtue of the family of the letter *ṛ*.
And [the vehicle] which is black, having the nature of the seed-syllable of air, is in the forehead within the air-mandala by virtue of the family of the letter *i* of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

At the beginning of the rite of piercing (kīlana) and so forth, the yellow [seed-syllable] consisting of the seed of earth is located at the navel in the mandala of earth, according to the power of the family of the letter *la*. || 156 ||

From the seed-syllable of emptiness (śūnyabīja), there arises a blue appearance for killing and a green one for life; the earth-totality (pṛthvīkṛtsna) is for traveling everywhere, and the wind-totality (vāyukṛtsna) for traversing the ocean; the fire-totality (vahnikṛtsna) is for the purpose of destruction, while the water-totality (toyakṛtsna) is for destroying the circle of the earth; the space-totality (khakṛtsna) is for traveling through the sky and for liquefying fire, while the emptiness-totality (śūnyakṛtsna) is for invisibility.

In the *Vimalaprabhā*, regarding the practice: from the seed-syllable of emptiness (*śūnyabīja*), for the purpose of killing, one visualizes [the deity] with a blue luster in the secret place within the mandala of gnosis (*jñānamaṇḍala*) according to the family of the syllable *Aṃ*;
and for the purpose of reviving, one visualizes [it] as green in the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) within the mandala of emptiness according to the family of the syllable *A*.

Thus, it has been stated by the Blessed One that through the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇasaṃyama*) in these six locations according to the six families, the accomplishment of activities (*karmasiddhi*) is attained.
Now, the meditation on the totalities (*kṛtsna*) of earth and so forth is described, beginning with "earth" and so on.
Here, when the deity has been accomplished by the yogins, they should then emanate the earth-totality from the earth-mandala at the navel like a bridge over the ocean and meditate upon it.

By means of this meditation on the earth-totality, one goes upon the water as if on land when traveling across the ocean; thus, through the meditation on the earth-totality, one proceeds upon the water just as on dry land.

Likewise, for the purpose of destroying excessive rain by means of the wind-totality (*vāyukṛtsna*), one should emanate a wind-maṇḍala from the forehead and visualize the wind-totality above the clouds; by that, one destroys the rain from the clouds.
Then, one should visualize a gabled pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) composed of the five elements above oneself.
By that meditation, the yogin is not touched by water up to the peak of Mount Sumeru, nor does the rain from the clouds enter even while it is falling; thus it is stated in the Root Tantra.
Likewise, having emanated the air-totality (*vāyukṛtsna*) above the fire for the purpose of destroying the rain, there is the fire-totality (*vahnikṛtsna*).

Here, one should visualize a flame produced from the transformation of the fire-seed syllable within the fire-mandala at the throat, rising above the earth; by means of those flames, one should imagine the circle of the earth melting like molten gold.
In this way, for the purpose of liquefying the earth, the fire-totality (vahnikṛtsna) should be meditated upon.

Thus, for the purpose of cooling the complexion, one should emanate the "all-water" (*toyakṛtsna*) from the heart of the deity; having emanated this all-water, which is produced from the water-seed upon the water-mandala, one should visualize it at the crown of the fire.
By that means, the fire becomes cool and is no longer capable of burning.

Regarding the "totality of space" (*ākāśakṛtsna*) in the practice of traveling through the sky: one should meditate on the totality of space as being devoid of substance within the space-maṇḍala at the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*). By that, traveling through the sky occurs;
likewise, by that very meditation, one becomes invisible during disturbances such as those caused by thieves—this is the rule. || 157 ||

Now, meditation for the pacification of calamities caused by animals is described: Meditation on the five-faced [lion] indeed occurs from the fire-seed syllable (*ra*) when there is a threat from the lord of elephants; meditation on the white Garuda occurs from the water-seed syllable (*va*) when there is a threat from the king of serpents; meditation on the eight-legged rhinoceros-lion, resembling a cloud at the time of dissolution, occurs from the wind-seed syllable (*ya*); and meditation on the one called the rhinoceros (the lion) occurs from the seed-syllable born of wrath (*kṣa*) when there is a threat from the Daityas, according to the lineage of the mountain-clans of the enemy of horses. || 158 ||
Regarding the passage beginning with "meditation" (*dhyāna*) and so forth:
here, when fear arises for the lord of elephants, one should then meditate upon a five-faced lion produced from the seed-syllable of fire—that is, from the letter *ra*—at his throat;
that is the meditation on the five-faced lion (*pañcānanadhyāna*) concerning the subduing of the lord of elephants.
Thus, in the event of a defeat by the lord of serpents, [the mantra] consisting of the water-seed-syllable (*va*) becomes white like that in the heart within the water-mandala;
it consists of eight feet, meaning eight syllables.
In the event of fear from rhinoceroses—that is, fear of lions—it is entirely [white] on the forehead, consisting of the wind-seed-syllable (*ya*) within the wind-mandala.

The one called Khaṅga is for the enemy of horses; in fear of buffaloes, it is yellow according to the lineage of the earth family, arising from the seed-syllable *la* at the navel in the mandala of the earth;
the one born of Wrath is for the destruction of the Daityas, dark blue on the crown in the mandala of emptiness.

In the blue secret *jñānamaṇḍala*, the seed-syllable *hūṃ* or the seed-syllable *kṣaṃ*—born of wrath and bringing happiness to yogins regarding the destruction of the *dātyas* and others—becomes manifest; such is the rule of meditation for the destruction of the animal realm. 158.

[Chapter on] the Great Summary of Various Means of Accomplishment: Now, the rule for the initial accomplishment of ritual actions is stated— The illustrious mantra and the form of the Buddha must first be accomplished by the pervasive yogin; afterwards, the ritual actions, possessing immeasurable qualities and residing within the divisions of the sun, will be perfected.

But if the mantra and the form are not accomplished, nothing whatsoever can be perfected, even within the abode of the three worlds. Therefore, O King, when one's own mind is free from defilement, one should accomplish the mantra and the form. (159)
Regarding the phrase "the glorious mantra" and so forth:

here, for the sake of accomplishing the activities of yogins, the "glorious mantra" to be first practiced is *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*; it is to be practiced according to the procedure for recitation (*jāpa*) and fire-offering (*homa*) to be described below, for the sake of accomplishing other mantras.

Thus, the image of the Buddha—that is, the image of emptiness—must be made directly perceptible for the sake of accomplishing the higher meditations (*aparadhyāna*). In this way, O Lord, the yogin must first accomplish the glorious mantra and the image of the Buddha; afterwards, the activities (*karmāṇi*) are accomplished through the twelve divisions (*dvādaśabheda*), which consist of immeasurable qualities like the divisions of the sun. However, as long as the mantra and the image are not accomplished within the abode of the three worlds, nothing at all is accomplished. Therefore, O King, once one's own mind is free from defilement, one should first accomplish the mantra-image of the Lord; such is the rule. (159)

Now, for the sake of attaining the siddhis of the sword and so forth, the sādhana of the Lord of Asuras is described: O King, one who has fallen on the battlefield or likewise a thief hanging [there], on the eighth day during the night of spirits (bhūtarātra), one should bathe him in the cremation ground with eight jars;

having worshipped him with perfumes, incenses, lamps, various kinds of food offerings, and red flowers, one should perform the placement of the vajras (vajranyāsa) according to the natural order upon the head, heart, crown, navel, and throat. || 160 ||

By the words beginning with "hero" (śūra), it is meant that here on the battlefield, a heroic prince or another warrior has fallen by the strike of a single iron arrow; likewise, a hero who is hanging from a tree,
or a thief, on the eighth day of the night of spirits or on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
"O King"— this is the address.

In the world of the funeral pyre, that is, in the cremation ground, one should bathe that corpse with eight jars [of water] prescribed for the rite of subjugation (*vaśyakarma*), as well as with the waters of *Jayā* and *Vijayā*.
Then, having worshipped with perfumes, incenses, lamps, various kinds of sacrificial oblations (*caru*), and red flowers, and having donned a red garment,
one should perform the *vajra*-placement (*vajranyāsa*) according to the natural order on the head, heart, crown, navel, and throat— namely,
*oṃ* on the forehead, *hūṃ* at the heart, *haṃ* at the crown, *'ho* at the navel, *āḥ* at the throat, and *ikṣaḥ* at the secret place.

Thus, having performed the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) consisting of the previously mentioned heart, head, crest, armor, eyes, and weapon, one should effect the protection of both the deity and one's own body through union with the deity. || 160 ||

Having fashioned within a triangular pit a central lotus with its seed-syllable mark using vermilion powder, one should place the marks of the Jinas on the petals in the cardinal and intermediate directions, as well as the respective marks of the goddesses.

Outside, upon the three lines, there are no marks; likewise, in the circle of the ten directions, there are the marks of the Krodhas. To its left is a *preta*, whose lotus-hand holds a sword, with its feet outside the mandala.

Then, in the previously mentioned triangular *kuṇḍa*, the inner lotus is red with the aforementioned vermilion powder; it is "with its emblem," meaning there is the emblem of an arrow (*bāṇa*) in the pericarp (*kaṇikā*). Alternatively, according to the statement, "In all rites, [there is] a vajra," there is a red vajra.
Regarding the emblems on the petals—"the emblems of the Jinas":
there is a sword on the eastern petal, a jewel on the southern, a lotus on the northern, and a wheel on the western.

"In every direction and intermediate direction likewise," refers to the respective emblems of the goddesses as previously stated regarding the defects of the Mothers: namely, a knife in the southeast, a thunderbolt-goad on the leaf of the Daityas in the southwest, a thunderbolt-noose in the northwest, and a trident in the northeast.
On the three outer lines, within the circle of the ten directions, there are likewise the symbols of the wrathful deities;

just as those of the Tathāgatas are in the cardinal directions, so those of the goddesses are in the intermediate directions; above is the vajra of Uṣṇīṣa, and below is the axe of Sumbharāja, for the protection of the three enclosures.

Thus, having placed the marks in the dust mandala according to the previously stated procedure, having installed the ritual jars and other implements upon the cremation ground mandala, having performed the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), and having performed the worship of the chosen deities with perfumes and other offerings, one should then present the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) to the guardians of the field (*kṣetrapāla*) and others. Then, that *preta*—in its own dwelling—is placed to the north of the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) and to the south of the southern gate of the dust mandala; thus, between the mandala and the pit, the *preta* is positioned with its left foot forward, meaning with the right foot [pointing] northward and the head toward the north.
"With an asikarakamala" means with a sword in hand, held upward and encircled by three lines.

Having performed self-protection with the vajras of the Lord of Jinas against the previously mentioned defects of the Mothers, the mantra-practitioner, while performing this very act of licking meat mixed with blood on the right side of the hearth (kuṇḍa), should offer oblations one thousand times—ten times a hundred—reciting the mantra ending in *phaṭ*: *oṃ hrīṃ phreṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. Having bound that mantra, he remains in the vajra-posture, truly unshakable like Mount Meru, until midnight.

Thus, having performed the self-protection (*ātmarakṣā*) as previously described with the Vajras of the Lord of Jinas within the mandala, the mantra-practitioner (*mantrī*), while performing the fire-offering (*homa*) in this manner with blood and flesh on the right side of the hearth (*kuṇḍa*), should proceed as follows:

having kindled the fire from a Kṣatriya’s house with *khadira* wood in this hearth, and then having performed the invocation of the Fire-god (*pāvakāvāhana*) and so forth according to the previously stated procedure, he should offer one thousand times—that is, one thousand units—of "great meat" (*mahāmāṃsa*) together with blood using his own mantra through the yoga of the deity. His mantra is:
*oṃ hrīṃ phra hūṃ phaṭ*; this is his mantra.
By this [mantra] as well, its ritual placement (nyāsa) should be performed:
*oṃ* on the forehead, *hrīṃ* on the throat, *phreṃ* on the heart, *hūṃ* on the navel, and *phaṭ* on the secret place—this is the placement.
Having assumed the vajra-posture, remaining truly unshakable like Mount Meru, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) for one watch until midnight. || 162 ||

When the homa is complete, he who blazes forth with his tongue lolling, possessing sharp fangs and three eyes, roaring and causing the earth to crack with his feet while terrifying the practitioner, stands within the center of the fire-pit and laughs "kahakaha" and dances with a fearsome body; seeing him, the terrified mantra-practitioner, his mind destroyed, goes to the city of Yama in an instant. (163)

[Chapter on Various Methods, verses 161–167] Then, when the thousandfold homa is completed, he blazes forth, with his sword dangling from his mouth, possessing sharp fangs and three eyes; roaring and causing explosions, he terrifies the practitioner with his feet even as they strike the earth. Having entered the body of a *preta*, that lord of the *asuras* remains in such a state within the interior of the fire-pit, laughing "kahakaha" and dancing with a terrifying form.
Seeing that, the minister, his mind destroyed, goes to the city of Yama in an instant. || 163 ||

The mantra-practitioner should not fear even the Lord of the Asuras while in the cremation ground for the sake of attaining accomplishment. Seeing that his mind is unshakable, the Lord of Beings says this again:

"I am accomplished; I have been mastered by you, O brave one! Speak, what shall I do for you now? When this has been said, the practitioner should pray in his own mind for whatever he desires for the benefit of others. 164.

"May your lordship grant me the eight worldly supernatural powers (*laukikī-aṣṭasiddhi*): the power of touch, the sword, the nectar of mercury, the fruit-pill, the eye-ointment that brings delight, and the medicinal paste for the feet;
as well as hatred, eradication, the destruction of worlds, paralyzing, attracting, and subjugation—may all these attain perfection for me. And he replied, "I shall do all of this. (165)

Having accomplished the lord of spirits (bhūtendra), O King, the practitioner goes wherever he wishes—in the netherworld, in the atmosphere, in the abode of the best of gods, on the peak of Mount Meru, or across the ocean; mounted there with sword in hand, he performs the welfare of the world even while dwelling upon the surface of the earth. Therefore, for the sake of the benefit of sentient beings and out of supreme compassion, the lord of asuras should be accomplished. || 166 ||

From this point forward, the three verses beginning with "one should not fear the Lord of Asuras" and ending with "the Lord of Asuras is to be accomplished" are easy to understand; such is the rule for the accomplishment of the Lord of Asuras. (164–166)

Now the characteristics of mantra are stated: O Lord of Men, the first syllable of the name of the male and female deities becomes the Mind-Vajra; furthermore, all the syllables of the name constitute the Speech-Vajra, and beyond that is the Body-Vajra.

Therefore, there are many kinds of individual limb-mantras, which are sometimes accomplished through recitation (*pāṭhasiddha*), and sometimes they are to be meditated upon, worshipped, or recited according to the divisions of Mind, Speech, and Body, following the family of one's own Jina. || 167 ||
"Beginning with the first letter of the name," and so forth.

Here, among the stable and moving phenomena within the three realms, whatever is the name of a thing, the first letter of that name is the "first letter of the name" (*nāmādya*); that itself becomes the mind-vajra. O Lord of Men, for all deities and goddesses, it is the speech-vajra, known as the "all-name. For example, here, names such as Tārā, Pāṇḍarā, Māmakī, and Locanā are themselves the speech-vajra.

Thus, for all phenomena (*bhāva*), even every name-syllable (*nāmākṣara*) is likewise [the body-vajra], and beyond that is the body-vajra (*kāyavajra*). Here, as in the examples: *oṃ tāre tutāre ture svāhā*, *oṃ pāṇḍaravāsini varade svāhā*, *oṃ māmakī kiri kiri svāhā*, *oṃ locane vasude svāhā*—these syllables in excess of the name, together with the syllables of mind and speech, are body-vajras. Therefore, the garland-mantra (*mālāmantra*) which follows after that body-vajra is called the "limb-by-limb mantra" (*pratyaṅgamantra*).
Just as the hands, feet, and so forth are limbs of the body, so too are the components of the name those of the mantra-name;
and that [name] is of many kinds,
sometimes being established through mere recitation.

Here, as in the Chapter on Consecration (*abhiṣeka-paṭala*), the mantra for each limb (*pratyaṅga-mantra*) is as follows: *Oṃ āḥ hūṃ ho haṃ kṣaḥ ha, kṣ m l v r ya, Kālacakra, subduer of the difficult-to-tame, ender of birth, old age, and death, conqueror of the three worlds, great lord of heroes, vajra-body, vajra-limbed, vajra-eyed,* and so forth. This mantra for each limb—whether established through recitation (*pāṭhasiddha*), accomplished in a previous life, or accomplished again in this life—becomes perfected;
thereafter, one performs the ritual action.

Here, the mantra is to be meditated upon (*bhāvya*) by means of the mind and so forth, beginning with the name; it is to be worshipped (*yājya*) as the name-mantra, and it is to be recited (*jāpya*) as the name augmented [by syllables].

"According to the power of one's own Buddha-family" means that it is to be meditated upon through the distinctions of the rosary and so forth by way of the distinction of mind; it is to be worshipped by way of the distinction of speech; and it is to be recited by way of the distinction of body—this is the rule.
In this context, one should meditate on the form of the deity without the initial *oṃ* of the name;
however, at the beginning of every name, one should worship with the *oṃ* of Kāyavajra.
Likewise, for each limb, having added the mantra of Ādikāyavajra and the *hūṃ phaṭ* of Cittavajra, one should recite it.
In this way, there is a differentiation of body, speech, and mind for all sentient beings. || 167 ||

Now, the number of recitations for the general mantra-sādhana is stated: For each class of mantra, ten million recitations (koṭijāpa) are prescribed; from that, a fire-oblation (homa) consisting of one-tenth the number is accomplished according to the influence of the natural qualities (guṇas).

Only then does it become effective for pacification and other rites, yielding fruit; otherwise, it does not attain success. Furthermore, the source of the mantra (mantrayoni) is to be mastered through meditation, recitation, fire-oblations, vows, and observances. || 168 ||
Regarding "each one" and so forth:

here, for each individual class of mantra, the recitation of ten million (*koṭi*) is well-known as the *kāyavajra* [practice]; from that ten-million-fold recitation, the fire offering (*homa*) is one-tenth, which constitutes a fire offering of one million.

"By means of the substances mentioned in the Initiation Chapter, according to the power of the natural qualities of the Vāgvajra, and by virtue of the qualities such as pacification (*śānti*) and so forth, [the mantra] is accomplished through the ritual of the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), the seat (*āsana*), and so on;

only then does it subsequently become capable of granting results in pacification and other rites, for otherwise it does not attain accomplishment. Thus it is said: 'The goal is to be accomplished through meditation, recitation, and fire-offerings (*homa*), joined with vows and observances; and the source of the mantra is likewise to be accomplished.'"

In this context, whatever the specific commitment (*samaya*) of each deity may be, that deity is to be accomplished through that commitment and those observances and restraints (*vrata-niyama*); otherwise, they are not accomplished.

Likewise, if the initial syllable of the name of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is an enemy of the first syllable of the practitioner’s (*sādhaka*) name, then death occurs for the practitioner;
or if it is neutral (*udāsya*), then suffering arises.
Now, if it is a friend, then success is achieved; by means of a consonant that is a friend to the vowel, there is immortality, but by a consonant that is an enemy, there is disease.
All other enemies consist of the syllables of wind; there is no recitation (*japa*) of the vowels, which are the syllables of water, within the mantra,
by means of that vow and that discipline.
Furthermore,
it is said: "There is no death by an enemy" in the sixteenth chapter, verses 167–168.
The Great Chapter on Various Means: Vowels are [the friends] of consonants, and consonants are [the friends] of consonants.

Thus, water-syllables are the friends of fire-syllables; fire-syllables are the friends of earth-syllables; earth-syllables are the friends of wind-syllables; space-syllables are the friends of all; and all syllables are the friends of space.
Likewise, water is the friend of earth, wind is the friend of fire, fire is the friend of wind, and earth is the friend of water; such is the group of friends.
Water is the source of wind; earth is the source of fire; fire is the source of water; and wind is the source of earth.
Having thus understood everything, one should then accomplish the mantra-deity; such is the rule in the *Mūlatantra*.
Likewise, the Blessed One said in the *Mūlatantra*: "The letters *a*, *ku*, *ha*, and *ka* are guttural, characterized by vowels and consonants."
They always abide as friends to the elements, such as wind and the rest, which are empty.
The letters *i*, *cu*, and *yaś* are palatals (*tālavya*), characterized as both vowels and consonants;
they are born from the wind element and are enemies of those born from the water element.
The retroflex consonants ṛ, ṭu, ra, and ṣa, characterized as both vowels and consonants,
arise from the fire element and are the enemies of those born from the earth.
The labials and those beginning with the letter *u* (the labio-dentals), characterized as vowels and consonants,
are born from the element of water and are the enemies of those born from fire.
Furthermore, those dental consonants characterized by vowels and consonants that arise from the earth element are enemies to those born of the air element.
Air is always the friend of space and is neutral toward it due to the power of air; water's friend is earth, and fire is neutral toward it due to the lack of power.
Water is the friend of earth, as are fire and wind; however, excluding the *praṇava*, the first syllable of a mantra constitutes its *kula*.
That very mind is the cause for the accomplishment of the images of the mantras, when the first syllable of a mantra is conjoined with other consonants.
Then, that which was previously to be grasped by those two, due to the cause of initial utterance, becomes twofold through the distinction between vowels and consonants.
The enemy and friend of the vital breath (prāṇa), as well as that of the body, are now declared: the vowels are remembered as being either enemies, friends, or indifferent to the vital breath.

The consonants are the enemies of the body, while the vowels are its friends; those consisting of both are indifferent. A vowel as an enemy would take away the life-force of the practitioner, without a doubt.
Because ordinary fire lacks power,
wind is the friend of fire;
because ordinary earth lacks power, it is [the friend] of [fire].
Fire is always the enemy of wind; water is neutral toward it due to lack of power.
Wind is the enemy of fire; earth is neutral toward it due to lack of power.
[As stated] in the *Vimalaprabhā*, this causes disease and other afflictions in the body.
The enemy, characterized by the consonants, acts within the body;

those five [consonants] beginning with *ka* that possess the nature of consonants even within a single group— earth and the other elements belonging to them must be known, they must be known in the accomplishment of mantra.
Ṅa, ña, ṇa, ma, and na—these are the friends of those born from air and the other elements; gha, jha, ḍha, bha, and dha—these are the enemies of those born from water;
and ga, ja, ḍa, ba, and da—these are the enemies of those born from earth.

The letters kha, cha, ṭha, tha, and tha are the enemies of those born under the fire element (vahni-janman); the letters ka, ca, ṭa, pa, ta, and ta are the enemies of those born under the wind element (vāyu-janman).
A letter situated at the beginning of a mantra is an enemy whether it belongs to its own class or to another.
"The color of practitioners is twofold: innate and name-derived," and so forth; such is the rule of the Blessed One in the Root Tantra.
Furthermore, in that very same [tantra], the sixfold activity of the first syllable is explained.
For instance, for the sake of accomplishing the consonants of mantras and so forth, as well as the vowels,
six types of ritual action are prescribed for those performing service and recitation:
first one should perform *tāḍana* (striking), then *āveśa* (possession), and after that *dāhana* (burning).
Then the practitioner of mantra performs nourishment, followed by feeding and satisfaction; then,
struck by the King of Weapons preceded by the mantra and pervaded by the void with the letter of emission (visarga), he enters the state of swoon.
Through one hundred thousand recitations, the mantra-deity becomes transfixed in the mind;
having abandoned ego-grasping, she enters the body of the practitioner.
Thus, overcome by the vital wind (*vāyu*), she undergoes possession (*āveśa*) for the yogi.
When the Earth is overcome by fire, it is consumed; likewise, when it is nourished by water, it flourishes. When the deity is recited while stationed at the crown of the head, she departs;
when she is gratified at the crown of the head, pervaded by the digit of the Bindu, she becomes a granter of boons.

Thus, in the *Ādibuddha-mahātantra*, the preliminary service (*pūrva-sevā*) by means of six hundred thousand recitations is proclaimed by the Muni for the sake of attaining the desired accomplishment:
*phaṭ*, *hūṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, and likewise *vaṣaṭ*.
The practitioner of the vow should perform the six rites at the end of the mantra according to their respective order;
having first offered to Vairocana, he should again commence the recitation.
Having performed ten million recitations, he should then perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) consisting of one-tenth that number.

The Great Chapter on Various Means of Accomplishment: By means of the procedure taught in the tantra, everything is accomplished from that; the deity grants a boon, and when perfected, she grants whatever is requested by the practitioners.
The location is other than what is found in the book, the caste is different, the ritual action is different, as are the time, the mantra, and the lineage.
Those men on earth who perform the practice using mantras recited for all rites that lack a foundation in the [proper] direction, being devoid of the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*), undergo suffering;
for what indeed is that "tradition" if it is found merely in books and the like?

Likewise, those practitioners who are devoid of the true essence of mantra seek to enjoy space as revealed through written recitations of provisional meaning; they attempt to accomplish the rites for deities and others by means of mantras read from books.
Through firm vigor of one's own mind, or by the recitation of mantras,

the desired worldly accomplishment (*laukikī siddhi*) shall arise for practitioners who seek the welfare of others— through mantra-recitations, as well as through fire-offerings (*homa*) and the sequential performance of worship rituals.

"Those devoid of ritual action do not achieve success; this is the word of the Teachers, the Bodhisattvas, and the gods as it truly is. Therefore, with every effort, that very [practice] is adopted by the wise."
Thus, having performed the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), one should accomplish the syllable of the mind;
herein [is] the striking of the mantra and so forth, as follows— first, the Tārā mantra is shown:
By that same procedure, the others are to be understood:

one hundred thousand recitations of the mantra for striking, *oṃ htāḥ phaṭ*; *oṃ ytāḥ hūṃ* for causing possession; *tāḥ voṣaṭ* for burning; *oṃ vtāḥ namaḥ* for nourishing; *oṃ ltāḥ svāhā* for increasing; and *oṃ tāṃ vaṣaṭ* for pleasing. Having performed six hundred thousand recitations and offered sixty thousand oblations (*homa*), then there are ten hundred thousand recitations of the Vāgvajra mantra: *oṃ tāre svāhā*.
Then, the fire offering (homa) consisting of one-tenth [of the recitations],
followed by the body-vajra recitation: *oṃ tāre tuttāre ture svāhā*.

One should perform the fire offering (*homa*) up to ten hundred thousand times, reaching the limit of ten million; in this way, the deity of the mantra becomes a granter of boons for yogis, and not otherwise.

Each mantra—whether it be that of the mind, speech, or body—is to be meditated upon, worshipped, and recited; the rule in the *Mūlatantra* of the Blessed One is that these consist of six hundred thousand, ten hundred thousand, or one hundred million recitations.

Now the accomplishment of the pill (*gulikā*) is described: The perfected pill, bound with the three metals and containing the flesh of a bird, bestows the power of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*). By means of the lamps of dogs, horses, and so forth, it removes hunger, thirst, and other diseases from the body.

With their eyes and bile, it becomes an ointment for excellent men that pierces the earth, grants invisibility, and captivates the minds of young women when accomplished in a glorious cremation ground.
[From the *Vimalaprabhā*, the commentary on the *Sādhanā* section, beginning with "siddha" etc.]

In this regard, first, having accomplished the mantra for the preparation of the pill (*gulikā*) according to the previously mentioned procedure, one recites: *oṃ kālacakra ājñāsiddha gulikāṃ sādhaya svāhā*.
Thereafter, there occurs the deity’s authorization for the preparation of the pill.

In this regard, the procedure is as follows: having prepared the *palala* (pounded meat) of one of the thirty-six groups of *khecarīs* mentioned in the Chapter on Consecration—namely, those consisting of five, sixteen, eight, or eight [groups]—and having made a powder dried in the shade, one should mix it with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). Then, having ground it with Akṣobhya, one should make pills the size of chickpeas. Thus, they are "perfected" when bound with the three metals. Here, by means of the purification of body, speech, and mind, through the divisions of Moon, Sun, and Rāhu, the three metals are silver (*tāra*), copper (*tāmra*), and magnetite (*kāntaloha*). When each is bound individually, they are said to be "bound with the three metals."
The pill made from the flesh (*palala*) of birds, when prepared according to the sequence to be described, bestows the power of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*).

Likewise, a pill prepared and bound with the flesh of land-dwelling and water-dwelling creatures such as dogs, horses, and so forth, removes diseases such as hunger and thirst from the body when applied with the three metals (*triloha*). This is the rule for the preparation of the pill (*gulikā*).
Now, the preparation of the collyrium (*añjana*) is stated, beginning with "with eyes," and so forth.
Having first accomplished the mantra for the preparation of the collyrium (*añjana*) as before, one should then accomplish the collyrium itself with the mantra:
*oṃ kālacakrājñāsiddhāñjanaṃ sādhaya svāhā*.
Then, having taken the eyes of birds and ground them into a fine powder, one should meditate upon it with the *bodhicitta*.
That very same ointment serves for the attainment of hidden treasures (*nidhāna*) and for the piercing of the earth (*bhūprabheda*).
Furthermore, having prepared an ointment from the bile of dogs, horses, and so forth, one should saturate it with female menses;

that very ointment brings about invisibility (*antardhāna*). When accomplished in a glorious cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), it is enchanting to young women and effective for both invisibility and subjugation (*vaśya*).

Then, on the night of the eighth day of the dark fortnight, or during the day of the Manu-period, having drawn the mandala and performed protection all around it, and having placed balls of meat or collyrium in its center and worshipped it with very fragrant flowers, one should perform the mantra-recitation until they emit rays like the sun in the sky; then, having extracted what is to be grasped from that [light]. || 170 ||

In this regard, the procedure is as follows: on the night of the eighth day of the dark fortnight, or on the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight—known as the "day of the Manu"—having drawn the mandala and having performed the protection rites all around it as previously described for the practice of the Lord of the Daityas, one should then place either a pill or collyrium contained in a skull within the center of the mandala's hub. Having thus placed the meat, the pill, or the collyrium in its center and worshipped it with very fragrant flowers, and having likewise offered the previously mentioned oblations and so forth, one should then perform the recitation of the mantra.
By this previously mentioned method and by the command of Kālacakra, one should recite the mantra as long as rays of light are emitted, whether toward pills or ointments.

Then, having extracted what was to be grasped from that limit, if they do not emit rays of light, then one should perform the mantra-sādhana again until the deity grants a sign of response (*pratyādeśa*).
Then, having taken men according to the number of pills, one becomes a pill-vidyādhara.
In this way, one becomes a Vidyādhara by means of a mirror;
by means of a sword, a Sword-Vidyādhara;
and likewise by means of a jewel and so forth.
The mantra for that is: *oṃ kālacakra ājñāsiddha khaḍgaṃ sādhaya svāhā*.
Thus, the rule is that "Kālacakra" is placed at the beginning in the case of the jewel and so forth.
Having fashioned an iron sword there, one should accomplish it according to the specific deity.

Having made the jewel of crystal, the lotus of silver, and the wheel of gold, the vajra of all metals, and likewise the bell and the curved knife of iron—this is the rule for the ritual of the insignia (*cihna-sādhana*).
In this way, one should accomplish all weapons, such as the trident, the spear, and so forth.
Whichever weapon one accomplishes here, by that insignia one becomes a *vidyādhara* of that particular family (*kula*) by the command of Kālacakra.

Now, if by the rule of the deities one attains the seven-fold revolution like the perfected elixir (*siddharasa*), then the *khecarī* accomplishments arise without [further] practice; such is the rule in the Root Tantra.
Thus ends the procedure for the practice of pills and so forth. || 170 ||

If the messenger is alive and has gone toward the northern direction (the quarter of the sky), the question is peerless and yields the fruit of great happiness; however, one bitten by a snake will meet death if the messenger is said to be dead or if the question is "equal" (neutral).

Indeed, if the messenger utters the name of a serpent or similar creature, the person bitten meets death. If the inquiry occurs during the inhalation of breath, it is auspicious; if during the exhalation, it shall be inauspicious. (171)
The messenger, with his left foot foremost, indicates a young woman; if he touches a man with his right hand or a limb of his own body, that person has been bitten in that very spot.

A wide-open gaze of the eyes and face portends death, as does a black sound at the root of the ear; if there is even a slight throbbing in the heart-lotus, one should perform a ritual of protection there.

First, there is the protective rite which brings happiness to both the victim and oneself; having applied Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, and Space to the thumbs and other fingers respectively, one should place the letters from *la* to *ha* in order upon the thighs, belly, heart, the center of the face, and the forehead. Then, with the syllables *hūṃ*, *kṣū*, *hya*, *hya*, and so forth, the ten serpents—both even and odd—are assigned according to the distinction between short and long vowels. (173)

The short seed-syllable on the left side reaches the ear and throat, while the long one on the right side reaches the armpit, belly, and thighs; through the application of emanation and withdrawal, one performs protection by means of the syllables called *Jina*, joined with the seed of the serpent and the syllables *huṃ kṣūṃ*. Thus, the bitten person, their heart swiftly struck down, enters a state of paralysis. When the earth-seed is at the forehead and the seed at the feet, paralysis occurs quickly; when the water-seed has entered the head and the fire-seed is in the belly, one attains freedom from poison.

The transference of poison occurs indeed in the seed-syllable of Vāyu at the forehead and in the fire at the heart; when it has entered the void at the crown of the head, alas, the poison that had reached the feet is truly severed. || 175 ||

A white drop on the forehead renders even the three types of poison non-toxic; a red one effects *stobha* (paralysis) and *praveśa* (entry); one resembling a dark cloud effects *stambhana* (immobilization); and a yellow-colored one [effects the same]. Regarding the flow of the vital breath (*prāṇapravāha*), one should apply a mixture of the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*) for the state of non-toxicity. Alternatively, with the mouth wide open, one should apply borax (*ṭaṅgaṇa*) to the uvula with the finger. [From the *Vimalaprabhā*: "In the case of non-toxicity, one should employ that which is blended with the three pungents. || 176 ||
Vajrī, Jāti, Kumārī, Trikaṭu, salt, Lāṅgalī, Devadālī, Brāhmī, Carā, Aśvagandhā, Dinakara, and Vandhyākarkoṭakī;
[along with] feces, flesh, semen, and blood—all these made into equal pills and ground with Akṣobhya—when applied by smell, destroy spirits, fevers, or the stable poison of serpents. (177)

During the seven-day cycle beginning with Sunday, at the conclusion of each seventh division of day and night, Kulikā—whose form is death—flows for half a *nāḍī* between the void (*śūnya*) and Mars (*manda*).

One should not engage in the sport of snakes, nor should one consume any of the three kinds of poison; for one bitten by a snake during that very time goes to the city of Yama. This occurs at midday and midnight, during the periods of day and night, when one is struck by a weapon upon reaching the ground.
Due to the division of the days of the week, the Kulikā—the single vein of the time-bite—flows through the middle of the junctions as the Void and the Blind.
Furthermore, at dawn and when the sun has set, the Kāla-vein likewise flows; these mouths of Rāhu should be correctly understood at every daily occasion. (179)
In the sun [sign], the serpent Ananta has its course during the day and night; in the first portion of the day, the remaining serpents arise here according to the division of the seven days.
The durations in *nāḍīs* are 0, 6, 5, 3, 4, 8, 7, 3, and 3, starting from Sunday; due to the difference in the movement of the eight hooded snakes, there may be poison. (180)

The Brahmin is Ananta, white as snow; the Kṣatriya king is Kulika; Vāsuki is Śaṅkhapāla, red; the Vaiśya is Mahābja, resembling excellent gold; and Takṣaka is likewise. Karkoṭaka is Abja, resembling a dark cloud; and the two Śūdras are Viśva and Varuṇa, possessing all colors. Their places of birth are the elements of water, fire, earth, air, and ether.

From the feet to the waist it is yellow, and likewise from the navel-suture to the throat it is white; from there up to the creeper-like eyebrows it is red, resembling a dark cloud; and from there indeed, extending to the crown, it is of universal color (variegated) and accompanied by a multitude of hoods.
When meditated upon with the five elements and sealed with their respective mudrās, this [Garuda] removes the poison of serpents, as well as diseases caused by spirits and the like. || 182 ||

One should meditate upon Kāraṇa, the Lord of Birds, within the lotus of one's own heart, atop the sun, adorned with serpent ornaments, five-colored according to his entire family, and radiant. Having first recited the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ) and the end-syllable *svāhā*, and then having muttered the mantra of the Lord of Birds ten million times, one should accomplish the Lord of Birds together with the host of hooded serpents.

When this is accomplished, the lords of serpents, the sons of the serpent-king, spirits, yakṣas, and planetary deities on this excellent earth, as well as ḍākinīs and mātṛs, enter into a state of servitude.

All the hosts of planets are drawn by the power of the mantra; even one bitten by the God of Death is restored to speech. Therefore, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, a person should first practice the sādhana of the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa).
Therefore, the *gāruḍa* meters from the one hundred and seventy-first verse onward are easy to understand;
for that reason, they have not been written [here] with commentary. || 171–184 ||

Now the yantras for pacification and other rites are described: First, the *sādhya* [name] is placed in the center; then, in the eight petals [of the lotus], starting from its own directions, are the eight consonants beginning with *ya*. In the sixteen petals, there are the letters beginning with *e*, and in the thirty-two petals, the letters from *ka* to *hakṣa*. In the four petals of the junctions (*sandhi*), the letters ending in *la* are placed along with their respective vowels. In the four petals of the Vedas, the eight [letters]; in those of the kings (sixteen), the thirty-two; in those of the teeth (thirty-two), the sixty-four; and in those of the twice-born (four), the *sādhya* is placed in the center. In the first [set of] petals, the group of four [consonants] beginning with *ya*; in the sixteen, those beginning with *e*; and in the thirty-two, the ten groups multiplied by three (thirty) [consonants] from *ka* to *hakṣa*. In the four petals of the junctions, the letters ending in *la* together with their vowels, and the *sādhya* is likewise placed in the four petals multiplied by the number of lunar days (thirty) and the yugas (four).
"In the Vedas," and so forth.

Here, on materials such as banyan leaves mentioned in the *Abhiṣeka-paṭala*, diagrams for rites of pacification (*śānti*) and other purposes are to be inscribed using sandalwood paste and the like with a cool-pointed stylus.
The sequence there is as follows: four petals in the first circle, eight in the second, sixteen in the third, thirty-two in the fourth, sixty-four in the fifth, and thirty-two in the sixth.
Just as there are six wheels in the body—at the crown, the heart, the forehead, the throat, the navel, and the secret place—so too there are six circular diagrams in the drawing of the yantra.
In that [diagram], the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is placed in the center of the four-petaled lotus.
Regarding the "Vedas," this refers to the four petals; on them, in the cardinal directions, one first places the pair *a* and *aṃ*.
A in the east, Ā in the north, I in the west, and AḤ in the south.
Thus, regarding the first circle:
on the petals of the eight lotuses—that is, on the eight leaves—are the letters beginning with *ya*. *I* and *ī* are in the east and the southeast (*agni*).
Ṛ ṝ are in the south and the southwest;
u ū are in the north and the northeast;
la la are in the west and the northwest.
Thus is the second circle.

Likewise, regarding "among the kings," in the third circle of sixteen petals, [the vowels] beginning with *e* are placed in the four petals starting from the east: *e, ai, ya, yā* in the eastern petals; *ar, ār, ra, rā* in the southern petals; *o, au, va, vā* in the northern petals; and *al, āl, la, lā* in the western petals. Thus is the third circle.

"In the petals" means in the thirty-two petals; "the ten multiplied by three" means thirty consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ha*. Regarding "in the twice-born [petals]," these are as follows:

in the five petals starting from the east, *cha, ja, jha, ña*; in the five petals to the south, *ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa*; in the north, *pa, pha, ba, bha, ma*; and in the west, *ta, tha, da, dha, na*. Thus, beginning from Īśāna (northeast), on the eastern petal one begins with the syllable *ma*, and across three petals [there are] *ka, kha, ga*. In the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is stated that beginning from the southeast (Āgneya), in the south one begins with *ña*, and across three petals [there are] *gha, ṅa, cha*.
Starting from the southwest (nairṛtya), on the three petals beginning with the letter *ṇa* in the west, [the syllables] are *sa pa ṣa*;
starting from the northwest (vāyavya), on the three petals beginning with the letter *na* in the north, [the syllables] are *śa ka ha*.
Thus, it is on the thirty-two petals in the fourth circle.
Regarding "six oceans" (abdhi-ṣaṭ), this refers to the sixty-four petals;
the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is to be placed on the four petals—in the east, south, west, and north—just as it is, and likewise in the center.
Thus, the name of the *sādhya* is in five locations.

Regarding the phrase "in the Yugas multiplied by the lunar days" (*tithiguṇitayugeṣu*), this refers to the sixty petals; in order, the letters ending in *la* (*lāntāḥ*) are with their respective vowels (*samātrāḥ*).

Thus, *ha ya ra va la*, together with their twelve vowels (*mātrās*), constitute the sixty [syllables] on the sixty petals. Then, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise, the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhyanāma*) is placed: *ya yā yi yī yū yṛ yu yū yḷ ylu yaṃ yaḥ* on twelve petals. Then, to the south of the name, *ra rā ri rī ru rū la la raṃ raḥ* on twelve petals.
To the north of the name, *va vā vi vī vṛ vṛ vu vū vla vlu vaṃ vaḥ* on twelve petals.

In the west, on the twelve petals, are the letters *la*, *li*, *lī*, *ḷ*, *ḹ*, *lu*, *lū*, *ḷḷ*, *llū*, *laṃ*, and *laḥ*—these being the name of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Then, on the eastern petal is the first letter of the *sādhya*'s name; on the western petal is *ha*; on the northern petal is *haiṃ*; on the southern petal is *haḥ*. Thus, moving counter-clockwise, [the letters] from *hi* to *hī* extend to the northeast (*īśāna*); *hu* and *ha* extend to the southeast (*agni*); *huhū* extends to the northwest (*vāyavya*); and *ha la hala* extends to the southwest (*nairṛtya*).

The first syllable of the *sādhya*'s name is placed in the pericarp (*kaṇikā*), the second on the eastern twilight-petal, the third on the southern, the fourth on the northern, and the fifth on the western.
The syllables of mind, speech, body, and gnosis—*te*, *hūṃ*, *āḥ*, and *oṃ ho*—should be written together with the initial syllable of the name. || 185 ||

From the first [vowels] and each of the individual vowels, by virtue of the crocodile (*makara*) and the jar (*ghaṭa*), there are five long and short [vowels]. On the outer petals, there are also thirty-two syllables such as *vajratīkṣṇa* together with the heart-mantra.

Furthermore, for rites such as pacification (*śānti*) on the exterior, there are the mandalas of *va-ya-ra-la*; their syllables have the head at the center, and for subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), they have the foot moving like a flame. (186)
Now, according to the [signs] Capricorn and Aquarius, there are five long and short vowels starting from the first vowel;
here, in the signs beginning with Capricorn, the presiding deities are *kā*, *khā*, *gā*, *ghā*, *ṅā*, and so forth.

To the right of the previously established seed-syllable of the mind (*citta*), in clockwise order, they are *cā*, *chā*, *jā*, *jhā*, *ñā* in Pisces; likewise, *trā*, *jhā*, *ja*, *cha*, *ca* in Aries; thus, on the ten petals.

Likewise, on the south [petal] are the ten letters beginning with *ṭa* for Vāgvajra; on the north, the ten beginning with *ya* for Kāyavajra; and on the west, the ten beginning with *ta* for Jñānavajra. On the remaining twenty petals—specifically the five petals on the west—are the five long vowels beginning with *ā*; on the east, the five short vowels beginning with *ṅa*; on the south, the five long vowels beginning with *sa*; and on the north, the five short vowels beginning with *ka*. Thus, there are sixty syllables in the fifth circular array on the thirty-two outer petals.

Here, in the secret lotus, through the purification of the thirty-two petals, there are thirty-two syllables on the petals within the sixth circle, together with the heart-mantra, beginning with *Vajratīkṣṇa* and so forth.

They are as follows: starting from the northeast (*īśāna*) and ending at the southeast (*āgneya*), one has "O Vajratīkṣṇa, cutter of suffering" (*vajratīkṣṇa duḥkhacheda*). Then, in the south, "to the embodiment of wisdom-knowledge" (*prajñājñānamūrtaye*). Likewise, in the west, "O Lord of Body and Speech" (*kāyavāgīśvara a*).
And likewise in the north, "homage to you, Arapacana" (*arapacanāya te namaḥ*). These are the syllables beginning with *Vajratīkṣṇa*.

Having thus drawn the yantra consisting of six wheels according to the procedure taught in the chapter on consecration, and also for external rites such as pacification (*śānti*) and so forth, the mandalas of *va*, *ya*, *ra*, and *la* are indeed those [of the wheels].
This yantra, for the purposes of pacification, nourishment (*puṣṭi*), the removal of fever, and the neutralization of poison,
one should encircle the yantra with a water-mandala, or else with the syllable *va*.
Then one should cast [the victim] into the center of a moon-maṇḍala or into the midst of an elephant;

likewise, for killing and similar rites, one should encircle [the victim] with a wind-maṇḍala, for subjugation and similar rites with a fire-maṇḍala, and for paralyzing and similar rites with an earth-maṇḍala.
The remainder should be performed as stated in the Abhiṣeka-paṭala.
In this yantra, since the letters are said to have their heads within the womb (*garbha*), they should be drawn with their heads toward the womb;
since it is said that "their feet move like peacocks," all [letters] should have their right feet [toward the center],
and for all of them, Meru is situated to the north.
The "embryo-center" (garbhakaṇikā) is used for subjugation and attraction. || 186 ||

For pacification and other rites, the mantra-practitioner should write the lines of the *garbha-cakra* with a quill whose tip is as flickering as fire. As previously stated, this wheel effects pacification, nourishment, subjugation of the world, destruction, eradication, attraction, subjection, paralysis, and delusion within the abode of the three worlds. It is to be accomplished through recitation (*jāpa*) and fire-offerings (*homa*). First, in this context, the mantra beginning with "Mahāvajratīkṣṇa" and so forth [is to be employed]. (187)
Likewise, in rites such as pacification (*śānti*), the "womb-feet" (*garbhapāda*) face north with their heads moving like a flame;
thus they have their heads to the south.

Similarly, in rites such as killing (*māraṇa*), the "eastern feet" (*pūrvacaraṇa*) have their heads to the west; in rites such as immobilization (*stambhana*), the "western feet" (*paścimacaraṇa*) have their heads to the east.
The mantra should be written on each leaf according to the aforementioned method; this is easy to understand. Thus ends the rule for the six-cakra yantra. || 187 ||

Now the Yantra of Yamāntaka is described: on the eight-spoked, twelve-spoked, sixteen-spoked, and intermediate [circles], located in the cardinal and intermediate directions, the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is in the corners and the center; from the base of Mount Meru, Yamarāja becomes manifest.
From that center of the inner circle, *danirayakṣet* arises; from that, at the end, *oṃ hoḥ ṣṭrīḥ*; outside of that is *vikṛtādānanāt*; and twice *hūṃ phaṭ*. || 188 ||

Regarding "eight-spoked" and so forth: here, on a *nyagrodha* leaf or similar surface, the yantra is to be drawn; the first circle has eight spokes, the second twelve spokes, and the third sixteen spokes.

In that regard, "located in the directions and intermediate directions on the eight spokes" means that the first syllable of *Yama* and the others is located in the cardinal direction, while the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) are located on the petals in the intermediate directions. And on the sixteen spokes, [they are] on every other petal among the eight; thus the person to be accomplished is in the corners.

In the first circle, he who prevails in the center of the pericarp is *Ya*; in the twelve-spoked [wheel], *Ra* is in the east, *Jā* in the second, *Sa* in the third, and *Do* in the fourth petal of the first eight-spoked [wheel].
Furthermore, on the right, in the twelve-spoked [wheel],
there is *ru* on the fifth petal, *ṣa* on the sixth, and *ṇa* on the seventh; then again, on the eight-spoked [wheel], there is *yo*.
Furthermore, on the western petal of the twelve-spoked [wheel],
there is *ni* in the eighth, *ra* in the ninth, and *ya* in the tenth.
Furthermore, on the eighth spoke, [the syllable] *kṣe*;
again, on the twelfth and eleventh spokes, and likewise on the twelfth, it is said: *yama rājā sa do me ya ya me do ru ṇa yo da ya*.
"Ya, da, yo, ni, ra, ya, kṣe, ya, ya, kṣe, ya, ca, ni, rā, ma, ya"—thus, according to the *Mūlatantra*, these sixteen syllables are [placed] by the Sole Lord upon the sixteen petals.
Likewise, in the center, Yamarāja arises from the base of Meru; from that, from the center of the womb-enclosure (*garbhāra*), there is *da* and *ni*; and from that, *ra* and *ya*, hence "niranta."

Thereafter, regarding the eight-spoked and twelve-spoked [wheels], there is a rule: on the sixteen-spoked wheel, one should write this mantra—*oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana huṃ huṃ phaṭ*—between each petal, alternating with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). || 188 ||

Thus, O King, within the intermediate enclosure (kakṣāntarāla), this mantra containing the name of the person to be acted upon (sādhyanāma) is employed; it prevails in causing enmity, death, and subjugation. The syllables *ya*, *ma*, *rā*, *kṣe*, *da*, *me*, *do*, and *sa* are to be placed at the beginning. Furthermore, for paralyzing, attracting, deluding, strengthening, pacifying, and eradication, the letter *ya* enters from the womb [of the mantra] according to its qualities, and everything else is to be arranged externally as before. (189)

Thus, O King, this mantra containing the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) occurs within the intermediate compartments for the rites of inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*), causing death (*mṛtyu*), and subjugation (*vaśya*).
Here, in the center, the presiding deity (*adhideva*) prevails: *ya* for inciting enmity, *ma* for causing death, and *rā* for subjugation;
likewise, *kṣe*, *da*, *me*, *do*, and *sa* are the first [syllables] of each.

In this context, for the purpose of immobilization (*stambhana*) the syllable *kṣe*, for attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*) the syllable *da*, for delusion (*mohana*) the syllable *me*, for increasing strength (*balakaraṇa*) the syllable *do*, for pacification (*śānti*) the syllable *sa*, for eradication (*uccāṭana*) the syllable *cca*, for inducing fever (*jvarakaraṇa*) the syllable *ṇa*, for paralysis (*stobhana*) the syllable *rū*, for victory (*jaya*) the syllable *jā*, for the alleviation of affliction (*santāpaśamana*) the syllable *yo*, and for the warding off of enemies (*śatrunivāraṇa*) the syllable *ni*— these enter into the interior [of the seed-syllable] by the power of their qualities. Thus, according to the nature of the ritual action, whichever letter is the presiding lord within the interior, the letter *ya* is written in its place.
As before, everything is on the outside; this is the rule for the Yamāntaka machine. || 189 ||

Now the Mañjuśrī yantra is described: From the head of the letters, *ma* arises first, embraced by the vowels; it is the letter at the end of the letters (*va*) by virtue of belonging to the Vajra family, and I am said to be the fifth.

Wisdom is represented by two dots (*bindu*) in the supreme enclosure of the vowels; this *me* is also *u*, and thus *maṃ muḥ haṃ huḥ saṃ suḥ* [are formed] on the petals of the lotus and the earth-petals, as well as on the *mañju* petals. (190)
Regarding the passage beginning with "of the letters" (*varṇānām*):
here, "from the head of the letters" means that the *bindu* is at the head of the letters; from that head, the letter *ma* arises in front, embraced by a vowel.
The anusvāra, when embraced by the vowel *a*, becomes the letter *m*;

furthermore, when embraced by the letters beginning with *ka*, it becomes the end of the respective class (*vargānta*), thus becoming *ṅa, ña, ṇa, na, ma, na, no*. By virtue of the lineage of the Vajra family, I am said to be the fifth.
Therefore, I am the *bindu*; through the two *bindus* and the *visarga*, in the supreme enclosure of vowels between the two *akāras*, this "me" is indeed the *ukāra*.
Thus, "maṃ" is the Means (*upāya*) and "muḥ" is Wisdom (*prajñā*). In this way, there are eight syllables—haṃ, huḥ, saṃ, suḥ, maṃ, juḥ, ri, and ya—to be placed upon the eight petals.
In the second [mandala], which is circular with twelve spokes, it is indeed the "ark-leaf" (arkapatra). || 190 ||

Externally, Śrī-Vajraghoṣa prevails, joined with Mantabhadra as well as HŪṂ PHAṬ; in this [mandala], one should place the name of the target (*sādhya*) within the pericarp (*kaṇikā*), and likewise issue the command for the illustrious Samāja and so forth.
Thus, in the previously mentioned wheels as well, the name of the target is always to be written. All of this is accomplished for men through the word of the Lord of Jinas and by my grace. || 191 ||
Externally, on the first petal is Śrī, on the second Va; in this sequence, Jra, Ghoṣa, Samantabhadra, Hūṃ, and Phaṭ—these are the twelve syllables. All else is as before.
Thus, the one to be accomplished (sādhya) is here in the pericarp (kaṇikā).
The first syllable of the name of the person for whom the rite is being performed [should be placed] in the pericarp;
then, at the time of recitation, there is the invocation of Śrī and so forth, as follows:
Oṃ Śrīvajraghoṣa Samantabhadra, bring about peace, bring about peace for such-and-such a person! Namas!

In this way, for rites such as nourishment (*puṣṭi*) and so forth, *svāhā*, *hūṃ*, *phaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ* should be placed at the end; likewise, when drawing the diagrams (*yantra*), on the very same leaf, and also in the previously mentioned wheels (*cakra*), the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) should always be written. All of this is accomplished for men through the word of the Lord of Jinas and by my grace—thus [ends] the diagram (*yantra*).
The procedure for writing. || 191 ||

Whatever sound arises in the region of the heart of excellent men is heard within the cavities of the ears; therein the mind of the person enters into a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*), joined and become one with it.
Whatever sound is uttered in the world of living beings, that very thing the yogi hears; and this consciousness of hearing from afar must be cultivated by the powerful yogi. (192)

Having assumed the paryanka-bandha posture, with an open mouth, one should touch the teeth against one another; the external wind, drawn in and joined with that nectar, enters the center of the navel.
When restrained within the excellent body, it removes heat, hunger, thirst, and even poison; or else, the white drop at the forehead, surrounded by the vowels, releases nectar.

Even when the mouth is closed and the nostrils are sealed, the external air is drawn in with force by the *prāṇa*; the *apāna* wind, struck [against it] like lightning and fire, through the power of time and the practice of yoga, attains a state of equilibrium within the midst of the moon, sun, and fire. It removes hunger, thirst, and the need for food, and bestows immortality upon the body.

Having practiced for six months the yoga of fixing one's gaze upon one's own shadow while standing in the sunlight with the face turned away, and having looked at a hidden treasure with a steady stare, one should thereafter look toward the sky; then the smoke-colored *samarasa-puruṣa* (the person of equal flavor) will be seen.
He reveals a fissure in the earth; then, having entered the shadow of a tree, a garland of points (*bindu-mālā*) is meditated upon in the expanse of the sky.

That power which proceeds from the center of the navel to the supreme state, the end of the twelve, the end of the digits (kalā), is firmly restrained at the navel; resembling lightning and fire, it rises in the form of a staff. 1. From the wheel of practice (*sādhanā-cakra*) to the other wheel, she moves with a soft and graceful gait through the central channel (*madhya-nāḍī*); until, by force, like a needle, she touches the external skin at the aperture of the crown (*uṣṇīṣa-randhra*). (196)

The *mudrā* conforms to illusion; at that time, one should forcefully impel the downward breath (*apāna*) into the upward path. Having pierced the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*), it proceeds to the excellent city when the pair of winds is restrained.

Thus, through the piercing of the vajra in the mind along with its objects, one attains the state of a sky-walker (*khecara*); furthermore, this Mother of the Universe becomes for yogins the very nature of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*). || 197 ||
Like a form in the sky or in a mirror, illuminating the three worlds, she flashes with many rays resembling lightning and fire;

though appearing as non-different from external bodies, yet devoid of objects, she shines situated in the ether. She alone embraces the mind and consciousness of the world in its manifold forms. (198)

Having abandoned this stained-hearted *karmamudrā* and the conceptualized *jñānamudrā*, one should meditate upon the *divyamudrā* for the sake of perfect awakening—the mother of the supreme Victors—stainless, changeless, equal to space, all-pervading, accessible to yogis, immutable, possessing the splendor of gnosis, removing the impurities of existence, and permeated by Kālacakra. (199)

Consciousness is not of the nature of atoms; likewise, such [atoms] do not exist here in the three realms of existence. "Consciousness itself is the wisdom of the Buddha, abiding nowhere"—thus will the Buddhists teach.

By means of that which is devoid of syllables, men shall go toward emptiness; having grasped that emptiness, the husband taught that which is the immutable innate bliss of the body in the Mantra Vehicle. (200)

Go to the cow, the house, the arrow, the horse, and the elephant as your lords; enter the objects of the senses, for you are pure. This is the restraint during the time of sacrifice for those whose sense-objects are like poison, through the yoga of knowledge.
That which is the drinking of blood along with the cow-hide and the Soma-creeper by the initiated—the nectar of Soma that resides in the vulva (bhaga) is the form of all-pervading bliss. 201.

Brahmā is the body, Hara is speech, and Hari is the mind of living beings; they are the three Vedas. You are the syllable Oṃ, the three letters, the moon, the sun, and the fire, as well as the three channels and the [three] qualities (guṇas). Kaula is in the body, while Kulānya is situated in the qualities of the sense objects; Atharvaṇa is in the form of sound (nāda). In the center of that is the Unstruck (anāhata), which is devoid of sense objects, beyond qualities, and imperishable.

[Chapter, verses 196–209] The Great Chapter on Various Sadhanas: This secret was indeed taught of old by Brahmā, the yogi, at the Vedānta; yet, due to the loss of knowledge over time, the sages here have taught the killing of living beings.

O base man, that engagement in it yields fruitless results; for even charcoal, when sprinkled with streams of milk, might somewhere in this world take on the color of the moon for the sake of attaining heaven. (203)
