Those men who are deceived by Vedic statements devoid of ritual application and lacking in traditional observances, having performed a protection rite for their own wives during the day and night for the sake of obtaining sons, [believe] that a gift given by a son indeed becomes [a benefit] for the father who has gone to the world of the dead; therefore, this "wish-fulfilling gift" (*kāmadāna*), which yields the fruit of happiness for the virtuous, has been concealed by wicked Brahmins. (204)
If a noble horse belongs to another man, yet a great stallion is born from that great mare, will there not again be prosperity for the owner through the power of the horse?
Since lustful men perform protection [of their wives] every day, who are you and what is your own wife? Alas, when death has arrived, it is an inauspicious bondage of karma. (205)

In the world of mortals, the gift of a cow, the gift of land, and likewise other gifts that grant enjoyment—such as the gift of medicine and food which removes all disease and relieves hunger and thirst; and the gift of everything desired, which yields the fruit of human happiness—are indeed meritorious. How much more so at this time [of the Kali age], when a beloved wife, a sister, or even a fortunate daughter should be offered as a secret gift! 206.

The prostitute is the *karmamudrā*, and the secret woman is the *samayamudrā*; the wife of another is the *dharmamudrā*, who is independent and delights in many objects, while the *jñānamudrā* is one's own wife.

The prostitute is twelve years old and delights in supreme bliss; the woman of noble family (*kulastri*) is sixteen years old; she is independent at twenty years; she becomes one's own daughter at thirty years; and she is one's own wife at thirty [years]. (207)

Previously, for the sake of Buddhahood, the earth—abounding in elephants, horses, chariots, and various golden objects—was given by the Buddhas; furthermore, their heads, along with blood and flesh, were offered.

Yet, through these, the desired Buddhahood did not arise; therefore, the gift of desire was bestowed, and by that secret gift, Buddhahood was born for men within the family of the Conquerors' progenitor. (208)

Gold is equal to copper, the jewel on the crown of the gods is equal to a fragment of glass, a virtuous courtesan is equal to a low-born woman in the granting of desires, and a noble wife is equal to a piece of leather; a pure-bred horse is like a donkey, and a preeminent lord of elephants is obtained by means of a goat. If such things can be obtained through the gift of a wife, O Lord, what gain is there not for one born into the lineage of the Conqueror? (209)

In the sphere of loving-kindness, giving does not bestow the fruit of equal happiness because of the influence of beings who are [merely] similar; likewise, in the sphere of equanimity, it is so because of the influence of beings who are Māras.

Because of being inferior or superior, when both the spheres of compassion and sympathetic joy are bestowed, the two accumulations are fulfilled, yielding the fruit of immutable bliss for the sake of others by those who have attained the Sugata state. 210.
O King, for whom the caste system is the authority, for him the Veda is the authority; for whom the Veda is indeed the authority on this earth, for him sacrifice is the authority.

For whom sacrifice is the authority, for him the slaughter of various animals and men is the authority; for whom slaughter is the authority, for him sin—which causes the fear of hell—is the authority. (211)

For the sake of providing lodging and food, the Blessed One has taught the consecration of a glorious monastery; indeed, there the donor provides medicine and the gift of sustenance to pacify illness.
In the absence of such giving, the monastery becomes a mere dwelling on the surface of the earth—a haunt for animals. O King, wherever the Saṅgha resides, there also reside the Buddha and the Dharma.

Human beings who have gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha do so for the sake of liberation. The Buddha is established here in this abode; the Dharma is indeed this book written here. The Saṅgha, wearing the saffron robes, bestows the supreme bliss of adornment for a hundred thousand births. The Teacher is the Buddha himself, and his teaching is the Dharma upon the excellent surface of the earth. (213)

The Saṅgha established therein is one whose heart is joyful and who is compassionate toward all sentient beings; it is described here as fourfold, yet again as twofold: the Śrāvaka and the Unsurpassed.
Furthermore, it consists here of Bhikṣuṇīs and Bhikṣus, as well as Mahopāsakas and Mahopāsikās, Yoginīs and Yogins, and lay followers (Upāsakas and Upāsikās) who delight in innate bliss. || 214 ||

For the sake of merit and wisdom, the yogi always gives various kinds of gifts, especially food and other necessities that bring supreme happiness; this is the gift of what is desired by the practitioners.
Those givers who always bestow these with joyful hearts and devoted minds, being filled with merit and wisdom, go in this very life to the state of supreme bliss. (215)

In this chapter, regarding the Great Chapter on Various Means (Nānāsādhanamahoddeśa): Those disciples who are unawakened and openly revile the Teacher, the Jina, quickly go to the Avīci hell, most terrifying, having been slain by the Lords of Obstacles.

Who among men is equal to that monk, the preeminent Lord of the Jinas, who performs self-consecration through the power of mantras, and who stands in the state of vows and observances as a celibate practitioner? (216)

Everyone performs austerities while delighting in supreme bliss—whether as a mendicant, a wandering ascetic, a naked one, a shaven-headed one, or one with matted hair; whether devoted to sacred learning and recitation, or a scholar who has lost the path.

This is due to the ego-grasping of the doer, always clinging here to self and others, to son and wife, to the distinction between what is edible and inedible, and to the distinction between the worthy and unworthy recipient. (217)

Having withdrawn from the entire Buddha-field—which bestows the fruit of human happiness—and from attachment to body, speech, and mind, the one of evil intellect would look toward another Lord [in] a field, a sacred site, or another region, by means of violating vows and observances, by falling from a mountain, in battle, during an eclipse of the sun, or through the destruction of various weapons and fire while being intent on the pleasures of the senses. ||218||

In the past, all of this was even orchestrated by the Māras for the sake of drinking blood; yet it was only when he had gone to battle at a sacred ford, fasting, and was slain in combat; or when he died for the sake of releasing the sun’s rays, or for the sake of his home, wealth, or the welfare of Brahmins—that [this body was taken]. Therefore, this body of one's own, which is the abode of equal pleasure and pain, must be protected from others.

Having heard this king of tantras and the conduct of the supreme Victors, and having received initiation, whoever again gives way to envy shall enter hell for as long as eight [aeons]. Therefore, initiation should not be accepted by men as long as envy remains in the mind. (220)

Due to the power of impure fruits, hell-beings wander upon the ground as sharp as a needle’s point; yet by means of this—perfect generosity and ethical discipline within the family of the Conqueror’s progenitor, and the fullness of patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, aspiration, power, and perfect primordial knowledge—the yogi, having quickly made his mind joyful through the gift of a wife, establishes himself here in this birth. Those deluded men who, having formed bonds of passion in this life, have gone to hell, [are those who failed in these]. 229.
For the sake of the fortune of the earth, one whose heart is extremely fickle seizes a sharp sword and enters from all sides into a battle crowded with warriors and consisting of four divisions;
yet, seeing a herd of elephants, the sword falls from the palm of that terrified man. In this case, the fault does not lie with the sword, just as it is with a mantra-born [power]. (222)

Having attained [the state] through the sequence of the supreme mantra, one should accomplish the gods, the serpents, and the deities on the ground of Rudra by means of self-consecration; and the goddesses belonging to the family of the pledge (samaya) through meditation, recitation, and offerings.

The practitioner of mantra should perform the consecration according to the pure sequence with a mind of unceasing great bliss; for from that, the wish-fulfilling jewel of gnosis arises, and this is the path of the Victor.
Fire is never without its fuel; a fowler is never without his snare; a goldsmith is never without gold; and for the disputants, there are no enjoyments without their arguments.

Likewise, the mind of a yogi is never without attachment to a woman; yet when the body is pierced [by the central channel], that which pierces the body is not bound, and it bestows the innate bliss (*sahaja-sukha*) here in this world. (224)

In a garden or on a mountain devoid of people and wild animals, one should accomplish peaceful mantras; fierce mantras in a fierce cremation ground or in the abode of the best of gods for the rites of immobilization (*stambhana*) and delusion (*mohana*).

For subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), the mantra-practitioner attains the supreme bliss of the Lord through the application of all mudrās. In other places or with other wombs, there is no accomplishment for men even in hundreds of thousands of lifetimes. (225)

Having performed the recitation of mantras in his house, village, during the day, at night, or at the time of twilight, the weary, deluded, and disenchanted practitioner says again: "There is no accomplishment of the mantra.
He does not properly recognize the empty place or the time that has passed into the dead of night; instead, he applies medicinal ointments to his feet, toes, and head as if afflicted by disease.

Neither meditation, nor mantra recitation, nor ritual implements, nor great maṇḍalas, nor seats, nor fire-offerings, nor mantra-consecrations, nor the invocation and dispatching of the families of the Victors within the colored powder [maṇḍala] grant the accomplishment of mudrās or the supreme bliss of the Lord in the context of all mudrās. Therefore, for the sake of liberation, that [mudrā] should be meditated upon by the yogin at every daily occasion. 227.

O Lord of Men, when one has entered into swoon or sleep, one's own mind becomes devoid of intrinsic nature; yet in the state of waking, it manifests as having an intrinsic nature. That [mind] does not reveal the path of liberation for living beings.

The mind-vajra of yogins, which is distinguished from both existence and non-existence, which bestows equal bliss, and which is embraced by its own wisdom—when that mind has attained innate bliss, it is the giver of liberation. // 228 //

In the chapter on the Great Summary of Various Means (*nānāsādhanamahoddeśa*): *Oṃ āḥ hūṃ hoḥ*. First, having purified it here according to the sequence, one should always awaken the liquor; having set it ablaze, one should contemplate it as being like the molten moon, gradually.

From that vessel, with a drop [of liquid] from the tip of the ring finger of the hand whose palm is like the moon, one should draw a triangle resembling the sun on the ground outside, and a circle in its center. (229)

Having meditated upon the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*) within that [maṇḍala], which encompasses even the three realms of existence, that mantra-practitioner performs the libation and other rites daily with his thumb and ring finger.

First, the practitioner offers a bali-oblation here for the lords of regions and villages, using their names at the beginning, middle, and end; then two morsels for Hārītī, and again a bali-oblation for the King of Wrath.

At the abode on the surface of the earth, when the command of the Lord has been given, one offers the first morsel to the female messengers (*dūtīs*) and recites this verse of giving for the sake of auspiciousness with what remains after they have eaten.

At the time of sleep, one performs the ritual placement of limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) upon one's own face, head, throat, heart, navel, private parts, and crown, using the limbs and faces belonging to both families, during both worship and sexual union. (231)
Therefore, the forty verses following the one hundred and ninetieth are easy to understand.

From the verse beginning with "The sound which in the region of the heart" up to "the mouthful of the messengers," several verses are easy to understand; however, several other verses have been stated by way of ellipsis in the *Abhiṣeka-paṭala* (Initiation Chapter) for the sake of practical necessity.

Now, for the sake of attaining both supramundane and mundane accomplishments, the objective support of the deity (*devatālambana*) is explained: The objective support of the deity may be of two kinds: direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). That which is direct perception arises from the yoga of reality (*tattva*), like the moon in the sky, as the manifold *saṃbhogakāya*.

When not directly perceived, there is inference; it is a conceptualization based on reality, like a corpse, which is to be viewed in paintings and so forth for the sake of meditation by yogins of unrefined intellect. (232)
"Direct perception," and so forth.
Here, according to the disposition (*āśaya*) of sentient beings, the object of focus for deities may be both direct perception and inference for yogins.

Of these two—direct perception and inference—that which is direct perception, through the yoga of reality, becomes like a constellation of stars in the sky; that is, it is the manifold *saṃbhogakāya*.
The three realms of existence throughout the three times are perceivable by the fleshly eye and are like illusions or dreams.
Herein, first, the beginner yogi perceives the universe with the fleshly eye, devoid of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*);
thereafter, he perceives it with the divine eye through the power of the ritual for the superknowledges.
Then he sees with the Buddha-eye by virtue of the limit of those free from passion;
thereafter, he sees with the wisdom-eye by virtue of the limit of the bodhisattvas.
And from that, one sees with the eye of wisdom that, through the power of the mind directed toward perfect enlightenment, one is liberated from all substrates;
such are the five eyes of the Tathāgata, beginning with the fleshly eye, in relation to the vision of emptiness.

"Other beings are like those blind from birth regarding the object of the vision of emptiness"—this detailed explanation is to be stated in the forthcoming *Paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*. This is the rule for the cultivation of reality (*tattvabhāvanā*).

Furthermore, when reality is not established through direct perception, inference is [required], yet that which is to be shown in paintings and so forth is a conceptualization based on unreality, like a dead body.

Thus, having fashioned images or paintings of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or having drawn a maṇḍala circle with fixed forms that are pleasing to behold, this is the rule for the cultivation of conceptualization for the sake of meditation by dull-witted beginner yogins. || 232 ||

Now, the method for the cultivation of conceptualization is stated: First, whether it be the form or the mandala, it should be cultivated in reality upon a cloth; through the yoga of reality in space, one's own mind is seen as the entire [deity] without exception.

By the power of the guru’s discipline, for half a year or one year, until it becomes stable, then through union with the mudrā, after only a few days, it attains the state of being non-leaking (akṣaratva). ||233||
Regarding "form" and so forth:

here, for beginner yogins, by means of the power of their own minds, a single deity—such as "form"—drawn upon a cloth painting (paṭa) is to be meditated upon; or else, even a mandala is to be meditated upon first on a cloth painting, though not as the ultimate reality, but as one's own mind.

Furthermore, in reality, because of the union with reality (*tattva-yoga*) within space—that is, through the union of emptiness and compassion—one's own mind, appearing as the entire and complete visible mandala-circle of all forms, is without conceptual construction. Thus, whether it be form and so forth imagined [as such], or painted on a cloth, this image of emptiness is non-conceptual; for half a year or one year, according to the Guru’s injunctions, one should practice until one's own mind becomes stable.
"From that, through union with the *mudrā*":

here, when the mind has become stable within one's own heart by the power of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), meditation (*dhyāna*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and concentration (*dhāraṇā*), then, "through union with the *mudrā*, in a few days"—the rule being that these are eleven hundred and twenty-five days according to the *Kālacakra*—in these many days the *bodhicitta* attains the state of being unchanging and becomes stainless; such is the connection [of the words].

In this regard, a *dharmabhāṇaka* (preacher of the Dharma) who serves as a supervisor for the painting of cloth-scrolls (*paṭa*), the copying of manuscripts (*pustaka*), or the making of images (*pratimā*) must be sought out. By him, the cloth-scroll, manuscript, image, and so forth, should be produced through both fierce and peaceful rites;

having bestowed the aforementioned offerings and other gifts, worship of the *ācārya* must be performed, and a communal feast (*saṃghabhojya*) and a *gaṇacakra* should be provided at the time of offering the *argha*.
Just as there is a procedure at the time of consecration, so too at the time of offering the *argha* water, it must be performed according to one's capacity; this is the rule. || 233 ||

Now, the rule regarding the vajra-word is stated: In every king of tantras, this vajra-word of the yogins has indeed been taught; yet, out of supreme compassion, it was concealed by the Lord of the Universe for the sake of maturing the ignorant. Therefore, having analyzed it, the yogin should meditate upon it at every daily occasion—the Unstruck (Anāhata), the Mother of the Victors’ Noble Sons, the Mudrā—for the purpose of attaining accomplishment. Thus ends the fourth chapter on the Means of Achievement. Kālacakra. 234.
ka. evaṃ; vāgurā ga. eṣāṃ ca; teṣāṃ kha.
ga. ca. cha. citraṃ; ka. kha. ga. ca. cha. niṣiktā.
ca. vikalpitaṃ ga. 'sva' is not present ca. a book appearing as a cloth.
In the chapter, the "Great Summary on Various Means" (*nānāsādhana-mahoddeśa*), beginning with the words "In all," etc.:

here, in every king of tantras such as the *Samāja* and others which are *upāya*-tantras, and in the *Cakrasaṃvara* and others which are *prajñā*-tantras, the "vajra-word" is indeed the previously mentioned imperishable bliss (*akṣarasukha*) of the yogins.
This was stated by the Blessed One: "For example, the Blessed Buddha, the Perfectly Awakened One, is born from the syllable A."
The letter A is the foremost of all phonemes, of great significance, and the supreme syllable.
For it is the Great Vital Breath, indeed non-arising, devoid of verbal expression, the foremost cause of all speech, and the perfect radiance of all words.
Beginning with these words and ending with "Homage, homage to the Gnosis Body" (*jñānakāya namo namaḥ*), the Gnosis Body is described in one hundred and sixty-two verses in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*;
that very same [Gnosis Body] is called the "Vajra-word" (*vajrapada*) in every king of tantras.
That very [bliss], concealed out of supreme compassion for the sake of maturing the ignorant, was taught as the bliss of the two organs to the ignorant;

therefore, having opened that vajra-position day and night at every moment, it should be meditated upon by the yogin with sharp faculties and the aforementioned eye for the sake of the sign of the accomplishment of the mudrā. For the sake of the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, what is that?

"The Unstruck Kālacakra is the progenitor of the best of Jinas"—this is the rule of the Blessed One to be understood by yogins in all other tantras for the sake of attaining the state of perfect Buddhahood.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, the Great Instruction on Various Sadhanas, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the commentary on the *Laghukālacakra-tantrarāja* in twelve thousand verses, which follows the *Śrī-mūla-tantra*. The commentary on the Chapter on Sadhana is completed.
[The earth was awakened by the King of Jewel-Light, who is awakened by the three mandalas; its purposes are most wonderful.]

Thus has been explained the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), the method for accomplishing various goals for the sake of others, which is most desired to be realized. By my having written down this chapter on the method of accomplishment, may the entire world become stainless, possessing the single eye of primordial wisdom, and reach the jewel-peak of the supramundane, non-dual source of bliss, through the merit obtained by me, Āvukadattaka.
